News.title: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
News.content:
The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits.

Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits.

He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures.

The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms.

But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation.

"That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future."

The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage.

There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned Â£5bn welfare cuts last year.

But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential".

McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers".

The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs.

He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow.

In his wide-ranging 250 page report, external, Milburn proposes:

An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s, which would end the health-top up of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales

Instead, a new "youth allowance" would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently

A reduction in employers' National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in the retail and hospitality sectors, meaning employing those young people would be cheaper

A huge expansion in post-18 college places and a legal right to work, education or training

A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England to give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan

Primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet, and schools obliged to offer work experience

The report calls for the government to spend around Â£5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support.

And it urges ministers to "kickstart the reform programme" next year, with an initial Â£500m, from "repriotising" existing spending.

News.title: 'It's hard to keep going': Neets speak to BBC about struggling to get a job
News.content:
A government-backed review has proposed wide-ranging measures to help get young people into work.

The BBC spoke to young people not in education, employment or training - also known as Neets - about their experiences trying to find jobs.

Read more about the Milburn review.

News.title: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
News.content:
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.

Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.

Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.

"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.

News.title: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
News.content:
"Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives.

You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government.

Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade.

There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government).

Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Thursday's meeting.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe.

It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage.

Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme.

"Small stepsâ¦ to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy."

News.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
News.content:
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.

Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.

US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.

The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.

For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.

Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

News.title: Government risks missing climate targets if EV rules weakened, adviser warns
News.content:
The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".

The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around Â£800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.

The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of Â£12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.

Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".

Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.

In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars

SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.

"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.

News.title: Largest British study to check social media ban's effect on youth mental health
News.content:
The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.

Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.

And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.

Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.

"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.

"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."

Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.

People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

News.title: US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline
News.content:
A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports.

The NSA - America's largest intelligence organisation - said it had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" but that "mission-critical capabilities" were not affected.

The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information.

It comes after a string of technology outages in the US in recent days that have affected flights, banks and other infrastructure.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

"NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."

It did not specify when the issue began, nor when it would be resolved.

The issue was not a cyberattack, multiple US news outlets reported.

Tens of thousands of people work at the NSA, which is responsible for collecting signals intelligence, overseeing cyber threats, and protecting US government communications.

Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday.

Sources familiar with the situation told CBS that operations at the NSA's headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, had not been affected but that some activities had been redirected to other facilities around the country.

Tuesday's outage follows a series of technological outages.

Last week, a massive Microsoft outage impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world - including the US and Canada - while a network failure grounded all US flights.

On Monday, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.

Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have affected other banks and that it was not a cyber security incident.

News.title: Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd
News.content:
Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".

The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.

But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast, external, detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.

"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.

"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."

The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".

"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.

"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.

"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.

"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."

Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.

But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.

"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.

"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.

"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.

"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.

"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.

"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

News.title: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.

Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive Â£1m to scale up their projects.

One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.

The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.

They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.

He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".

Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.

The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.

"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

News.title: Channel 4 admits it doesn't know number of Married At First Sight UK sex abuse complaints
News.content:
Channel 4's bosses were also questioned at length about Brand by MPs in the hearing.

Brand's work on Channel 4 included hosting Big Brother sister show Big Brother's Big Mouth and its celebrity equivalent from 2004 to 2007, a chat show in 2006, and appearing on Big Fat Quiz of the Year.

Addressing Dogra and Channel 4's chairman Geoff Cooper, MPs said the member of staff who made two complaints about Brand "fell through the cracks".

In response, Dogra said: "I'm not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice. We have apologised in public in the past and in private."

She accepted that the woman's complaints were "not handled properly" and added that "it's almost unforgivable that happened twice".

When asked by the committee if junior members of staff could raise complaints against a star without fear of losing their job, Dogra replied she "can't say 100%" that that would be the case.

"What I can do is set the standard, set the tone, make sure that the facilities are available, make sure that my staff and the production companies understand the repercussions of not complying, and understand the kind of culture that I'm trying to set, and we're trying to set as an industry."

She also said she found the "cultural personality" around Brand "horrendous".

"I find it distasteful, and I look at the jokes... that is the lowest form of humour, because these are jokes that are made at the expense of someone else's physical safety.

"I don't believe it should have been acceptable then, and I certainly don't think it's acceptable now."

During the session, Dame Caroline also put to Channel 4 bosses that in both the MAFS UK and Brand cases, the broadcaster appeared like "a child with their hand in the cookie jar".

The committee chairwoman asked: "To what extent can you reassure us that Channel 4's priority is genuinely the welfare of the staff who work there, the staff who have worked there, and the people who take part in your shows - rather than purely when the world is looking at you and you suddenly feel that you've got a reputational reason to take a look at these shows?"

Dogra responded by saying that when Channel 4 commissioned the review, "we didn't even know whether the Panorama programme would be made".

She added: "We had received a right-to-reply letter and the programme came out six weeks later, but it equally it could not have been made. We always intended to do the review."

In the instance of the woman who tried to complain about Brand, she added: "I'm not sure there are more apologies we can give. Because none of those things should've happened."

If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

News.title: Henry Nowak killer applies to appeal against conviction
News.content:
The man jailed for murdering Henry Nowak has applied to appeal against his conviction.

Vickrum Digwa, who stabbed the 18-year-old student with a large dagger in Belmont Road, Southampton, on 3 December 2025, has also asked the Supreme Court to review his sentence, his lawyers have confirmed.

Earlier this month the Court of Appeal raised his minimum term from 21 to 25 years, after the Attorney General argued it was unduly lenient.

The BBC understands Digwa wants to argue that his conviction for murder is unsafe on four grounds. The applications do not mean Digwa will automatically get any further hearings or reviews.

Imran Khan and Partners, Digwa's lawyers, said: "An application has been lodged seeking to appeal against Vickrum Singh Digwa's conviction.

"That application concerns the safety of the conviction and is separate from the proceedings concerning sentence."

News.title: Church of England should protect 'every belief', King says
News.content:
King Charles has said the Church of England does not just protect the Christian faith, but also the space "for every belief" within British society.

He was speaking in his role as Supreme Governor of the Church at the inauguration of a new term of its national assembly, General Synod.

While such comments have caused fierce theological debate in the past, they are consistent with the King's long-expressed beliefs.

Similar statements about the Church were also made by Queen Elizabeth II in a landmark speech given during her Diamond Jubilee.

The late Queen attended 10 Synod inauguration ceremonies since the assembly was established in 1970, though the then Earl of Wessex attended on her behalf at the last inauguration in 2021.

The day's ceremony started with a worship service at Westminster Abbey. The King and members of Synod then moved the short distance to Church House, the Church's administrative headquarters, for the Sovereign's address.

Speaking to the nearly 500 members of the assembly - including all the Church's bishops as well as clergy and lay people, many of whom were newly elected for a 5-year term - the King talked of his own deep faith and the way it guided him.

He then talked of a clear vision of the Church's public role.

"At a time when our society can feel divided, it is all the more important that the Church of England continues to extend its ministry among all the people of this country," the King said.

"The Church protects not just the Christian faith of all of us gathered in this room, but the very space for faith itself â of every belief â within our whole society and national discourse," he continued.

News.title: Protest against talk by academic who made Arday plagiarism claim
News.content:
Hundreds of people have gathered to protest against a talk at an Oxford University college by the academic who accused the late Professor Jason Arday of plagiarism.

Stand Up To Racism organised a demonstration against Nathan Cofnas's talk at Oriel College, organised by Oxford Reform UK, on Tuesday evening.

Protesters, some with face masks on, appeared to try to block the entrance gates to stop people getting into the college before the talk.

Dozens of protesters held signs saying "Nathan Cofnas not welcome" and "Remember Professor Jason Arday".

Chants of "Nathan Cofnas shut him down" could be heard.

Cofnas, who has advocated for "race realism", wrote a blog accusing Prof Arday of plagiarism in his doctoral thesis.

News.title: Train attacker feared 'conspiracy by devil'
News.content:
A knifeman accused of trying to kill passengers on a moving train had a delusional belief his life was at risk because of a "conspiracy by the devil", a court has heard.

Anthony Williams denies 10 counts of attempted murder on a Doncaster to London King's Cross service which had to make an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire on 1 November last year.

Cambridge Crown Court heard Dr Bernard Chin, a consultant forensic psychiatrist instructed by the defence, diagnosed Williams with schizophrenia.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies four other counts of attempted murder in relation to earlier attacks in his home city and London.

At the start of the defence case, barrister Gillian Jones KC told jurors: "I'm not going to call Mr Williams to give evidence."

The judge, Mr Justice Calver, told jurors: "You must not hold this against him in any way."

News.title: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
News.content:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.

The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.

The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".

"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".

Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".

The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.

It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.

The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".

The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.

Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."

It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.

News.title: Conservative influencer Brett Cooper admits she has left MAGA: ‘There was a lot of gaslighting that took place’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Conservative influencer Brett Cooper has left MAGA, admitting that “there was a lot of gaslighting” in President Donald Trump’s base.

In October 2024, weeks before Trump would go on to defeat then-Vice President Kamala Harris for a second term in the White House, Cooper was all smiles in a photo she posted to Instagram, wearing a MAGA hat on horseback. She captioned the photo, “Sry Kamala, this is what joy looks like.”

Two years later, Cooper is disheartened with the movement she so fiercely backed.

“I’m not part of [MAGA] any more,” Cooper, a 25-year-old with 1.7 million YouTube subscribers, told the Financial Times in a new interview. “I think I’ve moved on.”

open image in gallery Conservative influencer Brett Cooper said in a new interview, ‘I’m not part of [Maga] any more,’ as President Donald Trump dodges blame for Republicans’ massive losses in the midterm elections ( Brett Cooper via Instagram )

Cooper’s rift from the MAGA movement started with the Trump administration’s handling of files related to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein last year.

Trump begrudgingly signed a bill to release the files after months of resistance, with critics not only questioning the transparency of the administration, but also whether a more sinister cover-up was taking place. The president, who ran in the same social circles as Epstein decades ago, has denied claims of a cover-up, telling reporters, “I have nothing to hide.”

Cooper remembered seeing a social media post from Trump suggesting that those still demanding answers about Epstein’s crimes and associates were no longer part of MAGA.

“Ok, well, I guess I’m not!” she recalled thinking.

open image in gallery Cooper, like other Republicans, took issue with Trump starting a war in Iran more than eight months ago that caused gas prices to soar — after the president promised no more prolonged military conflicts ( AFP via Getty Images )

She, like other Republicans, also took issue with Trump starting a war in Iran more than eight months ago that caused gas prices to soar — after the president promised no more prolonged military conflicts. She also didn’t like the administration’s response to economic concerns, as many Americans struggled with stubborn inflation.

“There was a lot of gaslighting that took place,” Cooper said. “It’s just been so belittling.”

Cooper, a former Daily Wire host, now focuses her conservative values on more cultural and entertainment videos rather than politically heavy episodes for her podcast, The Brett Cooper Show.

Despite her dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, she still voted Republican in the midterm elections, where Democrats took control of the House and the Senate. Trump has dodged blame for the massive losses.

“It’s just kind of closing the chapter,” she said. “We’re excited to see what’s next.”

open image in gallery Podcaster Joe Rogan, who endorsed Trump in the 2024 election, admitted after the GOP midterm shellacking, 'They didn’t just lose the podcast bros. They lost most of the country' ( AFP via Getty Images )

Podcaster Joe Rogan, who endorsed Trump in the 2024 election, admitted after the GOP midterm shellacking, “They didn’t just lose the podcast bros. They lost most of the country.”

Rogan and other podcasters helped Trump to victory in 2024, but nearly halfway through his term, they are showing some buyer’s remorse.

Since Trump returned to the Oval Office, Rogan has criticized the Iran war, the president’s massive immigration crackdown and the administration’s handling of the Epstein files.

“When you get into a war that no one wants to be in, when you got militarized police in the streets wearing masks and no ID,” Rogan said while reflecting on Republicans’ election losses.

News.title: Chipotle launches clothing line including hoodie with secret pouch for your burrito
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Chipotle Mexican Grill has launched a limited-edition sweatshirt featuring an insulated, concealed pocket built to hold a burrito, bowl, salad or tacos, ahead of its retail launch on Wednesday.

Priced at $53 with free shipping and a complimentary entrée card, the oversized, unisex "Sneak It In" hoodie will be sold exclusively at ChipotleGoods.com beginning November 18 at 9 a.m. PT for customers in the United States and Canada while supplies last.

Each garment is lined to keep food warm and includes a separate compartment for napkins. The sweatshirt is available in three colors: black, gray and maroon, which the company markets as Nothing To See Here Black, Got the Goods Gray and No Burrito Here Brown.

The Mexican fast-casual chain developed the item in response to social media posts showing customers bringing outside meals into movie theaters, according to a company news release.

"Everything about going to the movies has gotten better over the years," Kirby Ann Connell, Chipotle’s senior director of social and influencers, said in the release. "Bigger screens, better sound, more comfortable seats. But the food? We're still choosing between popcorn, candy and nachos."

open image in gallery Chipotle Mexican Grill has unveiled a limited-edition hoodie with a hidden, insulated pocket designed to hold a burrito, bowl, salad or tacos, ahead of its retail release on Wednesday ( Getty )

Connell added: "Movie nights deserve real, craveable food. And since our fans were already sneaking Chipotle to theaters, we figured we'd make it a little easier. Sometimes innovation is as simple as putting a burrito pocket in a hoodie."

In announcing the apparel on X, the restaurant wrote, "saw u sneaking burritos into the movies so we made a hoodie to help u out."

The post drew immediate interest from consumers and other brands, with footwear company HEYDUDE replying, "now this is a need."

open image in gallery The limited-edition ‘Sneak It In’ sweatshirt costs $53, includes free shipping and a complimentary entrée card and goes on sale Wednesday ( Chipotle )

To support the concept, Chipotle cited a 2024 YouGov survey indicating that 63 percent of Americans admitted to sneaking food or drinks into a cinema.

In addition to the direct sale, U.S. members of the Chipotle Rewards program can enter a sweepstakes to win one of the hoodies through November 22. Members can redeem 10 rewards points per entry for up to 20 entries, and a mail-in entry option is also available without a purchase, according to the promotion's official rules.

The free entrée card included with each sweatshirt purchase remains valid through December 31, 2027. The company also announced a separate holiday promotion running from November 27 through November 30, offering a $10 bonus code to the first 15,000 U.S. online buyers who spend at least $50 on e-gift cards.

News.title: Kalshi stops taking bets based on Trump’s comments over fears of manipulation: report
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prediction market platform Kalshi has reportedly stopped offering contracts that allow users to wager on what President Donald Trump will say during public appearances, following a federal regulatory order over concerns that the markets could be manipulated.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued a directive on Friday instructing the company to temporarily suspend all contracts tied to the president’s remarks on specific dates, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. Kalshi had previously said that its platform used security protocols to prevent market manipulation.

Concerns surrounding the contracts intensified earlier this year after a former White House teleprompter operator, Gabriel Perez, allegedly used inside information from the president’s speeches to place winning wagers on the site. Perez later reached a settlement with federal regulators over the incident.

Following that case, Democratic lawmakers have signaled plans to investigate prediction platforms as they prepare to assume control of key congressional committees after their wins in the November midterm elections.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee next year, wrote to the White House last week requesting details on its response and saying that the teleprompter episode “should have been a wake-up call” to enforce stricter ethics policies.

open image in gallery Prediction market platform Kalshi has reportedly stopped bets on what President Donald Trump will say in public after federal regulators ordered a pause over concerns that the markets could be manipulated ( Getty Images )

Despite dropping markets tied directly to the president’s remarks, Kalshi intends to keep other contracts involving the administration active, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke to The Wall Street Journal. A contract tracking what Vice President JD Vance will say at an event on Wednesday remains live, as do wagers on which senior officials might depart the administration this year and whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will keep his position.

The suspension marks a shift for Kalshi, which has long argued that so-called mention markets serve as a legitimate tool for businesses to hedge risk. At a New York event last month, Kalshi chief regulatory officer Sudhir Jain defended the company’s decision to keep listing Trump-related contracts even after regulators flagged them for insider trading risks.

open image in gallery Kalshi had previously defended its Trump-related contracts as a legitimate way for businesses to hedge risk, even after federal regulators flagged them for insider trading concerns ( AFP/Getty )

“There are mention markets with true hedging utility, with true business cases, and we list those,” Jain told The Wall Street Journal at the time. “If you look at what we used to list, and what we list right now, we have significantly trimmed. We want to focus on the ones which we list right now, which are related to Trump, related to earnings, related to some keynote addresses, but very, very limited. I think we have cut that down by more than 50 percent.”

Although mention markets generate relatively low trading volumes compared to other contracts, they have drawn considerable attention online, where prediction-market influencers frequently livestream their wagers on major broadcasts like the State of the Union, as reported by The Wall Street Journal.

open image in gallery The regulatory crackdown comes as the CFTC investigates rival platform Polymarket, and after Donald Trump Jr. stepped down as a Kalshi adviser following his firm’s investment in the competitor ( Reuters )

The CFTC, currently led by Trump appointee Michael Selig, has sought to balance support for the growing prediction-market sector with stricter oversight. In addition to pausing Kalshi’s Trump contracts, the agency has opened a broad investigation into Kalshi’s main rival, Polymarket.

Still, the CFTC has defended prediction platforms in court against state regulators who argue the sites operate as unlicensed gambling operations, intervening in cases across a dozen states — including Louisiana, where a judge ordered the platforms to stop operations last week.

Kalshi also previously had ties to the president's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., who worked as an adviser to the firm until recently. The company stated that the two sides mutually agreed to part ways after 1789 Capital, a venture firm where Trump Jr. is a partner, increased its financial stake in Polymarket.

News.title: Jeff Bezos says the new James Bond wasn't picked until Friday
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The choice of Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond came just three days before the announcement, Jeff Bezos said Tuesday.

“We ran a really tight process and we made the final decision on Friday,” the Amazon founder said, speaking onstage at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference in Menlo Park, California.

Bezos offered the most insight yet into the behind-the-scenes process of casting one of the most iconic roles in cinema — something that's fueled much speculation over the years, and much discourse since Pattinson's selection was announced Monday morning.

Bezos' comments also indicated that he, as Amazon's executive chairman, was directly involved in the casting. Amazon MGM Studios assumed creative control of the long-running franchise last year, tapping Denis Villeneuve to direct the still-untitled film.

A “big group” of contenders was whittled down to five finalists who performed three scenes each in screen tests, Bezos said.

“We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists and it was — it was really interesting, you know. Full costume, real sets, other actors with them,” he said.

He didn't disclose the names of the finalists, but actors reportedly considered for the role included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.

“Then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all those screen tests and reviewing all that,” Bezos recounted, calling all the performers “extraordinarily talented.”

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performances. And it was kind of immediately undebated,” he added.

But there was one thing working against the 40-year-old Pattinson: They thought he might be too famous. The six previous Bond actors — Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig — were little-known or drawn primarily from stage and small-screen work before being catapulted into fame as the secret agent.

“We sort of thought maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” Bezos said. “But in the screening test, it was so obvious, he is James Bond.”

News.title: Cambridge Dictionary chooses 'human' as word of the year in response to AI fears
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Fears of artificial intelligence inspired the Cambridge Dictionary to flip back to the 15th century for the word that best captures the 2026 cultural zeitgeist.

“Human,” the dictionary's word of the year, is not just a throwback but also a backlash of sorts that reflects the debate over how AI has blurred the lines between machines and people.

“AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children."

The adjective derived from the Latin “humanus” and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as “having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines.”

Dictionaries typically choose a novel word — sometimes slang that has crossed into the mainstream — or an existing word that has taken on a new meaning.

Artificial intelligence has factored heavily in Word of the Year distinctions across several dictionaries in recent years.

“AI” itself was chosen by Collins Dictionary in 2023 — a year when Cambridge picked “hallucinate,” in reference to the tendency of AI to fabricate information. Merriam-Webster last year named “slop” its word of the year for low quality content produced by AI while Collins went with “vibe coding” for the AI-assisted software development method.

“AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human," Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who has promoted the smart use of AI, said in a comment on the Cambridge Dictionary selection. "The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”

Other word contenders for 2026 included “agent,” for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and “analogue” for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology.

News.title: Nabeel Rajab, prominent Bahraini human rights activist, dies at 62
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist from Bahrain who helped lead the island nation’s 2011 Arab Spring protests and spent years in prison for challenging its monarchy, died on Tuesday. He was 62.

His family found him unresponsive at their home in Turkey on Tuesday morning, friends and activists said. The Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which Rajab once led as president, confirmed his death in a post on X.

“We extend our sincere condolences and heartfelt sympathy to his esteemed family. We pray that God may encompass him with his vast mercy and reward him abundantly for his efforts and contributions,” the group wrote.

Ebrahim Sharif, an activist and close friend of the family, said Rajab's wife and daughter took him to a hospital in Istanbul, where he was pronounced dead. He said after speaking with Rajab's brother that the family believes Rajab likely died of a heart attack.

Rajab for decades was one of Bahrain's leading human rights activists. He frequently posted on social media about Bahrain's treatment of dissidents, and was an unusually visible figure in a country where voicing criticism can carry enormous risk.

In 2002, Rajab helped establish the Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which became a platform for him and his colleagues to call for democratic reforms in the island nation, where a Sunni monarchy rules over a predominantly Shiite Muslim population.

He rose to international prominence in 2011 as the Arab Spring uprisings swept the region and demonstrations erupted in Bahrain.

As one of the movement’s best-known voices, he joined thousands of demonstrators occupying Manama’s Pearl Roundabout and kept protesting even after a violent crackdown by security forces. He and the protesters described their demands as fair elections, constitutional democracy and an end to preferential treatment for Bahrain’s Sunni minority.

Bahrain ultimately put down the uprising with the help of troops from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Though Bahrain’s constitution guarantees freedom of speech, Rajab was prosecuted under laws criminalizing remarks that insult foreign countries or government agencies or spread false rumors during wartime.

He was imprisoned on multiple occasions in the years that followed. The detentions drew international criticism from the United Nations, human rights groups and some of Bahrain’s closest allies, including the United States, which bases its Navy’s 5th Fleet in the island kingdom.

He was released to home detention in June 2020 during the coronavirus pandemic while serving a five-year sentence over tweets criticizing the Saudi-led war in Yemen and alleging prison abuse.

“Nabeel really stood out for standing up for the most vulnerable even when he knew the cost would be extremely heavy,” said Sayed Ahmed AlWadaei of the London-based Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy.

Rajab left Bahrain with his family early in the Iran war, as authorities cracked down on Shiite-led protests. Rajab accused the government of torturing an imprisoned activist and feared he would be arrested if he returned, he told The Associated Press at the time.

The International Federation for Human Rights, where Rajab served as deputy secretary-general from 2010 to 2020, called him an inspiration.

“The world has lost a truly exceptional human rights defender. He paid for his commitment to a more just world with many years in prison and constant harassment by the Bahraini authorities. This must have taken a toll on his health,” said Alexis Deswaef, the group's president.

___ Schreck reported from Bangkok and Metz from Jerusalem.

News.title: Ukraine inflicts devastating damage on Crimea Bridge in major symbolic blow to Putin
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Ukraine inflicted catastrophic damage on the bridge linking Russia and Crimea on Tuesday, delivering a major symbolic blow to Vladimir Putin.

Russian authorities said they opened a ⁠terrorism investigation following ⁠two Ukrainian ​attacks on ⁠the bridge over the Kerch Strait, adding ‌that the ‌structure had suffered damage.

All train and vehicle traffic on the Crimean Bridge has been suspended while specialists assess the damage, Russia’s ministry of transport reported on Tuesday morning. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier described damage to the bridge as minor.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky celebrated the strike, which he said was the result of a seven stage operation carried out over a number of weeks between the SSU and armed forces.

"We ⁠have long been ​telling ⁠Russia: Enough of ‌striking bridges, cities and villages, energy infrastructure, railways and ‌grain ships. Enough ‌of war. But every time Russia chooses further ⁠escalation," Zelensky said in his nightly video address.

open image in gallery Anton Gerashchenko claimed a Flamingo cruise missile had hit the bridge ( Pravda Gerashchenko )

A Flamingo cruise missile was deployed to carry out a “precision-guided strike”, he said, alongside a range of other missiles and drones including Neptune missiles and Ruta drones.

He shared a video compilation of the strike, which showed a missile going towards the bridge. The strike itself appeared not to be recorded, as the president said the “communications uplink worked flawlessly until the very last seconds.”

Anton Gerashchenko, Ukraine’s former minister of internal affairs, said the operation had dealt out “critical damage” on the bridge.

“Last night, the Kerch Bridge, a symbol of occupation and Russian aggression against Ukraine, sustained critical damage during a powerful combined missile and drone attack.”

Ukrainian sanctions commissioner Vladislav Vlasiuk reshared a photo of the bridge with one of its arches missing on Tuesday morning, captioned: “Crimean Bridge. Sanctioned.”

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, asked “residents and guests” of the region to avoid the bridge following the “enemy” strike.

“The enemy has attacked the Crimean Bridge again. At this moment, traffic is suspended. We ask residents and guests of Crimea to refrain from traveling towards the bridge and to take the restrictions into account when planning their routes. We will provide further updates on the situation. I remind you of the need to trust only official sources of information.”

The ⁠attacks, on Monday and Tuesday, killed two people and shut down the ‌bridge, ‌the ⁠Russian-installed governor said.

The 12-mile long (19km) Crimea Bridge is one of two routes available to Moscow, connecting the transport networks of Russia and Crimea after the Ukrainian peninsula was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. It has been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine and is widely viewed as one of Putin's signature infrastructure projects.

It consists of a separate roadway and railway, both supported by concrete stilts, which give way to a wider span held by steel arches at the point where ships pass between the Black Sea and the smaller Azov Sea.

Few countries have ‌recognised Crimea as part ​of the Russian Federation.

The bridge ‌has been attacked by Ukraine several times since Putin sent Russian forces ​into Ukraine in February 2022. A truck bomb in October 2022 ‌killed four people and limited the ⁠bridge's capacity for several months.

open image in gallery The bridge is deemed one of Putin’s most significant infrastructure projects ( AFP/Getty )

The overnight strike was part of the largest Ukrainian drone attack on Russia since the start of the full-scale war in 2022, as the defence ministry said it shot down 1,441 ‌drones over 22 regions, ​surpassing Monday's figure of 1,336 which itself had ‌set a new record.

Air defence systems had ⁠repelled a massive drone attack on the industrial areas of Ufa and Salavat ‌in Russia's Bashkortostan ​region, home to a number ‌oil refineries, state media reported, ​citing local officials.

Russian attacks have also intensified ⁠in the past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv. Two bridges over the ​Dnipro River sustained damage late on Monday, which prompted some water and power cuts and traffic restrictions.

President Zelensky said on Tuesday: “We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation – and every proposal has been met with loud rejection. Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region.

“We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine’s defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered.

“I thank the true warriors of the Security Service of Ukraine, all our Defense Forces, our intelligence agencies, and EVERY manufacturer of weapons effectively used to defend Ukraine, Ukrainians, and our national interests. Glory to Ukraine!”

News.title: Le Pen pledges to lower France’s retirement age to 60 if she wins next year’s election
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Marine Le Pen has pledged to tear up Emmanuel Macron’s flagship pension overhaul and allow French workers who started their careers young to retire at 60 if she wins the 2027 presidential election.

Unveiling her economic programme on Tuesday, the National Rally front-runner sought to convince sceptical bond markets that she can deliver one of her party’s core promises to working-class voters without worsening France’s already-strained public finances.

At the centre of her proposal is a new €900bn (£750bn) retirement fund built up over a generation alongside France’s existing pay-as-you-go system, financed by redirecting a portion of existing employer payroll contributions.

“We are going to bring down one of the last privileges in our country, the privilege of access to the financial services that make a minority wealthy today, while also improving the financing of our national economy,” Ms Le Pen told reporters.

open image in gallery Le Pen has pledged to lower France’s minimum retirement age to 60 ( Reuters )

The far-right leader promised that hundreds of thousands of people would be able to leave work two to three years earlier than under Mr Macron’s legislation, which gradually lifts the minimum retirement age from 62 to 64.

France’s current statutory retirement age of 62 years and nine months is already well below the 65-to-67 benchmark across most major economies, even as French life expectancy ranks among the highest.

“For those who wonder whether the French social model will still be standing when they retire, I have heard them,” she said. “This reform is a promise for the future and an act of faith in the French model.”

“Hundreds of thousands of workers will retire earlier, gaining two to three years compared with what [Mr Macron’s] reform would have imposed,” she added.

President Macron’s 2023 pension changes provoked months of mass strikes and street protests before the government agreed to freeze their implementation in exchange for Socialist support on the budget.

But the higher retirement age threshold remains due to come into force in January 2028, shortly after the next president takes office.

open image in gallery Macron’s pension reforms have drawn widespread criticism, triggering mass demonstrations last year ( AFP/Getty )

How to fund France’s generous retirement system – the single biggest drain on the public purse, projected to cost more than €430bn (£360bn) next year – has become a central test for the National Rally’s economic credibility.

Ms Le Pen has committed to finding €138bn (£115bn) in wider public spending reductions by 2032, arguing that her overhaul would eventually generate up to €20bn (£17bn) in annual savings.

Economists and market analysts remain unconvinced that those figures add up if Mr Macron’s age increase is reversed.

To keep costs in check, National Rally is shifting emphasis away from a fixed age threshold towards the total number of years paid into the system.

Workers who entered employment early would qualify for retirement between 60 and 62 after 40 to 42 years of contributions, while university graduates would generally need to remain in work well into their sixties to receive a full pension.

News.title: Testosterone ads banned over low sex drive claims
News.content:
Five adverts that claimed symptoms such as low energy and lack of sex drive were linked to low testosterone levels have been banned by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

An investigation by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), published on Wednesday, found that the adverts exaggerated the link between low testosterone and several common symptoms, including loss of motivation and changes in mood, which could have many possible causes.

The adverts, which included three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads, were created by Voy, an online health platform and prominent seller of weight loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The ASA said: “While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn’t have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation”.

It also ruled that one Facebook ad, claiming that low testosterone affects one in four men over 30, was “misleading and not supported by the evidence Voy provided”. Voy disputed this.

“We’ve banned the ads and have told Voy to ensure that future ads don’t mislead people about the symptoms or prevalence of low testosterone,” the ASA added.

Catherine Drewett, investigations manager at the ASA, said: “People should be able to trust the health claims they see in ads. This ruling makes clear the standards we expect from advertisers promoting health tests and services and the importance of ensuring their claims are supported by strong evidence”.

In response, Voy said the language in the ads was “deliberately conditional”, arguing it “did not state or imply that the advertised symptoms were definitively caused by low testosterone”.

The ASA launched its investigation after receiving multiple public complaints.

News.title: Saucepan racks, fitted sheets and dehumidifiers: Your tricks for drying laundry in winter
News.content:
As temperatures drop and laundry piles up, drying clothes indoors can become a headache. But when Laura de Barra gave her verdict on the best heated clothes airers, Telegraph readers had a lot to say. So, we asked you what works in your homes.

While some of you have relied on heated airers for years, others have found a standard clothes horse or an overhead airer paired with a dehumidifier preferable. Several of you argue that you can’t beat the efficiency of a tumble dryer.

Here are your tried and tested tips...

Heated airers

These readers explain why they’ve relied on their heated airers for years, offer advice on what makes a good model and how to avoid damp and mould problems.



After seeing a review for the Lakeland heated airer printed in The Telegraph in 2008, Clive Ruffle, 67, from Surrey, felt enticed to buy one. “It had a price offer and a coupon to send to the newspaper,” he recalls.

“It’s still going strong and has been very useful to us,” he says. “I was quite surprised to see the dryer we bought those years back still available.”

The options to fold the airer away flat and use only half of it, where one side is folded down, are the two major features that attracted Clive to the product.

“The drying speed is good, and we’ve never felt frustrated by it,” he says. “The heated bars are very effective and if we choose to heat, clothes are usually done in the day. They take a bit longer without the heater.”

To avoid damp or mould problems, Clive keeps his upstairs windows open, “even on the coldest days,” he adds.

For a more affordable option, Caroline Morrell, 65, from Greater Manchester, recommends buying a tiered Minky heated clothes airer, which she uses with a Beldray cover.

News.title: ‘I lost my family when I contracted HIV’: why virus is still taboo in Iraq
News.content:
Hassan Mehdi never imagined that telling his family he had contracted HIV would cost him his home and his family.

The initial symptoms of the virus weren’t too worrying: a skin allergy, a rash, and swollen lymph nodes in his neck. The dermatologist told Mehdi, not his real name, that he was probably suffering from a seasonal allergy. But he then began to think about his dating and sexual history and did an HIV test at home. A faint line appeared, indicating it was positive. “I tested once again at home and got the same result,” he said.

His worst fears were then confirmed by doctors at a public HIV centre.

“Mentally and psychologically, I collapsed,” Mehdi told The Telegraph, his voice thick with pain. “I decided to take a break and leave my job as a graphic designer, and I shut myself in my room.”

The doctor urged Mehdi to tell his family about the diagnosis. He also asked him to sign a paper promising to disclose his status if he married, not to stop treatment and not get a tattoo. It also warned that he could face legal consequences if someone accused him of spreading the virus.

When he finally broke the news to his mother, he hoped she would support him. But instead, he was met with hostility.

He said: “After informing my mum, she started to spread the news with my relatives, and they warned her that if I stayed at home and mixed with them, I would infect them all. Additionally, my elder brother heard and told me: ‘If I see you in the street or anywhere else, I will kill you.’ That was the last sentence I heard from him before I packed my bag to leave home forever,” he said.

“I lost my family when I told them I had HIV,” he adds. “To a religiously extreme family, HIV/Aids is taboo,” he added.

To fight the virus and adjust to a new life away from the town where he grew up, he immersed himself in gym workouts, a strict diet, and his treatment regimen. Close friends, social gatherings, and special cultural events became his sanctuary.

News.title: Bosses ‘increasingly reluctant’ to hire as employment costs soar
News.content:
Job vacancies fell to their lowest level in 12 years outside the pandemic as employers braced for the impact of the Government’s workers’ rights reforms.

Vacancies dropped by 22,000 to 690,000 in the three months to October, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

This was the lowest since February to April 2021 – and the worst performance since the three months to September 2014 when taking out the impact of Covid lockdowns.

Bosses are grappling with higher employment costs in addition to the Government’s looming deadline to implement the Employment Rights Act on Jan 1. Under the changes, a cap on claims for unfair dismissal will be scrapped and the time a worker needs to have been employed before they can make a claim will be cut from two years to six months.

Martin Beck, the chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “The problem isn’t that businesses are firing workers. It’s that they’re increasingly reluctant to hire them.”

News.title: Wall Street slides as Nvidia casts shadow over tech stocks
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Asian stocks fell sharply at the start of a huge week for AI following the shock exit of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang over a string of extramarital affairs.

South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi fell 3.6pc and Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.4pc after another night of drama for the $4tn (£3tn) chip giant.

Just hours after Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, called for a “dramatic shake-up” at Nvidia , it emerged Mr Huang was considering a possible comeback.

Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the boss of Epic Games, were among prominent figures to sign a public letter demanding that Nvidia “bring Jensen back”.

Meanwhile, several unnamed tech executives set up a “war room” to coordinate a “Stand With Jensen” campaign, according to The Financial Times.

The Wall Street Journal also reported overnight that Nvidia could be looking to scale back some of the aggressive financing it has deployed to prop up other AI companies.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies said: “These concerns are more real and are likely to have an impact on a number of companies in the supply chain.”

Taiwan’s Taiex, a beneficiary of the global AI frenzy, sank 6pc, with shares of its leading chipmaker TSMC down 5.7pc.

Allies in Silicon Valley, including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the boss of Epic Games, have pushed for Mr Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia despite an ongoing investigation into his conduct by the company’s board.

The chip giant will unveil its latest quarterly results on Tuesday after triggering a wave of turmoil for the tech sector.

AI giant Anthropic is expected to list in New York this week with a valuation of $1.4tn, doing so at a time when valuations are coming under pressure.

By Monday morning, several major AI supplies had suffered a drop in their share price, with chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung down 4.3pc and 4.5pc, respectively.

OpenAI investor SoftBank Group also slipped 3.7pc, while memory maker Kioxia dropped 7.7pc. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron was also down 7.1pc.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “Nvidia’s results tomorrow may outweigh everything and will largely put a bow on a bumper earnings season in what has been a bumpy period for markets.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Asian stocks mostly fell Monday as the tech sector struggled to recover from the crisis at Nvidia after boss Jensen Huang stepped down.

Mr Huang, a pivotal figure in the artificial intelligence boom, resigned Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The 63-year-old’s departure raised concerns about the chip titan, which is at the centre of a build-out that has helped propel global markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the world.

Reports that Mr Huang was in talks for a spectacular return to the hotseat, did not appear to be having much of an impact in Asia, with Taiwan’s Taiex index plunging 6pc as chip giants TSMC and MediaTek were hammered.

South Korea’s Kospi sank more than 3pc owing to steep losses in SK hynix and Samsung, while Japan’s Nikkei lost more than 2pc with Advantest plunging 11.1pc and Kioxia 7.7pc.

There were also losses in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Bangkok, Manila and Jakarta, though Hong Kong, Mumbai and Wellington rose.

News.title: How an NHS midwife overhauled maternity care in the world’s most dangerous place to give birth
News.content:
In her nearly 20-year career as an NHS midwife, Isata Dumbuya saw only one woman die. But in her first week working in a government maternity hospital in rural Sierra Leone, she witnessed the deaths of four mothers.

Her Sierra Leonean colleagues seemed resigned to such tragedies. Yet for her, these avoidable deaths were a huge shock: they brought home the enormity of her career change, and the challenges she now faced.

She had returned to Sierra Leone to pass on her NHS experience and training, but she had never seen anything like this.

“I did not know what to do – in all my experience,” she recalls. “There were [medical] conditions that I was seeing there that I had never seen in my life because they would not be allowed to happen in the UK.”

After a long and successful career in the UK, the mother-of-five had been inspired to return to her birthplace after seeing reports of the appallingly high mortality rates faced by mothers.

At the time women in Sierra Leone had a one-in-17 lifetime chance of dying during pregnancy, delivery or its aftermath. Today the lifetime risk is one in 52.

She found the government hospital in Kono overwhelmed, short-staffed and poorly organised.

Her new colleagues were exhausted and fatalistic from the relentless deaths.

“In this time, the only thing I was useful for was crying.

“I [had a lot of doubt] because I’m like ‘I can’t do this’. I really don’t know how.

“And also, when you are looking at the people around, they are so fine with it, because they had to do some serious level of emotional shutdown to cope with all this.”

News.title: England stun world champions Spain in one of their greatest victories
News.content:
There was so much to admire. England began the night testing Spain’s first-phase passing to breaking point. They began the second half counter-attacking Spain for two goals from Ezri Konsa and White. Then after Elliot Anderson’s red card, this was a different England. With Trafford in inspired form, they held off the relentless Spain for long enough.

Harry Kane scored his 93rd England goal from the spot and was replaced before the end so that Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy could give the midfield one more lease of life. By the end, the excitement meant that Kane was unable to take his seat on the bench, and he stood alongside Tuchel in the technical area, cajoling and advising.

England have beaten Spain on Spanish territory in recent times, but it was the nature of this performance, its many qualities when the moment required them, that made it so significant. This was the end of a 43-game unbeaten streak for the European and world champions, and it was ended by an England team in their best form in recent years.

Only three who started this game – Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice – started the final of Euro 2024, lost to Spain. Tuchel’s pool of talent is deeper than it was for his predecessor but there is also a greater maturity to the way they play. The England manager called it the greatest performance of almost two years in charge “given the circumstances… who we play, where we play” and as ever for England just slightly too late.

The defeat by Argentina in the semi-final in Atlanta just stings that little bit more when one considers the craft and resilience England showed on this night. They were under the hammer after Anderson threw an arm over the shoulder of Lamine Yamal and was dismissed before Mikel Oyarzabal converted the penalty that followed. “Thirty minutes against Spain in Spain feels like three hours,” Tuchel said, although Spain had a long way back after the blitzing they took at times in the first hour.

Sports.title: Chelsea star Pedro Neto restrained by Craig Bellamy as he clashes with Wales bench after being sent off for Portugal
Sports.content:
Next

His complaints to referee Sven Jablonski fell on deaf ears but tempers flared as he left the pitch.



The winger clashed with members of the Welsh bench and had to be restrained by manager Bellamy.

The situation eventually calmed down and Neto made his lonely walk down the tunnel.

Bruno Fernandes had given the visitors the lead before goals from David Brooks and Sorba Thomas put the Welsh ahead.

Wales came close to re-establishing the lead before half-time.

Sports.content:

ASHLEY YOUNG says Manchester United should forget building a new team around Bruno Fernandes – and go for Morgan Gibbs-White instead.

New boss Mauricio Pochettino has a big decision looming over his Portuguese skipper who has turned down two new contract offers at Old Trafford.



He turned 32 earlier in the autumn and is having a below-par season for the Red Devils by his high standards.

While Young, 41, played on at the top level until he was 40, he feels the time is right to start looking to the future rather than relying on Fernandes.



And his choice would be to raid Nottingham Forest for England ace Gibbs-White, 26 – who would be pivotal to United going forward.

Young said: “Bruno has been unbelievable for the club. The standout performer. But there’s been so much that’s come out that we’re hearing about him turning down another contract.



“You want to build around a player but he’s 33 next year. I know age is nothing but a number but he’s not at his peak. I wouldn’t say he’s past it, but he’s getting older now.”

United blew their summer budget on three midfielders in Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos – but Young thinks they need to spend again.

Gibbs-White has been heavily linked with moves to Tottenham and Manchester City in recent years but is still at the City Ground.

Young told the Overlap Daily in association with Sky Vegas: “For me, I would go and sign Morgan Gibbs-White.

“Now, I’m just throwing that name out there, but you’re thinking a No10, you want to build a team around a player.”

Young has no doubt that Poch will want to make big changes to the playing squad once he gets his feet under the table at Old Trafford.

He added: “There’s a lot of players there that shouldn’t be playing for Manchester United, shouldn’t be in that squad.



“And I’m sure Pochettino is going to be looking at that squad and going, right, what do I need? Or how long is it going to take me to change this squad?

“Straight away, first and foremost, he’s got to go in and he’s going to put his stamp on it straight away.”

PAUL INCE claims Manchester United’s midfield have “no legs” and accused them of “wasting” £50million on Andrey Santos.

Former Old Trafford star Ince says the “basket case” Red Devils are too lightweight in the middle of the park and lack power.



Along with Santos from Chelsea, Youri Tielemans arrived from Aston Villa and Carlos Baleba joined from Brighton in a £155m midfield revamp.

The trio have been locked in a battle with Kobbie Mainoo and captain Bruno Fernandes for the three central positions.



This is just one of the problems new head coach Mauricio Pochettino will have to try to solve when he starts work on Wednesday after jetting in from the USA.

Guv’nor Ince, who won seven trophies in his six years at United, told SunSport: “Fernandes is a world-class player but has got no legs.



“Mainoo, he’s got no legs. So where are the legs in the middle of the park? If you’re going to be a top team, you’ve got to have legs.

“Those players, they’re not powerful. They’ve got no legs. The times you see them running back to their goal.”

Brazilian Santos, 22, signed for United in July despite being sent out on loan four times by Chelsea and generally used as a squad player by the Blues.

The Red Devils moved for him because he fit their age profile and had Prem experience.
