Sports.title: Josh Kelly’s Footwork Could Test Jaron Ennis’ Patience
Sports.content:
Trainer Stephen Edwards thinks Jaron “Boots” Ennis will stop Josh Kelly late in their junior middleweight unification, though he sees a familiar problem standing in the way. Kelly has the footwork to make Ennis chase him. What Edwards wants to see is whether Boots walks him down behind a steady jab or gets impatient trying to take his head off.

“His feet are a bigger deal than his hand speed. His hand speed won’t be a problem for Boots,” Edwards said to Sean Zittel’s channel. He brought up Amir Khan to explain the difference between throwing fast punches and throwing shots an opponent can see coming. Even if Kelly and Ennis look evenly matched for speed in the opening rounds, Edwards believes Ennis will read Kelly’s tells early.

Ennis’ corner has already dealt with this style

Derek “Bozy” Ennis trained Philadelphia southpaw Ray Robinson, who fought Kelly to a draw back in 2019. Edwards thought Robinson deserved the decision that night and believes having gone through that camp will give the Ennis corner plenty of confidence. Bozy brought up the draw himself at the launch press conference, so the history is already on both teams’ minds.

Kelly has obviously had years to improve since then. Edwards gave him full credit for beating Bakhram Murtazaliev, an opponent few wanted to go near. A 2019 draw only tells you so much about Kelly at 154 pounds today, especially after he proved he can beat a heavy-handed champion marching forward. The Robinson tape gives Bozy a starting point. The Murtazaliev win shows what Kelly can do when real power comes after him.

Ennis has his own history to study, too, and it goes deeper than one bad night. Across two full fights with Karen Chukhadzhian, Boots never looked comfortable dealing with that constant movement. In their rematch in front of his own fans in Philadelphia, Chukhadzhian tagged Ennis with clean right hands and made him look awkward for long stretches. It wasn’t until Chukhadzhian finally gassed out down the stretch that Ennis took control of the fight.

The problem for Kelly is that copying that blueprint takes more than quick feet. Kelly isn’t quite as slick as Chukhadzhian, and he doesn’t carry the same power or willingness to stand in the pocket and trade. Against Kelly, the temptation for Ennis will still be to load up on another power shot whenever the first one misses, giving Kelly room to step away and make him reset. Using a sharp jab to herd Kelly toward the ropes will make finding clean openings much easier, especially if Kelly lacks the pop to make Ennis respect what is coming back.

“Boots doesn’t choose the conservative route,” Edwards said. Ennis likes putting combinations together and hurting guys once he gets close. Kelly can use that aggression against him by making Ennis reach and getting away before the follow-up lands. How many rounds Kelly can pull that off without giving away points on the cards is another question.

Edwards expects the cost of all that movement to catch up with Kelly in the second half. In his view, Kelly will have to keep moving even when he wants a round to catch his breath, because standing in range gives Ennis the chance to land his heaviest shots. That is where Edwards sees the late stoppage coming. Kelly’s best chance to change that is turning his early escapes into real scoring opportunities. If all that footwork only keeps him safe, Ennis will take his time closing the distance and break him down.

Sports.title: Israil Madrimov Exposed Terence Crawford, And Walking Away Won’t Fix It
Sports.content:
Terence Crawford should come out of retirement to fight Israil Madrimov again if he wants his Mount Rushmore claim taken seriously. Beating Canelo Alvarez gave Crawford a historic achievement, but it did nothing to settle the argument over whether he deserved to beat Madrimov.

That is the stain on his legacy. Crawford left their August 2024 fight with a unanimous decision and the WBA junior middleweight title after looking completely out of ideas against the only prime A-level opponent on his resume. The scores were 116-112 and 115-113 twice, a narrow escape that looked like a gift decision to plenty of observers who saw him clearly lose.

“A win over Canelo will put me on Mount Rushmore, I really believe that,” said Crawford before their fight.

All that Mount Rushmore talk sounds like deep insecurity, as if Crawford is trying to talk himself into credentials he never earned. Truly secure all-time greats do not campaign for their own spot on the mountain. Listening to Crawford demand historical elevation after struggling so badly against Madrimov is like watching a PFC insist on being promoted to General right after failing an inspection.

Once Crawford asks for that kind of company, counting belts and pointing to an unbeaten record cannot be the whole discussion. His overall resume was already thin, padded out with unheralded contenders and aging names well past their best days. When he finally stepped in against a sharp, prime operator in Madrimov, his superiority vanished.

Madrimov gave him an awkward problem he could not solve. His feints, changes of position, and sharp right hands prevented Crawford from settling into the comfortable control he had enjoyed against lesser opposition. Crawford had to think before committing, hesitating for long stretches without throwing a punch.

The case for Madrimov winning rests on the cleaner, more effective work in the close rounds. Crawford’s supporters can point to his jab and late activity, which is precisely why running it back matters. This was not a beaten challenger begging for another payday. It was a prime opponent who exposed the limits of Crawford’s aura.

“I thought Israil Madrimov did enough to edge it here tonight,” said Eddie Hearn after the fight. Hearn promoted Madrimov, so his interest was obvious, yet his objection reflected what millions of viewers saw unfold in real time.

For fans who scored it for Madrimov, Crawford’s victory carries a permanent asterisk. Walking away without fixing it leaves a glaring hole in his career, especially since that shaky performance should have disqualified him from landing the Canelo sweepstakes in the first place.

The Canelo opportunity was already being discussed before Crawford faced Madrimov, creating an obvious financial incentive for the bigger attraction to survive. It explains why critics viewed the scorecards with suspicion, and why beating Canelo feels like an escape hatch rather than proof of all-time greatness.

Crawford could answer the boxing question tomorrow if he actually believed his own hype. Come back and face Madrimov again. Prove the first performance was an off night, take away Madrimov’s best weapons over twelve rounds, and earn the rank he keeps trying to claim.

There would also be a clear tactical reason to watch. Madrimov would need to turn his success with isolated clean punches into sustained offense, while Crawford would have to find ways to attack without spending rounds frozen by feints.

Crawford earned the money to retire, but he has not earned immunity from criticism. Until he clears up the mess he left behind against the best prime fighter he ever faced, his Mount Rushmore talk will keep sounding like a man trying to convince himself more than anyone else.

If Crawford wants another fight to save his legacy from that gift decision, Madrimov is the only call that counts.

Sports.title: Rafael Predicts WBA Will Let Teofimo Bypass Catterall
Sports.content:
Jack Catterall might win every argument with the WBA and still watch his biggest payday walk out the door. Dan Rafael thinks the sanctioning body will end up letting Teofimo Lopez bypass his mandatory to fight WBC welterweight champion Ryan Garcia in early 2027, simply because the sanctioning fees on a unification are too big to turn down.

“The Catterall side that thought that this was over was mistaken because it’s not over,” Rafael told Pro Boxing Fans.

Right now, that is Rafael’s read on how boxing politics usually play out rather than proof that a special permit has been approved. Lopez’s team insists they filed their request on November 5 and are appealing the WBA’s ruling, which leaves Catterall sitting in limbo despite doing everything by the rules.

According to Rafael, talks for Lopez against Garcia are already deep down the road, even if nothing is signed yet. He expects that fight to happen either as a two-belt unification or with just Garcia’s WBC title on the line if Teofimo dumps his strap.

For Catterall, the worst part is watching Teofimo keep his belt while taking the bigger money fight. Catterall beat Shakhram Giyasov in May for the secondary strap and turned down step-aside cash to force his shot, yet Rafael points out that big names almost always get greenlit when a unification is on the table.

“They’re going to see a lot of money that can be made on a sanction and involvement in a major event like Teofimo–Ryan Garcia,” Rafael said.

Even if the WBA stands firm and refuses the exception, Catterall still gets burned. Teofimo would likely vacate rather than risk his money fight against a skilled southpaw for a fraction of the Garcia money. Catterall would get upgraded to full champion by email, getting the belt without the career-defining fight he actually wanted.

WBA Orders Teofimo vs. Catterall breaks down the mandatory dispute and whether Lopez will vacate the title to chase the Ryan Garcia fight.

Sports.title: David Benavidez Risks Losing His Edge By Going Into Businessman Mode
Sports.content:
David Benavidez says he is done handing over 10 percent of his purse to a promoter once his December 5 cruiserweight unification against Michal Cieslak is in the books. After a decade with Sampson Lewkowicz, Benavidez told Reuters he wants to negotiate his own contracts starting next year.

“I paid my dues. After this, I’m saving the 10% for myself,” said Benavidez to Reuters.

Once fighters start thinking like businessmen instead of athletes, their careers usually hit a brick wall. In leagues like the NFL, NBA, or NHL, the schedule forces athletes to show up and compete every week regardless of who stands across from them. Boxing has zero structure like that, so a self-managed fighter can sit on the shelf for a year, turning down tough fights while praying for one giant lottery ticket.

Look at Shakur Stevenson right now for proof of how badly that mindset backfires. After beating Teofimo Lopez back in January, Stevenson wasted ten months chasing a Devin Haney payday that fell apart, lost his Zuffa Boxing deal, and got stuck with a dangerous WBO mandatory against Raymond Muratalla that brings little money.

Benavidez is heading down that same slippery slope after launching DB Promotions on Brian Custer’s channel in October. Even though he insists, “I’m still PBC all the way,” while keeping Al Haymon, TGB Promotions, and Luis De Cubas in his corner, his eyes are already drifting past the best fighters in his own division.

Assuming he beats Cieslak in Glendale, Arizona, to add the WBC strap to the WBA and WBO belts he took from Gilberto “Zurdo” Ramirez in May, Benavidez will hold three titles at 200 pounds. Instead of rushing to unify all four belts against Jai Opetaia, Benavidez told Reuters that facing Oleksandr Usyk does far more for his bank account.

Usyk holds all the leverage at the negotiating table and does not need Benavidez. If Benavidez spends 2027 acting like a cautious promoter instead of an active destroyer, his popularity and sharpness will vanish long before Usyk ever signs a contract.

Sports.title: Bakhodir Jalolov, Not Derek Chisora, Should Replace Jai Opetaia Against Deontay Wilder
Sports.content:
Jai Opetaia is reportedly out of his December 11 fight against Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua card in Cardiff, and Derek Chisora has already jumped in to offer himself up as a substitute. Chisora wants an eight-round rematch at Principality Stadium, admitting that eight rounds are all he has left in the tank while promising they would be worth watching.

The problem is that plugging a 42-year-old Chisora into the ring with a 41-year-old Wilder for a shortened fight turns the top of a global Netflix event into an old-timers’ exhibition. Fans already sat through Wilder edging Chisora by split decision over 12 rounds in London back in April, a slog nobody outside a local pub crowd was begging to run back, especially when one fighter openly concedes he cannot last 10 or 12 rounds. If Turki Alalshikh wants to save the credibility of that co-main slot, a much stronger option sits right in front of him, though it is the exact kind of fight Wilder’s team might hesitate to touch.

That option is Bakhodir Jalolov.

At 32, Jalolov brings the kind of pedigree and physical threat that makes a late replacement worth tuning in for. He is a two-time Olympic super-heavyweight gold medalist going up against Wilder, the 2008 Olympic bronze medalist. That angle sells itself on an international broadcast without needing manufactured trash talk.

More importantly, Jalolov is ready right now. He is coming off a 10-round unanimous decision win over Solomon Dacres at The O2 on October 17. He is already in shape, injury-free, and ranked fourth by both the IBF and WBO and tenth by the WBC. Like Opetaia, Jalolov (18-0, 15 KOs) is a southpaw, only instead of a 200-pound cruiserweight moving up, Wilder would be staring across the ring at a natural 6-foot-7 heavyweight with real punching power.

Jalolov also solves the entertainment question. He took some criticism in his recent UK outings against Dacres and Agron Smakici for fighting at a controlled, safety-first pace because neither opponent had the firepower to make him uncomfortable. Wilder takes that comfort away on sight. Even at 41, Wilder carries the kind of right hand that forces an opponent to stay alert every second of every round. Jalolov would not be able to coast behind a jab when one mistake puts him on the canvas, and Wilder could not afford to give away early rounds against a giant technician who knows how to manage distance.

The real question is whether Wilder’s side wants any part of a tall, undefeated Olympic champion on a little over three weeks’ notice. Taking on Jalolov carries the risk of getting outboxed from the outside or stopped late, whereas Chisora would be a familiar, eight-round payday.

If the goal in Cardiff is to deliver a serious night of heavyweight boxing rather than a nostalgia act, Jalolov has the credentials, the conditioning, and the danger factor to make the co-main event matter.

Sports.title: Hearn Wants Mayweather to Risk 50–0 Against Garcia
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn wants Floyd Mayweather Jr. to end his exhibition run and put his 50 and 0 record on the line against reigning world champion Ryan Garcia. In an interview this week, Hearn compared the idea of Mayweather returning to face an active titleholder to George Foreman winning the heavyweight crown back in the nineties.

Hearn views it as an exciting idea, yet notice who he is leaving out of the conversation. Hearn promotes unified junior middleweight champion Jaron Ennis, and he is certainly not pushing Mayweather to step into that human guillotine. Even though casual fans would pay big money hoping to see Mayweather finally get flattened, matching a guy turning 50 in February 2027 against Ennis would look like a sanctioned mugging rather than a sporting event.

Ryan Garcia is a completely different story. Despite holding a world title, Ryan has looked vulnerable whenever an opponent survives his early power and takes away his leaping left hook. His clear loss to Rolly Romero exposed how quickly he runs out of ideas when he has to lead, and even when he dropped Devin Haney badly in 2024, he got wild and could not finish the job.

If Ryan were a relentless volume puncher with power, a 49-year-old Mayweather would be in huge trouble. Even in his mid-thirties back in 2014, Mayweather got smothered against the ropes and took heavy shots in two close fights against Marcos Maidana because he could not dodge nonstop punches from every angle. Ryan is a single-shot hunter who needs space to set up his left hook, giving Mayweather plenty of breathing room to use his upper body slip, low crouch, and stiff jab to steal quiet rounds on the outside.

“If you want to come back, fight the reigning world champion, someone like Ryan Garcia,” said Hearn on the Mr. Versace podcast. “I think that’s a thrilling narrative and storyline. I mean, it’s like Foreman coming back, isn’t it? “That’s, for me, that’s worse than losing your O,” Hearn said of the exhibition run.

For Mayweather, trading his unbeaten record for one last monster payday makes total sense if the rumors about his cash crunch are true. You cannot spend an undefeated record, and if he loses at 50, nobody holds it against him anyway.

Ryan is the one walking into a career-risk situation. If he loses to a 50-year-old retiree, that embarrassment follows him forever, and it is tough to see him having the thick skin to brush off that kind of permanent stain.

Sports.title: Matchroom’s Teremoana Title Timetable Starts With Ahio
Sports.content:
Matchroom wants Teremoana Teremoana in a world title shot within 18 months, yet they are still praying Hemi Ahio survives long enough on Wednesday in Melbourne to give their prospect some actual work. You cannot have both without throwing him in against live heavyweights who can hit back.

“Probably coming earlier in his career than we maybe thought,” said Matchroom CEO Frank Smith on the Punch Podcast, discussing the step up against Ahio. “I would say within the next 12 to 18 months, he’s going to be in a position to challenge for a world title. If he carries on on a trajectory he’s going on.”

Going into Wednesday’s 10-rounder for the vacant IBF Intercontinental title, Teremoana already sits at number 15 in the IBF rankings. Winning that regional strap will push him straight toward the top 10, which sounds great on a press release until you look at who he has actually beaten.

His last five opponents lasted an average of 1.2 rounds. On Tuesday, Teremoana tipped the scales 16.7 kilograms heavier than the 36-year-old Ahio while holding a six-inch height advantage. Even though Ahio brings a 25-1 record into Pullman Melbourne Albert Park, oddsmakers have Teremoana as a -1000 favorite to score another stoppage.

If Teremoana blasts Ahio out inside two rounds like everyone expects, Matchroom learns nothing. Nobody finds out if his gas tank holds up past round five, whether his jab stays sharp when he gets tired, or how he reacts when a contender takes his best right hand and fires back.

Climbing the IBF ladder with quick knockouts over regional opposition is easy. Being ready for a real world champion by early 2028 is a completely different story. If Smith is serious about that 18-month clock, Matchroom has to stop protecting his undefeated record and put him in with a top-15 heavyweight who can actually win rounds off him next.

Sports.title: Vito Mielnicki Jr. Passes on Hernández, Targets Zayas
Sports.content:
Vito Mielnicki Jr. wants no part of dangerous Cuban middleweight Yoenli Hernandez right now, and Matchroom Boxing is helping him steer straight toward a much safer commercial target in Xander Zayas instead.

Matchroom CEO Frank Smith confirmed that Mielnicki passed on fighting Hernandez and is already lined up for the undercard of the Jaron Ennis vs. Josh Kelly three-belt unification on February 27 in Atlanta. The plan from there is to match Mielnicki against Zayas next summer.

“He wants to fight Xander Zayas next summer. That’s a fight that we’ve been working on. He was already lined up to have a fight on our undercard of the Boots-Kelly show. That was already planned. And then his focus is to fight Xander next summer,” said Smith on the Punch Podcast.

It is easy to see the business logic behind the move, even if hardcore fans are not going to like it. Hernandez is a big, heavy-handed 160-pounder who has been tearing through opponents and is now negotiating to fight Michael Zerafa for a WBO middleweight title. Going up against an experienced Cuban like Hernandez would be a real problem because of how good this guy is. We saw how quickly Denzel Bentley gave up his title recently rather than face Hernandez. He knew better.

Mielnicki is ranked No. 2 by the WBO at 160 after beating Austin Williams in September, so the path to Hernandez was wide open if he actually wanted the smoke.

Instead, Mielnicki is focusing on fighting Zayas in an arguably more winnable fight, who just confirmed he is moving up to 160 pounds in early 2027 after getting stopped by Ennis in their junior middleweight unification back in September. Notice the subtle detail in Smith’s pitch. Zayas is no longer a 154-pounder, meaning any summer fight between them will happen at middleweight, where both guys are trying to rebuild or cash in without touching the division’s biggest punchers.

Zayas brings a recognizable name and a built-in New York and New Jersey ticket-selling angle against Mielnicki without carrying anywhere near the physical threat of Hernandez. That is smart matchmaking by Eddie Hearn and Smith, though it tells you plenty about where Mielnicki’s team thinks his ceiling is at 160.

Everything now comes down to who Matchroom puts across from Mielnicki on February 27 at State Farm Arena. If they feed him a soft touch just to keep him busy until summer, fans will see right through the Zayas buildup.

Ghana News.title: Ghana’s nuclear journey: From Nkrumah’s vision to a new investment commitment
Ghana News.content:
Ghana’s proposed US$200 million investment in nuclear power readiness marks a significant step in a journey that began more than six decades ago. It renews an ambition rooted in the country’s earliest development agenda: building the energy capacity to sustain industrialisation and economic transformation.

During a recent discussion in the media, I expressed support for this investment. Its importance becomes clearer when placed within the history of Ghana’s efforts to include nuclear power in its electricity generation mix.

In 1961, under President Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana decided to undertake the Ghana Nuclear Reactor Project. Its immediate purpose was to establish a research reactor for scientific research, training and radioisotope production. The longer objective was to develop the human resources and technical knowledge necessary for nuclear electricity generation.

The establishment of the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission gave that ambition an institutional foundation. Nuclear science formed part of a broader vision in which education, infrastructure and energy would support an industrial economy.

Nkrumah recognised that economic transformation required deliberate preparation for future electricity demand. Factories, mineral processing facilities and expanding cities would need dependable power. His overthrow in 1966 interrupted the early nuclear power agenda, although Ghana’s scientific work in nuclear technology continued.

An important milestone followed during President Jerry John Rawlings’ administration. The Ghana Research Reactor, GHARR-1, achieved first criticality in December 1994 and was formally commissioned in March 1995. It served research and training purposes, giving Ghanaian scientists practical experience in reactor operations and nuclear applications. That experience helped strengthen the country’s technical foundation for future development.

The modern policy drive towards nuclear electricity gained renewed momentum during the energy difficulties of the 2000s. In 2007, President John Agyekum Kufuor’s administration established a presidential committee chaired by Professor Daniel Adzei Bekoe to assess the potential role of nuclear power. Its recommendations informed Cabinet’s decision in 2008 to include nuclear energy in Ghana’s electricity generation mix.

Successive administrations continued the preparatory work. A major legal development came during President John Dramani Mahama’s first administration with the passage of the Nuclear Regulatory Authority Act, 2015, Act 895. The Act established an independent regulatory authority and provided a framework for licensing, inspection, enforcement and the protection of people and the environment from radiation risks.

This legal foundation is central to the credibility of Ghana’s ambitions. Nuclear power requires institutions capable of examining technical proposals, enforcing standards and holding operators accountable throughout the life of a facility. Regulatory competence must develop alongside the programme itself.

Ghana’s preparations also underwent international scrutiny. The International Atomic Energy Agency conducted an Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review in 2017 and a follow-up mission in 2019. In 2022, under President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, Ghana formally announced its transition into Phase Two of the programme, involving preparatory work towards construction following a policy decision.

This history reflects contributions by successive governments, scientists, engineers and public institutions. It demonstrates the value of continuity in national development. Projects requiring decades of preparation depend on administrations preserving institutional knowledge and advancing the work they inherit.

The latest commitment under President Mahama’s administration provides an opportunity to move that work forward with a defined funding proposal and timetable.

The 2027 Budget proposes US$200 million for a 24-month nuclear readiness programme, running from January 2027 to December 2028. The preparations include site studies, technology selection, environmental assessment, financing, licensing, safeguards, emergency planning and the safety case. The stated target is to complete readiness and sign an engineering, procurement, construction and financing contract for a fully state-owned nuclear power plant by December 2028.

The nature of this commitment must be communicated accurately. The US$200 million is intended for readiness activities. It represents preparatory expenditure rather than the full construction cost of a nuclear plant. The Budget also explicitly recognises that completing readiness in 2028 does not mean nuclear electricity generation will begin in that year.

That distinction should help establish realistic public expectations. The quality of preparation will influence the project’s eventual cost, safety, financing and delivery.

My support for this investment rests on the need to plan for Ghana’s future productive capacity. Our electricity policy must account for the demands of an economy seeking to manufacture more goods, process more of its natural resources and support increasingly sophisticated businesses.

Nuclear power deserves consideration within that long-term planning. Its suitability must be assessed alongside other generation sources, the capacity of the national grid, financing conditions and projected demand. The objective should be a dependable electricity system that supports competitive production.

There is also an opportunity to build Ghanaian skills and expand participation in a technically demanding industry. A nuclear programme can create work across engineering, construction, environmental management, law, finance, security and technical services. The extent to which Ghanaians benefit will depend on deliberate training, credible local participation requirements and opportunities for domestic businesses.

Training must therefore be connected to identifiable roles. Universities, technical institutions and professional bodies should be involved early enough to prepare people for the work the programme will require. Local participation must similarly be supported by standards, certification and supplier development.

As a lawyer and energy policy analyst, I consider governance fundamental to the success of this investment. Transparent procurement, rigorous technology assessment and financing terms that protect the public interest must guide implementation.

The regulator must have the resources, expertise and independence to make decisions on safety grounds. Communities must receive clear information and meaningful opportunities to participate. Waste management, emergency preparedness and eventual decommissioning must be incorporated into planning and financing from the outset.

These requirements give substance to the investment. Public confidence will grow through demonstrable competence, openness and accountability.

Ghana’s nuclear journey has endured interruptions, renewed commitments and years of institutional preparation. The proposed investment offers President Mahama’s administration an opportunity to advance this national undertaking through measurable progress.

The task now is to turn funding commitments into sound decisions, capable institutions and a credible route towards implementation. That is how an ambition first pursued in the early years of independence can contribute to Ghana’s next stage of development.

Our energy ambition must match our development ambition.

The writer is a lawyer, law lecturer, author and energy and public policy analyst.

Ghana News.title: Child Online Africa calls for AU action on online violence against children
Ghana News.content:
Child Online Africa has called on the African Union (AU) and its member states to take urgent and coordinated action to protect children from online violence, sexual exploitation and other forms of digital abuse.

The organisation has launched the #AfricaESafetyNow campaign ahead of the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, scheduled for November 18 to 19, 2026, in Manila, Philippines.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, November 17, the organisation said Africa had reached a critical point in addressing the risks children face as they increasingly engage with digital platforms.

It acknowledged that technology provides opportunities for learning, innovation and development but warned that children are also exposed to online violence, cyberbullying, harmful content and sexual exploitation.

“The protection of children online can no longer be treated as an optional policy concern or left entirely to individual families. It is a shared responsibility that requires decisive leadership, coordinated continental action and accountability from governments and technology companies,” the statement said.

Child Online Africa wants the AU to move beyond policy commitments and establish concrete measures to protect children across digital spaces.

Its proposals include the development of a continental legal framework or protocol on child online safety, with clear and enforceable protection standards.

It is also calling for a dedicated African eSafety Commission, or an equivalent continental mechanism, to coordinate action and ensure accountability among member states.

The organisation further wants the AU to accelerate implementation of its Child Online Safety and Empowerment Policy through a clear and adequately funded roadmap.

Other recommendations include expanding age-appropriate digital literacy and online safety education in schools and communities, while strengthening the capacity of parents, teachers and caregivers.

It also urged governments to hold technology companies accountable through safety-by-design measures, stronger privacy safeguards, effective reporting systems and appropriate enforcement.

The organisation acknowledged the AU's adoption of its Child Online Safety and Empowerment Policy in 2024 as an important recognition of the need to protect children online.

However, it said the policy must now be backed by political commitment, institutional coordination and adequate investment.

“What is now required is the political will, institutional coordination, investment and accountability to translate that commitment into meaningful protection for children,” the statement said.

Ahead of the Manila conference, Child Online Africa said African countries should approach the discussions with a common position on protecting children from violence in both physical and digital environments.

It argued that online safety should form an integral part of the broader child protection agenda, rather than being treated as a separate concern.

“Violence against children does not end at the school gate or stop when a child enters the digital world. Online safety must be recognised as an integral part of the broader child protection agenda,” the statement said.

The organisation is calling on African governments, civil society groups, child-rights advocates, parents, educators, young people, development partners and technology companies to support the campaign.

It is urging the public to sign its petition, share its message and demand concrete action from the AU.

The petition, titled Africa's Children Are Under Attack Online: Demand the African Union Act Now to Save Them!, seeks to turn public concern into pressure for measurable policy action.

“Africa's children deserve more than promises. They deserve protection,” the statement said.

The statement was signed by Awo Aidam Amenyah, Executive Director of Child Online Africa, an Accra-based organisation advocating for child online protection across the continent.

Ghana News.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
Ghana News.content:
Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May

As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.

On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The move not only restricts exports of advanced chips, but also access to the computing power Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.

South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, a US-based think-tank.

China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

A blow to Asia's AI boom

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.

These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.

But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.

The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.

A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".

Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".

A headache for China

The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

Beijing has made tech self-sufficiency a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and a half months.

"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.

Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.

The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.

But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

Ghana News.title: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
Ghana News.content:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.

The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their financing and ability to support construction in the West Bank.

Settlement construction, which is illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".

"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".

Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".

The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.

It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.

The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".

The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.

Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."

This follows the UK's expansion of its human rights sanctions regime last month, which allows the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.

Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.

"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.

"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.

"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."

'New approach'

In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".

That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel, which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.

Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

Ghana News.title: Six in court accused of high-value Pokemon card theft
Ghana News.content:
Six men charged with stealing high-value Pokemon cards from a warehouse in Nottinghamshire have appeared in court.

Nottinghamshire Police said a group allegedly drilled through the wall of a business premises in Aurillac Way, Retford, before stealing 26 boxes of cards in December.

Liam Duce and Liam Parker, both of HMP Lancaster Farms; Daniel Milligan, 27, of Wharfe Street in Otley; Brandon Coates, of Broom Terrace, Leeds; Matthew Middleton, of Pawson Street, Leeds; and Mohammed Hussan, of Whiteacre Road, Newcastle-under-Lyme, Staffordshire, were charged with conspiracy to commit burglary between 25 and 28 December.

They appeared at Mansfield Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

Duce, 25, and Parker, 29, appeared via video-link from HMP Lancaster Farms and were remanded in custody.

Coates, 20, Middleton, 44, and Hussan, 32, attended court in person. The court granted them bail with conditions, including not contacting their co-defendants and not going to Obsidia Ltd, a trading card business in Retford.

Milligan, who appeared in court virtually, was also granted bail on conditions.

All six defendants were told to appear at Nottingham Crown Court on 15 December for a plea hearing.

Ghana News.title: ‘We’re a capitalist society’: Grindr defends $120 a month premium tier
Ghana News.content:
The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, Grindr, has defended its $120 (£91) per month premium subscription service, which launches globally today.

Edge offers AI-powered services, such as daily personalised profile recommendations, to provide better matches and limit scrolling.

The company's CEO, George Arison, told BBC News it would be a "very different Grindr experience" which was aimed at a "small community of users" - and was unapologetic about its cost.

"I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not," he said.

Grindr has long offered a free service and two additional tiers that cost between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.

Users in San Francisco reacted mixed to the app's new, more expensive version, according to BBC News.

"The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," said one user who told the BBC the company's newest offering "just seems really out of touch with the community."

"I think that's really disheartening, and it kind of leaves a bad taste in my mouth," added another user, Adrian, who declined to give his last name.

"The cost doesn't bother me," said a user named Michael. "All of these apps have premium tiers, so saying that Grindr shouldn't have that when it exists across all these other apps used for connection doesn't make sense."

He noted that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.

'It's a choice'

Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.

On its earnings call earlier this month, the company said almost 400,000 users had registered for the service in the first 72 hours that it was available for testing.

Inside Grindr, Edge is viewed as a way to drive future growth in an industry has struggled in recent years.

For those who can afford it, the service promises insights into a user's compatibility with prospective matches. It also resurfaces a user's past connections alongside summaries of previous interactions.

The current $120 monthly fee comes after the company tested charging hundreds of dollars more. And Arison has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.

Arison told the BBC he's not concerned that introducing an ultra-premium offering will pit "haves" against "have-nots" on the social networking platform.

Edge users "being willing to pay more for that set of features will result in us being able to subsidise the product for everybody else," Arison said.

"It's a choice that people make on whether they want to be on it."

An 'AI-first company'

The use of AI to develop the Edge service is part of Grindr's attempt to become what it calls an "AI-first company."

Arison said the company was investing in AI to build products faster and cheaper.

In September, as the debate over AI safety raged throughout Silicon Valley, Arison told the BBC that his concerns about what he called an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic" had prompted him to instruct some of his engineers to stop using Anthropic's technology.

Anthropic is set to sell shares to the public for the first time this week.

Although Grindr still uses Anthropic's Claude Code tools, Arison said the company is on track to phase them out of its workflows by next year.

He said Grindr once heavily used Claude Code but is no longer its primary tool for writing code.

"Anthropic's built an amazing set of products, and they should be very proud of what they've done," Arison said. "They should aim to win with the awesome products they have, rather than regulatory capture that they're trying to win with, oftentimes."

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain
World.content:
Iran claims drone strike on US radar was retaliation for alleged airspace violations by US military drones.

Share Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain on social media

Kuwait’s army has said the Gulf country is under attack by drones while the United States and Iran traded blows, marking escalating tensions in the region as a peace deal remains elusive.

The military said in a statement on X on Tuesday that “any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defence systems intercepting hostile attacks”.

The US earlier carried out several attacks on Iran’s southern island of Qeshm, in the Strait of Hormuz, hours after Iran said it launched a drone attack on a US radar system in Bahrain.

“The American attack on locations on Qeshm island caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas,” Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, told the official IRNA news agency on Tuesday.

He said the situation was under control and relief agencies were on full alert. IRNA reported five to six explosions on the island on Tuesday evening.

A US official told Al Jazeera the strike hit a missile launch site on Qeshm, in response to Iran’s earlier attack on a US base in Bahrain.

US Central Command said Iranian drones aimed at a US radar system at an air base in Bahrain “were intercepted without any damage to US equipment or personnel”.

Bahrain attack

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it carried out a “precision operation” with drones on the US-operated radar at the Sheikh Isa air base, in response to “repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones”.

Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, said its air defences intercepted the attack, and blasts were heard over the capital, Manama, according to the AFP news agency.



It was the third Iranian drone attack on Bahrain in five days after a lull of several weeks. Friday’s strike was the first Iranian attack on a Gulf country since early September, AFP reported. Reuters said it came after a Bahraini court sentenced 64 people, mostly Shia clerics, to life in prison for allegedly colluding with Iran.

Kuwait’s armed forces said on Tuesday night that its air defences were responding to “hostile drone attacks” and urged the public to follow safety instructions.

It did not say where the drones came from or whether there were casualties or damage.

Tankers hit in Hormuz

Iran’s armed forces said three oil tankers struck naval mines while trying to cross the strait on Tuesday. The US military says it cleared the main routes of mines.

Since the war began on February 28, Iran has tried to restrict traffic through the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil, insisting that ships use only routes it has authorised. The US has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and has escorted tankers.

Another tanker, the Panamanian-flagged Tara Gas, was struck on Monday about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, in Oman, causing a fire in its engine room, according to the security firm Vanguard.

Vanguard and India’s ports minister initially said all 25 crew, 24 of them Indian, were safe. But the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the vessel was hit a second time and the crew were “currently unaccounted for”. India’s ports minister later said the crew had abandoned the vessel after a second attack and that one Indian sailor was missing. Another Panamanian-flagged tanker, the On Phoenix, was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast on Monday.

Ongoing diplomacy

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, discussed safeguarding shipping and diplomatic options in Muscat, Oman’s news agencies said.

A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, arrived in the Middle East on Monday, and US President Donald Trump is due to hold a three-way summit on Thursday in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the Iran war is on the agenda.

World.title: Israel parliament elects Gadi Eisenkot ally Matan Kahana as new speaker
World.content:
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.

Israeli lawmakers have elected Matan Kahana as the new parliament speaker, marking a step towards reversing domestic policies from the outgoing government led by Benjamin Netanyahu.

Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot – the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu – was voted in on Tuesday, receiving 66 votes in the 120-member chamber.

Netanyahu’s Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate. He received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.

The Israel parliament speaker is an important office given that it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.

“I will be a Knesset speaker for everyone, irrespective of race, religion or gender,” said Kahana during his inauguration speech immediately after the vote.

Kahana, a 54-year-old former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of Netanyahu’s domestic agenda, especially regarding contentious reforms to the judiciary.

Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having been in and out of office for three decades.

The vote took place weeks after October 27 parliamentary elections in which neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a majority in the Knesset, with the two blocs trading barbs since then.

Eisenkot’s wide-ranging bloc secured 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s finished with 53. Two Arab-majority slates won an unprecedented 19 seats on the back of anger over Netanyahu’s hard-right government.



On Tuesday, the two lists voted for Eisenkot’s candidate Kahana as parliament speaker, with one Arab Knesset member absent.

Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s parties met on Sunday to discuss the possibility of joining a unity government but the meeting appeared to be largely a formality, with both men saying they should be prime minister.

Netanyahu, who has reportedly been urging US President Donald Trump to resume the war on Iran, has talked up the threat from Tehran as he insists on the need for a unity government.

Sweeping reforms

With Kahana at the helm and if Eisenkot retains the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties, he has an opportunity to deal serious blows to Netanyahu’s legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.

Eisenkot has said he wants to rescind sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.

Eisenkot has also vowed to quickly set up a state commission of inquiry to investigate security failures that led to Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack.

Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel’s security, has refused an independent probe, instead proposing one whose members would be chosen by politicians.

Kahana, who is now a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, served in a short-lived non-Netanyahu government in 2021 and 2022 as minister for religious services, during which he clashed with ultra-Orthodox Jews by seeking to reduce the power of the Chief Rabbinate.

Kahana himself is an observant Jew, part of Eisenkot’s efforts to form a broad coalition that ranges from secular liberals to religious conservatives.

As parliament speaker, Kahana succeeds Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally who has held the position since 2022.
