Contributing, Senate President Godswill Akpabio urged INEC to enforce the provisions of the Electoral Act 2026 against electoral violence, stressing that offenders should face the consequences prescribed by law.

Akpabio said Sections 121 to 128 of the Act provided for offences relating to electoral violence, intimidation and the snatching of Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) machines, ballot boxes and other electoral materials.

He said the lawmakers had recommended penalties ranging from 12 months to five years’ imprisonment, without an option of fine for aggravated offences involving attacks with dangerous objects.

According to him, Section 92 also empowers INEC to suspend elections in areas where violence is reported and reschedule them within 24 hours.

He added that the Electoral Offences Commission Bill 2025, passed alongside the Electoral Act, provided for a dedicated mechanism to address electoral offences, including vote-buying, violence and attacks on electoral officials.

Akpabio said the enactment of the laws placed responsibility on the executive to ensure their effective implementation.

In another resolution, following an additional prayer by Senator Sampson Ekong (Akwa Ibom South), the Senate urged the Federal Ministry of Information and the National Orientation Agency to intensify public enlightenment campaigns against political violence.

Ekong said legal provisions alone would not adequately address the problem without sustained public awareness, particularly among young people who could be recruited into violent political activities.

Also contributing, Senator Binos Yaroe (Adamawa South) urged state governors to ensure that opposition parties and candidates were not denied access to public facilities, including arenas and hotels controlled by state governments.

He said restrictions on such facilities could undermine the principle of a level playing field for political parties and create avoidable political tensions.

Senator Ali Ndume (Borno South) supported the motion and proposed that security agencies prohibit the carrying of dangerous weapons during political campaigns.

He called for the arrest of anyone found carrying knives, sticks or other harmful objects at campaign venues, irrespective of political affiliation.

Ndume also proposed the establishment of mobile courts to ensure the prompt prosecution of offenders during campaign activities.

He said political campaigns should be conducted with legitimate campaign materials rather than weapons, adding that the measures should apply equally to all political parties, including the ruling All Progressives Congress.

Ndume further cautioned against campaign slogans that could heighten political tensions, citing slogans such as “Tinubu Must Go”, “Atiku Must Go” and “Obi Must Go”.

He said political disagreements should be resolved through peaceful engagement rather than violence.

Senator Sumaila Kawu (Kano South) also expressed concern over the presence of supporters carrying dangerous weapons at political gatherings.

Kawu described it as a shame for candidates contesting elections into the Senate, House of Representatives or governorship positions to be surrounded by supporters carrying weapons.

He questioned the conduct of politicians who, despite making laws against electoral violence, allowed their supporters to engage in activities capable of undermining the electoral process.

“It is a shame to see candidates contesting for the Senate, House of Representatives or governorship surrounded by supporters carrying dangerous weapons. Where are we going as lawmakers when we appear to encourage conduct that violates the laws we enacted?” he said.

The Senate urged political parties, candidates and their supporters to embrace peaceful political engagement and respect the rule of law ahead of the 2027 general elections.

World.title: COP31: African workers declare ‘no more empty promises’ as unions demand climate justice, decent jobs
World.content:
By Victor Ahiuma-Young

Representing 18 million organised workers across 52 African countries, the International Trade Union Confederation–Africa, ITUC-Africa, has challenged world leaders at COP31 to move beyond climate change rhetoric and deliver concrete action, demanding climate finance, decent green jobs, workers’ protection and a just transition that puts African workers at the centre of decision-making.

The African workers, under the banner of ITUC-Africa, issued the message at the COP31 Political March in Antalya, Turkey, declaring that the continent’s workforce would no longer tolerate empty promises and delayed commitments on climate action.

In a statement by its General Secretary, Akhator Joel Odigie, the regional labour organisation warned that African workers were bearing the devastating consequences of climate change despite contributing comparatively little to the crisis.

Speaking under the theme, “Deliver, Don’t Delay – Move from Dialogue to Action,” Odigie said the climate emergency was no longer an abstract environmental concern but an immediate threat to workers’ lives, livelihoods and fundamental labour rights.

“We are the 18 million organised workers of Africa, represented here by ITUC-Africa across 52 countries. We are the ones who build, transport, farm, mine, and power this continent. And we are the ones who will pay the highest price if COP31 ends in more talk and no delivery,” he declared.



He stressed that workers were already experiencing the devastating effects of extreme weather conditions, including unbearable workplace heat, destructive flooding and prolonged droughts that threaten agricultural production and community livelihoods.

“The climate crisis is not abstract for us. It is the unbearable heat on a construction site, the flood that destroys a community, the drought that kills a harvest,” Odigie stated.



Citing International Trade Union Confederation data, he disclosed that extreme workplace heat already claims nearly 19,000 lives annually, while heat stress could wipe out working hours equivalent to 136 million full-time jobs by 2030.

“This is a labour rights crisis. And it demands a labour response,” he insisted.

Workers reject slow progress on climate commitments

ITUC-Africa expressed concern that despite COP31 being presented as the “COP of implementation,” progress on translating climate commitments into tangible benefits for workers and vulnerable communities remained inadequate.

The organisation particularly criticised the slow progress on the Just Transition Work Programme, arguing that workers’ rights and participation must not be relegated to the margins of climate negotiations.

According to Odigie, although procedural progress had been recorded, the mechanism’s design remained unresolved, with no substantive agreement reached on how it would operate.

“The Just Transition Work Program—the one space where workers’ rights should be front and centre—has made procedural progress, but its mechanism design is still open, with no substantive agreement yet,” he said.

He maintained that the ongoing negotiations in Antalya represented a critical opportunity to move from discussions to concrete commitments that would guarantee workers a meaningful role in shaping the continent’s economic and environmental future.

Demands climate finance, not debt

A major concern raised by the African labour movement is the persistent inequality in global climate financing, particularly the limited resources reaching African countries despite the continent’s vulnerability to climate change.

ITUC-Africa noted that while the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap seeks to mobilise $1.3 trillion annually by 2035, sub-Saharan Africa receives less than three per cent of global climate finance, with much of the funding provided through loans rather than grants.

The organisation also highlighted the funding gap surrounding the Loss and Damage Fund, stating that although $826 million had been pledged, only $456 million had actually been received.

Odigie further expressed disappointment that the African Group of Negotiators’ push to triple adaptation finance had not received a standalone agenda slot.

He argued that African countries should not be forced to accumulate more debt to address a climate crisis they contributed relatively little to creating.

“So when we say ‘deliver,’ we mean: stop congratulating yourselves on roadmaps and start signing the cheques, with grants, not debt,” he declared.

The labour movement called on developed countries to provide new, additional, predictable and adequate climate financing, primarily through grants and highly concessional public financing.

It also demanded debt relief, progressive taxation and windfall taxes on extractive industry profits as alternative ways of mobilising resources for climate action and essential public services.

“Africa should not be forced to borrow its way out of a crisis it did not cause. We reject loans as climate contributions,” the statement stressed.

New form of economic colonialism

ITUC-Africa also warned that the global transition to clean energy must not become another avenue for exploiting Africa’s natural resources while denying its people the economic benefits of industrialisation.

The organisation argued that Africa must move beyond exporting unprocessed critical minerals, including lithium and cobalt, and develop the capacity to process these resources locally.

It insisted that the continent’s mineral wealth should support industrial development, create decent employment opportunities and improve the living standards of African workers.

“The global energy transition must not become a new colonialism. Africa must use this shift to industrialise, not remain a supplier of unprocessed raw materials,” Odigie declared.

He called for local processing of critical minerals to ensure that the jobs and economic opportunities generated by the global green transition remain within African economies.

The organisation also warned against the potential impact of the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism on African producers and workers, arguing that the costs of the global transition should not be unfairly transferred to developing economies.

Another major demand is the establishment of an effective Just Transition Mechanism that guarantees workers formal representation and meaningful influence over decisions concerning employment, investment and industrial transformation.

ITUC-Africa maintained that workers must be involved in designing and implementing national transition pathways rather than being subjected to decisions reached without their participation.

It called for the operationalisation of a mechanism capable of providing technical assistance, capacity-building and financial support to countries pursuing climate-friendly economic transformations.

“A mechanism without worker participation is a shell. Trade unions must have formal representation and meaningful influence—not token consultations—in decisions affecting employment, investment, and industrial transformation,” he said.

He added that the proposed Belém–Antalya Mechanism must be developed in partnership with workers and their representative organisations.

“The proposed Belém–Antalya Mechanism must be built with us, not for us,” he emphasised.

Protect jobs, workers’ safety

The African trade union body further demanded comprehensive employment and social protection measures to ensure that the transition to a green economy does not leave millions of workers unemployed or economically vulnerable.

It called for employment-impact assessments, skills development, retraining, redeployment opportunities, job or income guarantees, occupational safety and health protections, and universal social protection to be incorporated into every transition plan.

The organisation stressed that women, young people, migrant workers and those employed in the informal economy required specific protection because of their vulnerability to economic and environmental disruptions.

Particular attention was drawn to extreme workplace heat, which ITUC-Africa said must be formally recognised as an occupational hazard, with enforceable safety measures introduced to protect workers.

The organisation argued that climate policies would remain incomplete if they addressed environmental sustainability without guaranteeing decent working conditions, employment security and social protection.

In a message, ITUC-Africa warned that COP31 must not become another international climate conference where vulnerable populations are asked to wait while governments and global institutions continue making promises without delivering results.

Odigie argued that the consequences of global warming were already being felt, making urgent action essential to prevent African workers from bearing an even greater share of the crisis.

“The question is not whether we will transition—the question is whether that transition will be just, or whether it will leave millions of African workers behind while a few extract the profits of a green economy built on our backs,” he warned.

He insisted that African workers were not attending the climate negotiations merely to appeal for sympathy but to demand their rightful place in decisions that would determine their economic future.

“We are not here to beg. We are here to negotiate. We are here to demand. And we are here to stay,” he declared.

Reaffirming the organisation’s position, he outlined four central demands: climate finance through grants rather than debt; an operational Just Transition Mechanism with workers fully represented; African industrialisation rather than continued extraction of raw materials; and decent, green and unionised jobs for the continent’s workforce.

He said: “Deliver the finance—grants, not debt. Deliver the Just Transition Mechanism—with workers inside, not outside. Deliver industrialisation—not extraction. Deliver decent, green, unionised jobs for Africa’s workers.”

Odigie concluded with a call for world leaders to translate their climate commitments into measurable outcomes, stressing that African workers would continue to press for accountability and justice.

“Move from dialogue to action, now,” he declared, ending his address with the rallying cry, “Amandla!”

World.title: NDIC urges corps members to save in insured banks
World.content:
By Vincent Ujumadu

AWKA — The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) has urged members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) in Anambra State to cultivate sound financial habits and ensure they save their money in banks insured by the corporation.

The advice was given during a financial literacy and sensitisation seminar organised by NDIC officials at the NYSC orientation camp in Awka South Local Government Area of the state.

The corporation urged the corps members to embrace what it described as a smart financial lifestyle built around earning, saving, investing and spending wisely.

The Communications Manager of NDIC, Chinenye Chimezie-Amadi, advised the corps members to exercise caution when choosing where to save their money, stressing the importance of using deposit-taking institutions insured by the corporation.

She urged them to develop the habit of budgeting, distinguishing between their needs and wants, and setting aside part of their earnings for emergencies and future investments.

According to her, many people earn money without keeping track of how they spend it, making it difficult for them to build savings.

“Our presence at the orientation camp is to help you learn a kind of life you need to live in future as you begin to make decisions for yourselves.

“Some people won’t have savings, but you see them carrying expensive hairs and mobile phones. That is living a false life. We are looking at a situation where you save for emergency and for your future,” she said.

Amadi urged the corps members not to dismiss the possibility of saving because of their present earnings, saying even small amounts could accumulate into substantial savings when set aside consistently.

She also advised them to prioritise essential expenses before discretionary spending and develop the habit of paying themselves first by setting aside a portion of their income.

On the choice of financial institutions, she warned against depositing money in unregulated schemes offering unusually high returns, urging them to verify that their banks were insured by NDIC.

“Even when you have a house, you still need to set aside your house rent as a way of saving. If you do it consistently, you will be surprised at the amount you save,” she said.

The NDIC Controller, Enugu Zonal Office, Mr Chidi Nwankwo, urged the corps members to acquire financial literacy skills ahead of their transition from national service into the labour market.

Speaking on the topic, ‘Know Your Deposit Protection: A Practical Guide for NYSC Corps Members’, Nwankwo explained the corporation’s role in protecting depositors and outlined the applicable deposit insurance limits.

He advised the corps members to confirm that any deposit-taking bank with which they intended to transact was insured by NDIC, explaining that eligible deposits were protected within the limits prescribed for different categories of financial institutions.

According to him, deposits in deposit money banks are insured up to N5 million per depositor, while those in microfinance banks, primary mortgage banks and payment service banks are covered up to N2 million.

Using an example, Nwankwo explained that a depositor with N6 million in a deposit money bank that subsequently fails would receive insurance compensation of up to N5 million, while recovery of the remaining N1 million would depend on the realisation of the failed bank’s assets.

He encouraged the corps members to understand the scope of deposit insurance and make informed financial decisions to protect their savings.

World.title: Atiku’s fuel subsidy reversal plan not realistic — Fashola
World.content:
Minister of Works and Housing, Mr. Babatunde Fashola(SAN)

Former Lagos State Governor, Babatunde Fashola, has challenged Atiku Abubakar to explain how he intends to fund his proposed return of fuel subsidy if elected president in 2027, describing the plan as unrealistic.

Fashola said the former vice-president had not addressed the practical difficulties that could undermine the proposal, particularly Nigeria’s inability to fully meet its crude oil production targets and persistent security problems in oil-producing areas.

He made the remarks on Tuesday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today.

The former Minister of Works and Housing questioned the source of the crude oil needed to supply local refineries and support a subsidy arrangement, given the country’s production challenges.

“If we have refineries working, what is our current oil quota? Are we optimising it yet? No, because they are legacy issues, challenges with security people, vandalism. So where is this magic crude oil going to come from? People are entitled to ask,” he said.

Fashola insisted that Atiku must demonstrate that the proposal can work rather than rely on promises to win public support.

“If he can explain, good, let the people choose. But without proof, it is like abracadabra,” he said.

He maintained that his criticism was directed at the policy and not the former vice-president personally.

“The proposal is not realistic. I am looking at the proposal, not the personality,” he said.

Fashola also questioned the consistency of Atiku’s position, noting that the former vice-president had supported subsidy removal during the 2023 presidential campaign.

He said the change in position raised questions about the basis for the proposed reversal and what measures would make the policy sustainable.

Fashola further argued that bringing back subsidy would involve legislative processes, as lawmakers would have to amend the existing legal framework to accommodate the policy.

He wondered whether members of the National Assembly would be willing to support such a move, given its potential implications for public finances.

The former governor also drew on his experience in the Buhari administration, saying subsidy payments had previously constrained the funds available to state governments.

“I was in a government that was paying subsidy, and the states were not getting money. So are we going to go back to partial, near-zero returns, states borrowing money to pay salaries? Is that where you want us to go?” he asked.

Atiku announced in August 2026 that he would restore fuel subsidy if elected president in 2027. He proposed a temporary, audited arrangement focused on petroleum products refined locally, arguing that it would help bring down fuel and transportation costs and ease the burden on households.

Tinubu announced the removal of fuel subsidy during his inauguration on May 29, 2023, as part of his administration’s economic reforms.

World.title: Military aircraft crashes, 19 dead
World.content:
File image of Russian flag.

A military transport plane crashed on Tuesday in the Siberian region of Kemerovo, killing all 19 onboard, Russian media reported, citing a statement from Moscow’s defence ministry.

“An An-12 military transport aircraft crashed in the Kemerovo Region while on a scheduled flight. The plane went down in an uninhabited area. There were 19 people on board, including the crew, they all perished,” the Russian defence ministry was quoted as saying by state news agency TASS.

The preliminary cause of the crash is a technical malfunction, TASS added.

“A commission from the Russian Aerospace Forces is working at the site to establish all the circumstances of the incident,” the ministry’s statement was quoted as saying by RIA Novosti.

Kemerovo region’s governor, Ilya Seredyuk, said earlier on Telegram that there had been an “aviation incident” near the village of Yagunovo.

He added that “an aircraft, which was in transit through our region, has presumably crashed”.

Seredyuk posted a video from the site in which multiple fire engines and ambulances could be seen, their lights blaring in the dark.

Vanguard News

World.title: Benue Justice Commissioner resigns with immediate effect
World.content:
By Peter Duru, Makurdi

The Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Benue State, Prof. Timothy Ornguga, has resigned his appointment with immediate effect, barely one year and two months in office.

The Attorney-General announced his decision in a resignation letter dated November 13, 2026, addressed to Governor Hyacinth Alia through the Secretary to the State Government, SSG.

The letter, titled, “Resignation from the Appointment as Honourable Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Benue State,” formally communicated his decision to step down from the position with immediate effect.

He disclosed that he had served the state for one year, two months and two weeks, expressing appreciation to Governor Alia for the confidence reposed in him and the opportunity to serve.

The resignation letter, which bears an official receipt stamp dated November 16, 2026, stated: “I write with profound respect and deep sense of responsibility to formally tender my resignation from my appointment as the Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Benue State. The resignation is with immediate effect. Having had the privilege of serving in this esteemed capacity for the past one year, two months, and two weeks.”

He further stated: “I consider it an honour to have been entrusted with the responsibility of serving our dear state and contributing in my own capacity to the administration of justice, the promotion of the rule of law and the advancement of good governance. I am sincerely grateful to Your Excellency for the confidence reposed in me and for the opportunity to serve.”

Contacted, the Media of the former Justice Commissioner, Jude Ekpendu confirmed the development.

Meanwhile, efforts to ascertain the circumstances surrounding his resignation were unsuccessful as the Commissioner for Information and Orientation, Chief Solomon Iorpev, said he was unaware of the development when contacted.

World.title: FGN bonds undersubscribed by 9% in November auction
World.content:
By Elizabeth Adegbesan

The Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) bond auction in November 2026 was undersubscribed by 9.5 percent , attracting a total subscription of N1.81 trillion against N2 trillion offered by the Debt Management Office, DMO.

This reflects decline in investors’ demand for the Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) debt instrument.

According to the November FGN Bond Auction result released by DMO , investors bid N1.81 trillion for bonds worth N2 trillion with total allotments rising by 25 percent to N1.5 trillion in November, down from N1.2 trillion allotted in October 2026.

Four instruments were offered during the auction consisting 21 percent FGN March 2028 , 19.3 percent FGN April 2029, 17.94 percent FGN August 2030 and 19.89 percent FGN May 2033, with an offer of N700 billion, N250 billion, N750 billion and N300 billion respectively.

Investor interest was strongest for the May 2033 bond, which attracted N766.4 billion in bids from 233 successful applicants.

The bulk of allotments also went to this bond, totaling N676.6 billion.

The March 2028 bond received N162.99 billion and a non competitive allotment of N50 billion while the April 2029 bond received N241.03 billion and a non competitive allotment of N30 billion.

The August 2030 bond received an allotment of N336.12 billion.

Clearing yields for the bonds were as follows: March 2028: 16.89 percent, while that of other bonds were 16.99 percent.

The results reflect continuous declining appetite among investors for Nigerian government debt, even as allotments tightened compared with previous months.

World.title: 2027: Weigh alternatives before rejecting Tinubu’s reforms – Fashola tells Nigerians
World.content:
File: Babatunde Fashola

…Says cost-of-living crisis is global

…Subsidy return will hurt federation revenue

…Defends Lagos-Calabar highway

By Juliet Umeh

Former Lagos State Governor, Babatunde Fashola, has urged Nigerians to weigh opposition parties’ proposals before rejecting President Bola Tinubu’s reforms, saying the country should not “abort this journey mid-term” without considering the alternatives.

Fashola, a former Minister of Works, spoke on Channels Television, where he said voters should be helped to make informed choices ahead of the 2027 general election.

“What are the other parties offering that is different, that is better, that is compelling as a reason to interrupt the process of reform and restructuring that is already underway?” he asked.

He acknowledged the hardship many Nigerians face but said the cost-of-living crisis was not unique to Nigeria.

“Anybody who is right-thinking will concede that the cost-of-living challenge is now a global challenge,” he said, citing the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and conflicts that disrupted energy and food supplies.

Fashola said: The government had introduced measures including a higher minimum wage, support for students through the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, NELFUND, and tax reforms.”

He said the policies were aimed at easing pressure on households, while acknowledging that there was “a distance between policies, programmes, projects and results.”

On the removal of petrol subsidy, he said a return to the policy would have consequences for government revenue and the funds available to states and local governments.

“Subsidy is not just about ‘I said it, I did not say it’. It has to be paid for somewhere. One of the things that suffered because of that was the monthly receipts into the federation account.”

Fashola challenged politicians proposing a return to subsidy to explain how they would fund it and what they would do differently.

“I want to see rigour, I want to see detail, I want to see numbers,” he said, adding that Nigeria also needed to explain where the crude oil for subsidised supply would come from, given constraints on production.

Fashola said the government deserved credit for maintaining the subsidy removal, despite the hardship it had caused.

“What this government deserves commendation for is not falling over on the sword and saying because the people like it, let’s bring it back,” he said.

He cited the introduction of compressed natural gas, or CNG, as one of the measures aimed at reducing living costs.

Defending the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Fashola said it had reduced travel time to the Lekki Port.

“It took me 40 minutes from Ikoyi to get to that port. Traditionally, when I went to visit that site when I was governor, it used to take me all of one and a half hours. A 90-minute journey is now 40 minutes.

“Go and calculate the fuel savings in that corridor, and the relief to people’s disposable income,” he said.

Fashola also pointed to jobs created by construction activity along the route, saying: “I wish that somebody will commission a survey about how many people are earning a daily living from the construction activity that is going on there.”

Asked about the project’s cost, Fashola said the Bureau of Public Procurement was responsible for reviewing contract prices and issuing certificates of no objection.

On questions about Tinubu’s fitness to govern, he said: “Nothing suggests to me that he’s not fit.”

He described the president as “much more mature” than when they first worked together and said Tinubu was still reading, giving directives and managing government affairs.

World.title: Resolving Uncredited Pension Funds Imbroglio
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

With huge accumulation of uncredited pension fund put at N99.28 billion, all eyes are on PenCom on judicious utilisation of the funds to the benefit of contributors, writes Ebere Nwoji.

Few months ago, precisely in July this year, the National Pension Commission( PenCom), said uncredited pension funds deducted from salaries of Nigerian workers as at March 2026, stood at N99.28 billion.

The commission said the figures represented deductions made by employers from their workers’ salaries as part of their pension contributions to be saved in their Retirement Savings Accounts (RSAs), but which were not credited or paid into the accounts.

The commission disclosed this at the one-year anniversary of the introduction of the Pension Contribution Remittance System (PCRS), organised by PenCom in collaboration with the Pension Operators Association of Nigeria (PenOp), and the Nigerian Employers’ Consultative Association (NECA) in Lagos.

According to the Director, Surveillance Department, Saleem Muhammad, about 70 Percent of the uncredited funds came from private sector employers while the remaining 30 percent came from public sector employers.

According to Muhammad, accumulation of this huge uncredited funds which have entered the pension system but cannot be allocated was one of the weaknesses of the manual remittance system initially used by pension sector operators.

He further said the situation was created by invalid RSA PINs, missing schedules ,incorrect PFA details and data inconsistencies.

The commission said having made efforts to identify the true owners of the contributions without success, it would soon take a decision on what to do with the huge funds.

This disclosure by the commission created concern in the minds of Nigerian workers, retirees and job seekers as such they are eager to know what decision the commission would take or has taken on the uncredited fund . It is indeed a concern because some owners of the fund according to PenCom are casual workers of big organisations like Julius Berger who are now out of job. These contributors are somewhere suffering in poverty and penury because having lost their jobs some have not been able to secure another job since then but cannot access their contributed money to keep life going while looking for another job.

Loss of job by contributors

Section 7 subsection 2 of the PRA 2014, which references section 16 subsection 2 and 5 permits workers to access 25 per cent of their Retirement Savings Account upon job loss.

The act said such a contributor must have remained unemployed for at least four months after disengagement and must be under 50 years.

Some including those that worked with public sector retired with nothing to fall back on where as their money is somewhere waiting to be traced.

Both the employers who deducted the money and who supposed to remit the same to the pension fund custodian designated by the PFA could not liaise with either the PFA, the PFC or even PenCom officials to trace the owners of the fund right from onset before the accumulation of this almost N100 billion.This is so whereas organisations were asked to appoint pension desk officers who see to the welfare of their workers on the issue of contributions.

Workers’ plight

Few years back, THISDAY was approached by an elderly man at the customer care department of one of the PFAs with office along Ikorodu road who was lamenting that he worked for 25 years in Julius Berger as a truck driver, retired that particular year but when he wanted to process his retirement entitlement, his pension desk officer told him there was nothing in his RSA. Downcast by this news from his pension desk officer, the retired Julius Berger truck driver approached THISDAY for an assistance in the area of telling Nigerians his plight.

Obviously this must be one of the owners of this uncredited N100 billion funds. This calls for the need for carefulness, periodic trainings of desk officers of both public and private organisations to avoid a repeat of this ugly situation.

It is true that it was against the backdrop of this situation which was created by manual remittances of deducted funds by the employers that prompted PenCom and PFAs to initiate the introduction of the Pension Contribution Remittance System (PCRS), an electronic or digital way of remitting the deducted funds, care must be taken to guard against its own errors that may result in accumulation of even high quantum of unremitted funds which will be at the detriment of Nigerian workers.

Experts’ View

But before PenCom takes decision on what to do with the already accumulated funds, THISDAY sampled the opinion of some actuarial experts and pension analysts on way forward for PenCom on the funds.

A UK trained actuarial scientist, chartered insurer and Chairman /CEO Anchor Actuarial Services Limited, Dr Pius Apere, on where PenCom should channel the uncredited contributions for the benefit of Nigerian workers said: “In my professional opinion, the National Pension Commission (PenCom) should consider retaining uncredited pension contributions in the Pension Protection Fund (PPF) for the following reasons: Potential Future Identification of Unidentified Contributors: A significant proportion of the unidentified contributors whose pension contributions constitute these uncredited funds are likely to be casual workers. Such individuals may subsequently secure part-time or full-time employment with other employers and become fully captured under the new Pension Contribution Remittance System (PCRS) being introduced by PenCom.”

“Consequently, retaining these funds in the Pension Protection Fund (PPF) would preserve their potential to benefit workers who may become eligible for pension-related support in the future. The funds could be utilised to finance the Minimum Guaranteed Pension (MGP) and/or PenCare for eligible retirees, thereby providing a social safety net for Nigerian workers, particularly those whose pension contributions may remain uncredited or unidentified,” he said.

Furthermore in what he titled anticipated increase in funding requirements for MGP and PenCare, Apere noted that current eligibility thresholds of N52,500 and N70,000 for the Minimum Guaranteed Pension (MGP) and PenCare, respectively, might be reviewed upwards in the future to reflect prevailing economic realities, particularly inflation and the rising cost of living.

According to him, any upward review of these thresholds is likely to increase the financial obligations of the Pension Protection Fund (PPF), potentially placing additional pressure on the Fund. This may necessitate the sourcing of additional funds by PenCom to ensure the sustainable financing of the MGP and/or PenCare.

Reasoning along this line, Apere who was former Managing Director of Linkage Assurance plc, advised that retaining the uncredited pension contributions in the PPF would therefore strengthen the fund’s financial capacity and provide an additional pool of resources to meet these anticipated future obligations.

In another suggestion he titled, “Investment Potential of the Pension Protection Fund,” he said in accordance with the applicable regulatory provisions, any surplus funds available in the Pension Protection Fund (PPF) were expected to be invested before they were eventually utilised to finance the Minimum Guaranteed Pension (MGP) and/or PenCare.

Accordingly, he said retaining the uncredited pension contributions in the PPF would not only strengthen the Fund’s financial position but also create an opportunity for the funds to generate investment returns over time.

Such returns, he explained, could further enhance the Fund’s capacity to meet its future obligations and promote the long-term sustainability of the pension system.

In conclusion, he said with the introduction of the Pension Contribution Remittance System (PCRS), the incidence of uncredited pension contributions is expected to reduce significantly or potentially be eliminated over time, as the system is designed to improve the identification, tracking and reconciliation of pension contributions.

In his words: “In view of the foregoing, I strongly recommend that PenCom consider retaining the existing uncredited pension contributions in the Pension Protection Fund (PPF), rather than channelling the funds to other purposes.

“This approach would preserve the funds for potential future beneficiaries, strengthen the financial sustainability of the PPF and provide additional resources to support the Minimum Guaranteed Pension (MGP) and PenCare programmes. Ultimately, this would ensure that the uncredited pension contributions are deployed in a manner that promotes the long-term interests and welfare of Nigerian workers and retirees.”

A member of Nigerian Union of Pensioners under the Contributory Pension Scheme who preferred to be anonymous said it will be good if PenCom could look side ways to see similar agencies that have similar cases of unclaimed, uncredited fund belonging to unidentified Nigerians and what such agencies did with the funds.

The NAICOM Example

Taking a look at a sister agency like the National Insurance Commission( NAICOM) and unclaimed policy holders’ funds he said PenCom should borrow a leaf from what NAICOM did to contain cases of unclaimed policy holders funds and what the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) did with Nigeria’s massive pool of unclaimed capital market dividends.

THISDAY recalls that NAICOM handled unpaid and unclaimed insurance claims through several key mechanisms.

Two years back, as quantum of unpaid claims due to surrounding controversies which compelled the claimants to abandon such claims mounts with lots of reports flooding the policy holders’ complaint box of NAICOM, the commission consistently enforced strict measures to clear the backlog of unpaid and unclaimed insurance settlements. As regulator, NAICOM centered its decisions and enforcement actions on mandating transparency through the Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA) and penalising non-compliant underwriters.

As operators claimed that owners of most of the outstanding claims have disappeared and were no where to be found to process their claims for them to pay, at their Insurers’ Committee meeting, NAICOM issued a direct mandate to underwriters through their umbrella body, the NIA, to address unclaimed settlements.

The commission did not stop there rather it’s Chief Executive and commissioner for insurance Mr Ayo Omosehin, under his Zero-Outstanding-Claims Directive, charged insurance chief executives to clear their backlogs and ensure that no unresolved, genuine claims was carried over into their financial accounts.

After repeated warnings, NAICOM published a comprehensive list titled “Complaints Against Insurance Companies” on its official portal. The publication exposed over 1,582 unresolved claims complaints across life and non-life policies lodged by corporate and individual policyholders. This was endorsed by NIA this way lots of unclaimed claims operators claimed no body had claimed were settled.

World.title: NIA Charges Technical Committee on Proactive Engagement
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Ebere Nwoji

The Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA), has charged its Technical Committees to strengthen their contributions to industry development through proactive engagement, strategic recommendations and effective collaboration in addressing emerging challenges in the insurance sector.

NIA Chairman, Mrs. Ebelechukwu Nwachukwu, gave the charge recently during a breakfast meeting with Chairmen and Secretaries of the Association’s Technical Committees.

The meeting provided an interactive platform for the NIA leadership and representatives of the Technical Committees to assess their activities, identify areas for improvement and explore strategies for enhancing their effectiveness and contributions to the growth of the association and the Nigerian insurance industry.

Addressing the committees, Nwachukwu commended the them for their invaluable contributions to the association’s activities and the development of the insurance industry over the years.

She, however, challenged them to demonstrate greater commitment, innovation and responsiveness in discharging their responsibilities, stressing that their expertise and recommendations remained critical to the association’s strategic direction and industry advocacy initiatives.

According to her, the NIA Governing Council places significant expectations on the technical committees, particularly in providing informed recommendations that serve as the foundation for counncil decisions on market conduct guidelines, regulatory policies and other critical industry matters.

In her welcome address, the Director-General of NIA, Mrs. Bola Odukale, expressed appreciation to the leadership and members of the Technical Committees for their unwavering commitment, professional contributions and continued support to the NIA Secretariat and the insurance industry.

She reiterated the secretariat’s commitment to strengthening its working relationship with the committees and providing the necessary institutional support to enhance their operational effectiveness and delivery of their mandates.

World.title: Optimus Bank’s H1 Profit Before Tax Rises 104% to N24.55bn
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Nume Ekeghe

Optimus Bank Limited grew its profit before tax (PBT) by 103.9 per cent to N24.55 billion in the first half of 2026, up from N12.04 billion recorded in the corresponding period of 2025, as stronger interest income and an expanded balance sheet supported its earnings.

The bank’s improved financial performance, captured in its audited results for the half year ended June 30, 2026, coincided with an upgrade of its credit rating by Agusto & Co. to A- Long-Term and A1 Short-Term, with a Stable Outlook.

Interest income, one of the key drivers of the performance, more than doubled to N42.42 billion, representing a 101.9 per cent increase from N21.01 billion recorded in the same period last year.

Profit after tax (PAT) also rose by 84.3 per cent to N15.96 billion, compared with N8.66 billion in H1 2025, reflecting the bank’s stronger earnings during the period.

The growth in profitability was accompanied by an expansion in the bank’s balance sheet, with total assets rising by 65.3 per cent to N472.69 billion as of June 2026, from N286.02 billion at the end of December 2025.

Commenting on the performance, the Managing Director of Optimus Bank, Dr. Ademola Odeyemi, said the results reflected the progress made in building a resilient institution with the capacity to sustain growth and deliver value to customers.

“Our H1 performance reflects the progress we are making in building a strong, resilient, and growth-focused institution. The significant improvement in profitability, strengthened capital position, and rating upgrade by Agusto & Co. reinforce our commitment to building a bank that customers and businesses can rely on,” he said.

World.title: Afreximbank Commits $75M SME Finance Facility to Development Bank
World.content:

Emma Okonji

The African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) has committed a $75 million finance facility to the Development Bank of Nigeria (DBN) to expand access to finance for Nigerian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including eligible businesses in the creative economy.

Announced during CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos, the facility reflects the event’s focus on connecting creative enterprises with finance, investment and markets. Executive Vice President, Intra-African Trade and Export Development, Afreximbank, Mrs. Kanayo Awani, and Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, DBN, Dr. Tony Okpanachi, led the ceremonial signing on behalf of their institutions.

“Our partnership with DBN goes beyond providing capital. We are taking an integrated approach that combines finance with capacity building, export-readiness support and access to markets. Our objective is to help Nigerian SMEs build productive capacity, strengthen their competitiveness and make the transition from promising local businesses to sustainable exporters. At the same time, we will work with participating financial institutions to strengthen their capacity to better understand, finance and support SMEs throughout their growth journey,” Awani said.

“This partnership with Afreximbank represents another important step in DBN’s commitment to expanding access to finance for Nigerian MSMEs and enabling them to build resilient, competitive and sustainable businesses. The $75 million facility will provide much-needed financing through our Participating Financial Institutions, while creating greater opportunities for businesses, particularly those in the creative and export-oriented sectors, to strengthen their productive capacity and access new markets,” Okpanachi said.

World.title: UBA Deepens Fight Against Phishing, Scam
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Nume Ekeghe

United Bank for Africa (UBA) Plc, has stepped up its fight against fraud, advising customers and the public to stay alert to phishing scams where criminals increasingly use fake bank messages, cloned websites and impersonation accounts to steal account details and money.

The bank in a statement noted it is slated to hold the 2026 edition of its Fraud Awareness Week, from Monday, November 16 to Friday, November 20, 2026, with the theme “Fraud Dynamics: Staying One Step Ahead.”

UBA’s Group Chief Internal Auditor, Eugene Inotu, who spoke ahead of the campaign, said the bank wants every customer to recognise a phishing or fraud attempt before it causes harm.

“Fraudsters are counting on panic. They want you to click before you think, so the strongest defence is to pause,” Inotu said. “UBA will never ask for your PIN, password, OTP or BVN through a link, a text message, an email or a phone call. If a message asks for any of these, it is not from us, no matter how genuine it looks.”

Continuing, Inotu said, “Fraud keeps changing shape, and our customers need to keep pace with it. This year’s Fraud Awareness Week is about staying one step ahead, so that every customer knows how to spot a scam, verify a request and report it quickly.”

Offering practical guidance, UBA’s Group Head, Brands, Marketing and Corporate Communications, Alero Ladipo, urged customers to treat every unsolicited link with suspicion and to confirm requests only through the Bank’s official channels.

She said, “Avoid clicking links in messages you did not ask for. Type the UBA website address directly into your browser or use the official UBA Mobile App, and download banking apps only from official app stores. If a request looks unusual, confirm it through our verified channels, including Leo, our virtual banking assistant, and our official contact centre.”

Continuing, she said, “If you receive a suspicious message or notice a transaction you did not initiate, report it to us directly at once using our verified phone numbers or website you know is real, not the details provided in the suspicious message so that we can secure your account.”

Polaris Bank, in partnership with Evolve Charity Trust, has distributed learning materials to 640 students across 10 public secondary schools in Nigeria as part of efforts to improve access to education, particularly for the girl child.

Now in its sixth year, the initiative forms part of the bank’s Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programme aimed at easing the financial burden of education on families, encouraging school attendance and reducing the number of out-of-school children.

Speaking on the initiative, the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Polaris Bank, Mr. Kayode Lawal, said the intervention underscored the bank’s commitment to expanding educational opportunities for underserved children.

“The initiative is designed to support 50,000 students by 2028, building on its current reach of 24,000 students across 49 locations. World.title: Stanbic IBTC Empowers Women Entrepreneurs
World.content:

Nume Ekeghe

Stanbic IBTC has reinforced its commitment to women’s economic empowerment and enterprise development, bringing together women entrepreneurs, professionals and business leaders at Bloom Weekend 2026, a two-day event designed to equip women with the knowledge, connections and resources to build and scale sustainable businesses.

Anchored on the theme, ‘Bloom into Growth: From Business Owner to CEO’, this year’s edition focused on the transition from running a business to building a structured, professionally managed enterprise capable of achieving sustainable growth.

The conversations centred on the realities of business expansion, with participants exploring the importance of effective leadership, financial discipline, sound business structures and strategic planning in moving enterprises beyond their early stages.

The first day featured the Ladies at the Table Empowerment Series (LATTES), alongside a series of practical masterclasses designed to provide participants with actionable insights for their entrepreneurial and professional journeys.

Speaking on the initiative in Lagos, Executive Director, Business Development, Stanbic IBTC Pension Managers, Nike Bajomo, said: “Many businesses begin with an idea, a skill or a passion, but sustainable growth requires more than determination. It requires structure, sound financial management, access to the right capital, a trusted brand and effective leadership. Bloom Weekend is about equipping women entrepreneurs to make that shift, to think beyond where their businesses are today and build for where they want to be tomorrow.”

The two-day experience reflected Stanbic IBTC’s wider commitment to women’s empowerment and enterprise development. By combining leadership conversations and practical business learning with opportunities for greater visibility and connection, Bloom Weekend provided women with support across different stages of their growth journeys.

World.title: PMAWCA: Dantsoho Seeks Regional Port Cooperation to Cut Cargo Costs, Delays
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Eromosele Abiodun

The Port Management Association of West and Central Africa (PMAWCA) has called for stronger cooperation among ports in the region to reduce cargo clearance delays, lower logistics costs and improve the competitiveness of West and Central African economies.

The President of PMAWCA, Dr Abubakar Dantsoho, disclosed this while speaking at the opening ceremony of the association’s 46th Annual Council and Joint Gulf of Guinea Commission-PMAWCA Forum in Sipopo, Malabo, Equatorial Guinea.

Dantsoho who is also the Managing Director of the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), said regional ports must prioritise strategic collaboration over destructive competition to address common challenges confronting the maritime industry.

He said closer cooperation among ports would improve operational efficiency, strengthen logistics resilience and ensure that the benefits of maritime trade extend beyond coastal countries to landlocked nations whose economies depend on efficient ports and transport corridors.

According to him, the region’s Atlantic coastline, stretching from Mauritania to Angola, serves about 20 coastal countries, while five landlocked countries, including Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Chad and the Central African Republic, depend directly on the efficiency of its ports and transport networks.

“When a single port along our coast suffers congestion, it is a household or a market in Bamako, Niamey, N’Djamena, or Bangui that bears the cost,” he said.

He noted that although West and Central African ports had undergone significant transformation over the past decade through the construction of deep-water terminals, public-private concessions and the deployment of modern port infrastructure, structural challenges continued to undermine their efficiency and competitiveness.

He identified prolonged cargo dwell times, high port charges, expensive corridor transportation and inadequate interoperability among customs and port operations as some of the major constraints affecting regional trade.

“Cargo dwell times remain excessively long across too many terminals, and high port and corridor transit costs continue to inflate the final price of consumer and industrial goods.

“Despite the deployment of single-window platforms, our customs and operational procedures still lack seamless interoperability, both between neighbouring ports and with hinterland administrations,” he said.

Also speaking, the Executive Secretary of the Gulf of Guinea Commission, Mr. Jose Mba Abeso emphasised on the need for member states of PMAWCA to stand with maritime safety and fight against illegal fishing, drug trafficking, human trafficking and illicit acts.

Abeso said, “I would like to leave aside one aspect which is the protection of critical sea infrastructures such as subsea cables as well as the protection of gas, piping, and the future climate that will connect Cameroon with Equatorial Guinea and Nigeria with Equatorial Guinea as well.”

World.title: Does Elon Musk ‘owe’ South Africa anything?
World.content:
President Cyril Ramaphosa’s claim that Elon Musk’s humble beginnings are attributed to his South African education, and that the world’s richest man should “give back” to his country, has been met with angry reactions on social media.

The president was speaking during a work trip to the US, where he was invited to speak at Semafor’s World Change discussion this week

Musk – who was born in Pretoria – left home just before his 18th birthday to study in Canada, his mother Maye’s birthplace. He later resettled in the US.



Apart from being a South African, he also holds both Canadian and US citizenship, the latter obtained through naturalisation in 2002.

CYRIL RAMAPHOSA SUGGESTS ELON MUSK’S SUCCESS IS A CREDIT TO SA

Speaking to ABC News host Jonathan Karl, President Ramaphosa recalled meeting Elon Musk for the first time in late 2024. He claimed that he was keen for the world’s richest man to create investment opportunities.

He shared: “I’ve always been awed by his brilliance. But also, I‘d like to chat to him about remembering his country



Ramaphosa added: “Even as one is a citizen of another country, you should still be loyal to your own country”.

The president claimed that Musk – who has accused South Africa of enforcing “super-racist laws” over his failed Starlink bid – had received a better education than black people during Apartheid. He attributed this to Musk’s success.

He continued: “The education that he would have received, a much better education than the Apartheid government [spent on mine]. So if one does not understand that, they will never be able to understand precisely what needs to be done to remedy the harm that was done.



“What you have become today is by dint of your own origins. Where you were initially educated, where you began dabbling in these things… it’s because of the knowledge and education that was made available to him

“This endowment that he now has was formed in South Africa, and he should be one of those that say, ‘I would like to contribute to the development of South Africa and give back to this country that made me who I am today’”.

"I have met Elon Musk in the past, and I've been awed by his brilliance. But I'd also like to chat to him about remembering his country," South African President Cyril Ramaphosa tells @jonkarl.



"What you've become today is by dint of your own origins … It is because of the… pic.twitter.com/YJpqozgjQR  November 16, 2026

‘HE DOESN’T OWE YOU ANYTHING’

On the X app, which Elon Musk owns, a clip of Ramaphosa implying that the former president should not only be loyal but also contribute to his country left many users outraged by the president’s “entitlement”.

Here are a few responses…

@dickyd64: “Now he’s trying to take credit for@elonmusk success! What arrogance!”



@greybtc: “Claiming to have made Elon Musk is quite a reach 💀”

@MyT_Words: “Right; Elon’s brilliant mind and relentless curiosity and pursuit of truth and understanding and all the time he spent educating himself with anything available at all that he could get his hands on and years of work and angst and struggle and inventiveness had nothing at all to do with it”

@Pirate747John: “Elon doesn’t need your approval or owe you anything”



After leaving South Africa at the age of 17, Elon Musk briefly stayed in Canada – his mother Maye Musk’s place of birth – before settling down in the US.

In 2002, he became a naturalised citizen.

World.title: South Africa and England draw Polo Test Match at Val de Vie
World.content:
South Africa and England played to a 6-6 draw in the second Polo Test Match at Val de Vie Estate in the Cape Winelands. Image: Supplied

South Africa and England played to a 6-6 draw in the second Polo Test Match at Val de Vie Estate in the Cape Winelands on Saturday, 14 November.

The closely contested encounter saw England captain Matt Perry take home the Most Valuable Player (MVP) award, while both teams were unable to repeat or overturn the result of last year’s international fixture.

South Africa, captained by Jannie Steenkamp, had beaten England 8-6 in 2025.



The visitors returned to Val de Vie this year hoping to level the series, but the teams finished the match honours even.

Geely brings star power to polo event

Geely South Africa was the official vehicle partner of the event and welcomed celebrities, sports stars and other distinguished guests to Val de Vie Estate.

Guests watched the match from a private hospitality terrace overlooking the Pavilion Polo Field, with the Paarl-Franschhoek mountains providing the backdrop to the ceremonial march-on.



The Cape Riviera-themed occasion also featured a display of Geely vehicles, including the Riddara and E5.

“Val de Vie Estate was an ideal setting to welcome our guests and introduce more people to Geely,” said Greg Maruszewski, chief operating officer of Geely South Africa.

“We were delighted to support the International Polo Test as Vehicle Partner and be part of an occasion that brings international sport to the Cape Winelands.”



Springbok stars among celebrity guests

Several prominent South African rugby stars attended as Geely guests, including Francois Hougaard, Evan Roos, Scarra Ntubeni, and Seabelo Senatla.

Fashion entrepreneurs and models were also among those attending.

The afternoon concluded with a live performance by Sunset Sweatshop on the polo lawns. The band brought its blend of goema-rock, reggae, funk and folk to the event.

World.title: Orlando Pirates v Sundowns among six matches affected by fixture changes
World.content:
Orlando Pirates will have several fixtures rescheduled due to their CAF Champions League commitments.

The Buccaneers are the only South African team still competing in the continental competition, with the group stages set to get underway later this month. Their participation has consequently affected their Betway Premiership schedule.

This week, the Premier Soccer League (PSL) announced several fixture changes, including the highly anticipated clash against Mamelodi Sundowns.



The matches affected are against Golden Arrows (November 28), Stellenbosch FC (December 5), Polokwane City (December 19), Mamelodi Sundowns (January 9), AmaZulu FC (January 16) and Kruger United (January 22).

This means six of Pirates’ league fixtures, which were initially scheduled for Saturdays, will now be played during the week.

Orlando Pirates eyeing CAF glory

The Soweto giants will lose five weekend dates for their Betway Premiership home matches at the Orlando Amstel Arena. Meanwhile, Sundowns will also have to face the Buccaneers midweek rather than on a Saturday.

Pirates’ away fixture against Richards Bay FC, scheduled for December, is also subject to change depending on whether they reach the Carling Knockout final, which is scheduled for December 12.

The Orlando Pirates clash against Mamelodi Sundowns has now been moved to January 5.

World.title: AFCON 2027 qualifiers: Bafana Bafana lead group after Kenya win
World.content:
Bafana Bafana's two legs against Kenya are shaping the AFCON 2027 qualification race. Image: Kigali Today (Flickr), Bafana Bafana (X).

South Africa’s path to AFCON 2027 qualification is back on track.

Bafana Bafana entered their Group D clash on 17 November second on the log.

Here’s what the win in Nairobi means for Pitso Mosimane and the team.



AFCON qualifiers: Bafana Bafana in tight race

With Kenya already through as co-host, the race to AFCON 2027 is down to just two teams.

Guinea strengthened their standing with a win over Eritrea to lead the Group D log, according to SuperSport.

Before Tuesday’s crunch fixture, South Africa were trailing by two points, with a game in hand.

Eritrea, meanwhile, were mathematically eliminated after a fourth straight loss.

With Kenya already having a place in the main tournament, they still posed a major obstacle for Bafana Bafana.

In the first leg at the Orlando Stadium, the Harambee Stars scored in the 90th minute to seal a 2-2 draw.



An Amos Wanjala own goal in the ninth minute put the co-hosts on the back foot.

According to FlashScore, veteran Michael Olunga then equalised with a 44th-minute penalty.

Relebohile Mofokeng seemed to have won the game for Bafana with his strike at 77 minutes.

However, Ryan Ogam was on target to equalise for the visitors as the teams shared the points.

What the Kenya result means for the qualification race

Bafana Bafana bounced back with a nail-biting 2-1 win in Kenya on Tuesday.

Mofokeng was the hero for his country, scoring two crucial goals in the second half.

Despite this, South Africa was still under pressure after Kenya pulled one back through Mohammed Bajaber.

It was eerily similar to how the match in Johannesburg had gone.

However, Bafana Bafana’s defence held firm to clinch the crucial three points in the race to AFCON 2027.

With this result, South Africa are one point ahead of second-placed Guinea.

The remaining fixtures will be played in March next year, including the return leg against the Guineans.

World.title: ‘90% fake’: MaMkhize’s ‘designer’ fashion up for auction [video]
World.content:
MaMkhize's personal items have gone on auction again. Images via X

Hundreds of supposedly designer fashion items from MaMkhize’s wardrobe have gone under the hammer at auction in a bid to recoup her R120 million outstanding SARS debt. However, an industry expert has claimed that up to 90% of the goods are fake

The auction includes the listing of clothes, handbags, shoes, jewellery and other accessories whose authenticity could not be confirmed

Over the years, the businesswoman, real name Shauwn Mkhize, has also been accused of tender fraud, corruption, and forgery.



MAMKHIZE: MORE PERSONAL ITEMS GO ON AUCTION

Last week, over 1000 personal items, including designer clothes, handbags, shoes and jewellery, went under the hammer at a court-ordered auction.

On Monday, another 400 items were listed.

The auction house, Bidders Choice, has stated that many of the goods in the auction could not be authenticated.

The auction forms part of SARS’s ongoing efforts to recover over R120 million in MaMkhize’s outstanding taxes – both personal and business-related. The matter dates back to November 2024, when the Durban High Court granted SARS a search and seizure warrant.

Since then, several auctions have taken place over the year, with items such as luxury cars, movable assets, and even designer alcohol going under the hammer.

Last month, the High Court ordered that five properties in Sandown, Johannesburg, linked to MaMkhize and her family, be sold.



FAKE?

Meanwhile, an industry expert has boldly claimed that nearly all the designer items currently on auction are counterfeit.

In a video posted by TimesLIVE, Sandton boutique owner David Leven – speaking from the auction at Mooikloof – stated that a friend who had previously done authentication work for SARS told him that of the items on auction, that “90% were fake”

Pointing to a green crocodile-skin Hermès Birkin bag, Levin said: “It’s not real….I’m in the industry [I know my stuff]”.

WATCH | David Leven, owner of a high-end Sandton boutique, attended the auction of Shauwn Mkhize’s items out of curiosity. Despite it being his first auction, he believes 90% of the items are fake, a view shared by some bidders at the venue.



Video: @Koena_xM pic.twitter.com/QGBq1ZK30n — Sowetan (@Sowetan1981) November 16, 2026

It’s not the first time the authenticity of MaMkhize’s personal items has been called into question.

Last year, Bidders Choice claimed that only 23 out of 200 designer handbags and luggage pieces were authenticated.

World.title: Gayton McKenzie says sorry to Tatjana Smith, launches attack on Swimming SA
World.content:
Tatjana Smith celebrates after winning a gold medal at the Paris Olympics in 2024. Image: Anton Geyser / Team SA

Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie has ordered a full investigation into Swimming South Africa (SSA) following Olympic champion Tatjana Smith’s decision to pursue her swimming career under the Dutch flag.

McKenzie also issued a public apology to Smith, accusing the national swimming federation of treating one of South Africa’s greatest sporting champions disgracefully.

READ | Roland Schoeman blasts Swimming SA after Tatjana Smith’s shock Netherlands switch



Speaking at a media briefing at Parliament on Tuesday, 17 November, Gayton McKenzie said he had lost complete faith in Swimming SA and believed the federation needed urgent intervention.

Smith shocked South African sport last week when she announced that she intended to represent the Netherlands, following growing tensions with Swimming SA over sponsorship arrangements, fines and prize money.

READ | THIRD South African Olympic swimmer to pursue career under another flag



Gayton McKenzie said he had no ill feelings towards the swimmer for her decision, arguing that the federation’s treatment of her had contributed to her departure.

“She’s been treated in the worst possible way. They should be ashamed.

“And what angered me the most is that immediately after we got the news that Tatjana is going to swim for the Netherlands, they tried to cover up and make her the scapegoat,” he said.



€46 000 penalty and withheld prize money

Gayton McKenzie highlighted Smith’s lengthy battle to receive money owed to her following her performances at the 2023 World Championships in Fukuoka, Japan.

According to the minister, Smith was invoiced €46 000 for an alleged sponsorship infringement after she failed to wear a particular sponsor’s brand.

Swimming SA subsequently withheld her prize money, resulting in a prolonged dispute over payment.



McKenzie said Smith only received the money in 2024 after instructing her lawyers to pursue legal action.

The minister also said his department had ensured that all money owed to the swimmer by the department was paid without delay.

“We paid her as fast as she swims. We want to thank her for the years that she’s given, for the medals that she’s given us, for what she’s done for this country,” he said.



Gayton McKenzie described Smith as South Africa’s greatest Olympian and said she deserved an apology for the way she had been treated.

SASCOC given 90 days to investigate Swimming SA

McKenzie has written to the South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee (SASCOC), requesting a full investigation into Swimming SA’s administration and financial affairs.

The investigation will examine the federation’s sponsorship agreement with Arena, including the penalties imposed on athletes and who was responsible for paying them.



McKenzie also wants investigators to establish whether other swimmers have been fined or had prize money withheld.

However, the investigation will extend beyond the sponsorship dispute.

The minister said SASCOC had also been asked to examine how money was spent on the Franschhoek High-Performance Centre and identify alleged shortcomings in Swimming SA’s constitution.



He believes Smith may have been made a scapegoat for broader administrative problems within the federation.

“I’ve asked it to establish how the Arena sponsorship agreement works, what penalties were levied and who paid them, and whether other swimmers were fined or had money held back.

“I’ve asked it to look at how money was spent on the Franschhoek High-Performance Centre and the flaws in the federation’s constitution. And that’s why our swimmers are choosing to represent other countries,” McKenzie said.



SASCOC’s acting head, Lwandile Simelane, has pledged to complete the investigation within 90 days.

McKenzie said regulations require SASCOC to deal with the matter first, making its investigation an important initial step before further action can be considered.

McKenzie says Swimming SA needs urgent intervention

The minister has also called for a task team to help stabilise the federation, describing its current condition in particularly strong terms.



“I’ve asked SASCOC to deploy a task team to stabilise the federation, because the federation is in ICU. And we should not run away from that,” he said.

McKenzie warned that Smith should be the last South African athlete to experience such treatment from a national sporting federation.

“But I want to assure South Africans that she’s the last athlete who will be treated in such a fashion by these federations. That is not how a national federation should treat the people it exists to serve,” he said.



Tatjana Smith’s departure raises questions about South African swimming

Smith won Olympic gold in the 200m breaststroke at Tokyo 2020 and silver in the same event at Paris 2024.

Her decision to pursue representation by the Netherlands has raised wider questions about athlete welfare, funding and the administration of South African sporting federations.

McKenzie’s intervention now places Swimming SA’s sponsorship arrangements, financial management and governance under scrutiny.



The outcome of the 90-day SASCOC investigation could prove significant for the federation and the future of South African swimming.

For now, McKenzie has made his position clear: he believes Smith deserved better and wants those responsible for the federation’s administration to answer questions about how it operates.

World.content:

Police have taken over the investigation.

Emergency officials remain on high alert across the city.

World.title: Number Of The Day | 25 Basis Points | 17 November 2026
World.content:
Black Friday's Biggest Trap Is Not The Price Tag. It's The Payment Plan.

Black Friday has become one of the few occasions when spending money can feel like an act of financial discipline. Retailers frame discounts as opportunities to save, countdown clocks create urgency, and consumers are encouraged to believe that delaying a purchase could mean losing out. In a country where household budgets are already under considerable pressure, the appeal is understandable. Buying something at a reduced price seems sensible, especially when the product has been on a wish list for months. But the psychology of a bargain often obscures a more uncomfortable question: does paying less for an item actually mean spending less money?

The answer depends on how the purchase is financed, what the buyer can afford and how much of their future income has already been committed. A consumer who purchases a discounted appliance outright may realise a genuine saving, provided the advertised reduction is legitimate. Someone who finances that same appliance through interest-bearing credit faces a different calculation. The final amount paid can include interest, initiation fees, monthly service charges and potentially penalties if repayments are missed. By the time the account is settled, the original discount may have been significantly reduced or eliminated. What appeared to be a saving at the checkout can become an expensive commitment spread across several months or years.

This distinction matters because retailers and financial institutions have become increasingly effective at presenting affordability in terms of monthly payments rather than total expenditure. A purchase costing several thousand rand can appear manageable when reduced to a relatively small instalment, particularly if the first payment is deferred. Yet the size of an instalment says little about whether a household can sustainably afford the obligation. It does not account for existing debt, unexpected expenses or the possibility that borrowing costs might change. Consumers are effectively encouraged to evaluate purchases against the money available today, even though the financial consequences will extend well beyond the promotion.

The timing of Black Friday makes that calculation especially important in South Africa. November arrives immediately before a festive period associated with travel, family gatherings, celebrations and additional household spending. For parents, the December holiday is followed by the financial demands of a new school year, including uniforms, stationery, transport and fees. A purchase financed in November does not disappear when the festive season ends; it continues competing for income during months that may already be financially demanding. The apparent convenience of spreading repayments can therefore create pressure precisely when households need greater flexibility.

Interest rates complicate the picture further. When borrowing becomes more expensive, households with variable-rate debt may find themselves allocating more income to existing repayments. That leaves less room for discretionary purchases, emergency savings and unexpected costs. It also changes the true cost of taking on additional credit. Although interest-rate adjustments are designed partly to manage

inflation by influencing demand, their effects are experienced most directly through household cash flow. A relatively small change in borrowing costs can matter considerably to someone whose budget has little capacity to absorb another expense.

None of this means that Black Friday discounts are inherently misleading or that consumers should avoid credit altogether. There are legitimate opportunities to purchase necessary goods at better prices, and responsibly structured borrowing can serve a useful purpose. The difficulty arises when the promotional price becomes the sole measure of value. A meaningful financial decision must consider whether the product is necessary, whether the discount is genuine, what the purchase will cost in total and whether the household can accommodate the repayment without compromising more important obligations. These questions require more attention than an advertised percentage reduction, but they also offer a much clearer picture of what a bargain is actually worth.

Perhaps the most useful way to approach Black Friday is to reverse the logic of the promotion. Instead of asking how much money can be saved by purchasing something immediately, consumers could ask how much money they would retain by waiting, paying cash later or deciding not to buy it at all. That shift does not eliminate the pleasure of finding a good deal. It simply restores the consumer's financial circumstances, rather than the retailer's deadline, as the most important part of the decision. A genuine bargain should leave a household better off after the excitement of the sale has faded, not quietly consume the income it will need in January.
