World.title: Rassie Erasmus handed six-game ban for referee comments
World.content:
LONDON - Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-game ban by World Rugby on Tuesday for outspoken criticism of officials following a rare defeat for the world champions against France.

Erasmus questioned the decision by the television match official not to intervene on a series of French tackles.

"If he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" he said in a press conference in Dublin on Monday, ahead of the Springboks' clash against Ireland this weekend.

The 54-year-old will be banned from "any match-day involvement" with his players and coaches and will not be allowed to even enter the stadium.

"The panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity," World Rugby said in a statement.

"Teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."

Erasmus is no stranger to disciplinary action for aiming at officials.

In 2021, he was banned for two months by World Rugby for an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' first Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions.

The following year, he also received a two-match ban for a series of social media posts criticising officials in a defeat by France.

South Africa Rugby has requested a full misconduct hearing.

"The organisation respected the process but had requested an opportunity for its coach to contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives," said a spokesperson for SA Rugby.

Erasmus could miss the final of the Nations Championship on November 29.

South Africa trail New Zealand by one point at the top of the southern hemisphere standings with one round of fixtures to go.

World.title: Deutsche Bank shares drop after reports on mass data leak
World.content:
MUNICH - Shares in Deutsche Bank plunged on Tuesday after international media outlets published reports based on millions of leaked emails and other documents that shine a light on questionable past business practices at the German banking giant.

The leaks deal with the bank's business over the past 20 years, including ties to Russian oligarchs, the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and Donald Trump before he became US president.

The data, shared by unidentified whistleblowers, raised questions about internal controls at Germany's largest bank and reignited questions regarding chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution.

The investigation, dubbed "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank shares fell by nearly six percent shortly after the opening of the Frankfurt Stock Exchange.

According to the reports, the bank at times prioritised commercial interests over compliance with international sanctions, anti-money laundering regulations and even its own internal procedures.

The data originated from two whistleblowers and was channelled through South African and Indian journalists to more than 50 media outlets worldwide.

The documents reportedly detail, among other things, how Deutsche Bank courted oligarchs and sought to expand its Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

Documents cited by the media outlets indicate that Sewing was among the participants in the working group that developed the Russia strategy.

The reports also note that the bank's announced withdrawal from the Russian market after the Ukraine invasion remains incomplete.

As of last year, Deutsche Bank still employed 162 people in the country and its local subsidiary generated a pre-tax profit of 61 million euros ($67 million).

The data also contain new details regarding the bank's long-standing business relationship with Epstein as well as its dealings with Trump.

Furthermore, the documents indicate that the bank set up controversial tax-optimisation schemes for wealthy clients, and suggest that criminal networks were able to funnel money through the bank.

The documents also offer insights into arms deals involving problematic states, the bank's support for clients in environmentally damaging industries, and the holding of donation accounts for Germany's far-right AfD political party despite internal opposition.

Deutsche Bank does not dispute that the records are genuine, though it refers to them as "purported internal documents" and noted that some of the incidents cited date back more than two decades.

The bank said that it reviewed these matters with regulatory authorities at the time and that it had invested seven billion euros between 2019 and 2025 to strengthen its control systems.

It is now "a different bank", it said, pointing to record profits in 2025 and progress made in terms of compliance.

World.title: Dead Melbourne Cup racehorse found dumped in bin
World.content:
MELBOURNE - A dead Australian racehorse has been found in an industrial rubbish bin on the outskirts of Sydney two weeks after running in the prestigious Melbourne Cup.

Trainer Bjorn Baker said Tuesday he was "deeply distressed" after a member of the public stumbled across the carcass of thoroughbred So You Are, which finished eighth in this year's race.

The five-year-old horse was euthanised on Monday after a bout of severe colic, local media reported.

"Like everyone who has seen the footage I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in a statement on social media.

"He was a much-loved horse and he deserves to be treated with respect and dignity after his death.

"I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances and I expect a full explanation of what occurred."

Horse vets REC Equine Specialists apologised and said the animal should have been buried respectfully, national broadcaster ABC reported.

"After his death So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," the company said.

"What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone else who cared for him.

"We are deeply sorry."

Racing NSW said So You Are was awaiting burial when video of the abandoned horse was recorded, and the footage was subsequently shared online.

"The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect," the regulating body in New South Wales state said in a statement, according to ABC.

"Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner.

"If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action."

World.title: Tatjana Smith 'treated in the worst way': McKenzie
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said on Tuesday he had ordered an investigation into the national swimming federation following the departure of the country's most decorated Olympic athlete, swimmer Tatjana Smith, for the Netherlands.

In an emotional video on social media, the 29-year-old two-time Olympic gold medallist announced last week she would no longer represent South Africa at international events because of financial challenges.

"She's been treated in the worst possible way," sports minister Gayton McKenzie said at a press conference where he announced an investigation into Swimming South Africa, the sport's national governing body.

The review would include charges that the federation withheld prize money from Smith because she wore her own sponsored and specialised swimsuit and goggles at the 2023 World Aquatics Championships in Fukuoka, Japan.

As she had not worn only the brand of the national sponsor, the federation had withheld her winnings for taking gold in the 200 metres and silver in the 100 metres.

"In May 2024, two months before the Paris Olympics, the greatest Olympian this country has ever produced had to instruct lawyers to get her own prize money from her own federation, only then was it paid. The interest on it was paid much later," McKenzie said.

"They should be ashamed," he said. "Tatjana has been treated like an enemy of this country,” McKenzie added, issuing an apology to the swimmer.

"At the end of the day, I hope that investigation will deliver what I wish for, for us to have new people to run our swimming," he told AFP after the briefing.

Smith won the 200 metres breaststroke at the 2020 Tokyo Games, which were delayed one year by the COVID-19 pandemic, and the 100 metres breaststroke at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

She also won two silver medals in the pool, making the Johannesburg-born swimmer the most decorated South African Olympian.

World.title: What Kenyans expect from Ruto's State of the Nation Address
World.content:
As President William Ruto prepares to deliver his fourth State of the Nation Address today, Kenyans will be looking beyond the government's achievements to demand answers on a raft of unresolved grievances that have defined his four years in office.



From the high cost of living and rising taxation to corruption, abductions, unemployment and questions surrounding the legality of his expanded Cabinet, the President faces growing pressure to demonstrate that his administration has listened to citizens and acted on their concerns.



The address comes against the backdrop of a presidency that has repeatedly promised economic transformation, fiscal discipline and accountable leadership, but has also faced waves of public discontent over the rising cost of living and the perceived disconnect between government policies and the realities facing ordinary households.
