World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 17, 2026
World.content:
South Africa Investigates Shootings That Left 17 Dead

South African police are investigating two separate mass shootings that left 17 people dead in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng. Eight men were found shot dead inside a minibus outside Pietermaritzburg. In a separate shooting, six men and three women were killed inside a shack in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria. Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning. Police have said the incidents are unrelated. They have launched manhunts for the suspects. The motives remain unknown amid growing concerns over gun violence and organised crime in the country. In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.

Five EU Countries Plan Rwanda Migrant Deportation Hub

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Five European Union countries, Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, plan to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda in 2027 as part of efforts to increase the removal of people who have exhausted their legal right to remain in their countries. Under the proposed arrangement, deportees will be able to settle in Rwanda or return to their countries of origin. The initial phase is expected to focus on single men, with the centre potentially accommodating about 100 people. However, the plan has been criticized by human rights groups over safety concerns for migrants and Rwanda's human rights record. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has also criticised the proposal, questioning its humanity and effectiveness. The five countries maintain that the scheme will comply with EU and international law.

Guinea Arrests Over 1,200 in Illegal Gold Mining Crackdown

Guinea has banned illegal gold mining in its northeastern Siguiri region. At least 1,263 suspected miners were arrested, including nationals from Burkina Faso, Mali, Togo, Nigeria, Ivory Coast and Ghana. Authorities said that the crackdown aims to protect the environment from mining activities that damage soil, vegetation and water sources, as well as improve regulation of the sector. However, the operation has sparked criticism over alleged human rights abuses, mistreatment and deportations of foreign miners. The crackdown comes as Guinea begins operations at its first gold refinery in Conakry, with the government seeking to process more of its gold locally. Officials said the ban applies to all illegal miners, not only foreign nationals. Neighbouring Burkina Faso and Mali have raised concerns over the treatment of their citizens caught up in the operation.

Declining Aid Exposes Refugee Children to Exploitation, UN Warns

The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and Oxford University have warned that declining humanitarian funding is leaving refugees in Bangladesh and Ethiopia increasingly vulnerable to trafficking, child labour and exploitation. Since 2024, more than 170,000 Rohingya refugees have fled to Bangladesh, where conditions have worsened because of deteriorating shelter conditions and reduced access to clean water. Ethiopia's child protection programs, family reunification services and schools for refugee children have been hit by funding shortfalls. Children, especially those separated from their families and unaccompanied minors, are at greater risk of sexual violence, forced labor and early marriage, the organizations warned. In Ethiopia, planned child protection needs were only 18% funded in 2025, leaving thousands of vulnerable children without adequate support. The studies call for predictable humanitarian funding to strengthen protection services and prevent further exploitation.

DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Remains Out of Control - Africa CDC

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has warned that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo remains out of control, six months after it was declared, with more than 11,200 infections and 5,500 deaths reported. Director-General Jean Kaseya cited insecurity, attacks on health workers, unpaid medical staff and shortages of resources as major obstacles to containing the outbreak, which has spread to eight provinces. He also warned of further regional transmission, particularly to the Central African Republic and South Sudan. Vaccine and treatment trials are underway. The absence of an effective vaccine targeting the Bundibugyo strain remains a major challenge. Kaseya is urging international donors to release billions of dollars in pledged funding to strengthen the response.

Close 

Harare Halts Housing Demolitions Until Further Notice

Harare City Council has suspended all housing demolition operations with immediate effect until further notice. Acting Town Clerk Warren Chiwawa issued a memorandum instructing all council departments and operational teams to stop demolition activities unless authorised by his office. The directive requires strict compliance across the municipality, with no further demolitions permitted until a new instruction is issued. Chiwawa warned that all departments must ensure the suspension is communicated to their staff and operational teams.

World.title: Liberia: Weah Targeted for Arrest? - a Reality or Mere Propaganda
World.content:
Is former President George Manneh Weah being monitored and considered for a possible arrest by the Liberian government?

That is the boggling question confronting Liberians, mainly his supporters, as unconfirmed and unproven reports about such plans have been swirling in the past few weeks, leaving many to wonder if truly the former President is on the radar for arrest.

The swelling question is whether the information has any iota of reality or mere political chicanery intended to stir tension and debate.

What is true is that there is no official government statement to the effect, neither has the government rebuffed such reports.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Recall that it is not the first time news about Weah's arrest has emerged in the last few months, and the Liberian government had clarified they harbored no such plans to arrest the former president.

The government has maintained that no one or no office is above the law, an indication that Weah or any other official, current and former, can be arrested if there are justifiable reasons to do so in keeping with law.

More so, alleged plans to arrest Weah began filling the air in the immediate aftermath of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor's arrest back in August in connection to her alleged involvement in a major drug case.

However, the current information about Weah's arrest is fast spreading and reaching the nooks and corners of the political and social landscape, causing nervousness and provoking sharp reactions from his supporters, some of whom are warning the Unity Party administration to desist from pursuing actions that could plunge the country into any mess of confusion, possibly war.

The information is not just growing and spreading, it is creating more tension to the already hazed atmosphere amid the rising economic strangulation already being faced by Liberians as the government is struggling to remedy the situation.

A recent World Bank report showed a scaring picture of the government's 'economic challenges. The exchange rate is reaching its most downward trend, as it is at US$1 to $820 Liberian dollars, a dramatic drop from $190 to $1 US dollar.

But the drop of rate is not affecting prices of goods, thereby exerting additional pressure on the household economy and more hardship on citizens.

The alleged plan of Weah's arrest is said to be tied to the ongoing fight against drugs initiated by the government to rid the country of illegal narcotics and other substances.

Liberian blogger "LAW LAW" in one of his latest podcasts alleged the government has hatched plans, quoting alleged information he received, to arrest the former President.

He claimed the plan is to provoke a situation where Weah supporters, the opposition community and the Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) will come out to resist the arrest, and a potential chaos ensues.

In the wake of that, he claimed the government's plan is to portray the CDC as the one that has created the mayhem. He urged the CDC and Liberians not to fall the government's plan or allow it to manipulate the process, adding "the international community is aware of the plan that the government is the one masterminding the plan to create a false narrative about the CDC."

Adding fuel to the fire was a widely shared post by Philipbert Semogar Jargba-Wleh Browne in his "Justice or survival: what should the National Security Council do when the evidence points to a popular president?"

He wrote, "Assume, for the sake of argument only, that President Weah was involved in cocaine trafficking, that the Government of Liberia holds overwhelming evidence sufficient to convict him before a court of competent jurisdiction, and that he is so popular that any attempt to arrest him would plunge the Republic into another round of civil war: if you were the National Security Council, would you arrest him in the name of justice and accountability and damn the consequences, or would you pretend the investigation never took place and the evidence was never found in order to preserve the stability and longevity of the Republic?"

He framed it as 'HYPOTHETICAL' and not real, and meant for illustration purpose only.

Browne who claimed to be knowledgeable of national security issues further stated: "No emotional outbursts, no political sentiments, just plain honesty and truth. If you were the head of the National Security Council, what would be your approach? I will start the ball rolling in the first comment."

The post, though clearly marked hypothetical, was shared and misinterpreted in many quarters as evidence that an arrest was imminent.

The controversy intensified in August, when former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor was arrested at the Roberts International Airport on August 19, 2026, in connection with an investigation into the seizure of about four tons of cocaine in Duazon, Margibi County, in July.

The drugs were reportedly valued at US$317 million.Howard-Taylor was later charged with drug trafficking, money laundering, criminal conspiracy, and related offenses.

On August 25, she was remanded at the Monrovia Central Prison after the court rejected her lawyers' request for compassionate detention.

Her arrest became a major political flashpoint, particularly within the CDC, where concerns arose that the investigation might expand to include other prominent figures linked to the Weah administration.

Former President Weah later threatened to mobilize CDC supporters and other Liberians to oppose what he characterized as efforts by the Boakai administration to target and intimidate opposition politicians and former officials under the pretext of combating illicit drugs.

Other Liberians are now having their say in the alleged Weah arrest plan. One of them is the political leader of the Economic Freedom Fighters of Liberia (EFFL), Emmanuel Gonquoi.

Weighing in on the issue, he repeated the highly popularized phrase "no one is above the law," calling for equal justice and warning against political protection for former leaders.

His remarks come as a cocaine-trafficking controversy and allegations of a possible government action against former President Weah continue to heighten political tensions.

The controversy surrounding Weah has taken a new turn, as Gonquoi publicly challenged the idea that the former Liberian president should be exempt from criminal investigation or potential arrest because he once held the presidency.

In a strongly worded Facebook post published Saturday, November 14, Gonquoi questioned whether Weah has special standing that puts him beyond the reach of Liberia's justice system.

He maintained that no one, regardless of political status or past service to the country, should be above the law.

Titled "The Difficult Truth," the post addressed supporters of the former ruling Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC), the government of President Joseph Boakai, and Liberians involved in the increasingly heated debate over Weah's potential legal exposure.

"So, Former President Weah is above the Laws in Liberia? Is he above our Country values?" Gonquoi asked, before urging the government to investigate the former president if credible information links him to criminal activity.

"If he is link[ed] to any crime, he should be investigated and if possible arrested," he wrote. Although Gonquoi did not identify a specific criminal accusation against Weah or provide evidence connecting him to an offense, his remarks have placed the former president at the heart of an increasingly sensitive national debate, regarding whether Liberia's commitment to equal justice can withstand the political influence and loyalty surrounding its former leaders.

Gonquoi, however, publicly rejected any attempt to use political mobilization to obstruct the government's anti-drug investigation.

In August, Gonquoi warned that he would mobilize against protests aimed at disrupting the investigation, arguing that the drug crisis was too serious to be turned into a partisan political contest.

His latest remarks appear to broaden that stance beyond the investigation itself, prompting questions about whether Weah should be treated differently from other citizens if investigators establish a legitimate basis to question him.

At the center of Gonquoi's argument is a constitutional issue that has become increasingly prominent in Liberia's political debate: the scope of presidential immunity and whether it can protect a former president from criminal accountability.

Article 61 of Liberia's 1986 Constitution grants the President immunity from suits, proceedings, arrest, and detention for acts carried out in the exercise of presidential authority in accordance with the Constitution and other laws.

However, the same provision states that the President is not immune from prosecution after leaving office for a criminal act committed while in office.

On the other side, Wantoe Teah Wantoe, a member of the CDC, warned the UP government against what he called reckless statements.

"I know the Unity Party government and its supporters are intelligent people, and I expect them to understand the difference between political intelligence and outright recklessness. Do not mistake President Weah's silence, patriotism, and commitment to peace for weakness," Wantoe wrote.

"This is a former president who received nearly 50 percent of the votes in the 2023 presidential runoff and peacefully transferred power in the interest of our democracy. It is deeply disrespectful to even think that you can use political power to intimidate, threaten, or manufacture a case against former President George Manneh Weah."

Close 

According to Wantoe, the presidency of Liberia is not an ordinary political position, and a former president must not be treated as a target for political games.

"There is a difference between lawful accountability and the reckless belief that controlling the government gives anyone the right to use state institutions against political opponents," he wrote on social media at the weekend.

"President Weah is protected by the Constitution of Liberia. Article 61 provides presidential immunity for official acts, while Articles 20 and 21 guarantee due process and the rights of accused persons. These constitutional protections cannot be ignored for political convenience."

Even putting immunity aside, Watoe said President Weah's record of patriotism, respect for the law, and commitment to democracy deserves recognition.

He further stated, "If these reckless statements are intended to test public opinion about a possible arrest of President Weah, let there be no misunderstanding: Liberians have every right to respond firmly, peacefully, and constitutionally to any politically motivated action against him."

"Fighting impunity must never become an excuse for selective justice. The government should focus on jobs, the economy, healthcare, and the challenges facing ordinary Liberians rather than allowing reckless political statements to dominate national debate," he added.

He noted that former President Weah is not above the law, but he is certainly not beneath its protection, stressing "Let's respect ourselves."

"The most foolish and idiotic political strategy is to believe that reckless statements about President George Manneh Weah can somehow become evidence of wrongdoing."

For now, there is no arrest warrant, no charge sheet, and no official statement linking former President Weah to the cocaine case.

What exists is a toxic mix that a real drug investigation, a hypothetical debate about justice vs. stability, social media podcasts, and a deeply polarized political environment where every rumor travels faster than fact.

Until the government speaks clearly, either to confirm an investigation or to debunk the rumour, the question "Is Weah For Arrest?" will continue to hang over Liberia, stoking fear, anger, and speculation in equal measure.

World.title: Uganda: Muhoozi Returns to X With 10-Year Jail Threat for Media Critical of Museveni
World.content:
Nairobi — Uganda's Chief of Defence Forces Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba has returned to X with a fresh warning that media organisations and journalists who criticise or "belittle" his father, President Yoweri Museveni, could face 10 years in prison.

In a series of posts on Tuesday, Muhoozi also threatened to subject foreign media personnel he considers agents of foreign interests to trial by court martial, while announcing plans to introduce a new policy governing foreign media operations in Uganda.

"Any media from wherever insulting or belittling Mzee, Maama, Afande Saleh, or me will be imprisoned for 10 years," he wrote, referring to his father, mother and uncle, Gen Salim Saleh, a former military logistics chief who has repeatedly stepped in to contain diplomatic fallout from Muhoozi's controversial social media remarks and is widely regarded as a moderating influence on his nephew.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"I shall announce a new policy on the operations of ALL foreign media in Uganda soon. Their days of insulting our country are over," he added.

The posts mark his return to the platform after deactivating his account following a series of threats against Vice President Jessica Alupo over alleged links to what he described as a plot involving his former deputy, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu.

Muhoozi also announced that he had restored Elwelu's rank of Lieutenant General, weeks after publicly declaring that he had demoted the former deputy military chief to private.

"I was very, very angry with Elweru some weeks ago. I demoted him to a private. I was ready to do much worse. I now restore his rank as a Lt. General of our great army. He will face the Court Martial with his restored rank," he wrote.

Elwelu was arrested on November 2 over allegations of involvement in activities aimed at destabilising the country.

Muhoozi had previously accused him of treachery and threatened to take action against Vice President Alupo if she was found to have supported him.

Presidential ambitions

The army chief also used his return to X to restate his intention to succeed his father, declaring that he would contest the presidency after Museveni.

"I am going to stand for the Presidency of this country after Mzee. No one will stop me. I place my hope in Almighty God and my fellow countrymen and countrywomen," he posted.

The declaration comes amid growing uncertainty over the succession question within the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM), which has been in power since 1986.

An AFP report published on November 11 said the party's leadership had failed to agree on a proposal to designate Muhoozi as Museveni's successor, citing five party sources familiar with deliberations.

The report said a meeting of the NRM executive committee on November 10, convened to consider succession, ended without a decision on Muhoozi's candidacy after several members opposed the proposal.

Four members had reportedly voted in favour of his candidacy and three against before the vote was abandoned, with opposition to the proposal drawing loud cheers from some attendees.

One party source told AFP that Muhoozi's combative conduct on social media had created unease within the party.

Another said NRM Vice-Chairman Calvin Echodu had advised Museveni to retire his son from the army and give him a civilian role to prepare him for leadership.

Echodu reportedly also suggested that Museveni should seek another term in 2031, arguing that Muhoozi was not yet ready to take over.

Muhoozi, 52, currently heads Uganda's military and has increasingly become a central figure in the country's political succession debate as his 82-year-old father approaches four decades in power.

Controversial pronouncements

Muhoozi's latest statements add to a series of provocative social media interventions that have drawn domestic and international criticism.

Before deactivating his account, he threatened Vice President Alupo with arrest and dismissal from government over claims that she supported Elwelu's alleged treachery.

Close 

He also invoked previous confrontations with opposition figures, including Kizza Besigye, Kampala Lord Mayor Erias Lukwago and opposition leader Robert Kyagulanyi, popularly known as Bobi Wine, as evidence that his threats should be taken seriously.

In January 2026, Muhoozi threatened to kill Bobi Wine following Uganda's disputed presidential election, claiming that security forces had killed twenty-two "terrorists" belonging to the opposition National Unity Platform and expressing hope that the opposition leader would be next.

He also threatened to cut military ties with the United States after accusing its ambassador of aiding Kyagulanyi's escape.

The remarks attracted criticism from US Senator Jim Risch, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, who rejected an apology subsequently issued by Muhoozi and urged Washington to consider tougher measures against Uganda.

Muhoozi has also previously issued directives touching on government administration, including an order requiring ministers to obtain his permission before travelling abroad.

World.title: Kenya: Gachagua Faults Ruto's 'Usawa Ni Sawa' Over 'Tribal' State Appointments
World.content:
Nairobi — DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua has taken a swipe at President William Ruto's "Usawa ni Sawa" campaign, questioning the government's commitment to equal opportunities following a series of appointments involving people from the Kalenjin community.

Gachagua's remarks came shortly after the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) named Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer.

In a sarcastic post on X, the former Deputy President linked Ayabei's appointment to other recent selections, including Ronoh Kibet as KenGen Managing Director and CEO, and Lydia Sitienei Chelagat's nomination as Data Commissioner, which is awaiting parliamentary approval.

The appointments have revived Gachagua's criticism of what he describes as favouritism in the distribution of senior government jobs, even as Ruto promotes his "Usawa ni Sawa" message of equal opportunities for Kenyans.

Gachagua, who was impeached in October 2024 after facing several charges, including accusations of promoting ethnic divisions, has repeatedly accused his former boss of favouring members of his community in public appointments.

However, government allies have defended the selections, maintaining that the individuals were picked on merit and through competitive recruitment processes.

World.title: Rwanda: What to Know About Migrant Partnership Between Rwanda and Five EU Countries
World.content:
Rwanda's Minister of Interior Vincent Biruta (third right) joined senior officials from the five EU countries at a press conference announcing the new migration partnership.

The government and five European Union member states have announced a partnership to establish a migrant return hub in Rwanda, targeting the first transfers in 2027.

The proposed arrangement would cover people who have no legal right to remain in the participating European countries and are subject to enforceable return or removal decisions.

Announced in Vienna, Austria, on Monday, November 16, the initiative brings together Rwanda, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands. Negotiations will determine how the proposed hub will operate.

People transferred to Rwanda would have the opportunity to integrate into Rwandan society, voluntarily return to their countries of origin or move to another country where they have the legal right to reside.



ALSO READ: Rwanda, five EU countries announce migration partnership

Here are eight key things to know about the proposed arrangement.

1. It involves five EU member states

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands are pursuing the initiative with Rwanda as part of a broader partnership covering migration and other areas of common interest.

The participating countries describe the partnership as equal and mutually beneficial.

Austria's Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said the initiative would help curb irregular migration, disrupt people-smuggling networks and ease pressure on receiving countries.

2. Who would be transferred to Rwanda?

The proposed hub would receive migrants who have no legal right to remain in the five participating European countries and are subject to enforceable return or removal decisions.

Those covered must not be in need of international protection or have another legal basis to stay.

The initiative seeks to address difficulties in implementing return decisions, particularly where migrants' countries of origin do not cooperate with repatriation.

ALSO READ: What Rwandans say about UK asylum deal

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said return hubs could provide an alternative for people without the right to remain in Europe who cannot be returned to their home countries.

3. Migrants would have an opportunity to settle in Rwanda

People transferred under the arrangement would have the opportunity to integrate into Rwandan communities.

Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said Rwanda will work with its partners to develop skills and employment programmes to support those who choose to stay.

"These people who choose to stay in our country, to live in our country, will be integrated into our communities. And of course we work on a development programme to give them skills. They will need to be able to work," he said.

Biruta said the programmes would also benefit Rwandans through wider community development.

4. Returning home or moving elsewhere remain options

Settling in Rwanda would not be the only option.

Migrants would also be able to return voluntarily to their countries of origin or relocate to another country where they have the legal right to reside.

Biruta said the arrangement would offer a second chance to people who no longer have the right to remain in the participating European countries, allowing them to choose among the available legal options.

ALSO READ: What to know as Rwanda-UK migration dispute hearing starts

Support for integration and voluntary return would be developed with international partners.

5. European partners would cover the costs

The five European countries would meet the costs associated with the arrangement, including receiving migrants and supporting their integration in Rwanda.

Biruta said Rwanda's participation was driven by a commitment to finding a sustainable response to migration challenges.

He said partner countries would need to fund the support required by those transferred, including skills development and employment programmes.

6. International organisations are advising on the proposal

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, are engaging with the countries involved, although their roles differ.

IOM is providing technical input on the return hub process. It has indicated that it could provide care and assistance to migrants at the receiving government's request, provided the necessary safeguards are in place.

UNHCR is advising on compliance with international human rights standards and the protection of asylum systems, including ensuring that people who need international protection continue to receive it.

Their engagement should not be taken to mean that either organisation has agreed to implement the proposed arrangement.

The European Commission has followed the preparatory discussions, with implementation expected to comply with applicable EU and international law.

7. Rwanda's experience in receiving displaced people

Rwanda has cited its experience hosting refugees and asylum seekers as a basis for its participation.

Biruta highlighted the Emergency Transit Mechanism, established in September 2019 through a partnership between Rwanda, the African Union and UNHCR to evacuate vulnerable refugees and asylum seekers from Libya.

Close 

According to the minister, Rwanda has received more than 3,000 people through the mechanism, most of whom have subsequently been resettled in countries including Canada, the United States, Germany and Finland.

He said Rwanda's own history of displacement had shaped its understanding of the challenges facing refugees and asylum seekers.

The Emergency Transit Mechanism and the proposed return hub serve different groups: the former provides protection and assistance to people evacuated from Libya, while the latter would receive people found to have no legal right to remain in the participating European countries.

8. First transfers are targeted for 2027

The countries intend to develop the hub through a phased approach, with the aim of beginning transfers in 2027.

Denmark's Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov described the initiative as a breakthrough in efforts to reform Europe's migration system.

Greece's Migration and Asylum Minister Athanasios Plevris said it was expected to help reduce irregular migration and increase returns.

The Netherlands' Deputy Prime Minister Bart van den Brink said the partnership should strengthen the return system while giving migrants an opportunity to settle in Rwanda.

The announcement sets out the countries' intentions, but further negotiations are required to finalise the operational arrangements.

World.title: South Sudan: Bishops - 'Interim Government Must Respect the Constitution and Ensure a Democratic Transition'
World.content:
Juba — A clear mandate, respect for the Constitution and the law, and safeguards against any arbitrary exercise of power. These are the demands made by the Catholic bishops of Sudan and South Sudan to the interim government, warning against the risk that it could become an instrument of political exclusion or indefinitely prolong institutional uncertainty.

Ahead of the general elections, scheduled for February 11, 2027 (see Fides, 6/11/2026), the bishops expressed concern about the implementation of the 2018 peace agreement and the preparations of the electoral institutions. "We call for clarity and transparency, as well as respect for the constitutional and legal foundations governing the exercise of power, the mandate, and the limits of the interim administration," reads the statement delivered by Cardinal Stephen Ameyu Mulla, Archbishop of Juba, during the 52nd Annual Plenary Assembly of the Bishops, held in Torit from November 7 to 13.

The interim government, the bishops stated, must "safeguard national stability, ensure the continuity of essential public services, protect citizens' rights, and promote a peaceful and credible democratic transition." Any exercise of public authority must comply with the Transitional Constitution, the 2018 Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict, and the laws currently in force, while upholding the rule of law, institutional accountability, and the common good.



The bishops' statement comes nearly two months after President Salva Kiir dissolved the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity, established under the 2018 peace agreement, replacing it with an interim administration (see Fides, 24/9/2026). The decision followed amendments to the electoral law, which maintain the president's constitutional powers until the new government takes office.

The legal legitimacy of the new arrangement has been challenged by independent observers, who argue that ordinary legislation cannot establish structures and powers that are not provided for in the Constitution. The bishops stressed that the vote must "express the sovereign will of the people" and represent a peaceful and credible path towards constitutional democracy. Among the main challenges they identified are insufficient institutional, technical, and financial resources; security shortcomings; the failure to complete commitments under the peace agreement; political mistrust; and population displacement.

"The country must not be forced to hold elections in the absence of the necessary conditions," the bishops stated. The Church also called for dialogue among the government, the opposition, and groups that did not sign the 2018 peace agreement: "No lasting peace can be built through exclusion or unilateral decisions."

Close 

Finally, the bishops reaffirmed the Catholic Church's willingness to accompany the country on its journey towards peace and reconciliation through dialogue, civic education, and peacebuilding, working alongside political leaders, the international community, and the population.

World.title: Djibouti: Six Survivors Reach Berbera Port After Boat Sailing From Djibouti Sinks
World.content:
Berbera — Six crew members rescued after a cargo boat sank near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait have arrived safely at Somaliland's Berbera Port, where medical personnel and emergency teams are providing care, the Somaliland Ports Authority said on Tuesday.

Two other crew members died when the boat, Alfatah, sank on Nov. 16 while carrying cooking oil from Djibouti to Yemen's Salif Port, the authority said in a statement.

The survivors were rescued by M/V Adel 2 and brought to Berbera, where port teams received them and provided medical attention and emergency assistance.

"Six crew members rescued by M/V Adel 2 following the sinking of the boat Alfatah near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on 16 November 2026 have safely arrived at Berbera Port," the authority said.

Eight crew members were aboard Alfatah when it sank. The six survivors comprise two Yemeni, two Somali and two Indian nationals. Those who died were a Yemeni and an Indian national, according to the statement.

The authority said its account was based on information provided by the captain of M/V Adel 2 to the Berbera Port Communication Centre, alongside accounts given by the survivors after their arrival.

It praised the captain and crew of M/V Adel 2 for their "prompt humanitarian response" and efforts to rescue the six crew members.

The authority also extended condolences to the families, relatives and colleagues of the two men who died.

(Reporting by Mohamed Duale; Editing by Horn Diplomat Desk)

World.title: Pentagon detains senior US Army officer accused of spying for Russians after UK arrest
World.content:

A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel suspected of spying for Russia was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday, days after British counterterrorism police arrested him on suspicion of violating national security laws.

Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested Nov. 10 near Gloucester, England, on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.

British authorities previously said the allegations involved Russia, which the Kremlin denied any connection to.

SENIOR US ARMY SOLDIER ARRESTED IN UK ON SUSPICION OF SPYING FOR RUSSIA

The Associated Press, citing a U.S. official, reported that Tyner had not provided information to Russia.

Tyner's transfer followed consultations between British prosecutors, the U.K. attorney general's office and U.S. authorities, according to London's Metropolitan Police.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing, said investigators referred the case to the Crown Prosecution Service, which consulted the attorney general's office and U.S. authorities before transferring the investigation.

RUSSIAN SPIES ORCHESTRATED $40K MURDER PLOT IN NATION’S CAPITAL, US ALLEGES

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said in a statement.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the officer was in custody following a joint espionage investigation involving the FBI's Philadelphia field office, its London legal attaché office, British counterterrorism police, MI5, U.K. defense counterintelligence officials and U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk. That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase," Patel said.

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commander of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, warned service members against violating their oath to defend the Constitution.

"This case should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution," Stinchon said.

Tyner, who previously deployed to Afghanistan, Iraq and Qatar, served as a senior human resources officer with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester.

The British-led multinational force, which includes personnel from 20 nations, is designed to respond rapidly to military crises and operations.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied Russian involvement following Tyner's arrest, according to the AP.

"This arrest does not concern us in any way," Peskov said Nov. 11. "We don’t know what it’s connected to. We have nothing to do with this."

According to a Nov. 13 statement from the U.S. Army, Tyner entered active-duty service in January 2008 and deployed to Afghanistan from December 2013 to December 2014, Qatar from July 2016 to July 2017, and Iraq from December 2019 to July 2020.

World.title: Irish boxer Lee Reeves dies at 31 after three months in a coma following Dublin fight
World.content:
Irish boxer Lee Reeves died Monday night at 31. It's a tragic end. He spent the last three months fighting for his life after a bout in Dublin.

Reeves took heavy shots on Aug. 1 in a back-and-forth war with Gary Cully at Dublin's 3Arena. Both guys landed big punches all night. Then came the 10th round and Cully dropped Reeves twice to end it.

Reeves stayed down; medics rushed him straight from the arena for emergency brain surgery. The boxer stayed in a medically induced coma and moved back to University Hospital Limerick in October to be near his family. Things looked hopeful for a bit until his health took a turn for the worse after he caught a bad infection over the weekend, and died Monday.

IRANIAN BOXER ON DEATH ROW WINS HUMAN RIGHTS AWARD AS ATHLETES PUSH TO SAVE HIS LIFE

Tributes poured in across boxing on Tuesday, including from Cully on social media.

"What a character and a gent," Cully posted. "It's never been nothing but love between us, champ. Can't really believe I'm writing this, but RIP, brother."

Outside the ring, Reeves served as a soldier in the Irish Army's 12th Infantry Battalion. He also spoke out often about mental health after losing his mother to suicide in 2015. He even competed on "Survivor UK" in 2023.

Inside the ropes, fans knew the lefty as "El Champo." He won five Irish amateur titles before turning pro in 2018. The guy could scrap.

Reeves walked into the Cully fight on an 11-bout winning streak and a pro career record of 16-2 (11 KOs).

World.title: Kyle Whittingham addresses job security questions at Michigan, makes more headlines with UCLA comments
World.content:
The head coach of the Michigan Wolverines is jealous about a bunch of players from James Madison University, who'd have ever guessed it?

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

This weekend at The Big House matches up two programs with wildly different histories, backgrounds, geographic regions and recruiting success. Michigan, one of college football’s unquestioned blue bloods, against the UCLA Bruins, who for years were a punchline and in recent years have been better known for crowd shots of a two-thirds-empty Rose Bowl than for their on-field success.

MICHIGAN HIRED KYLE WHITTINGHAM TO FIX ITS MESS. INSTEAD, HE’S CREATED AN EVEN BIGGER ONE WITH WOLVERINES

Both teams have first-year head coaches, also with wildly different pedigrees. Michigan hired Kyle Whittingham after decades of sustained success in Salt Lake City with the Utah Utes, while the Bruins grabbed Bob Chesney whose most recent resume looks like this:

Head coach at Salve Regina (2010-2012)

Head coach at Assumption (2013-2017)

Head coach at Holy Cross (2018-2023)

Head coach at James Madison (2024-2025)

It's Michigan, though, with all their immense resources and recruiting prowess, including signing one of the most highly-regarded quarterback recruits in recent memory, Bryce Underwood, that's struggled. The Wolverines are just 5-5 on the season and are heading into Saturday with two-straight losses scoring a combined 13 points. They've lost to Iowa, Minnesota, Indiana, Michigan State and Oregon, and with UCLA and Ohio State looming, there's a reasonable chance the Wolverines miss out on a bowl bid.

For a program with their resources, it's been, well, an embarrassment.

On the other hand, the Bruins head into Ann Arbor as the most surprising team of the 2026 college football season. Under Chesney, UCLA hit the transfer portal and immediately turned the program around. While they've benefited from an easier schedule, they did beat a quality Oregon team on the road, never an easy feat, and held serve against opponents like Wisconsin, Illinois and Minnesota.

One more win guarantees them a spot in the Big Ten Championship game, and effectively secures their spot in the College Football Playoff. It's stunning, to say the least.

Whittingham, in his press conference this week, was asked how Chesney and the Bruins had done it, and gave a, well, interesting answer.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Transfer Portal. Look at their roster that's built. Man, what, 75% of their starters transfers for this year, and they hit the nail on the head with their evaluations in the portal. They did a great job of bringing in the right guys," he said. "The previous school that the head coach was at, got a lot of players from there. I think they took 20-plus players from there, something like that. And that's really how you do it in this day and age from just overnight, so to speak, is through the Transfer Portal. That's the only way you can do that and have such a marked change from one year to the next is you've got to have a really successful, great evaluation, and just get the right guys in, the pieces to the puzzle."

That "previous school" Chesney came from was... James Madison. So Whittingham's contention here is that UCLA has become a top-5 team headed for the College Football Playoff because they pulled players from... James Madison? Meanwhile Michigan is 5-5 and staring down a losing season with tens of millions spent on Bryce Underwood, Savion Hiter, and a long list of other former top recruits.

He's right about one thing though; nailing evaluations is more important than ever. Chesney clearly has a talent for evaluating the right players to fit his scheme and coaching style, and its paid off.

UCLA is starting a backup quarterback, Ty Dieffenbach, just like Michigan is starting their backup. The difference is that the Bruins' running game is so good and well-designed that the offense can score points anyway. Michigan with Tommy Carr looks hopeless, though Carr's 4/12 for 45 yards line against Oregon might be even worse than hopeless.

That must be tough to hear as a Michigan fan, that your team has struggled to even reach a bowl game because your roster isn't as good as a bunch of former James Madison players.

Michigan's struggles this year have raised questions about Whittingham's future in Ann Arbor, particularly because there's been a seeming disconnect between him and the team. As well as some online chatter that he's checked out on the season and hoping for a buyout.



"Yeah," he answered to a question about his interest in staying at Michigan. "But I guess anything I say, you can say, ‘Oh, that means he wants to get fired.’ To me, that’s ridiculous. Do I want to continue? Yes sir, I would like to continue. … That might be the most bizarre thing I’ve heard there."

"I don't know who spun it that way, but like I said, you can take anything and spin it any way you want and try to get the desired outcome you're looking for," Whittingham said. "That was not the intention."

Few, if any, predicted that the Kyle Whittingham hire would be such a disaster at Michigan. He was one of the most consistent coaches in the country at Utah, always punching above the Utes' program size and resources. Now at Michigan, one of the best jobs in the country, he's struggled and is searching for answers.

Not every team with a new coach can turn itself around overnight, and it remains to be seen how the Wolverines and Bruins fare in the coming seasons. But no two teams exemplify modern college football and its unpredictability than UCLA and Michigan. Given how this season's gone, would anyone be surprised if the Wolverines pull off the upset?

World.title: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
World.content:
LONDON — When European nations said they wanted greater involvement in Ukraine peace talks, this was almost certainly not what they had in mind.

Europe has long demanded more say in negotiations to end Russia’s war, fearful of being frozen out by Washington and Moscow. They dread a deal favorable to President Vladimir Putin — who will meet President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a historic three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.

The good news for them is that the United States says it is now pushing to include Europe in the next rounds of diplomacy. The bad news, say governments, officials and foreign policy analysts, is the alarming new suggestion from Trump’s team: that the entire future of European security should be up for discussion too — the same demand that Putin has pushed for years.

To the Russian leader, redrawing Europe’s security map means scaling back NATO’s presence, righting what he perceives as the injustices imposed on Moscow after the Soviet Union’s collapse. A succession of senior European officials have lambasted the idea, warning that Washington risks “walking into Moscow’s trap,” as Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, put it.

“This is all rather bizarre,” former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves said, summing up this sentiment in an interview with NBC News on Monday.

It’s not clear how or why the U.S. came to float a maximalist demand that Putin first made in 2021, one that was widely rejected by Western governments months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in recent days, as Washington ups its pressure for a breakthrough in peace talks, Russia and the U.S. have both revived the idea.

Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and envoy, wrote Friday that talks should tackle the “broader postwar European security arrangements.”

Earlier this month, he lamented “decades of mistrust” and “competing security concerns” between Russia and Europe, vowing to address these by building an “enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” Kushner has also stressed that NATO would remain central to European defense and that no country should have a veto over another’s alliances.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, flanked by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, following their meeting near Dublin last week. Paul Faith / AFP via Getty

Trump himself has also hinted that he seeks a final deal encompassing the entire continent. “It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” he told reporters in the Oval Office earlier this month. “I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”

Instead, the idea has been met with unease and dismay, viewed by many in Europe as echoing Putin’s hard-line war goals.

Whereas Kushner described Europe and Russia as neighbors unable to resolve their differences, the historical record shows the aggression has chiefly been directed one way. Russia seized Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022, while waging sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation against the West.

Kushner’s suggestion also touches on a central European fear: that Washington will pursue a deal at almost any cost, even if that emboldens Putin to expand his aggression.

“Why are two real estate agents pushing this idea?” Ilves said referring to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, another Trump envoy, both of whom made their fortunes in real estate before entering diplomacy.

“These people aren’t even diplomats,” said Ilves, who led his former Soviet republic from 2006 to 2016. “I’m not sure they have much of an idea of the long history of the development of security architecture in Europe relating to Russia.”

Asked about the criticisms, assistant White House press secretary Olivia Wales said the U.S. proposal sought to “strengthen existing European security arrangements, with NATO at their core, while developing practical mechanisms to prevent future conflict.”

Security guarantees for Ukraine “cannot be designed without understanding the broader security framework in which they will operate,” she said in an email, adding that any final agreement must respect Europe and Ukraine’s sovereignty “and be agreed by the relevant parties.”

European officials are nonetheless unnerved by Kushner’s remarks.

Kallas, the E.U. foreign policy chief, described Russia’s maximalist war demands as “really absurd,” while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pointed out that “Europe has a security architecture — we don’t need a new one.”

Elsewhere, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the rules were not the issue: “The problem is that Russia is breaking them.” And even Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was adamant that the “security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and NATO, not by Russia.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the idea as “dangerous,” saying that European security “should not be the main agenda.”

Ukraine’s view is that Russia is in no place to make such demands, given that it’s spent more than four years failing to win the war.

“At this stage, the most Putin can negotiate is a fair ceasefire along the current line of contact,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said. And “frankly, Europe does not need a new security order; it already exists, and Russia is constantly violating it.”

Kyiv and its European backers also argue that a ceasefire must come before any peace talks, accusing Russia of stalling so it can keep bombing civilian infrastructure ahead of the frigid winter.

If Europe accepts Russia’s demands about wider continental security before there is a ceasefire, Moscow “will try to create the impression that it’s our fault that the war continues, because we don’t want to accept all their demands,” according to Sven Biscop, a director at the Egmont Institute, a Belgian think tank.

He said he believed dialogue with Russia is a good thing, a view echoed by influential Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who in an interview with the Financial Times published Tuesday said that it had been “irresponsible” to outsource talks with Putin to the U.S., which he said could be leaning toward carving up Europe into spheres of influence.

Back in Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., urged Trump’s team to refuse Putin’s demands.

The Russian leader not only wanted control of Ukraine but “he wants to redesign NATO to accommodate his revisionist ambitions,” Shaheen said, adding that any discussions about European security infrastructure should be a “nonstarter,” for the U.S. which “has benefited from the Alliance.”

Amid all of this, any substantial progress toward ending the war remains elusive.

The latest round of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week produced no major breakthrough. Kushner said Washington was working toward what could be the largest prisoner swap of the war, while reporting that Russia had agreed to give Europe a seat at the table during the next round.

Putin met with Kushner and Witkoff at the Kremlin in Moscow last week. Vyacheslav Prokofyev / Pool / AFP via Getty

Russia hasn’t quite confirmed that, instead saying that it needs “to understand from the Europeans themselves” what they can “contribute to the peace process” before allowing them to join, as Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday.

There has been some internal wrangling among the European nations about who might represent them. Leaders have agreed on a team comprising the United Kingdom (which left the E.U. in 2020), France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and European Council. Kallas herself was left off the team.

“I don’t know who among the current leaders could be a sane dialogue partner,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the state-run news agency Tass on Monday.

He likened the chosen group of European countries to “the Quartet,” a satirical poem by Russian author Ivan Krylov. In it, a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear blame their failure to form a string quartet on the seating arrangement rather than their lack of musical ability.

That, at least, involved agreeing to a seating arrangement.

LIMA, Peru — They turned out in the millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a grueling 12-day tour of the South American nations, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

00:00 00:00 Pope keeps energetic pace in trip to South America after surgery 01:19

For some — particularly those in Argentina, which had not received a papal visit since Pope John Paul II in 1987 — it was the first time they would get to see a pontiff in person. A record 2.5 million people flooded onto the streets of Buenos Aires last week to try and catch a glimpse of Leo.

The Vatican dubbed it a “homecoming” tour for the 71-year-old, as the Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, spent the final six days in the country where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.

NBC News takes a look at some of the highlights from his trip.

Montevideo, Uruguay

After a 17-hour flight from Rome, Leo and his entourage touched down in Uruguay’s capital, Montevideo. Praising the Lord and thanking his wonderful medical assistants, Leo said that while some had questioned whether he would be able to make the trip because of his recent surgery, he “had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward.”

World.title: Waymo robotaxis banned from California freeways
World.content:
California banned Waymo robotaxis from state freeways after officials determined that the driverless vehicles pose an “imminent hazard to public safety,” the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles said Tuesday.

In a news release, the department said it had issued the Nov. 11 ban after one of the company’s autonomous vehicles tried to pass highway patrol officers conducting a traffic break on a San Francisco-area freeway this month.

The department also cited a separate incident in which three of the company’s vehicles entered an active construction closure on another San Francisco-area highway.

“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” the department said.

Similar restrictions were placed on the company after similar incidents earlier this year, the department said.

The ban will remain in place until Waymo can address the issue, according to the release.

In a statement, Waymo pointed out that the construction zone incidents did not involve injuries or collisions and said it is complying with the restrictions. The company temporarily imposed similar measures in other areas where the company operates.

Waymo’s robotaxis are in more than a dozen cities across the U.S. Waymo, which is owned by Google’s parent company, Alphabet Inc., first introduced the driverless taxis in San Francisco in 2024.

Waymo said it is working with state officials to “diligently and responsibly” resume freeway operations.

World.title: Nvidia sees strong growth in first earnings report without Huang
World.content:
Nvidia reported robust growth on Tuesday, as interim CEO Colette Kress hosted her first earnings call since the company's founder and former chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs.

The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

Nvidia expects revenue of $130 billion for its fiscal fourth quarter, with projected growth driven by strong demand for AI infrastructure, Kress said on a call with analysts discussing the latest results.

Wall Street analysts had expected third-quarter revenue of nearly $109 billion, according to financial research firm FactSet.

The financial results represent the first time Nvidia has reported earnings without Huang at the helm of the chip company he cofounded in 1993.

Strong beats

Nvidia's results for the period featured "beats on the top and bottom lines in Colette Kress' first print as interim CEO, five days after the board removed Jensen Huang, and the quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him," analysts with investment adviser Yorkville Ives said in a report.

The chip firm reported third-quarter data center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from one year ago, marking a record.

"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's chief financial officer, said in a statement.

During the earnings call, Kress and new Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones declined to answer questions about the company's progress in finding a permanent chief executive. But Jones said that the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

The company's search for a new chief is underway, Jones added, noting the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang. In the meantime, the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company, Jones said.

Nvidia shares rose nearly 4%, to $161.57, in after-hours trading.

Confidence boost

Adam Crisafulli, a Wall Street analyst with Vital Knowledge, said Nvidia's stronger-than-expected results should boost investor confidence.

"The headline numbers for [the fiscal third quarter] are strong, and the FQ4 guide is solid, too. Given how depressed sentiment is, this should be enough to spur a rebound," he said in a note to investors.

Huang resigned last week after admitting he had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy. Beyond spurring his shock exit from the company, the scandal has raised questions over whether the company's advanced chips were being used in China in violation of export controls.

The U.S. government is moving to close any loopholes in those rules. The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.

Kress addressed the new export controls in Tuesday's call, saying that "with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong." The company will study the new export controls, she added.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's board also said it formed a new committee to ensure that the company's policies comply with U.S. export controls.

Nvidia employees, investors and prominent tech industry leaders have rallied around Huang since his departure from Nvidia and called for his reinstatement as CEO. But the company's board is against reinstating the tech entrepreneur in his post, a source directly familiar with its thinking told CBS News.

Nvidia faces longer-term risks related to finding a new leader, stricter U.S. export controls and international sales, according to Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

"We're at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don't know what Nvidia's long-term leadership will look like," he told CBS News. "Jensen Huang's departure could create some near-term disruption, but a credible succession plan should go a long way toward steadying the ship. The next CEO will have big shoes to fill, but Nvidia's long-term opportunity does not hinge on one person."

World.title: NSA's classified internal network goes down, sources say
World.content:
Washington — The National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline Tuesday, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the situation, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.

The network, dubbed "NSA Net," is used for classified communications and information sharing within the nation's largest intelligence agency.

An NSA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance." The statement continued that "while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend National Security continues."

The spokesperson said that the agency's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.

Two U.S. officials told CBS News that, at this point, there is no evidence the disruption was caused by a cyberattack. Two sources familiar with the situation said the outage resulted from routine system patching, though the precise circumstances surrounding the disruption remain unclear.

The NSA has also implemented staggered arrival times for non-emergency personnel at Fort Meade, according to two sources familiar with the measure.

The news was first reported by CNN.

Multiple sources told CBS News that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems, which is why they decided to stagger arrivals. Sources referred to this as "Code Gray," part of a modified reporting schedule.

Sources familiar with Fort Meade's operations said the installation remains under normal operating conditions, with gates and campus-wide services unaffected. The sources explained that the NSA operates within its own secured campus and can establish unique reporting requirements for its personnel, independent of the larger installation.

In the meantime, some activities are being redirected to other NSA facilities around the country, according to sources familiar with the situation.

It was not immediately clear how long the network had been offline or when full service might be restored.

The NSA, home to one of the largest workforces in the U.S. intelligence community, is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats, and protecting U.S. government communications.

CBS News has reached out to the White House, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Pentagon for comment.

World.title: Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet
World.content:
Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet

toggle caption i Vahid Salemi/AP

CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain in the third Iranian attack in recent days on American military targets in the Persian Gulf island kingdom, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.

The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting, as Iran's targeting of Bahrain brought condemnations from the region. Analysts said stalled peace negotiations and Tehran's growing economic pressures were raising the risk of a substantial escalation.

Sponsor Message

Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military likewise said the attack inflicted no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.

Hours later, a U.S. fighter jet carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official said.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to "aggression" toward U.S. personnel.

A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.

The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month. Iran's attack Tuesday was its third on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.

toggle caption i AP

Iran may be shifting its strategy amid economic pain

Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.

Sponsor Message

U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.

Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.

Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.

Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.

Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.

"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."

U.S. expands its Middle East naval presence

With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.

Sponsor Message

The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.

Iran says it's responding to U.S. attacks

Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.

The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.

"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.

Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.

Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.

In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.

Iran may be losing patience as conflict drags on

The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

Sponsor Message

"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."

Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.

Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.

Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."

Iran has continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route.

World.title: Nvidia board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
World.content:
Nvidia board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO

toggle caption i Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

Nvidia said it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang, amid a push by the former CEO's allies to return him to lead the chipmaker he cofounded.

Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," board chair Harvey Jones said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang had said he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company.

Sponsor Message

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang wrote in a statement posted on social media. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."

Huang stepped down from the company last week after acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency, as well as with another woman who is an executive at Nvidia. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

Huang said he would be "honored" to return to the company if Nvidia's board agreed. His comments came as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."

"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.

Sponsor Message

Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors from the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd.

Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing the most advanced U.S. AI chips. They will also ask Huang about his involvement with Alice Huang, who was an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation.

Nvidia's board said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.

On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department announced new rules to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The Commerce Department and Justice Department also announced Monday that the DOJ is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

Nvidia sought to reassure investors about the company's future during its third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday.

"Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. And our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change," said Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer who is serving as interim CEO while the board finds a permanent leader.

Quarterly sales doubled to a record $115.8 billion and profit also doubled to $65.3 billion from a year ago. The company said it was raising its forecast for sales growth next year.

Sponsor Message

Nvidia shares were up 5% in after-hours trading on Tuesday. The company's stock price has dropped more than 16% since Huang admitting having an extramarital affair earlier this month.

World.title: Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia
World.content:
Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

A technology issue with United Airlines delayed departing flights yesterday evening, just as air travel was returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday. President Trump said yesterday that he hopes this incident will prompt Congress to allocate more funds to upgrade the outdated air traffic control system.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images North America

🎧 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the FAA will reevaluate future maintenance procedures, NPR's Joe Hernandez tells Up First. Mike McCormick, a former FAA senior executive and air traffic manager, told Hernandez that he thinks another nationwide ground stop is unlikely. McCormick says that in cases like this, the FAA sometimes imposes a maintenance moratorium, temporarily halting such work. The ground stop happened while L3Harris workers converted copper wires to a fiber optic system and installed a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.

President Trump is in Manila today to meet with allies at the ASEAN summit. Tomorrow, he travels to Shenzhen, China, for a joint summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. It's the first time those three have had a joint summit. The meeting will happen on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting in Shenzhen.



Sponsor Message

🎧 When leaving the White House yesterday, Trump said they would discuss his "favorite subject": Ukraine, NPR's Deepa Shivaram says. The White House had previously announced that Ukraine would not be on the agenda for the trilateral meeting. Shivaram says that Europe and Ukraine are concerned about how Ukraine may be discussed at the meeting, and what might come out of it, because President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will not be at APEC and Trump has recently been more lenient toward Putin and Russia.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has shaken Silicon Valley, prompting calls from some tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. Meanwhile, the U.S. government introduced a rule to block remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, closing a loophole that could allow adversarial governments to access American AI technology through overseas data centers. Nvidia is the world's dominant producer of AI chips.



🎧 Many prominent AI and venture capital figures have recognized Huang as a visionary whose company played a significant role in the AI boom, NPR's Shannon Bond says. An online petition supporting his reinstatement has garnered more than 160,000 signatures, but Bond says some of them may not be real. Elon Musk says he signed it. Brad Gerstner from Altimeter Capital, a key Nvidia investor, has urged the board to thoroughly investigate and keep all options open.
