Still, the early results suggest that looking past bad Chinese behaviour is paying dividends for Canadian businesses and the people they employ.

Xi agreed to drop his country's "anti-discriminatory tariffs," worth up to 25 per cent on some $400 million worth of Canadian pork and seafood products — a manoeuvre that delivers immediate benefits to those sectors by unlocking access to China's vast market for foodstuffs.

In addition to a commitment to take more lentils, fava beans, "wild aquatic products" and pet food, among other agri-food items, Xi is extending the tariff pause Carney secured in January for Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab, which has been an economic boon.

Indeed, since Carney's first meeting with Xi, and what the government says is 35 other ministerial visits and engagements to smooth over bilateral irritants, Canadian exports to China have surged.

Statistics Canada data and figures from the University of Alberta's China Institute show that Canadian trade with China hit a record $12.7 billion last quarter.

The dollar value of Canadian products sent to the Asian economic powerhouse has increased by 60 per cent over the last two years, a byproduct of Carney's move to restore relations with Beijing.

Kyle Larkin, president and CEO of the Canadian Meat Council, said pork producers have suffered under the Chinese restrictions and Carney's deal to eliminate many of them is "a great step in the right direction."

"We're very happy," he told reporters in China.

Vina Nadjibulla, the co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said U.S. trade actions necessitate Canada looking elsewhere for business — even if there are lingering concerns about cozying up to a country like China.

"China's behaviour hasn't changed, but Canada's strategic circumstance has," Nadjibulla said in an interview.

"We are now living in a world in which we do have to diversify and we do have to economically engage with China in certain areas. But I hope that we remain smart and strategic and do not forget the lessons of the past."

More Chinese steel, aluminum

In return for all this new access, Carney is opening the door wider to Chinese steel and aluminum imports by extending and expanding remission measures for products that cannot be found in sufficient quantities in this country.

Blair Dickerson, the president of the Canadian Steel Producers Association, said the changes are not expected to have much of an impact on the domestic industry.

"If there's something that we can't make in this country, then we're OK with it," she said in an interview. She added that the remissions are "not forever" and could be rescinded if companies here start to make those products.

There's also a vague commitment to "deepen co-operation" in "finance."

And Carney will continue to allow tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles to enter Canada annually at a reduced tariff rate — although the number imported so far is significantly below this year's quota of 49,000.

A backgrounder on the Carney-Xi deal distributed to reporters states that, after past BYD approvals, a second, unnamed Chinese company has just secured the necessary Transport Canada permissions to import its foreign-made cars.

A government spokesperson confirmed that Geely, an automotive conglomerate with stakes in brands like Zeekr, Polestar and Lotus, now has the green light.

Much of Canada's auto industry has fiercely opposed giving Chinese firms access, fearing a flood of cheaply made, state-subsidized vehicles will sink remaining Canadian auto and parts production.

While the Carney government previously expected significant manufacturing investment from Chinese EV makers in Canada, nothing has materialized — and the backgrounder released to reporters suggests none is coming soon.

Flavio Volpe, the president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association (APMA), told CBC News that Ottawa must resist any temptation to allow Chinese firms to ship "knock-down" car kits into Canada for assembly.

Volpe said Chinese firms have promised other countries like Brazil that these kits are just a first step until they can build local manufacturing capacity, only to renege on those commitments.

He said these kits use no Canadian parts, would imperil the homegrown sector and frustrate the U.S., which sends many parts to Canadian assembly plants.

"Does that scuttle any prospect of a trade deal with the Americans? Well, it certainly tweaks the Americans' attention," he said of the prospect of more Chinese-made vehicles in Canada.

While there's industry anxiety, Carney is showing an openness to working with these Chinese firms while the U.S. relationship is strained.

"We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market," Carney told reporters travelling with him on his nine-day trade mission.

"That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions."

World.title: Calgary high school says too many students are getting food delivered
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Calgary high school sent parents a memo this week asking them to rein in their children’s increasing use of food delivery apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash during school hours.

In the letter, St. Francis High School administrators said while the deliveries may be convenient, they can also be disruptive to classrooms, and pose security risks to have students interacting with individuals they don’t know on school grounds.

“As the safety and security of everyone at St. Francis is our priority, we ask that you please have a conversation with your child and ask them to not use any food delivery services during the instructional time of the day," the letter said.

Lee Martin, who represents Calgary Catholic teachers for the Alberta Teachers’ Association, told CBC News it's become more of an issue in recent years. He heard from one teacher just this week who said a driver tried to deliver food right to a classroom window.

“I think that as public educators we want our children fed,” said Martin. “However, this seems to be a bit out of control.”

A food drop-off cart outside an elementary school in Calgary's southeast. (Submitted by Lee Martin)

And it’s not only at high schools.

At one elementary school, he said upwards of 30 parents were either dropping off food or sending deliveries there daily, so the school set up a table in the foyer where students can go search for their bag at lunchtime.

A spokesperson for the Calgary Catholic School District said to their knowledge, St. Francis is the only school in its board addressing the matter.

In a statement, the Calgary Board of Education said it doesn’t have a specific policy on food deliveries, and it’s up to principals at individual schools to set guidelines if it is an issue.

“Students are discouraged from ordering deliveries into the building, though we are aware they may meet the driver in other locations on school property,” the statement said.

Students say it’s common, not necessarily an issue

Outside St. Francis, delivery driver Ali Nuru dropped off food for a student Tuesday. He says he’ll typically end up doing a couple of school deliveries a week.

“Most of the time I bring from McDonald's,” he said.

Delivery driver Ali Nuru says he typically delivers a couple of times a week to high schools, with McDonald's the No. 1 meal of choice. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)

Students said it’s fairly routine to see classmates meeting drivers in the parking lot to pick up their orders.

“A lot of times — I'm kind of snitching — but they'll be like, ‘Oh, can I go to the bathroom?' and then they just go meet the driver around the school, like the front of the school and then bring the food in with them,” said Grade 11 student Rebira Assefa.

However, she said it hasn’t been a big deal in her classrooms, with most students unbothered by it.

The bathroom excuse can be an issue though, said Grade 11 student Bradley White, since only so many students are allowed out of a class at a time.

“Like if someone's out for too long, then the teacher will be like, ‘OK, no one's allowed to use the bathroom for the rest of class because this person ruined it for everyone,’” said White.

Plus, he said it can be a distraction when someone orders an “excessive” amount of food for themselves and their friends, and brings it into class.

Cracking down on it, though, could be tricky.

“I don't really know how they would enforce a policy where you're not allowed to order something, because kids are going to do it anyways. They'll end up rebelling because you put another policy in,” said Grade 12 student Alysa Utigard.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: MAGIC: The Manufacturing of the Adversary
World.content:
“So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen, since what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.” — 2 Corinthians 4:18

By Lynn Cruz

HAVANA TIMES – Over time, Cuba could come to be seen as an island full of hostages. The story began with a revolution that promised to fulfill the ideals of the 1953 attack on the Moncada barracks. Fidel Castro had the exceptional ability to turn words into physical reality. A political animal and a lucky man, he awakened genuine hopes for social justice, sovereignty, and access to education and culture.

But when did the story begin to go wrong? Perhaps when one man’s power began to be confused with the destiny of a nation. Nationalizations, debts, and restrictions progressively narrowed the room for maneuver until the Revolution became a Leviathan. The consequences fell upon a people also trapped in a collective identity and a war against imperialism that outlived its central figure.

Fidel Castro lands in Washington, D.C.

From the Image to the Algorithm

In 1959, the Cuban Institute of Cinematographic Art and Industry (ICAIC) was established. Beginning in 1960, the ICAIC Latin American Newsreel, directed by Santiago Alvarez, produced 1,493 editions through 1990. Constructing political images required time, coordination, and control over the channels through which they circulated. That control also extended to the press. But editing is not correcting: it means making decisions about thought itself. Even documenting reality involves constructing a representation of it.

Fidel Castro died on November 25, 2016. He had been a speechmaking machine, a creator of political content whose voice occupied public and domestic spaces for decades. With the Internet and social media, the circulation of images changed. Post-truth found new means of expansion, and those in power learned to adapt. The Leviathan can mutate; its mechanisms of control do not disappear.

Since 2021, we have all become increasingly attached to the machine. What have algorithms changed? And what is changing now with artificial intelligence?

The Manufacturing of the Adversary

I want to focus on October 26, eight days before the US midterm elections. That day, Donald Trump and Truth Social seemed to speak with a single voice. Cubans, accustomed to seeing Granma present an official version of the truth, have historical reasons to distrust a platform that carries that word in its name.

Between 4:33 and 4:34 p.m., four Democratic figures appeared in succession: Adam Hamilton, Ilhan Omar, James Talarico, and Abdul El-Sayed. Four different contexts, reduced to controversies over identity, race, citizenship, gender, and religion. Six minutes later, the electoral endorsements began. At 4:52 p.m., Trump endorsed Sydney Gruters, a candidate in Florida’s 16th Congressional District, wife of then-state senator Joe Gruters, a Trump ally and the current chairman of the Republican National Committee. Her opponent, Kelly Kirschner, was portrayed as radical, reckless, and dangerous.

Attention shifted. What mattered was no longer what the candidates would do if elected, but which side they were on and what identity they represented.

Collage created in Photoshop using images of Sydney Gruters, Joe Gruters, Donald Trump, and Trump’s second inauguration ceremony.

Congressional District 16 is located on Florida’s west coast, in the Tampa Bay region along the Gulf of Mexico. Under the new 2026 electoral map, it includes portions of six counties: Manatee, Sarasota, DeSoto, Hardee, Polk, and Pinellas. It also includes part of St. Petersburg.

I met Kirschner personally. That is why I was not looking at an abstract confrontation between political parties: I was following people, their stories, and the communities they claimed to represent. His repeated invitations to his opponent to participate in a debate caught my attention. Accustomed to the absence of dialogue between those in power and the opposition in Cuba, I recognized a fundamental question: What happens when disagreement ceases to be an opportunity for conversation and becomes a spectacle?

Kirschner had built his career through community work. He participated in neighborhood mobilization efforts for Payne Park, a public park near Sarasota. As mayor, he promoted campaign finance reforms and, through UnidosNow, an organization he co-founded, helped first-generation students gain access to college. Gruters, by contrast, developed her career within political and administrative institutions. Her campaign defended familiar conservative priorities: taxes, border security, education, and family values.

Kelly Kirschner and his team connect with the community. Screeshot

Florida: The Stage for Magic

In 2022, after Disney criticized the Parental Rights in Education law, known by its critics as “Don’t Say Gay,” Governor Ron DeSantis pushed to eliminate the special administrative autonomy of Reedy Creek, a special improvement district created in 1967 by the Florida legislature to manage and provide municipal services (water, electricity, roads, fire protection) to the lands of the Walt Disney World Resort. The dispute became a political and legal battle.

Disney is a factory of stories. Florida became the stage for another kind of factory: one that manufactures adversarial characters. And onto that stage stepped Sydney Gruters. Sydney, Disney: two names that, when brought together, seem to suggest something more than a coincidence of sound. Magic ceased to be merely entertainment and became a metaphor for the power to manufacture realities.

There, politics, entertainment, and business shared the same landscape of representation. Disney, culturally associated with a liberal worldview, and DeSantis, a representative of Republican conservatism, appeared to occupy opposite extremes. Yet their interests revealed that party colors do not always define the principal boundaries of power.

I ask: “Mr. Trump, did you write the script for Sydney Gruters’ campaign?”

All we know is that there were flyers, a post on Truth Social, and a video that translated those words into images. The written word begins to abandon its role, and in its place—much like a memory—there emerges this fictional image.

AI-generated image: Kelly Kirschner transformed into a knight. On the right, Countess Sydney de Gruters, Joe Gruters, Donald Trump, and his technological court.

The Child as Political Territory

While major technology companies promote artificial intelligence literacy, pro-Gruters propaganda constructed another image of childhood: that of a child threatened by a cultural transformation from which someone had to protect them. A flyer from the super PAC Conservatives for American Excellence used AI-generated images to portray that threat.

I ask: “Mr. Trump, did you write the script for Sydney Gruters’ campaign?”

All we know is that there were flyers, a post on Truth Social, and a video that translated those words into images. The written word begins to abandon its role, and in its place—much like a memory—there emerges this fictional image.

AI-generated image.

When the defense of transgender rights became part of Democratic discourse, an aspiration toward inclusion emerged. But what happens when a cause ceases to be discussed and becomes an identity marker, a boundary separating one group from another? Childhood became the center of a dispute among adults. Children appeared less as individuals with rights than as figures in a political representation.

MAGIC

On October 28, six days before the elections, an artificial intelligence-generated video appeared on television showing Kelly Kirschner being arrested. The words Trump had posted two days earlier were now being transformed into images. First came the flyers, then the text, and finally the video, paid for by Gruters’ own campaign.

The image evoked the assassination of Lee Harvey Oswald during his transfer in police custody in Dallas in 1963. But the difference was fundamental: Oswald had actually been arrested; Kirschner appeared in a fictional situation, digitally fabricated. The image no longer needed to document an event. It could produce one.

It is easier to dismantle a lie than a fiction. A lie can be checked against the facts; fiction constructs a scene, creates associations, and leaves images in the memory. It does not need to prove what it tells: it needs the viewer to remember it.

Florida, After Texas

The Republican defeat in Texas has a central figure who was not on the ballot but had invested hundreds of millions of dollars to influence the outcome: Elon Musk. The businessman hoped to maintain Republican control of the state, but found himself facing a Democratic victory that threatens to change the conditions under which his technological projects can expand. The newly elected governor, Gina Hinojosa, has promised to halt permits for new data centers until safeguards are established for communities, water supplies, and the electrical grid.

Musk responded with a statement worth noting: Data centers in space were beginning to look like an attractive alternative.

But while Texas prepares to review the conditions governing that expansion, Florida offers another setting. There, tax incentives and legislation favorable to certain technological investments coexist with growing community resistance to the consumption of water, electricity, and land required by these facilities.

Could Florida become a new frontier for Musk’s technological interests?

District 16 was one battle over control of political representation. What is at stake in the rest of the country is much greater: who controls technology, who pays the price of its expansion, and who has the power to manufacture the images through which citizens interpret reality.

Propaganda can win an election. The infrastructure that makes it possible can determine who will have the power to construct the next reality.

And Cuba? Where will Cuba fit into all this? This increasingly abstract island.

Read more from Lynn Cruz’s diary here on Havana Times.

World.title: Journalist Who Reported on Drug Trafficking Murdered in Costa Rica
World.content:
Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez. Foto: Tomada de redes sociales

Camilo Rodríguez had reported death threats and declined to enter a protection program recommended by the Prosecutor’s Office.

By EFE (Confidencial)

HAVANA TIMES – Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who reported on drug trafficking cases through his social media accounts, was murdered on Monday, November 16, 2026, while driving his vehicle, apparently by hitmen riding a motorcycle.

The Judicial Investigation Agency reported that the case is under investigation as authorities work to identify those responsible for the crime.

Costa Rica’s Attorney General, Carlo Diaz, confirmed the victim’s identity to Channel 7 and said that Camilo Rodriguez had reported threats against his life and was receiving assistance through a victim and witness support program. However, he had declined to enter a protection program recommended by the Prosecutor’s Office.

The murder occurred in San Miguel de Santo Domingo, in the central province of Heredia, when the victim was driving his vehicle and was shot, apparently by two hitmen on a motorcycle.

Rodriguez frequently posted videos on social media denouncing drug trafficking and corruption cases. He even identified individuals by their full names, linking them to local and international criminal organizations.

“Part of the investigation will involve examining the victim’s background, reviewing all the people he publicly denounced on social media, as well as anyone else who might have had an interest in killing him. The Judicial Investigation Agency and the Prosecutor’s Office will make a major effort to identify those responsible for this death,” Attorney General Diaz said.

He also expressed regret over the crime, describing it as “a very strong indication that we do not have freedom of expression in this country and that if we denounce these acts, we could be subjected to a death like this.”

In his social media posts, Rodríguez often said that he turned over all his investigations to the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

The last Costa Rican journalists to be murdered were Parmenio Medina, in 2001, and Ivania Mora, in 2003.

Medina was the producer of the radio program La Patada, which exposed acts of corruption in Costa Rica. He was killed on July 7, 2001, near his home after three unidentified individuals shot him from a car.

Mora, meanwhile, was murdered while driving along a busy road in eastern San Jose, where two men shot her from a motorcycle before fleeing.

In recent years, Costa Rica has experienced record-high homicide figures, with approximately 900 killings annually. Authorities attribute 70% of these deaths to drug trafficking, with the vast majority committed using firearms.

The Judicial Investigation Agency has warned that, because of its strategic geographic location, Costa Rica has become a hub for the transit, storage, and reexport of cocaine originating in South America and destined for North America and Europe.

First published in Spanish by Confidencial and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: A Streetcar Named Cojimar
World.content:
The Hershey train stopped in Cojimar until 1957.

Photo Feature by Nike

HAVANA TIMES – I was reading a story written by a childhood friend in which he expresses his nostalgia for the first day he visited Cojimar and my family’s home.

The story inspired me to write this article for you.

In the 1930s, a train service was inaugurated in the town of Cojimar, allowing residents to travel to the city of Havana. The train ran along the entire length of G Street—which still exists today—where, until not too long ago, sections of the railway tracks could still be seen protruding from the pavement between 30th and 31st Streets.

Cojimar became part of the Hershey railway project in this area of Havana. The US businessman had built an entire town, complete with a sugar mill, housing, and hospitals for his workers. He did so around the time of the Great Depression in the United States because he needed sugar for his chocolates.

The train departed from the town of Casablanca, where the station was located. With the Hershey railway lines intersecting in the area, it was decided to establish a train service to Cojímar, connecting the town with Havana, where electric streetcars were already operating at the time. In the photographs, you will see a map of Havana’s streetcar network in 1930, marked in blue, with the Hershey electric railway connecting Casablanca and Cojimar marked in red.

The train entered Cojímar along G Street and crossed the entire town until it reached a block from the sea. There, it made a loop and headed back, passing very close to private farms.

There were several stops along the route, including one with a café called “La Línea” (The Line). Upon leaving town, the train followed the road known as “Los Curas” (The Priests), so named because there was a Franciscan monastery there. All that remains of the monastery today are two walls, but the road is still known by that name.

The last train departed at 11 p.m. The electric train, which was quiet and produced no pollution, was taken out of service in 1957 and replaced by gasoline-powered buses.

The train ended its journey at the Casablanca station. To reach Havana, passengers crossed the bay aboard a ferry that still operates today, known as “La Lanchita de Casablanca.” There is also another ferry in Regla, better known as “La Lanchita de Regla,” which still exists. Nowadays, however, there is almost always just one ferry serving both routes between Havana, Regla, and Casablanca.

In the 1930s, Cojimar was a very rural town, surrounded by farms with cows, horses, and chickens. People were accustomed to letting their animals roam freely. Cojimar was like one enormous farm, and many residents saw the streetcar as an intruder in their lives.

I mention this because accidents involving cows and horses began to occur. The residents who owned these animals went to complain to the mayor of Cojimar, asking him to demand that the railway company install a fence along the entire train route to prevent further accidents.

The mayor met with the company, and a dispute over the fence began. After several meetings, the company refused to build it, claiming it lacked the necessary funds. In the end, the townspeople had to fence in their animals, and there were no more accidents.

Civilization brings many good things for some people, while others find it very difficult to accept progress, even when it benefits everyone. For the animals that had to spend their lives confined, however, it was no benefit at all.

See more photo features here on Havana Times.

World.title: Cuban Police Prepare Block-by-Block Offensive vs. Starlink
World.content:
Satellite internet access is being sought as an alternative to the deficiencies of Etecsa, the state telecommunications monopoly. / CiberCuba

Some users are removing their antennas amid threats by the regime to confiscate the devices because they allegedly pose a risk to “national security.

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – On the rooftops of Los Sitios, one of Havana’s most densely populated neighborhoods, pigeon lofts and water tanks have begun sharing space with devices that Cuban authorities view with growing suspicion: Starlink antennas. Some remain in plain sight, while others are concealed behind makeshift coverings.

Caleb, 21, has observed this transformation from his pigeon loft, where he raises more than a dozen birds. “At first, I only saw water tanks and cages like mine, but now there are solar panels and Starlink antennas, too,” he tells 14ymedio. “Even though people cover them up, it’s easy to tell what they are.”

An old plastic tank, a curtain, or a mesh covering can be used to conceal a satellite terminal. Some nonmetallic materials allow radio waves to pass through, although they can weaken the signal, especially when they become wet.

A few days ago, Caleb’s mother passed along a warning. The woman remains involved with the Committees for the Defense of the Revolution (CDRs) and occasionally attends meetings with municipal or provincial officials. According to the young man, at one of these meetings it was reported that authorities were conducting a “block-by-block survey of who has Starlink.”

Caleb hurried to warn several acquaintances. Some, he says, have already removed their equipment, while others are planning to do so “until the storm passes.”

The concern is not limited to Havana rooftops. In various parts of Cuba, Starlink owners fear that authorities will intensify their search for antennas, identify their users, and impose new sanctions. Warnings are circulating among neighbors, buyers, and sellers as satellite internet spreads as an alternative to the deficiencies of Etecsa, the state telecommunications monopoly.

The battle against Starlink began in 2025

The Cuban Government’s battle against Starlink is not new. Since April 2025, authorities have announced restrictions and confiscations involving this equipment. That month, Customs reported the confiscation of 20 satellite internet kits and the seizure of other telecommunications devices.

In May 2026, the Official Gazette published two resolutions from the Ministry of Communications updating the procedures for technical authorization, equipment certification, and imports. The regulations establish controls over data-transmission and satellite communications devices, although their application depends on the characteristics of each device and the corresponding authorizations.

On November 9, the offensive took on an unprecedented diplomatic dimension that clashes with the immunity enjoyed by embassies. A communication from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, obtained by 14ymedio, reminded embassies and international organizations accredited on the Island that the importation and use of Starlink devices are also prohibited for them. The document refers to a diplomatic note from January 2025, confirming that the warning is part of an earlier restrictive policy.

But one of the authorities’ most revealing arguments does not appear in the customs regulations. Last Saturday, the government-aligned newspaper 5 de Septiembre published an article by Pablo Morales Concepción, territorial director of the Ministry of Communications Regulatory Control Office in Cienfuegos, presenting Starlink as a national security and sovereignty problem.

The official points out that these devices use encryption systems and that their traffic travels through foreign infrastructure, without any possibility of being audited by Cuban authorities. Among the risks he lists are the transmission of information without state supervision, the creation of parallel communications networks, and the circulation of unregulated content.

Morales’s stated concern goes beyond possible radio interference or the absence of permits. His article identifies the existence of communications beyond state supervision as a national security risk. That independence from Etecsa’s access infrastructure is precisely one of Starlink’s main attractions for many users on the Island.

Crackdown spreads fear

For Marcia, 66, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, the fear of losing that connection ceased to be an abstract possibility.

“My son sent me the money to buy a Starlink because communicating was becoming increasingly difficult, and he gets very anxious over there in Miami because he wants to know how I am and how his father is doing, since he suffers from ALS,” she tells 14ymedio.

In May, her son, who had emigrated, sent her $1,500. His mother contacted some informal sellers on Facebook who offered home delivery. A young couple arrived on an electric motorcycle, checked that the equipment worked, and set up the connection so that her son could pay the subscription from the United States.

The terminal, which according to the box came from Mexico, was installed on a balcony that could not be seen from the street. During the first few weeks, everything worked without difficulty. Marcia was able to see her son again through video calls and access websites she had previously been unable to open.

Until one day a police officer showed up at her home with a summons.

At the police station, she was told that her name appeared in a WhatsApp chat belonging to informal sellers who were under investigation for marketing Starlink equipment. The officers, she recalls, linked this activity to “National Security.”

Marcia explained that she had contacted the merchants because she was interested in an electric coffee maker that she ultimately did not purchase. She had never mentioned Starlink in the written messages, and the details of the purchase had been discussed over a phone call.

According to her account, she managed to leave without being penalized thanks to that explanation. She believes her gray hair and lack of a criminal record may also have worked in her favor.

“I got off by a miracle, because that same day there were other people at the station in the same situation, and some received fines. I also heard that several patrol cars had gone out to search a house belonging to people who sold Starlink.”

When she returned to her apartment, Marcia decided to get rid of the equipment and asked her son to cancel the subscription. “I can’t live with this fear,” she admits. “I’m now too old to be hiding, and what I saw at the police station was frightening, because they talked about Starlink as if someone were preparing a bomb in their house.”

Methods used to find Starlink terminals

To locate Starlink terminals, authorities could resort to various technological surveillance methods. One would involve using radio-frequency spectrum analyzers and radio direction-finding equipment, which can identify radio-frequency emissions and estimate where they originate. They could also use drones to observe rooftops and terraces or examine aerial images in search of the distinctive antennas used by the satellite service.

But the simplest, cheapest, and potentially most effective way to discover these devices is less sophisticated: informing on others. A neighbor’s complaint, surveillance by the CDRs, or a tip from someone who knows about an unauthorized connection can lead authorities to a home without requiring the deployment of expensive tracking equipment. In a country where the political surveillance apparatus has relied for decades on an extensive network of informants and collaborators, this is the cheapest and most effective tracking mechanism.

Informal Starlink sales have already resulted in criminal and administrative proceedings, according to reports circulated by government-aligned sources. Last October, a publication sympathetic to the Government reported prison sentences of four and five years for antenna sellers in Santa Clara. It also mentioned the seizure of 37 devices and fines of 100,000 pesos imposed on buyers.

On the outskirts of Matanzas, a 16-year-old uses a Starlink Mini to play online games with his friends. His father, who emigrated several years ago, sent him the money to buy the device and pays the subscription from abroad. “I have a group of friends who pay me a fee because I share the signal with them. We’re all from the same neighborhood,” says the boy, who requests anonymity.

To distribute the connection, the group has routers, Wi-Fi antennas, and network cables. They have also acquired EcoFlow power stations and solar panels to keep the equipment running during blackouts. The young man says his goal is “to play games and escape a little from everything that’s happening.”

“We don’t get involved in politics at all. I don’t know why they’ve suddenly taken issue with this,” he laments. “Most of the people I know who have Starlink use it for business, watching videos, playing games, and staying out of anything controversial.”

In his neighborhood, he explains, Etecsa coverage is very poor, and the nearby telecommunications tower frequently goes out of service because of a lack of batteries. The most recent blackout, he says, lasted three days. “Why do they want to take away the only thing that keeps us from having to get on a boat and leave this country?” he asks.

Meanwhile, in San Miguel del Padrón, another Starlink user acknowledges that his connection serves a very different purpose: managing bets on la bolita, the illegal numbers game that remains widespread in everyday Cuban life.

“There’s no way to get the winning numbers quickly unless you use one of these devices,” says the numbers-game operator. But finding out the Florida lottery results is only part of his business. Communication with customers takes place primarily through WhatsApp.

“People tell me which number they want to bet on and how much money they want to put on it, and all of that goes through the phone, no little slips of paper.” An assistant is responsible for collecting the betting money. Electronic transfers are also accepted on occasion, although the operator prefers to avoid them for fear that those transactions might attract the authorities’ attention.

The stable connection allows him to keep customers informed and reduce disputes over results or incorrectly recorded bets. “Without Starlink, I would already have ended up with a knife wound, because people get difficult when there’s an error with the numbers, or when several hours have passed and nobody has announced the winning numbers,” he explains.

He now fears that restrictions against the antennas will make an already illegal activity even more difficult. “I have friends with good connections who keep me informed, and these days they’ve been telling me to lie low and take the antenna out of my house because they’re going to come after me.”

His main concern is that too many people know the device exists. “My business is clandestine but public, and all it takes is one tip-off for them to come down on me,” he admits.

Ways Starlink setups are sold for delivery in Cuba

The expansion of Starlink also raises questions about the routes through which the devices enter the country, their sale, and the possible political use authorities could make of these distribution operations. The increasingly small and portable size of the devices makes it possible to camouflage them inside other electronic equipment, such as televisions.

A source involved in the international satellite telecommunications market told 14ymedio, on condition of anonymity, that during the first quarter of 2026, more than 1,000 Starlink Mini devices were purchased abroad for delivery to Cuba. According to the source, the order was so large that it exhausted the stock held by official Starlink distributors in that market. Suppliers reportedly even had to commit to future deliveries to complete the transaction.

The source maintains that the service offers more limited performance than conventional commercial connections but is sufficient for browsing the internet, using WhatsApp, accessing social networks, and viewing video platforms. In the source’s interpretation, the initiative was intended to facilitate access to communications independent of Etecsa in a country where blackouts, poor coverage, and the blocking of certain websites make internet access difficult.

What surprises the source most is not only the number of terminals purchased, but the apparent ease with which they reportedly entered Cuba and subsequently reached their recipients. Based on experience in the sector, the source considers it unlikely that an operation of such magnitude could have been carried out in such a short time without the knowledge, authorization, or cooperation of certain Cuban authorities.

According to numerous accounts published in internet forums, some of these devices work in Cuba without a subscription activated by the user or their relatives abroad. Although SpaceX has not publicly confirmed the existence of a specific free program for Cuba or how long it might last, the accounts are consistent with information provided to 14ymedio by this source, who says that certain devices are receiving service without their recipients paying a monthly fee.

The source also raises the possibility that authorities might eventually portray the mass entry of these devices as an operation of subversion organized from exile. In the source’s interpretation, the purchase and distribution of terminals financed from abroad could serve as grounds for accusing certain sectors of attempting to create a parallel communications infrastructure intended to disseminate information outside state control or facilitate the coordination of protests.

That hypothesis finds a point of convergence with the rhetoric already appearing in official media, such as the 5 de Septiembre article about Starlink’s alleged dangers to national security.

In this scenario, Starlink antennas have become something more than a technological alternative. For some, they represent the possibility of talking to relatives, keeping a business running, or escaping the everyday crisis for a few hours. For the authorities, according to the narrative beginning to take shape in official media, they constitute a tool that could encourage a social explosion. And, unlike what happened on 11 July 2021 [’11J’], there would be no way to disconnect the networks.

The ban surrounding these antennas in Cuba has affected Maykel, even though he has lived in Florida for years. When he went to send a package to his family in Havana through the Cubamax company, an employee warned him sternly: “Absolutely no sending Starlink to Cuba disguised in the package. Your family could go to prison if they receive something like that.” The emigrant took the threat very seriously and warned his relatives that “things have gotten very bad” regarding Musk’s devices.

The possibility of providing free internet through Starlink has also been part of discussions between Washington and Havana. Last April, a senior U.S. State Department official told the EFE news agency that a delegation from his country had proposed that the Cuban Government allow free, fast, and reliable access to Elon Musk’s satellite network. The proposal came weeks after the businessman publicly confirmed that Starlink was working in Cuba, although it could not be marketed there. So far, the Island’s authorities have not commented on the offer, but their current hostility toward these devices clearly reveals their position.

Meanwhile, on the rooftops of Los Sitios, some cautious owners have already opted to remove their equipment before the hunt for unauthorized antennas begins. They do not need to know whether the authorities have instruments capable of locating a device from a distance. It is enough for them to suspect that someone, from a nearby window or during a neighborhood meeting, might point out the roof where it is hidden.

Translated by Regina Anavy for Translating Cuba.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Tuesday, November 17, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Tuesday, November 17, 2026.

Trump Arrives in Philippines Ahead of ASEAN Summit and Meeting with Putin, Xi

Nov 17, 2026

President Trump has arrived in the Philippines on the first leg of a 48-hour trip to Asia. Trump landed in Manila aboard the new Air Force One, a luxury 747 jet gifted to him by the government of Qatar. He’s scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ahead of the ASEAN summit of Southeast Asian nations. Trump’s visit has drawn large protests in Manila, where police arrested hundreds of people over the weekend. Students, workers and progressive groups are demanding an end to the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran and are protesting against plans to build an artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub near Manila.

On Thursday, Trump will hold an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump also said he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un while in China.

Trump Says He “Would Not Mind” Seeing Jensen Huang Restored as CEO of Nvidia

Nov 17, 2026

The Trump administration said Monday it would investigate Megaspeed, the Singapore-based cloud computing firm that’s accused of sending advanced Nvidia computer chips to China, in violation of U.S. export controls. The investigation follows Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, after he admitted he’d had an extramarital affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. Megaspeed said on Sunday she had left the company more than a year ago. On Monday, President Trump responded to reports that Jensen Huang is in discussions with allies about a potential return to Nvidia.

Reporter: “Mr. President, do you want to see Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia?”

bq. President Donald Trump: “I would — I would not mind. I would not mind that. I like — you know, I threw out the name of Tim Cook. But I would say that the — Jensen’s reinstatement, I think he learned a big lesson, I guess maybe one lesson more important than another. But I would certainly not mind seeing that.”

Trump Takes “No Responsibility” for Largest FAA Ground Stop Since 9/11

Nov 17, 2026

United Airlines canceled dozens of departing flights and delayed more than 800 others on Monday after a system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes. United blamed a “technical issue,” without elaborating, and said in a statement there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

This comes after the FAA ordered a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop on Friday, causing over 18,000 flight cancellations and more than 28,000 delays. It was the largest disruption of its kind to U.S. air travel since the 9/11 attacks. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is due to brief senators about the incident today. On Monday, President Trump said Duffy had his full support, and blamed the Biden administration for the grounded flights.

President Donald Trump: “I don’t take any responsibility. They did a great job. Secretary Duffy, they acted incredibly. Everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.”

Shortly after taking office in January 2025, Trump signed an executive order freezing the remaining funds in a $25 billion Biden-era appropriation to modernize flight infrastructure. Trump and Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, DOGE, fired 400 FAA workers and granted 1,300 others early retirement offers or buyouts.

JPMorgan Chase Blames “Software Bug” After Customers Lose Access to Accounts and Services

Nov 17, 2026

Customers at major U.S. banks lost access to their accounts for several hours on Monday, after JPMorgan Chase reported a “temporary issue related to a software bug.” The outage began around 10 a.m. Eastern time and continued until early evening. It left thousands of people unable to use the money transfer service Zelle and caused problems for customers at several other U.S. banks, including Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Bank of America. JPMorgan Chase said the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack.

Meanwhile, Microsoft said Monday that last week’s global outage affecting services including Outlook, Teams and Copilot was due to a hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, along with increased traffic demand and reduced server capacity.

Israel Failed to Meet Commitments to Deliver Food and Supplies to Gaza

Nov 17, 2026

In Gaza, Israeli forces killed a young Palestinian man and wounded others in an attack east of the city of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza. Elsewhere, Israeli forces killed one Palestinian and injured five in the north, while in southern Gaza, Israeli forces shot and wounded three Palestinians, including a child, inside a school.

The latest killings come as Israel has failed to meet its aid commitments under the Gaza ceasefire deal. Data obtained by Haaretz showed decreasing food deliveries to Gaza, alongside severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair damaged infrastructure. The U.N. is also urging the protection of aid workers and hospitals. This is U.N. spokesperson Farhan Haq.

Farhan Haq: “Yesterday, an Israeli airstrike hit very close to a U.N.-led fuel convoy in Rafah. We are concerned that strikes at targets near our staff and vehicles, especially vehicles carrying fuel, expose them to unacceptable risks. Civilians, including humanitarian workers, must always be protected.”

Israeli Opposition Slams Netanyahu’s “Attempted Coup” over Framed Arab MKs

Nov 17, 2026

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing scrutiny after he claimed Israel’s October 27 election was stolen. Now there are new allegations that his administration interfered in the election. An investigation by Israel’s Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu aides gave police tips shortly before the vote, which led to Arab party workers being arrested on Election Day. The report also said the Shin Bet chief, whom Netanyahu personally appointed, tried to wiretap five Arab members of parliament. Following the report, the head of the opposition, Gadi Eisenkot, said, “Under no circumstances can Netanyahu remain at the helm of government for even one more minute. Under no circumstances must Israel be dragged into another election with him as prime minister.” Netanyahu had been pressuring Eisenkot to form a unity government with his right-wing Likud party.

Iran Attacks U.S. Radar Station in Bahrain, Says It Captured U.S. Drone

Nov 17, 2026

Bahrain’s military says it intercepted an Iranian drone strike targeting a U.S. radar facility — the third attack of its kind in recent days. The assault came after U.S. Central Command announced a third carrier strike group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, had arrived in the Middle East, adding about 10,000 sailors and Marines to U.S. forces in the region.

Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it had hacked the flight guidance system of a U.S.-made MQM-170 drone and landed it remotely, intact. It’s the latest in a series of similar claims by Iran. Meanwhile, three more vessels caught fire while transiting the Strait of Hormuz today, including a ship carrying liquefied natural gas and a supertanker holding more than 2 million barrels of crude oil.

Ukrainian Strike Damages Bridge Linking Crimea to Russia

Nov 17, 2026

Russia reports that Ukraine has carried out its largest drone strike of the war so far. According to Moscow, the attack damaged the major bridge connecting Russia with occupied Crimea and struck several oil refineries. Russian officials say their forces shot down over 2,000 drones and four long-range Flamingo missiles in a 24-hour period. Moscow’s mayor said about 600 of those drones were aimed at the capital. Meanwhile, Kyiv had 17 air raid alerts in one day, the most on record. Russian strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine, as attacks on energy infrastructure left 50,000 people without power.

Largest Union of U.S. Nurses Endorses Sen. Van Hollen for Senate Majority Leader

Nov 17, 2026

The largest union of nurses in the United States has endorsed Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen to lead the Senate Democratic caucus when the new Congress begins in January. In a statement, National Nurses United wrote, “The Democratic Party must not squander the chance midterm voters have given it to tackle our nation in crisis. Nurses and working people demand new Senate leadership that confronts the billionaire class, corporations, and governments to deliver transformative change for us. Sen. Van Hollen is the best person for the job.” The endorsement came after Van Hollen said he had a path to defeat New York Senator Chuck Schumer in a contested leadership challenge. Van Hollen was interviewed on CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen: “This is not about one person or any one individual. This really is a response to the call of the voters, who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies. But they haven’t fully hired the Democrats. They’ve given us a chance, and I think we need to earn their trust. And I think that begins by not going back to business as usual, not going back to the status quo.”

Meanwhile, Senator Van Hollen told Politico he supports New York Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker.

Study Shows U.S. Hyperscale Data Centers Produce Carbon Emissions Equivalent to Denmark

Nov 17, 2026

In climate news, a new study shows that U.S. hyperscale data centers produce carbon emissions equivalent to the entire nation of Denmark. Harvard researchers published the findings in Monday’s edition of Nature Sustainability. The study found just 403 of the largest U.S. data centers consume about 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a single year, rivaling many U.S. states, including Michigan. The study came as Turkey’s environment minister said from the COP31 climate summit in Antalya that world leaders must address AI’s growing energy consumption. This is Julie Cerqueira of the Natural Resources Defense Council.

Julie Cerqueira: “They’re not small buildings; they’re entire warehouses. They absorb entire communities. Oftentimes they’re up against neighborhoods. And so, I think it is right that communities think of them as major industrial projects, and that’s how we should treat them.”

Turkish Authorities Take Control of Pro-Opposition Media Outlet

Nov 17, 2026

In more news from Turkey, Turkish authorities raided the Istanbul headquarters of the pro-opposition Sözcü TV earlier today and took the channel off the air, while appointing a trustee to run the channel and its website. Four executives from Sözcü TV have also been detained. Since last month, the two remaining opposition channels have been brought under government control. This follows the Turkish government’s widespread crackdown on the main opposition party with dozens of mayors arrested since 2024.

Ecuadorian Fishermen Who Survived U.S. Boat Strike Sue Trump Administration

Nov 17, 2026

A group of 16 Ecuadorian fishermen who survived a U.S. military strike on their boat are suing the Trump administration. On March 17, two military drones launched from a U.S.-operated vessel exploded on their fishing boat, sinking it and severely burning two of its crew members. The fishermen say they were intercepted by English-speaking military personnel who then transferred them to the custody of Salvadoran forces. The attack came as part of Trump’s widespread military strikes on boats off the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific since September of last year that have killed as many as 250 people accused — without evidence — of being involved in drug trafficking. In the lawsuit, the 16 fishermen say they have no connection with the drug trade and that they were illegally targeted as they returned from a two-week fishing trip. Human Rights Watch reports Ecuadorian courts have acquitted at least 40 survivors of U.S. boat strikes of any wrongdoing, while 56 others have been released from custody without charge.

8-Year-Old Haitian Boy Reunites with Family After Weeks in Federal Detention

Nov 17, 2026

In immigration news, an 8-year-old Haitian boy has been reunited with his family after two weeks in a federal detention center in Texas. ICE took the third-grade student into custody earlier this month at a scheduled immigration appointment in San Diego. The boy had been living with his uncle since his father was deported last year. Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement, “His freedom should never have required a public outcry. No child should endure the trauma that he has been through.”

ICE Agents Pepper-Spray Pregnant U.S. Citizen

Nov 17, 2026

In more immigration news, outrage is mounting after a new video shows ICE agents pepper-spraying a 23-year-old pregnant U.S. citizen and forcing her to the ground on her belly. Lizbeth Vargas Andrade was filming an anti-ICE protest in Modesto, California, Sunday; she is also part of a group that monitors ICE activity in the area. In a video filmed by her husband, the agents are seen throwing her on the ground and aggressively cuffing Andrade with her stomach against the pavement. Her husband, Adolfo Talavera, can be heard shouting, “She’s pregnant with child!” as the agents move to detain his wife. Andrade says she also told the ICE agents she was pregnant. She was released from custody later that day with no criminal charges.

Press Groups Call for Justice After Mexican Journalist Found Dead

Nov 17, 2026

In Mexico, press freedom groups are calling for justice after Mexican journalist Eduardo Flores Salado was found dead in Acapulco over the weekend. Salado reported on security, missing persons and social issues. Authorities in the state of Guerrero have opened a homicide investigation. This is a community activist and one of Salado’s friends.

Alberto Serna Mogollon: “They slit his throat on Saturday, and yesterday, Sunday, he was found dead. It’s a crime that fills all of us in Guerrero with outrage, all journalists, and especially the LGBT community. Lalo was part of our LGBT community, our group. He was very supportive. He would send us his articles so we could get our activities out there in the press.”

The press freedom group Article 19 reports at least six journalists have been killed in Mexico so far this year. Reporters Without Borders ranked Mexico as the world’s second-deadliest country for journalists in 2025 — behind Gaza.

Read more news here on Havana Times.
