In Peru, retail revenue rose 7.4% when measured in Chilean pesos, and same-store sales, which compare shops open in both periods, rose 6.0%. Retail profit there tripled in Peruvian soles, and in Chilean pesos it rose to about 0.97 billion (about US$1 million) from 0.3 billion (about US$0.3 million).

Banco Ripley Peru’s loans grew 9.9% in Peruvian soles, and its profit rose 5.9%. Together with the Peru stores, it helped offset the weaker Chilean stores, the company said.

Mall Aventura, Ripley’s Peruvian shopping-mall unit, raised revenue 13.4%. Consolidated occupancy, including office towers, rose to 97.7% from 97.2%.

In Chile, the real estate segment’s profit rose 21.4% to 4.099 billion pesos (about US$4.1 million). Grupo Marina, a mall company in which Ripley holds 50%, helped.

Why the Bank Carried the Quarter

Banco Ripley Chile, the group’s consumer bank, lifted profit 46.7% to 13.164 billion pesos (about US$13.3 million). The bank alone earned more than twice the group’s net profit of 5.787 billion pesos (about US$5.8 million).

Its gross loan book grew 20.2%, and its revenue rose 17.0%. Its efficiency ratio, which is costs as a share of revenue, improved to 33.6% from 40.4%.

Faster lending carries risk. Cost of risk rose to 11.4% from 9.4%, which means the bank set aside more money for loans that may go bad.

Loans more than 90 days overdue stayed stable at 3.6%. The company ties the larger provisions to loan growth and a tougher economic and regulatory climate.

Retail Chile, the department-store arm, saw revenue fall 7.0% to 188.547 billion pesos (about US$190 million), and gross margin, the share of sales left after product costs, slipped to 28.8% from 29.4%. Online sales partly offset the decline.

Chief financial officer Werner Geissbühler said in the results release that the quarter showed the value of a diversified business. He said the bank and Peru did very well while Retail Chile faced a tougher consumer climate, where Ripley keeps prioritising cost discipline and the online channel.

What It Means for You

For a US investor, no US listing of Ripley is known. Any exposure would need access to the Santiago market, and this article is not investment advice.

What to Watch

Retail Chile is the line to follow, because its revenue fell 7.0% while the bank grew. Ripley’s next quarterly results will show whether the decline is easing.

The bank’s cost of risk is the second number to follow, because it rose to 11.4% from 9.4%. Loans more than 90 days overdue stayed at 3.6%, so any rise there would be an early warning.

Our Chile reporting is gathered on the Chile hub. It covers markets, politics and daily life.

What Is Not Known

Ripley’s share-price reaction to the results is not known. No analyst consensus for the quarter is confirmed, so no beat or miss is stated.

Nine-month totals rest on a single source and are left out. The full primary results document was not available at the time of writing, and the record is silent on any 2026 profit target.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Ripley earn in the third quarter of 2026?

Ripley earned 5.787 billion pesos (about US$5.8 million), up 53.2% from a year earlier. It reported the result on Tuesday, 17 November 2026.

Why did profit rise while store sales fell?

Banco Ripley Chile, the consumer bank, grew profit 46.7% to 13.164 billion pesos (about US$13.3 million), and Peru did well. Chilean department-store revenue fell 7.0%.

Can US investors buy Ripley shares?

Ripley’s shares trade in Santiago. No US listing is confirmed, so access needs the Chilean market.

What is the risk in the bank’s numbers?

Cost of risk, which is net provisions as a share of average loans, rose to 11.4% from 9.4%. Loans more than 90 days overdue stayed at 3.6%.

Sources: Ripley Corp, third-quarter 2026 results statement of 17 November 2026. Exchange rate of about 992 pesos per US$ from RT, a market-data provider, 17 November 2026.

World.title: Mexico Inspects Beach After SpaceX Debris
World.content:
Mexico: Environment

Profepa, the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection, began its work after the first material appeared at about 7:30 a.m., according to Tribuna, a Mexican news site.

The debris follows the explosion of a SpaceX rocket on 13 November, according to Contralínea, a Mexican investigative magazine. For US readers, it is a test of how a US company’s launches affect a neighbour’s coastline.

World.title: Peru Party Files Case Against Election Chief
World.content:
Peru: Politics

Renovación Popular, the right-wing party of Rafael López Aliaga, has filed a constitutional complaint in Congress against the head of Peru’s electoral court, according to Panamericana TV, a Lima television news site, on Tuesday 17 November 2026. The target is Roberto Burneo, president of the Jurado Nacional de Elecciones (JNE), the body that runs Peru’s election justice system.

The filing follows a JNE ruling that blocks López Aliaga from returning as mayor of Lima. For US readers, it shows how the fight over Peru’s 2026 municipal vote is moving from the electoral court into the legislature.

World.title: US Warns Travellers of Jalisco Blockades
World.content:
Mexico: Travel

The US Embassy in Mexico warned Americans in the western state of Jalisco about farmer road blockades on Tuesday 17 November 2026, saying the protests “can be unpredictable”, according to El Financiero, a Mexican business daily, on 17 November. Jalisco is home to Guadalajara, a city of several million people that many US visitors use as a base.

The blockades are part of a wider protest by white corn growers across central Mexico over prices and unpaid support. Five of the 25 protest points are in Jalisco, according to Expansión, a Mexican business magazine, on 17 November.

The Big Picture

White corn growers of the Bajío, Mexico’s central farming belt, announced blockades and rallies in Guanajuato, Jalisco, Michoacán and Querétaro, according to Expansión on 17 November. The protests were called the week before over selling prices, pending support payments and a lack of agreement with the federal government.

The Confederación Agropecuaria de México, a national farm group, called the mobilisation, according to Grupo Animal, a Mexican livestock news site, on 17 November. Its representative Mauricio Pérez Cabrera said in a video posted on Monday 16 November that “el campo mexicano está colapsado” (Mexican farming has collapsed), according to AFmedios, a Mexican news site.

What We Know

According to Expansión on 17 November, 16 of the 25 protest points are in Guanajuato, five in Jalisco, two in Michoacán, one in Querétaro and one in Campeche. El Financiero listed the Jalisco points on 17 November, including the Guadalajara–Colima highway at kilometre 40 and the Guadalajara–Mexico City highway at the Ocotlán toll booth.

El Financiero also named the Guadalajara–Nogales road at La Venta de Astillero, the La Barca–Atotonilco road and Federal Highway 80 at the Tepatitlán toll booth. The US Embassy gave its assistance numbers and urged citizens to enrol in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program, the US State Department’s free alert service, according to the same outlet.

Expansión reported on 17 November that Guanajuato growers want an income of at least 6,500 pesos (about US$353) per tonne of corn. It added that the proposal under review by federal and state authorities was 6,000 pesos (about US$326) per tonne, at 18.41 pesos per US dollar, the market rate on 17 November.

Why It Matters

For US readers, the risk is practical: a blocked highway can strand a rental car or delay a transfer between Guadalajara and nearby towns. Two of the five Jalisco points sit on routes toward Mexico City and Colima, according to El Financiero on 17 November.

Mexico is also a large buyer of US corn, so a farm revolt over prices can reach Midwestern growers through trade. Pérez Cabrera said pork and cattle producers struggle to compete with imports, according to Grupo Animal on 17 November, though no tonnage was given.

What the Government Says

Interior Secretary Rosa Icela Rodríguez said at the morning press conference on Tuesday 17 November that “no hay necesidad de bloquear” (there is no need to block), according to Expansión. She said support goes to producers “sin intermediarios” (without intermediaries) and totals 26 billion pesos (about US$1.41 billion).

Rodríguez said negotiations are led by the Agriculture Ministry and the interior ministry, with Deputy Secretary César Yáñez and Tonatiuh Ramírez, head of an Interior Ministry unit, according to Grupo Animal on 17 November. She added that unresolved cases will be reviewed and that some demands fall to state governments.

What to Watch

No new meeting date has been published in the sources reviewed. Travellers can check the US Embassy’s alert page and local road reports before driving in Jalisco.

What Is Not Known

No source reviewed says how long the blockades will last. Pérez Cabrera said no agreement had been reached to suspend them, according to Grupo Animal on 17 November.

The sources do not report any effect on Guadalajara airport or on flights. They also do not say whether the 6,000-peso offer was accepted.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Guadalajara airport affected?

None of the reports reviewed mention airport disruption. The blockades are on highways outside the city, according to El Financiero on 17 November.

What did the US Embassy advise?

It said the protests can be unpredictable and urged citizens to avoid the areas, according to El Financiero on 17 November.

What price do farmers want?

Guanajuato growers want at least 6,500 pesos (about US$353) per tonne, according to Expansión on 17 November.

What does the government say?

The interior ministry says dialogue is open and support goes directly to producers, according to Expansión on 17 November.

Sources: El Financiero, 17 November 2026 · Expansión, 17 November 2026 · Grupo Animal, 17 November 2026

World.title: Argentina’s Central Bank Rejects Stimulus
World.content:
Argentina: Economy

Argentina’s central bank will not loosen monetary policy to revive a weak economy, its vice president said on Tuesday 17 November 2026. Vladimir Werning rejected a “plan platita”, a handout of spare cash to boost spending, according to TN (Todo Noticias, an Argentine news channel and site) on 17 November.

For US investors in Argentine bonds and stocks, the message is that the inflation fight comes before growth. It lands as the economy shrinks and monthly price rises have turned up again.

The Big Picture

He said it is “very dangerous to propose loosening monetary policy to raise activity” (translated from Spanish).

He added that economists elsewhere may show different evidence, “but in Argentina it does not happen”. Those who demand the recipe, he said, “clearly do not know Argentina’s history”, according to TN.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What We Know

Werning also criticised calls for the dollar to “always float upwards” and for interest rates to move “always downwards”, calling them “silver bullets”, according to TN on 17 November. He said short-term measures are “palliatives for the symptoms”, and that cutting real wages or eroding savings would take Argentina back to December 2023.

Why It Matters

INDEC (Argentina’s statistics office) put October inflation at 2.2% a month on Thursday 12 November, according to Rankia, an Argentine finance news site, on 12 November. That was above September’s 1.9% and above the 1.8% that economists surveyed in the central bank’s monthly survey (REM) had expected.

INDEC’s monthly activity index (EMAE) showed output down 1.7% in August from a year earlier, according to Canal 26, an Argentine news channel, on 21 October. Cheaper credit would help borrowers, but the central bank fears it would feed prices that are already rising faster.

Markets and Country Risk

Werning said the recent rise in country risk, the extra yield investors demand on Argentine dollar bonds, is “merely political risk” and not doubt about the economic plan, according to TN on 17 November. He pointed to dollar interest rates for 2027 of 3.7%, which he called “a vote of confidence” in the model.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, traders gave 94% to Argentina’s 2026 annual inflation landing between 30.0% and 34.9%, and 2.7% to 25–29.9%, with about US$101,000 traded, as of 6:29 p.m. ET on 17 November. These are real-money bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What to Watch

INDEC is due to publish November inflation on Tuesday 15 December 2026, according to Rankia on 12 November; we could not check the date on INDEC’s own calendar. Prices have risen 26.3% in the first ten months of the year, according to the same report.

The next INDEC activity reading will show whether August’s contraction deepened. No date for any change in the central bank’s policy has been announced.

What Is Not Known

Werning did not name the past debts that took part of the central bank’s dollar purchases, nor say how much is left to pay, according to TN on 17 November. We could not confirm the current policy interest rate, and we found no named critic of the central bank’s line.

It is also unclear whether the government is preparing any spending measure. Werning’s remarks answered an idea in public debate rather than an announced plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Vladimir Werning?

He is vice president of Argentina’s central bank, the BCRA, which he spoke for at its annual monetary conference on 17 November 2026, according to TN.

What is a plan platita?

It is Argentine slang for a handout of spare cash, meant to lift spending. Werning said more money in circulation does not make the country grow, according to TN.

What is Argentina’s latest inflation?

INDEC reported 2.2% for October 2026 and 33.1% over twelve months, according to Rankia on 12 November. The November figure is due on 15 December.

How is the economy doing?

Output fell 1.7% in August from a year earlier, according to Canal 26 on 21 October, citing INDEC. Industry and trade fell.

Sources: TN, 17 November 2026 · Rankia on INDEC October inflation, 12 November 2026 · Canal 26 on INDEC activity index, 21 October 2026 · Polymarket: Argentina Annual Inflation 2026

Mexico: Security

A private Cessna 500 jet crashed near the airport of Durango, a city in northern Mexico, on Tuesday 17 November 2026, according to La Razón, a Mexico City newspaper. The paper relayed a report from AFAC, Mexico’s civil aviation agency (Agencia Federal de Aviación Civil), and said only the pilot’s death is officially confirmed.

The Big Picture

The crash happened at about 11:40 local time (UTC-6) on Tuesday 17 November 2026, which is 12:40 US Eastern and 17:40 UTC, according to La Razón. The aircraft came down about 500 metres from the runway’s end, at the threshold of runway 03 of Guadalupe Victoria International Airport.

The aircraft was a private Cessna 500 bound for Toluca, a city west of Mexico City, La Razón reported on 17 November. The flight plan listed two crew and four passengers, according to the AFAC report the paper relayed.

World.title: Killers of Costa Rica Journalist May Have Had Help Tracking Him, OIJ Says
World.content:
Investigators believe the two gunmen who killed journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri on Route 32 may have had help following him, said Vladimir Muñoz, acting deputy director of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). Muñoz said today that the attackers knew which vehicle the journalist was driving.

Investigators are examining whether a second motorcycle or another vehicle trailed Rodríguez and whether the gunmen received instructions before the attack. Agents are collecting security camera footage to reconstruct the routes the suspects used to reach the scene near San Miguel de Santo Domingo, in Heredia, and to flee.

According to the OIJ’s account, the attackers knew Rodríguez was alone in a red pickup. They pulled alongside, confirmed he was their target and opened fire, then circled the vehicle and fired again from a second angle. Muñoz said the men checked that Rodríguez was dead before fleeing toward San José. Based on how they acted, he said, they apparently set out to make sure he would not survive.

Agents have also searched Rodríguez’s home in Santo Domingo with authorization from prosecutors and the Heredia Criminal Court. Muñoz said they seized electronic devices, equipment and documents that will undergo forensic analysis as investigators try to establish a motive and identify those responsible.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said prosecutors will review the allegations Rodríguez published on social media, including the people he named, along with anyone else who may have had a reason to attack him. No arrests had been announced as of Tuesday afternoon, and the OIJ has not publicly identified any suspects.

Rodríguez, 50, had spent three days with his parents in Guápiles and set out for San José around 1 p.m. yesterday, according to his brother, Andrés Rodríguez. The Costa Rican Red Cross received the alert about the shooting at 3:21 p.m., about 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) from his home.

The journalist had filed about 10 complaints over threats in the past two years, according to the OIJ. Laura Lara, one of his lawyers, said he had worn a bulletproof vest for roughly three weeks as the threats mounted and had it on when he was shot. Lara said Rodríguez turned down the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection program because he believed it would restrict his work. Díaz had said yesterday that the journalist declined that protection despite the threats.

International press freedom groups added their voices on today Reporters Without Borders called the killing an alarm signal for press freedom in a country long regarded as a regional benchmark. The group urged authorities to determine whether the killing was linked to his publications and the threats against him.

José Zamora, Americas director of the Committee to Protect Journalists, said authorities should thoroughly examine any link to Rodríguez’s journalism and prosecute both the gunmen and whoever ordered the killing. The Inter American Press Association demanded an exhaustive and independent investigation.

His wake was scheduled for this evening at a funeral home in central Cartago, his brother said. A funeral Mass is set for Wednesday at 2 p.m. at the San Esteban parish, known as the Iglesia del Carmen, in Cartago’s El Carmen neighborhood. The OIJ has asked anyone with information to call its confidential line at 800-8000-645.

According to the attorney general, Rodríguez is the third journalist killed in Costa Rica, after Parmenio Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. Whether investigators reach anyone beyond the two gunmen is likely to define how this case is remembered.

World.title: Dollar Expected to Keep Falling in Costa Rica After Record Low of 446 Colones
World.content:
The U.S. dollar is likely to keep losing value against the Costa Rican colón for the rest of 2026, financial analysts said. Their forecast follows the exchange rate’s fall to the lowest level in the history of Costa Rica’s foreign exchange market. On Friday, Nov. 13, the weighted average rate on Monex, the Central Bank of Costa Rica’s (BCCR) foreign exchange market, closed at 446.10 colones per dollar. That was the lowest on record in Central Bank data and the eighth straight session of decline.

The close was 0.72 colones below Thursday’s 446.82 and broke the previous record of 446.80, set on Sept. 17. The Central Bank’s reference rates for Monday, Nov. 16, stood at 442.56 colones for buying dollars and 448.34 colones for selling them. By Tuesday, Nov. 17, the reference buying rate had slipped to 441.73 colones.

Traders exchanged $49.3 million in 228 transactions on Friday, at rates between 445.80 and 446.30 colones, according to BCCR data. The Central Bank bought $41.8 million of that total, or 84.8% of the day’s volume. Of those purchases, $32.3 million were stabilization operations and $9.5 million covered the needs of the non-bank public sector.

The bank uses stabilization purchases to absorb part of the dollar supply and moderate swings in the rate. Friday’s operations did not prevent a new low. Luis Alvarado, an analyst at Acobo Puesto de Bolsa, said the downward pressure could continue over the coming weeks, practically until the end of the year. He described the colón’s appreciation as a trend that has marked much of the past three years.

Pablo González, an economist at Mercado de Valores, called the recent lows small moves within an established trend. As long as the market has an excess of foreign currency, he said, a significant change in the short term is unlikely. Neither analyst forecast a specific floor for the rate.

The analysts pointed to a steady supply of dollars from foreign-currency-earning sectors, against weak demand. Seasonal factors add to the pressure in November and December, when companies convert dollars to colones to pay taxes and the aguinaldo, the mandatory year-end bonus.

The dollar opened 2026 at 497.07 colones on Jan. 2, according to BCCR records. At Friday’s close, it had lost 10.3% this year and stood more than a third below its 2022 peak. A weaker dollar lowers the colón cost of imported goods and of debts held in dollars. It also reduces the colón value of income earned in dollars, including salaries, pensions, remittances and tourism revenue.

The Central Bank publishes the Monex result after each daily session.

World.title: JetBlue Goes Daily From New York to Both Costa Rica Airports This Week
World.content:
JetBlue is scheduled to fly every day between New York and both of Costa Rica’s international airports starting Thursday, Nov. 19, up from Saturdays only. The daily nonstops from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) go to Juan Santamaría International Airport (SJO) near San José and to Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport (LIR) in Liberia, Guanacaste.

The flights appear in the Costa Rican Tourism Board’s (ICT) official timetable for November 2026, and airline schedule listings back up the change. The expansion comes as the winter high season gets underway, and it goes against the broader trend.

International aviation consultancies project roughly 14% fewer scheduled seats from the United States to Costa Rica between August 2026 and March 2027. Juan Santamaría is projected to lose the most, about 20%, while Liberia is expected to lose around 3%. JetBlue has made cuts of its own in Costa Rica. In July, the airline ended its route between Orlando and San José.

Its New York service is going the other way. With seven flights a week to each airport instead of one, you no longer have to plan a trip around Saturdays, which matters most for short stays and last-minute winter bookings. The first daily flights leave a week before U.S. Thanksgiving.

Daily service to both airports also lets you choose your arrival point by where you’re going. Liberia is closer to the beaches of Guanacaste and the Nicoya Peninsula, while San José is the better starting point for the Central Valley, the Caribbean coast and the southern Pacific.

JetBlue is the only airline flying nonstop between JFK and San José. The New York–Liberia route has more competition, and Delta is scheduled to add Saturday flights from JFK to Liberia starting Dec. 19, using 194-seat Airbus A321neo aircraft. JetBlue is also bringing its new first-class cabin, BlueFirst, to Costa Rica this winter. It starts on Fort Lauderdale–Liberia flights on Dec. 26 and reaches the JFK–Liberia and Fort Lauderdale–San José routes on Jan. 5, 2027, with introductory fares from $299 one way between New York and Liberia.

ICT’s timetable covers November only, and it is not yet clear how long the daily schedule will last into the new year. Airline schedules can change close to departure, so anyone with a booking should check flight times directly with JetBlue.

World.title: Costa Rica Wildlife Cameras Catch Heron Catfish Hunts and an Ocelot Latrine
World.content:
My camera traps continue to provide me with brief glimpses into the hidden lives of Costa Rica’s wild animals. Today we look at a new discovery and revisit one that has been providing me with interesting videos for years now.

Armored Catfish for Lunch

I found my first armored catfish something like five years ago on the banks of the Río Cañas while doing a camera trap study for a sugarcane plantation. It was a smallish, classically catfish-looking fish with armored plates. I poked at it and thought, ‘I wonder what eats a rock-hard fish like this?’

Fast-forward to 2026 and I’m implementing a camera trap project on a large property that used to be a sugarcane plantation and still has some of the canals that plantations use to move water round to irrigate the sugarcane. Water always attracts life, so I stuck some cameras on the banks of the canals, as well as a small lake on the property. While installing the cameras, I couldn’t help but notice that some species of fish was constantly shooting up to the surface of the water to gulp oxygen and disappearing to the bottom. They were moving some quickly, I could never see what they were.

After a few camera revisions, I’ve come to realize that they’re one and the same as my old crusty friend that I found on Río Cañas, the armored catfish. This realization came quite easily because I kept recording videos of large herons, mostly great blue herons and bare-throated tiger herons, with catfish in their beaks. Which of course answers the question, ‘What eats these rock-hard fish?’

Unisex Cat Bathroom

I’ve had a camera trap pointed at a hole in the base of huge Guanacaste tree every day since sometime in January 2023. Generally, a tree cavity is a good location for a camera trap. Lots of different species like to visit, hunt, and sleep in tree cavities. What makes this one extra special is this particular tree cavity happens to act as a communal unisex bathroom for ocelots.

Over the years, I’ve recorded 223 videos of ocelots with this camera. Sometimes they’re just passing by, sometimes they’re taking naps, but most of the time they’re pooping or smelling one another’s poop. Ocelots are known to use communal latrines to leave scent messages to the individuals whose ranges overlap in a given area. I just reviewed the bathroom camera yesterday, and I continue to record ocelots sending stinky messages back and forth.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica

World.title: Slain Costa Rica Journalist Filed 10 Threat Complaints Before His Killing
World.content:
Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri, the journalist shot dead yesterday afternoon on Route 32 in Heredia, had filed about 10 complaints over threats to his safety in the past two years, according to Vladimir Muñoz, acting deputy director of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). Investigators are now examining whether those threats are connected to his killing.

Rodríguez, 50, was driving a red pickup toward San José near San Miguel de Santo Domingo when, according to the OIJ’s preliminary account, two men dressed in black on a white motorcycle pulled alongside and opened fire. Muñoz said the attackers first shot at the driver’s side, then circled the vehicle and fired through the passenger window before fleeing toward the capital.

Muñoz said agents recovered nine to 10 shell casings outside the vehicle and that the number of shots could prove higher. An earlier account attributed to the OIJ on Monday evening cited seven to eight casings. Agents are reviewing security camera footage to trace the escape route and are checking whether the suspects had been following Rodríguez before the attack.

The case has been assigned to an interdisciplinary team from the OIJ’s San José Homicide Section, which is looking to identify both the gunmen and anyone who may have ordered the attack. No arrests had been announced as of this morning, and authorities have not established a motive.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said Monday that the scene resembled a contract killing, according to international wire reports. Díaz also said Rodríguez had declined to enter the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection program despite the threats, a point the OIJ confirmed, meaning he had no police protection. The public complaints Rodríguez made on social media, in which he named alleged drug traffickers, are one line of inquiry, which Muñoz described as broad. Further details are in our first report on the Route 32 shooting.

President Laura Fernández condemned the killing late last night, calling it a cowardly murder and a stain on freedom of expression regardless of the content of his statements. She said she had instructed all police forces to support the investigation so that those responsible are punished. Fernández had sued Rodríguez for defamation during the 2025 campaign over a video in which he alleged her home was built with money from a drug trafficker, according to wire reports. The shooting came on the same day the president said jailed gang members had ordered her own killing.

Former president Luis Guillermo Solís condemned the crime and called for a thorough investigation with no impunity for the gunmen or whoever planned the attack. In the Legislative Assembly, the 47 lawmakers present unanimously approved a motion for a minute of silence and a call for investigation, according to legislative reports.

National Liberation Party caucus leader Álvaro Ramírez said insecurity in the country had spiraled out of control, while Social Christian Unity Party lawmaker Abril Gordienko called the attack an alarming sign of the level of insecurity. Broad Front lawmaker José María Villalta said Rodríguez was killed for practicing journalism and urged investigators to pursue whoever ordered the crime.

Press organizations both here and around the world joined the condemnation. Yanancy Noguera, president of the Costa Rican Association of Journalists (Colper), said that the evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice, and the association demanded a swift investigation.

The Press and Freedom of Expression Institute (IPLEX) called for a prompt, independent, rigorous and exhaustive inquiry into both the perpetrators and anyone who ordered or financed the killing, while cautioning against drawing early conclusions about the motive. The Central American Journalists Network also condemned the attack and urged prosecutors and the OIJ to act quickly.

Rodríguez worked in radio, print and television before turning to social media, where he posted allegations about drug trafficking and alleged links between criminal groups and political and business figures. He said he had shared information on those links with the US Drug Enforcement Administration, a claim that has not been independently verified. He also sought public office, pursuing the Costa Rican Renewal Party’s presidential nomination in 2022 and heading the Aquí Costa Rica Manda party’s San José legislative list for the 2026 elections.

According to the attorney general, Rodríguez is the third journalist murdered in Costa Rica, after radio host Parmenio Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. The case lands as Costa Rica posts drug seizures the US Embassy calls historic, in a country that ranked first in the Americas in this year’s World Press Freedom Index.

Costa Rica has long counted press freedom among its democratic strengths, yet a recent survey found that four in ten Costa Ricans hold back their opinions on social media out of fear. How quickly investigators identify those responsible, and whether they reach anyone who ordered the attack, is likely to shape how safe people feel speaking out.

World.title: Costa Rica Has Never Beaten Argentina and Gets Another Shot Tuesday in Córdoba
World.content:
Costa Rica has never beaten Argentina. The Sele gets another chance tomorrow night in Córdoba, against an Argentina side that has looked unexpectedly vulnerable in its first days without Lionel Messi. Kickoff at the Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes is at 5 p.m. Costa Rica time (6 p.m. Eastern). The match will be shown free-to-air on Repretel Channel 6 and Teletica Channel 7, with streaming on the TDMAX app. Radio coverage is on Columbia 98.7 FM, Monumental 93.5 FM and Teletica Radio 91.5 FM.

It is the last match of 2026 for both teams, and both come off Friday losses. Costa Rica fell 2-0 to Ecuador in Quito in Bryan Ruiz’s first match as permanent head coach. Argentina lost 2-1 to Uruguay at La Bombonera in Buenos Aires. This is not the Argentina team Costa Rica faced in Los Angeles in 2024. Messi played his farewell match for the national team on Oct. 6 against Benin, less than three months after Argentina lost the World Cup final 1-0 to Spain.

Lionel Scaloni has since renewed his contract through 2030, but the rebuild got off to a poor start. Uruguay, now coached by Diego Forlán, scored twice early in the second half on Friday, first through a Leonardo Balerdi own goal from a set piece and then through Maximiliano Araújo. Julián Álvarez pulled one back midway through the half, in front of a crowd that left much of the stadium empty.

Scaloni said after the loss that he would make changes for Córdoba. Projected lineups in Argentina put Gerónimo Rulli in goal, with Enzo Fernández and Alexis Mac Allister in midfield alongside Nico Paz. Young attackers Gianluca Prestianni and Matías Soulé or Franco Mastantuono are expected to start with Álvarez up front. Defenders Aaron Anselmino and Mariano Troilo could make their senior debuts.

A changed, experimental Argentina lineup is the best chance Costa Rica could hope for. Even so, the runner-up at this year’s World Cup remains a heavy favorite at home. Costa Rica is rebuilding from a lower starting point. The team failed to qualify for the 2026 World Cup and went nearly a year without a win before Ruiz took over as interim coach in late September.

He won both of his Nations League matches, 3-0 at Nicaragua and 2-0 against Haiti. The Costa Rican Football Federation then appointed him permanent coach on Oct. 21, with the task of qualifying for the 2030 World Cup. Ruiz, 41, played for Costa Rica at three World Cups, including the 2014 tournament in Brazil, where he captained the team to the quarterfinals. He had never been in charge of a senior national team until this fall.

His official debut in Quito went against him. Jordy Caicedo scored for Ecuador in the 21st minute, and Moisés Caicedo converted a late penalty. Ruiz said afterward he was satisfied with how his team competed against a strong opponent and that what the group learned mattered more than the score.

Before the trip, he said winning was not the main goal against Ecuador and Argentina, though his team would still try to win. Defender Francisco Calvo put it more bluntly, saying the squad was not traveling to Argentina for a stroll. The trip has left the squad short of defenders. Keylor Navas was not called up because of knee discomfort. Defender Alexis Gamboa hurt his left knee in Quito minutes after coming off the bench and went home for an MRI.

Diego Mesén, who replaced Gamboa, was sent off three minutes later in his national team debut and is suspended for Tuesday. The federation called up veteran defender Kendall Waston to replace Gamboa. Waston will not join the team after his club reported he is still recovering from an injury, so Ruiz will work with a reduced squad.

Patrick Sequeira of Portugal’s Casa Pia is the only one of the three goalkeepers in the squad who plays abroad. Up front, the main threat is Manfred Ugalde, who returned to the national team after serving a suspension. The Spartak Moscow striker scored the last time these teams met, in March 2024, when his goal gave Costa Rica a 1-0 lead in Los Angeles. Argentina came back to win 3-1 on goals by Ángel Di María, Mac Allister and Lautaro Martínez.

The stadium has unhappy memories for Costa Rica too. At the 2011 Copa América, a mostly under-23 Costa Rica team lost 3-0 to Argentina at the Kempes. Sergio Agüero scored twice and Di María added the third.

A respectable result would give Ruiz something to build on heading into the new World Cup cycle. Another lopsided loss would end the year on back-to-back defeats and leave more questions than answers. Either way, it is one of the last big tests a young Costa Rica team will get before the road to 2030 begins.

World.title: Satellite Tracking Reveals New Findings on Marlin and Sailfish in Costa Rica
World.content:
Satellite tracking research is providing new insight into how marlin and sailfish move through the Pacific Ocean and recover after being caught and released, findings that could help shape the future of Costa Rica’s multimillion-dollar sport fishing industry. The research was among the highlights of the third annual La Alfombra Azul conference, organized by the Costa Rican Federation of Tourist Fishing (FECOP) on November 6.

Nearly 200 participants attended the event, which brought together scientists, conservation organizations, government officials, tourism operators, and representatives of coastal communities. Researchers from the Guy Harvey Foundation presented results from an ongoing research program in the Eastern Tropical Pacific that uses satellite tags and specialized sensors to monitor billfish populations.

So far, scientists have tagged 106 fish, including 46 black marlin, 30 blue marlin, and 30 sailfish. The tracking data has revealed differences in how the species move through the ocean, with blue marlin generally covering greater distances while black marlin tend to remain closer to shore.

The research has also provided information about what happens to these fish after anglers release them. Using sensors that monitor movement, scientists recorded average post-release recovery times of 8.9 hours for blue marlin and 4.9 hours for sailfish. The findings could help researchers better understand how catch-and-release fishing affects these species and identify practices that reduce stress on fish.

The research program, supported by fishing captains and crews who assist with tagging and monitoring, has contributed to 13 scientific publications. For Costa Rica, where sport fishing brings in international visitors and supports jobs in coastal communities, the findings have implications beyond scientific research.

Marlin and sailfish frequently travel across international waters, making their conservation a regional challenge that requires cooperation among countries. The conference also addressed a more controversial issue facing Costa Rica’s sport fishing industry: the use of fish aggregating devices, commonly known as FADs or plantados.

These floating structures attract fish and can make fishing more productive. However, their use has raised concerns about fishing pressure, environmental impacts, and conflicts between different fishing interests. Costa Rica currently restricts the use of these devices under measures involving the Constitutional Chamber, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport, and the Costa Rican Institute of Fisheries and Aquaculture (INCOPESCA).

Neighboring Panama, meanwhile, is evaluating their use in recreational fishing through a three-year pilot program. A technical study presented at the conference examined whether Costa Rica could develop a regulatory approach that distinguishes recreational fishing from other fishing activities while addressing conservation concerns.

The study, prepared by regulatory specialist Hannia Vega, explored market conditions and the potential use of satellite-based vessel monitoring systems to improve oversight. According to FECOP, 60% of the expert interviews conducted for the study raised concerns about fishing pressure and conflicts among users, while 50% identified possible benefits, including opportunities to extend the fishing season.

Dr. Bruce Pohlot, conservation director of the International Game Fish Association, said Costa Rica offers an unusual opportunity to study how marlin and other billfish interact with fish aggregating devices. Such research could help determine whether their use can be managed sustainably and what effects they may have on marine ecosystems.

Panamanian fisheries official Alexis Peña also outlined regulatory measures introduced in his country during 2026 to improve the management of marlin and sailfish and encourage catch-and-release practices. The discussions come as Costa Rica’s sport fishing industry works to strengthen its economic position while responding to growing conservation challenges.

A FECOP economic study based on 2019 data estimated that recreational and sport fishing generated approximately $500 million in revenue. The industry supports hotels, restaurants, transportation companies, marinas, fishing guides, captains, and crews, particularly in coastal destinations along the Pacific and Caribbean.

Catch-and-release fishing has become an important part of the industry’s conservation efforts. At Marina Pez Vela in Quepos, records from 45 fishing tournaments held between 2013 and 2026 show that more than 93% of recorded fish were released. FECOP is also promoting a new strategic roadmap for Costa Rica’s recreational and sport fishing industry, developed with funding from the U.S. Embassy and contributions from 110 participants.

The plan identifies fragmented industry representation, pressure on marine species, and gaps in regulation and technical capacity as major obstacles. It proposes five strategies aimed at improving cooperation and establishing common priorities. “Sport fishing needs to participate actively in decisions that affect its future,” said Damián Martínez Fernández, FECOP’s director of conservation and public policy.

He said the organization wants to turn longstanding industry concerns into concrete proposals supported by scientific evidence and the experiences of fishing communities. Beyond the scientific and regulatory discussions, the conference highlighted community initiatives from the Osa Peninsula, Paquera, Parrita, the Gulf of Papagayo, and Barra del Colorado.

These included programs involving youth training, community tourism, women’s participation in maritime activities, and the conservation of tarpon, an important species for recreational fishing on Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast. For FECOP, the goal is to ensure that an industry dependent on healthy marine ecosystems has a stronger voice in the policies governing their protection.

The satellite research offers one example of how scientific findings could help bridge the gap between economic interests and conservation, particularly as Costa Rica considers how to manage fishing practices in the years ahead.

World.title: Pura Vida: The Dream, the Reality and Everything in Between
World.content:
Is Costa Rica’s famous way of life everything we imagine it to be? Or is the real meaning of Pura Vida something we only discover once we begin living here?

Is “Pura Vida” a real way of life, or just a clever slogan created for the tourism boards?

If you ask an expat during their first month of trying to set up utilities, open a bank account, or navigate local bureaucracy, you might get a weary laugh.

But ask someone who has lived here through every season, and they may tell you something different.

Pura Vida is very real. But it isn’t something you purchase with a beach house, a beautiful ocean view, or a one-way ticket to paradise.

It’s something you learn to live. And sometimes, those lessons come with a little frustration, a lot of patience, and a good sense of humour.

The Vacation Version of Pura Vida

We all know the picture.

You arrive in Costa Rica, the sun is shining, the palm trees are swaying, and someone greets you with a warm smile and those two magical words: Pura Vida.

Your morning starts with fresh coffee, perhaps a walk along the beach, and nowhere you need to be.

Nobody seems to be in a hurry.

And you think to yourself, “I could get used to this.”

I understand that feeling completely.

There is something incredibly special about Costa Rica. The natural beauty, the warmth of the people, the appreciation for family, and the ability to enjoy life’s simplest moments. It’s easy to fall in love with this country.

But there is something nobody really explains when you’re sitting on that beach, sipping your morning coffee.

Vacationing in Costa Rica and living in Costa Rica are two very different experiences.

And that’s where the real adventure begins.

When a 15-Minute Errand Becomes a Two-Week Adventure

Let’s talk about something as simple as opening a bank account.

In Canada or the United States, you might walk into a bank with your identification, complete a few forms, and have everything organized relatively quickly.

Now imagine arriving in Costa Rica, excited to begin your new life.

You need a local bank account.

Simple enough, right?

Well, not necessarily.

Depending on your residency status, the bank, and your circumstances, you may be asked for additional documentation, proof of income, information about the source of your funds, or other paperwork.

You collect the documents.

You return to the bank.

Then you discover that something else is required.

And suddenly, what you thought would take 15 minutes has turned into several appointments, multiple conversations, and possibly weeks of waiting.

At some point, you begin to wonder whether you’re actually opening a bank account or applying for permanent membership in an exclusive club.

Welcome to the other side of Pura Vida!

And if you think banking is an adventure, just wait until you start arranging electricity, internet service, or navigating immigration paperwork.

You may hear, “Mañana.”

Tomorrow.

But you quickly learn that tomorrow isn’t always a promise that everything will be finished by lunchtime.

Sometimes, it simply means the process is still moving.

And if you arrive expecting everything to work exactly as it did back home, you may find yourself feeling a little overwhelmed.

The Part We Don’t Always Talk About

I think this is where some people become disappointed.

Not because Costa Rica isn’t beautiful. Not because the people aren’t wonderful.

But because they arrived with an expectation that life in paradise would somehow be free of everyday complications.

The truth is, Costa Rica is a real country, with real people, real responsibilities, and systems that don’t always operate the way newcomers expect.

And while it’s perfectly reasonable to want things to work efficiently, we also need to remember that moving to another country means adapting to a different way of doing things.

That doesn’t mean we have to love every delay.

Believe me, patience can wear thin when you’ve spent your entire morning trying to accomplish one simple task.

After living here for years, I’ve learned that there are days when you simply have to laugh. I’ve had mornings when a simple task seemed to take on a life of its own, and moments when I’ve wondered why I didn’t just stay home. You know those days when you set out to accomplish one simple thing and somehow end up spending half the day going in circles? Yes, those days!

But then something happens. Someone goes out of their way to help, a conversation turns into a new friendship, or you find yourself sitting outside at the end of the day watching the sun go down. And somehow, the frustration of the morning doesn’t seem quite so important anymore.

Perhaps the challenge is learning not to let those frustrations steal everything we came here to enjoy.

Pura Vida Doesn’t Mean Everything Is Easy

This is something I’ve thought about quite a bit.

Maybe we’ve misunderstood those two little words.

Maybe Pura Vida was never meant to promise that nothing would go wrong.

Maybe it was never about perfect roads, instant service, or having everything happen according to our personal schedules.

Maybe it’s about how we choose to respond when life doesn’t go according to plan.

It’s the person who takes a moment to help you even though they have their own responsibilities.

It’s the neighbour who checks on you.

It’s the stranger who offers directions when you’re completely lost.

It’s sharing a conversation over coffee instead of rushing through another day.

And yes, sometimes it’s learning to laugh at yourself when the simple errand you planned for Tuesday is still on your to-do list on Friday.

That doesn’t mean inefficiency should be celebrated or that genuine problems should be ignored.

It simply means we can recognize the challenges without losing sight of what makes this country special.

You Can’t Move to Another Country and Expect It to Become Yours

I believe this is one of the most important lessons for anyone considering a move abroad.

We bring our experiences, expectations, and habits with us.

That’s natural.

But if we spend every day comparing Costa Rica to Canada or the United States, we may never fully appreciate the life we’re trying to build here.

There is a difference between wanting to understand how things work and expecting everything to work the way we’re accustomed to.

Learning some Spanish helps.

Asking questions helps.

Doing your homework before making major decisions helps.

And having trustworthy local professionals and friends who understand the systems can make a tremendous difference.

Most importantly, approaching a new culture with curiosity and respect rather than frustration can change the entire experience.

Because the goal shouldn’t be to recreate the life we left behind, just with warmer weather.

The goal should be to embrace the opportunity to experience something different.

The Real Pura Vida Is Found in Everyday Life

Here’s what I keep coming back to.

Pura Vida isn’t always found in those picture-perfect vacation moments.

Sometimes it’s found in ordinary days.

The rainy afternoons.

The unexpected changes of plans.

The conversations with neighbours.

The small victories when you finally figure out something that seemed impossible a week earlier.

It’s learning that life doesn’t always have to move at the speed we’re used to.

That doesn’t mean we stop caring about getting things done. It simply means we learn to recognize which things deserve our energy and which things we need to let go of.

You can appreciate a more relaxed lifestyle and still plan ahead.

You can love Costa Rica and still acknowledge its challenges.

You can have a frustrating morning at the bank and still be grateful to call this beautiful country home.

Those feelings can exist together.

So, Is Pura Vida Real?

I believe it is.

But perhaps not in the way we first imagine.

It’s not a guarantee that life will be easy.

It’s not a promise that every problem will disappear the moment you arrive.

And it’s certainly not something that comes automatically with a beautiful home or a tropical address.

Pura Vida is something we gradually begin to understand through experience, patience, intention, and respect for the country and the people who call it home.

Some days, you’ll feel it while watching the sunset.

Other days, you might have to remind yourself of it while standing in line with a folder full of paperwork.

And maybe that’s the beauty of it.

Because the real gift of living in Costa Rica isn’t escaping life’s challenges.

It’s learning how to appreciate life, even when those challenges are part of the journey.

And to me, that’s where the real Pura Vida begins.

Pura Vida, always.

About the Author

Wendy Stoneham shares personal reflections on life in Costa Rica, the experiences of living abroad, and the lessons that come with embracing a different culture. She is also a real estate professional who has been helping people navigate the Guanacaste property market since 2018.

World.title: Belize City bartender denied bail after waitress alleges he choked her and threatened to kill her at bar where they work
World.content:
Belize City bartender denied bail after waitress alleges he choked her and threatened to kill her at bar where they work

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 44-year-old Belize City bartender was denied bail Monday after a 22-year-old waitress told police he punched her in the face and choked her, then returned the next day and threatened to kill her.

Jose Mario Aguillar Alfaro pleaded not guilty to one count of burglary and one count of threat of death in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court. The prosecutor did not object to bail, but the magistrate denied it and remanded Alfaro to the Belize Central Prison until January 19, 2027.

The woman told police she was trying to rest in a room at the establishment where they both work at about 2 a.m. on Saturday, November 14, when Alfaro opened the door and entered without permission. She said he told her to stop working, punched her in the face and began choking her. The woman said she managed to push him out of the room.

She reported that Alfaro approached her again at the same establishment at about 1:30 p.m. Sunday and told her, “I wah kill yuh and put yuh remains in a plastic bag.” She said he was standing about 20 feet away and holding what appeared to be a knife.

The woman told police she had known Alfaro for three years through work. She reported both incidents at the King Street Police Station on Sunday afternoon and gave police a recorded statement.

World.title: Murder charge against Robert Lamb dropped in 2023 killing of Gabriel Tillett; Kevin Lanza, Samuel Trapp still face trial
World.content:
Murder charge against Robert Lamb dropped in 2023 killing of Gabriel Tillett; Kevin Lanza, Samuel Trapp still face trial

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Robert Emmanuel Lamb, 26, is no longer facing trial for the murder of 18-year-old Gabriel Tillett, but he was escorted back to the Belize Central Prison on Tuesday because he remains on remand in a separate attempted murder case.

The Crown entered a nolle prosequi before High Court Justice Candace Nanton, formally discontinuing the murder prosecution against Lamb. Breaking Belize News understands the decision was made because there was insufficient evidence to proceed against him.

The Crown is still proceeding to trial against Lamb’s two former co-accused, brothers Kevin Lanza, 29, and Samuel Trapp, 31. Both appeared by video from prison, while Lamb appeared in person with attorney Dr. Lynden Jones. Justice Nanton granted an adjournment requested by Bryan Neal, who represents Lanza, and Orson “OJ” Elrington, who represents Trapp. The trial is expected to begin in early January 2027.

Tillett was found with multiple facial injuries inside Belize City’s Lord Ridge Cemetery on the morning of July 4, 2023. His brother identified him at the scene. As BBN previously reported, police said footage from a surveillance camera at Pitter Street and Antelope Street Extension, behind the cemetery, helped lead investigators to the three men.

Lamb has not been granted bail in the separate attempted murder case, which stems from an alleged attack and robbery involving businessman Deepak Rupuchand Katariya in Belize City on January 28, 2023. Lamb was arraigned three days later on charges of attempted murder, use of deadly means of harm, dangerous harm and robbery.

World.title: Caye Caulker Village and village councils across Belize to issue Trade Licenses under new act
World.content:
Caye Caulker Village and village councils across Belize to issue Trade Licenses under new act

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Rural Transformation, Community Development and Local Government issued a statement to clarify misinformation being spread by the Guardian newspaper.

The Ministry says that there has been no revocation of Caye Caulker Village Council’s authority to collect trade licenses.

On the contrary, this is the first time that Caye Caulker and many other rural communities will be able to issue trade licenses.

“The fees collected will be reinvested directly into our rural communities for the benefit of all residents and local businesses.

The revocation published in the Gazette was to allow for corrections on the tenure of the Boards. Subsequent Statutory Instruments (S.I. Nos. 105 and 106 of 2026) were published in the Gazette,” the Ministry explained.

In addition, the Ministry reminds that the Trade License Act, No. 19 of 2024, is now fully in effect for the new trade licensing year starting January 1, 2027.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture equips farmers in Corozal with Sustainable coconut tree management skills
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture equips farmers in Corozal with Sustainable coconut tree management skills

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Agriculture is equipping farmers in Corozal with Sustainable coconut tree management skills.

The Ministry noted that 16 coconut producers participated in an intensive one-day Coconut Tree Management Training held today at the Agriculture Department Office.

The workshop was organized by the Corozal District Extension Service in collaboration with the Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project Officer, Uziel Vasquez (CRESAP).

Facilitated by the National Fruit Tree Program Coordinator, Enrique Rivas and Israel Pech from the Research Unit at Central Farm, the training aimed to equip local farmers with modern, sustainable practices to optimize yields and build resilience in coconut farming.

Sessions covered industry insights, sustainable soil and plant nutrition, crop selection and cultivation, environmental factors and disease control and organic soil and plant nutrition.

In addition, farmers received coconut seedlings Brazilian Green Dwarf Coconuts.

World.title: Antonio Copo faces six charges after crash kills motorcyclist Dariel Perez in Guinea Grass
World.content:
Antonio Copo faces six charges after crash kills motorcyclist Dariel Perez in Guinea Grass

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Dariel Perez, 24, was on his way home from work Friday evening when his motorcycle collided with a vehicle in Guinea Grass Village, Orange Walk District. Perez was killed and his passenger, 25-year-old Ray Ramirez, was injured. Police have arrested and charged the other driver, 39-year-old Antonio Copo, with six offences.

Police Staff Officer ASP Stacy Smith said Perez and Ramirez were travelling toward Guinea Grass around 6:30 p.m. on November 13. According to the preliminary investigation, Copo was approaching from the opposite direction when he allegedly made a sudden left turn into the motorcycle’s lane. Perez and Copo are both residents of Guinea Grass Village.

Smith said Copo was charged with manslaughter by negligence, causing death by careless conduct, negligent wounding, driving without due care and attention, driving under the influence, and failing to give way when changing direction.

World.title: Colorful lights and Christmas ornaments to brighten Belize City for Holiday Season
World.content:
Colorful lights and Christmas ornaments to brighten Belize City for Holiday Season

By Zoila Palma: The Belize City Council, in partnership with Coca-Cola, will host its 9th Annual Christmas Tree Lighting Ceremony on Friday, November 27, 2026, at Battlefield Park and Mule Park in downtown Belize City.

The event begins at 6:00 p.m. and will feature festive displays, live entertainment and the Christmas edition of the Francis Reneau Concert Series.

The public is invited to bring family and friends to enjoy the holiday celebration.

See you there!

World.title: International News: More than 140,000 take part in nationwide cost-of-living protests across France
World.content:
International News: More than 140,000 take part in nationwide cost-of-living protests across France

By Zoila Palma: Today, more than 140,000 people took to the streets across France as public sector workers, students and private sector employees joined nationwide demonstrations demanding higher wages and improved public services.

The French Interior Ministry estimated participation at 146,000, including 28,000 in Paris, while trade unions put the turnout significantly higher at approximately 550,000 nationwide and 175,000 in the capital.

The demonstrations marked the third nationwide public sector strike since September, following failed discussions with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Friday.

Unions are demanding salary increases after the government ruled out a general pay rise for public employees for the fourth consecutive year. They estimate that public servants have lost 16 percent of their purchasing power since 2017, arguing that declining wages and worsening conditions are affecting essential services, including schools and hospitals.

Students also joined the demonstrations, with many expressing concerns about education, university access and the country’s economic future.

In Paris, nurse Aurelane Thos said deteriorating conditions in schools and hospitals and staff shortages were among the issues motivating workers to protest. University professor Nicolas Prevot also called for the protection of human rights and public services, while warning against the far right gaining political power ahead of next year’s presidential elections.

Although most demonstrations remained peaceful, authorities deployed security forces and temporarily prohibited the sale of firecrackers amid concerns about possible violence.

World.title: International News: Series of US outages raises cybersecurity concerns as FBI warns of AI-powered hacking tool
World.content:
International News: Series of US outages raises cybersecurity concerns as FBI warns of AI-powered hacking tool

By Zoila Palma: A series of major technical disruptions affecting U.S. transportation, banking and online services over the past several days has raised concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure, particularly as the FBI warns that cybercriminals are using an advanced hacking tool powered by artificial intelligence.

The disruptions included a nationwide flight ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday after an air traffic communications network became unstable, alongside outages affecting Microsoft 365 and payroll provider Workday.

CNN reports that the FBI had issued an urgent warning to private-sector cybersecurity officials earlier that Friday, identifying a tool known as ARTEX that was originally developed to help organizations detect weaknesses in their own computer systems.

However, the agency warned that malicious actors had gained access to the tool and were using it to target organizations globally across sectors including finance, government, technology, defense, energy, healthcare and telecommunications.

According to the FBI, some attacks using ARTEX have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.

The warning comes as additional disruptions were reported on Monday, when United Airlines experienced a technical shutdown that grounded flights, while JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo customers reported difficulties accessing their accounts online.

Although none of the incidents had been classified as the work of foreign adversaries or cybercriminals, cybersecurity experts noted the unusual concentration of major disruptions within a short period.

Experts also cautioned that AI-powered hacking tools could allow individuals with limited technical expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks at a much faster pace.

World.title: Fiscal watchdog backs another year of relief from Jamaica’s budget rules
World.content:
The town of Black River, the capital of St Elizabeth, is seen decimated by Hurricane Melissa last October.

Jamaica’s fiscal watchdog has backed a plan to keep the country’s budget rules suspended for another year, saying the cost of rebuilding after Hurricane Melissa is putting continued pressure on government finances.

The Independent Fiscal Commission said the government faces higher recovery costs while collecting less revenue than expected. Requiring it to meet the rules in 2027/28 could disrupt reconstruction, the commission warned.

The proposed extension still needs Parliament’s approval.

The rules are intended to keep the government’s finances and debt under control. Extending the suspension would give it more room to meet recovery costs while the economy recovers.

The government also plans to seek parliamentary approval for a separate change: moving the deadline for bringing public debt down to 60 per cent of the size of the economy, or less, from 2027/28 to 2031/32.

That would give it four more years to meet the debt target. The one-year extension of the suspension would not automatically change that deadline.

Fiscal Commissioner Courtney Williams validated the request for the additional year on November 13, following a review of the finance ministry’s submission and other economic data.

The commission found that Jamaica was still dealing with significant financial and economic damage from Melissa, which struck as a Category 5 hurricane on October 28, 2025.

Updated assessments by the Inter-American Development Bank and the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean put damage and losses at about US$12.2 billion, the commission said.

That is almost 40 per cent higher than the initial estimate and equivalent to more than half the value of everything Jamaica’s economy produced in 2024.

The larger damage estimate points to a more expensive rebuilding effort that will take longer to complete. Central government spending on infrastructure and other capital projects is projected to increase by J$21.8 billion in 2027/28.

At the same time, government income has fallen short of expectations.

Revenue and grants were J$27.8 billion below budget between April and September 2026. Most of that gap came from tax collections, which were J$22.6 billion below target.

The commission said some of the shortfall reflected when payments were received. However, it also linked weaker collections to continuing disruption from the hurricane and expects those pressures to last into 2027/28.

The economy is also expected to grow more slowly than previously forecast, limiting growth in tax revenue and making it harder to reduce debt relative to the size of the economy.

Public debt is projected to stand at 65.5 per cent of gross domestic product — the total value of goods and services produced — at the end of 2026/27. It is forecast to decline to 58.8 per cent by 2031/32.

The commission’s assessment clears a required step towards extending the suspension. The finance minister must now make an order and secure Parliament’s approval before it takes effect.

Changing the debt deadline would require a separate amendment to the Financial Administration and Audit Act.

The commission said the additional flexibility would leave financial scrutiny in place. The government would still have to report on its finances, Parliament would retain oversight, and the commission would continue monitoring public debt and other fiscal risks.

World.title: WATCH: Church’s Chicken expands Jamaica presence with second location
World.content:
Buoyed by strong sales at its Mall Plaza outlet, Church’s Texas Chicken is expanding its footprint in Kingston with the opening of a second location, signalling confidence in the Jamaican market and growing consumer demand for the international fast-food brand.

Supervisor Kevin Wilson said the outlet at Mall Plaza has done “exceptionally well”, fueling the move to launch the second location at the corner of King Street and Parade Square in downtown Kingston.

“We [Church’s Mall Plaza] were one of the best Church’s regionally and internationally so therefore … we are looking forward to maximizing on the [performance] of the first store, and doing even better,” Wilson said at the launch on Monday.

World.content:

The information contained in the article was published based on information received from law enforcement authorities at the time. It has since been established that Mr Lamond Sutherland was incorrectly identified, that the allegations and statements were false and that he was not in any way a party to the incident.

Jamaica Observer unreservedly retracts the article and sincerely apologises to Mr Lamond, Sutherland who is still very much alive, for any distress, embarrassment or damage to his personal and professional reputation which may have been caused by the publication.

World.title: ‘I will not be intimidated’ says House Speaker Juliet Holness
World.content:
House Speaker Juliet Holness speaking in Parliament on Tuesday, September 22, 2026. (Photo: Karl McLarty)

Embattled Speaker of the House of Representatives Juliet Holness has declared that she will not be intimidated by any member while carrying out her duties in the nation’s Parliament.

Holness made the remark in a statement at the start of Tuesday’s sitting of the House of Representatives, the first since the near brawl that came at the end of the last sitting on November 3.

WATCH: House in turmoil over Cuba censure motion

She told her fellow lawmakers that disagreement with the chair does not render its statements improper and it should not become a demand by any member for silence.

“Let me be equally clear, I will not be intimidated into silence or pressured into abandoning my responsibilities,” she stated while promising to continue to discharge her duties as speaker “with firmness, fairness and impartiality while respecting the rights of every member while upholding the authority of the chair”.

During the November 3 sitting of the House, Opposition Member of Parliament Mikael Phillips and Government member Desmond McKenzie had to be physically separated. Opposition members have alleged that the way the speaker conducted herself during the sitting led to the standoff. Even so, the relationship between Holness and Opposition members has been both testy and antagonistic.

During her statement on Tuesday, Holness emphasised that her role as speaker is separate and apart from her marriage to Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness. She also said the strength of Parliament rests not merely in the authority that it exercises, but in the principles it upholds and the standards it maintains.

She said while robust debate and principled disagreements are essential to democracy, “neither protest nor disagreement justifies disorder, obstruction or defiance of the chair”.

Holness said the standing orders governing the function of the Parliament are not merely guidelines made pursuant to the authority of the constitution of Jamaica. She said they govern parliamentary proceedings, protect members’ rights and establish the responsibility of the chair to maintain order.

She insisted that:“No member stands above these rules and their application cannot depend on whether a ruling meets with individual approval”.

Holness also noted that questions have been raised about her independence because of her marriage to the prime minister. She said while she has generally allowed her service to speak for itself, the constitutional position should be made clear.

She pointed out that she is the duly-elected three-term Member of Parliament for St Andrew East Rural and said it was her duty in terms of representing her constituents in the House.

“The mandate is mine in own right, neither conferred nor diminished by my marriage,” she remarked.

Holness pointed to section 43 of the Constitution which provides for the election of the speaker and the circumstances in which the office becomes vacant.

“I was duly elected to this chair and my marriage is neither a constitutional disqualification nor a measure of my independence or judgment,” she declared.

She told the House that any disagreement concerning her rulings are matters for parliamentary procedure to be assessed against the standing orders rather than her personal relationship.

“I stand by the rulings I have made and procedures grounded upon which they were given,” she said. She also told members that they are entitled to challenge decisions through the appropriate parliamentary processes but insisted that there is a clear distinction between legitimate scrutiny and personal attacks or intimidation intended to undermine her authority.

-Lynford Simpson

The ATL Vikings will have to wait a little longer to secure a historic Business House basketball title after suffering defeat to Sagicor B in game three of the League Division Two best-of-five finals, leaving them with a 2-1 series lead and their championship celebrations on hold.

World.title: Haitian trafficking network
World.content:
This file photo shows a group of Haitians who landed at Boston Beach, Portland, in 2023.

HEAD of the Portland police Superintendent Ainsley McCarthy has charged that the frequent arrival of Haitians on the shores of the parish is part of a broader trafficking network across Jamaica.

“We have a Haitian population here in Jamaica. For example, in Montpelier, St James, we have Haitians there. So these Haitians who come in from time to time, some of them are trafficked. They pay to get here, and then there are persons who pick them up to take them to other locations, most times outside of the parish,” McCarthy said during the latest episode of the Jamaica Constabulary’s

Force4good podcast.

McCarthy was supported by head of Police Area Two Assistant Commissioner McArthur Sutherland, who told the podcast that many of the Haitians are being employed by Jamaicans to conduct farming in the hills of Portland.

He said police have done numerous operations targeting that practice and, “We believe some level of coordination is outside of the Portland parish.”

According to Sutherland, last year the police had to intervene after a dispute between two of the immigrants during a party held on one of the farms left one of them dead.

“The matter is still before the court and that [Haitian] is still in custody. From an organised approach, we have sufficient reason to suspect — or I would say believe — that it is organised, to an extent. One of the evidence of that organisation is the fact that we see returnees — persons who were removed [and] returned. The last trip we had one such case, and we are dealing with it,” Sutherland added.

Last month, police apprehended 22 Haitians across Area 2 — which covers Portland, St Mary, and St Ann — within a one-week period, raising concerns about a possible human-smuggling operation along Jamaica’s north-eastern coastline.

In June, 17 Haitians arrived in the Passley Gardens area of Port Antonio. Days later an additional 11 landed on Jamaica’s shores. They were taken to Port Antonio Police Station for health and immigration processing.

According to Sutherland, Jamaica requires “infrastructural support” to successfully tackle the issue as there are multiple uncontrolled ports across the island.

“The maritime coastal domain awareness is critical, [and] Portland is no exception. We have been looking at this from several years back — from the days when we were looking at it as gun-for-drugs [trade]… where they bring down the weapon and in exchange they get the marijuana. We have not seen much of that activity. But the emergence now of, what I’d say, either people smuggling or people seeking refuge, whichever category you look at it from, we definitely need the right infrastructural support as a country to really handle that,” added Sutherland as he argued that an ongoing cross-border collaboration is needed.

That collaboration, he explained, would be “a very solid intelligence network that can identify the triggers and alert us so we can mobilise and respond to these situations as quickly as possible”.

“We know that at times they will get off the boat, out in the water, and swim towards shore in order to avoid detection. So it’s not necessarily that [the] boat [is] coming up on the shore. They have different approaches to getting here,” explained Sutherland.

He underscored that the Haitians do not arrive through a controlled port, making it difficult for law enforcers to conduct risk assessment and, in instances, health risks came to the surface and had to be treated with appropriately.

Meanwhile, McCarthy reported that through the support of the Portland Disaster Risk Management Committee and other agencies, law enforcers are better able to deal with the arrival of immigrants.

“Although it’s considered disaster risk management

— dealing with hurricane, earthquake

— we also come together to deal with the influx of illegal Haitians coming into the island. And we have the Red Cross that provides food, clothing, and meals also on a daily basis to these people while they’re here.

“We have the health department, who I just [need to] pick up my phone and I call Dr [Sharon] Lewis [medical officer of health for the Portland Health Department] and I say, ‘Doc, we have some visitors to the island and she should make special arrangement to get them medically examined.’ Then I will call PICA (Passport, Immigration and Citizenship Agency) and PICA comes in, does the interviews, and we get them out of the island as quickly as possible, in most cases. And where people apply for asylum, the matter goes through the court,” said McCarthy.

World.title: Dumb and dumber!
World.content:
CARNEY... these devices we walk around with in our hands, we become so dependent on these devices to answer questions, tell us what to do, how to think, that we’re thinking less (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

University of Technology (UTech), Jamaica chancellor, Ambassador Lloyd Carney has warned youngsters that increasing dependence on smartphones and other modern communication devices is doing more than wasting their time — it is making them dumber.

Carney issued the warning at all three of the university’s graduation ceremonies at Alfred Sangster Auditorium on the Papine, St Andrew campus over the weekend.

He urged graduates to reduce their social media use, citing studies which, he said, showed that high school students worldwide had experienced two consecutive years of declining thinking and problem-solving abilities.

According to Carney, the reported decline in thinking and problem-solving abilities marked a change from the pattern in previous years when each group of students leaving high school was expected to have stronger thinking skills than the one before.

“It’s the second year now in a row international studies have shown that students graduating high school from all over the globe, they have less cognitive skills, less logical thinking capability than students from two years ago. Two years in a row, our students are leaving high school not as smart as they used to be. Before there was always a progression every year, they’re a little bit smarter than the group before,” he said.

Carney said the findings had been linked to people’s growing reliance on devices, which, he believes, is reducing the amount of independent thought and analysis they exercise.

“These devices we walk around with in our hands, we become so dependent on these devices to answer questions, tell us what to do, how to think, that we’re thinking less.
