We’re not being as analytical in our way of thinking, and it is actually debilitating to us,” said Carney, who did not identify the studies he was pointing to, or provide details about the countries, number of students and methods used to reach those findings.

However, a study published in the Journal of Adolescence in 2025, which examined the academic performance of more than 1.78 million students aged 15 and 16 across 36 countries, found that results in mathematics, reading, and science had declined in many countries, particularly between 2012 and 2022.

The research, which analysed data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment, also found that declines were greater in countries where young people’s access to smartphones and use of electronic devices for leisure during school hours had increased.

At Sunday’s ceremony, Carney delivered the warning in even more blunt terms.

“These smart devices we walk around with, these phones, they are sapping your intellectual capacity because they want to think for you. So it’s to their benefit that you get dumber, and that’s exactly what’s happening,” Carney said.

He pointed to China and Singapore as the only two countries which, according to the studies he referenced, had not experienced decline in young people’s thinking skills over the two-year period.

The chancellor attributed this to restrictions in those countries on young people’s access to social media.

Carney also took aim at the pressure to create an image of wealth and success on social media.

“There are people borrowing money to rent a car to look like they have money so they can show on

Facebook, or whatever, that they have money. They are going into debt to pretend they have money, so that the billionaires in Silicon Valley can make money off of your foolishness. It is time to stop doing that,” he said.

Carney also warned that artificial intelligence (AI) could make it easier for people to misrepresent themselves and urged graduates to be careful about the information they share with such tools.

He said people should also avoid becoming so dependent on AI that they use it for every decision or task, arguing that technology companies had a financial interest in encouraging people to rely heavily on their products.

Drawing on his experience in business and technology, Carney said most everyday tasks in industry and business did not require expensive large language models, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Google’s Gemini.

He estimated that about 90 per cent of the work could be done using cheaper models.

Carney also shared a story of an engineer at one of his companies who left an AI model running for a month and generated a US$200,000 bill.

The chancellor also encouraged parents to lead by example if they wanted their children to spend less time on social media.

“If you want to curtail what your children are doing on social media, when you come home from work, read with them, play a board game, talk to them; imagine that, talk to them. If they see you on social media, spending your time talking to your friends on social media, posting on social media, your children are going to imitate what you are doing,” he said.

World.title: The bet pays off for Shaggy
World.content:
Shaggy (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Ahead of the release of his seventeenth studio album Lottery in May, Shaggy scored Billboard chart entries with two of the album’s singles — Til a Mawnin (featuring Sting) and Boom Body (with Akon and Aidonia).

The project, which bears his Ranch Entertainment and the New York-based independent label VP Records, didn’t crack the major charts, but it didn’t go unnoticed by Grammy voters.

On Monday, Lottery paid off for Shaggy when it was among six albums nominated in the Best Reggae Album category of the 69th annual Grammy Awards.

When the Jamaica Observer caught up with Shaggy moments after the nominations were released, the Boombastic deejay was quite upbeat when asked how he felt about receiving the nomination.

“Amazing! I titled the album Lottery because it’s how I’ve lived my whole career. Nobody hands you a winning ticket. You bet on yourself, put in the work, and see what comes back. Thirty-plus years in, having the Recording Academy recognise this record means the bet paid off again, and I’m incredibly grateful for that,” said Shaggy.

The album contains 13 tracks and features collaborations with Sting, Robin Thicke, Anthony Hamilton, Akon, Jeremih, Beres Hammond, Dexta Daps, Aidonia, 450, Mutabaruka, Vanessa Amorosi, Noah Powa, Olaf Blackwood, and Rayvon. It combines reggae, dancehall, and pop with elements of hip hop, soul, and R&B.

Shaggy shared that Lottery was the result of a combined team effort.

“A lot of work went into this project. I’m hands-on with everything I do — from writing to production. I brought in people I trust from different corners of music, like Sting, Robin Thicke, Akon, and Jeremih, so reggae and dancehall could sit next to R&B and pop and still feel like one; cohesive record. It was a real team effort, and I’m proud of everyone who contributed,” Shaggy disclosed.

This is Shaggy’s eighth nomination in the Best Reggae Album category. He was first nominated in 1996 for his platinum selling album

Boombastic. That album, released via Virgin Records, catapulted him to international success.

Since then he has racked up nominations for 2006’s Clothes Drop, 2009’s Intoxication, 2012’s Summer in Kingston, 2015’s Out of Many, One Music, 44/876, a joint project with Sting, which won the award, and 2023’s Com’ Fly Wid Mi.

Also receiving a nomination in this year’s Best Reggae Album category were Buju Banton (Too Too Bad), Chronixx (Exile), Ziggy Marley (Brightside), Runkus (Supernova) and Protoje (The Art of Acceptance).

This is the first nod for Runkus. He commented about the nomination on his Instagram story.

“Jah is glorious. Supernova Grammy nominated.”

Brightside has given Ziggy Marley his 7th solo nomination in the Best Reggae Album category. He earned nods for Wild and Free in 2012, Rebellion Rises in 2019 and won for Love is My Religion (2007), In Concert (2014), Fly Rasta (2015) and Ziggy Marley (2017).

This is Protoje’s third attempt at winning a Grammy. He was nominated previously for A Matter of Time (2019) and Third Time’s a Charm (2023).

Buju Banton won the Grammy in 2011 for Before the Dawn. He has eight nominations to date including Inna Heights (1999), Friends for Life (2004), Too Bad (2007), Rasta Got Soul (2010), Upside Down 2021 (2020), and Born for Greatness (2024).

Chronixx’s Chronology lost out to Damian “Jr Gong” Marley’s Stony Hill in 2018. This is his second nomination.

World.title: US scolds Ukraine over deep strikes ahead of fresh Russia peace talks
World.content:
“Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure ... have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate,” he said, adding: “The balance of advantage in deep strikes may well favor Moscow.”

The comments prompted an immediate rebuke from Ukraine’s NATO allies.

“Criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military … targets is quite a stupid thing,” German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius said after the meeting. “Instead of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about [Russia’s] terroristic strikes every night.”

“It's not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters. “In terms of deep strike capability, there's no doubt in my mind that it's helped to degrade [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's war machine.”

Ukraine has in recent months stepped up long-range attacks deep inside Russia, targeting depots of the online retailer Wildberries, military facilities, oil refineries and fuel export facilities. It says it has taken out 30% of Russian oil refining capacity. On Tuesday, Ukraine said it had destroyed part of the Kerch bridge linking Russia to Crimea.

Washington has long opposed deep strikes against Russia, particularly those that affect oil infrastructure. U.S. President Donald Trump last month accused Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. Zelenskyy has previously said the strikes give Ukraine “equal footing” in negotiations with Russia.

World.title: The 5 Labour groups that matter as Burnham shows his hand on welfare
World.content:
There’s a long way to go before MPs find out which of Milburn’s recommendations the government implements. A white paper and legislation are not due to be published until next year.

Getting Labour MPs — many of whom are long-standing anti-poverty campaigners — to back plans which ultimately aim to cut Britain’s massive welfare bill will be no mean feat.

Despite a huge majority in the House of Commons, Starmer was forced to roll back plans to reduce personal independence payments — which go to disabled people both in and out of work — after a well-organized campaign by senior Labour figures back in 2025.

POLITICO runs through the key figures from the governing party whose views on the report — and critically Burnham’s eventual proposal — are worth paying attention to.

1) The committee chairs

Treasury Committee Chair Meg Hillier and Work and Pensions Committee Chair Debbie Abrahams played a crucial role in halting some of Starmer’s welfare reforms.

Hillier wrote an amendment to Starmer’s welfare plans which would have stopped the bill at its first hurdle. More than 100 Labour MPs from across the party signaled they would back it, forcing ministers to change course and promise any changes would only be made after a review by Disabilities Minister Stephen Timms, which is due later this month.

World.title: Uganda in talks to host EU migration hub
World.content:
Bagiire said Uganda had a “discussion” with the Netherlands but “we haven’t got far.” He didn’t say which other countries Uganda had been speaking with but said the talks were not that advanced: “Let me say that the discussion is at a stage of a cup of coffee.”

In June, European diplomats said Uganda and Uzbekistan were being discussed as potential locations for EU migration centers. However, Uganda has three criteria that need to be met before it can host a hub, Bagiire said on the sidelines of a conference in Vienna hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development.

“If we are to establish a hub, it will be strictly for people of African origin; they should not have a criminal record; [and] no unaccompanied minors,” he said.

He added that the discussions involve “no more than 50” people, who would be sent to open facilities. “No detention, they’re not prisons — at all. People can integrate within the communities … they’re free to do whatever they need to do. The same way we treat our refugees,” he said.

World.title: Russia’s Lavrov says French troops in Ukraine amount to ‘direct participation’ in war
World.content:
Russia’s top diplomat accused Paris of directly taking part in the Ukraine war following a report that French troops are in the eastern European country carrying out noncombatant operations.

“We conveyed our concern through available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer support for Ukraine, but direct participation in the war,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters Tuesday at the East Asia Summit in Manila, adding that French troops were also “assisting in goal setting, providing satellite data and much more.”

Lavrov’s comments come a day after Radio France Internationale revealed Paris had kept troops in Ukraine for several months to provide training and equipment maintenance under the “Volia mission.” The troops, who are in the French military detachment in Poland, have been involved in the operation in Ukraine since at least summer 2026, RFI reported.

World.title: Brussels signals unwillingness to be Burnham’s EU sounding board
World.content:
A third EU diplomat said there could be a “gray area” in which both things are true.

While Britain can’t do “substantial negotiations” with the EU until there’s a “consensus” in the U.K., the same diplomat said it would be right for “some level of conversation with Brussels to see what’s sensible” so that realistic options can then be discussed with the British public.

But others agreed that the U.K. must provide sharper definition. A fourth EU diplomat said: “I think the next step in this process is that the EU needs a little more clarity on where the U.K. stands.”

A fifth said Burnham must first “include in his vision something that is realistic” which can then “be worked on together with the EU.”

Anand Menon, the director of the UK in a Changing Europe think tank, said a timeline where Brussels wants firmer proposals first should come as no surprise to Britain.

“The EU wants Britain to come to them and say this is the kind of relationship they want,” he said. “They want us to do that with a relationship that’s on offer rather than make up something that they are not willing to give.”

World.title: Le Pen defends retirement reform plan as opponents mock her economic credibility
World.content:
The far-right leader says her plan to lower the retirement age would be offset by savings and employer-funded pension schemes.

PARIS — Far-right French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen pushed back against the latest accusations on Tuesday that the math behind her pension reform doesn’t add up, arguing she and her team had done “a painstaking meticulous job” to create a system that is both “fair” and “economically efficient.”

“We are taking the situation seriously,” Le Pen said as she briefed reporters on the fine print of her proposal to bring down the retirement age to 62 for most workers. France’s retirement age is set to rise to 64 for most people in the coming years.

Le Pen and her lieutenants argued that while their proposal would cost more than €18 billion, that bill would be offset by more than €23 billion in savings from efficiency adjustments, thighter qualification rules for part-time workers, incentives for older people to stay in work and a host of other measures. Le Pen also floated introducing some private pension schemes, financed by employers’ contributions, in addition to France’s state pension system.

World.title: Polish far-right lawmaker Braun charged over hospital ‘citizen’s arrest’
World.content:
Grzegorz Braun faces up to five years in prison for allegedly detaining a doctor who had performed an abortion.

Polish prosecutors charged far-right European Parliament lawmaker Grzegorz Braun on Tuesday over an alleged incident in which he tried to carry out a “citizen’s arrest” of a doctor who had performed an abortion.

The Wrocław regional prosecutor’s office said it had sent an indictment to the court in the southwestern town of Oleśnica, accusing Braun of depriving the doctor of her liberty, violating her bodily integrity and insulting her. The charges carry a maximum sentence of five years in prison, prosecutors added.

Braun and several supporters entered the Oleśnica hospital in April 2025 to confront a gynecologist who had carried out a late-term abortion on a patient whose life was at risk. The doctor said Braun held her for more than an hour by blocking the exit with his body.

World.title: Crimea bridge destruction will impair Russian supply chains, says Ukraine
World.content:
The Russia-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksenov, confirmed the strike, saying the bridge was closed until further notice, but provided no details of the damage.

Russia launched a bombing campaign against Ukrainian bridges on Oct. 1, choking logistics and causing huge public transport problems. The Russian defense ministry reported hitting Kyiv’s North and South bridges across the Dnipro River, linking the two sides of the Ukrainian capital.

Ukraine said its attack against the $3.7 billion Kerch Bridge is part of its response to the Russian campaign. The road and rail bridge is a key supply line for the 2.5 million people living on the Crimean Peninsula, illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, as well as for Russian forces stationed there.

The road portion has collapsed, and the extent of damage to the parallel rail bridge is uncertain, although the Russian transport ministry said Tuesday that limited traffic will resume on a single railway track. Without the bridge, Russia will have to rely on ferries and overland transport through occupied Ukraine — both routes subject to attack by Kyiv.

"Partial destruction of the bridge affects logistics, supply chains, and the morale and psychological state of the families of Russian military personnel, intelligence officers, and officials," said Andrii Klymenko, head of the Black Sea and Baltic Strategic Research Monitoring Group.

Zelenskyy said the operation was carefully planned and gave a long list of the missiles and drones used.

World.title: Nvidia beats Q3 expectations in first report post-Jensen Huang
World.content:
The AI chipmaker said it doubled its third-quarter revenue and confirmed that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated as CEO after a Chinese spy scandal.

US AI chip giant Nvidia doubled its third-quarter revenues to more than $115 billion (about €104.59 billion), the company said Tuesday.

Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones also confirmed that the board of directors has no plans to bring back former CEO Jensen Huang.

Huang resigned on Thursday after a string of extramarital affairs came to light, including with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

What did Nvidia say about the results and Huang?

In a statement on Tuesday, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" as the firm tries to move on from the Huang affair.

"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress said in her first remarks since she was appointed last week.

She did not address Huang's resignation or the uncertainty surrounding his successor as Nvidia's CEO.

During an earnings call with Nvidia investors on Tuesday, Chairman Jones said the board had "unanimously accepted" Huang's resignation and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Huang pitches return after 'outpouring' of support

The results, which exceeded expectations, were announced hours after Huang said he would be willing to return to the company if the board agreed.

After Huang's resignation, tech industry figures such as Elon Musk, as well as US President Donald Trump, called for Huang to be reinstated as part of a campaign called "Bring Jensen Back."

In a post on X — his first public statement since the scandal plunged the company and AI sector into crisis — Huang acknowledged that he had made "serious mistakes in his personal life" and had failed to "live up to the standards expected of everyone at" the company.

Huang also said he had received an "outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers" for him to return.

Who is Jensen Huang?

Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia, which he led for more than three decades, turning it from a maker of graphics cards used in PC gaming into the dominant supplier of chips driving advanced AI models.

Under his leadership, Nvidia grew into one of the world's biggest — and most strategically important — companies.

Nvidia has been at the center of the AI boom that has pushed markets to record levels and spurred economic growth around the world.

Nvidia's chips are critical for training and operating advanced AI systems, making them crucial to governments, the military and the tech industry.

World.title: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers
World.content:
Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Swift response from government

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

The conviction in September of Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders was greeted with shock, disappointment and anger in Kosovo Image: Ermal Meta/Matrix Images/IMAGO

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

What is the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

Government set up working group

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

Speaking of Thaci's September conviction of war crimes in September, Prime Minister Albin Kurti has said that the government of Kosovo 'is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers' Image: Liam McBurney/PA Images/picture alliance

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

Parliament considers amending law

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute stresses that there is a fundamental difference between criticism of courts based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts Image: Bekim Shehu/DW

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

'Room for criticism of both sides'

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

World.title: EU, ASEAN pursue deeper trade ties, but hurdles remain as businesses struggle with informal barriers
World.content:
2027 could be a landmark year for EU–Southeast Asia trade, with several deals nearing completion. But the harder task will be to ensure that businesses actually use them.

The European Union and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) could be heading for a breakthrough year in 2027, when the two sides mark 50 years of diplomatic ties.

A long-awaited trade agreement with Indonesia is expected to take effect, while a deal with the Philippines is nearing completion and negotiations with Thailand and Malaysia are making progress. By the end of next year, the EU could have trade deals in place with six Southeast Asian states, up from just two today.

The anniversary could also revive the long-standing ambition of a broader trade agreement between the EU and ASEAN.

On November 17, the European Commission hosted a dialogue in Brussels to discuss trade relations with Southeast Asia, including progress on existing and pending free trade agreements (FTAs).

But attention is turning to what comes next. "Finalizing FTAs is only the beginning, not the end," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.

FTAs can reduce tariffs and remove trade restrictions, but that is of little use if businesses don't know how to use them, he added.

"Unfortunately, in many cases, this is where there is a failure. Communication and training are key," Humphrey said.

Indonesia and EU finally seal landmark trade deal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The hard work begins after signing

For Brussels, the priority should now be to tackle the less conspicuous obstacles to trade, he stressed.

Cutting customs delays, simplifying regulations, and helping smaller European businesses enter unfamiliar Southeast Asian markets will determine whether an FTA succeeds.

"European companies with little or no experience in Southeast Asia would benefit from greater on-the-ground support, particularly practical, firsthand guidance on informal business practices and the unwritten local rules," Alfred Gerstl, an associate professor at Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic, told DW.

One option is to expand the assistance offered by European chambers of commerce, trade delegations, and EU offices in Southeast Asia. This could range from helping firms find distributors to explaining local licensing requirements and how to qualify for preferential tariffs.

In Vietnam, for instance, sustained pressure from Brussels has helped improve market access for European pharmaceutical firms. In Indonesia, the EU has worked on trade facilitation while pressing Jakarta over import restrictions and halal certification requirements, said Camille Nessel, a researcher at the Universite Libre de Bruxelles.

Regular consultations with businesses on both sides could also help Brussels spot problems before they become trade disputes.

Trade policy has also acquired a geopolitical purpose in Brussels. "If trade policy is expected to reduce strategic dependencies, we are asking it to deliver on objectives that remain insufficiently defined, let alone demonstrating how to achieve them," Nessel told DW.

Diversifying trade and reducing dependencies

The EU wants to reduce its dependence on a handful of suppliers for the minerals needed for batteries and other clean technologies, while Southeast Asian producers, particularly Indonesia, want foreign investors to help develop domestic processing industries rather than merely buy raw materials.

The EU and Indonesia have already clashed over Jakarta's restrictions on nickel exports.

European investment in processing facilities, agreements on environmental standards, and greater regulatory certainty would give both sides concrete gains, said Nessel. "The real value of an FTA is not just opening a market but giving the EU the leverage to keep it open," she added.

Pasha Hsieh, Lee Kong Chian Professor of Law and Jean Monnet Chair at Singapore Management University, said Brussels should prioritize ratifying its investment protection agreements with Singapore and Vietnam.

Signed in 2018 and 2019, respectively, the agreements still require ratification by all EU member states before entering into force. "These delays underline the need to follow through on negotiated commitments," Hsieh said.

The issue is particularly relevant as the EU looks to develop investment protocols in other Southeast Asian states where investors have sometimes faced uncertainty over legal protections. Indonesia, for instance, has terminated numerous bilateral investment treaties, including agreements with the Netherlands and Spain.

Towards an EU-ASEAN trade agreement?

A larger question is whether the EU should continue pursuing bilateral deals with Southeast Asian countries or revive its original ambition of a region-to-region agreement with ASEAN.

The EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-wide FTA in 2007 but suspended them two years later amid disagreements over wide economic disparities among ASEAN members and political concerns. Technical discussions resumed in 2017, but little has come of them.

ASEAN already has regional agreements with China and several other economies. Beijing upgraded its free trade agreement with ASEAN in October 2025.

Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Region-to-region frameworks extend beyond trade. Humphrey, of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, called for negotiations to begin on a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and Investment Protection Agreement.

The EU-Singapore Digital Trade Agreement, which entered into force in February 2026, offers a possible model for wider cooperation, he noted, adding that common approaches to customs procedures, supply-chain standards, and green technologies could create greater alignment with ASEAN members that are not yet ready for full FTAs.

"European businesses have long complained of operating at a disadvantage due to the lack of a region-to-region deal. It is high time that both sides elevated their ambitions and embraced the idea of working towards such an agreement," Humphrey said.

The 2027 anniversary would be a convenient deadline for agreeing on what comes next, but Gerstl warned against mistaking another round of diplomatic ceremony for progress.

"There is a risk that attention will focus almost exclusively on the 2027 summit in Singapore and that the group photo will become the defining image of the event, only for momentum to fade in the years that follow," he added.

World.title: Deutsche Bank under fire after internal documents made public
World.content:
A cache of internal records outlines the bank's dealings with Jeffrey Epstein, Donald Trump and Russian oligarchs. The German lender has sought to deflect criticism by claiming its bad behavior is a thing of the past.

Deutsche Bank is in damage control mode again after an international consortium of more than 200 investigative journalists published internal documents from the global lender on Tuesday under the name "Inside Deutsche Bank."

The documents, published in Der Spiegel, Financial Times, Le Monde and The New York Times, among others, cover Deutsche Bank's business dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, now US President Donald Trump, and a host of Russian oligarchs.

Gleaned from nearly 15 million documents leaked to a journalist from India and another from South Africa, the e-mails and meeting minutes trace the bank's aggressive pursuit of business deals in Russia, and with high-profile Russian oligarchs, right up until Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — despite risk warnings from numerous managers.

Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing was among the executives who took part in the bank's Russia strategy working group. The bank also still employs more than 160 people in Russia and generated 2025 pre-tax profits of €61 million ($67 million) there through a local subsidiary.

Money laundering, oligarchs, terrorists: How corrupt are the banks? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Not just about Deutsche Bank's business with Trump, Epstein and Russians

In all, the documents cover the past 20 years of the German lender's business dealings and raise questions about the efficacy of internal controls by showing that Deutsche Bank had repeatedly put financial interests before international sanctions compliance and anti-money laundering rules.

Other red flags raised in Tuesday's reports suggest that Deutsche Bank sought to set up tax-optimization schemes for wealthy clients, that criminal networks may have been able to move illicit cash through the institution, that it helped facilitate arms deals, that it helped companies in environmentally damaging industries and that it held funds for the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Has Deutsche Bank really changed its ways?

Beyond more recent negative headlines involving alleged anti-money laundering and compliance failures, Deutsche Bank has been trying to restore its public image ever since its involvement in the US subprime mortgage rate scandal helped trigger the 2008 global financial crisis — a fiasco that ultimately cost the bank more than €20 billion in penalties and settlements.

When Sewing later took over in 2018, he promised to turn the institution around. Although he has made Deutsche Bank profitable once again, he did so at the cost of massive job cuts, and some compliance failings have continued.

Sewing to the German business daily Handelsblatt that some mistakes had been made under his leadership.

"When you look at the events today, you naturally ask yourself whether you could have done some things differently," he told the paper. "I am not without mistakes," he said, but added that the course he set for the bank "has always been right and remains so."

The bank's shares fell by up to 6% in Tuesday trading.

German government wants 'full transparency' from Deutsche Bank

Deutsche Bank issued a statement claiming that the reports were old news and that the institution had long ago turned over a new leaf.

In an e-mailed statement to the press, Deutsche Bank Supervisory Board Chairman Alexander Wynaendts wrote, "During my tenure I haven't seen a single decision from Christian Sewing that I was not comfortable with."

A Tuesday statement from the bank described the revelations as "legacy" matters and claimed they would have no lasting negative financial impact on the institution.

Nevertheless, German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Tuesday called on Deutsche Bank to "provide full transparency regarding how it has addressed past failures and internal control deficiencies and how it will effectively prevent these in the future."

Further, Klingbeil said authorities must investigate and "take necessary action" where appropriate.

World.title: Saudi Arabia: Rights groups raise alarm over rising number of executions
World.content:
Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression?

Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.

The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.

In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.

"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.

According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM , the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.

Saudi police forces reacted to peaceful protests by opening fire at the demonstrators in Quatif in 2011 Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

Is the Iran war affecting Saudi domestic repression?

Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.

"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Leah Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.

This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.

Major sports events in Saudi Arabia are either postponed or canceled due to the ongoing attacks from Yemen's Houthis and Iran Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Saudi Arabia's repression against the Shia minority

Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST , echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.

Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.

However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.

"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.

What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

World.title: US and Mexico lose measles-free status
World.content:
The United States lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization has said. Bolivia and Mexico have also lost their measles elimination status.

The ​United States is experiencing its highest number ​of cases in more than three decades. Some 7,700 people in the country have been infected and 13 have died since 2025.

As ​of November 12, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have confirmed 5,412 measles cases and 6 deaths. US states have reported a total of 10 deaths from the highly contagious virus this year.

Pennsylvania has been the worst-hit state, reporting seven measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases.

Why are measles caseloads rising despite readily available vaccines?

Tuesday's declaration by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but is the latest sign of measles' avoidable resurgence.

"Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death," PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa said.

Thanks to a series of functioning vaccines, measles had been virtually eradicated throughout most of the developed world for decades.

Vaccine hesitancy and disinformation has risen in recent years in the US, seemingly fueled at least in part by the COVID pandemic.

The rising influence of renowned vaccine critic Robert F. Kennedy Jr., now the US Health Secretary — who dropped out of the 2024 presidential election campaign to form an alliance with Donald Trump — was one of the clearest indicators of this.

"This is a serious warning for our region, but it is not an irreversible setback," PAHO Director Barbosa said. "We know how to prevent measles, and we know how to stop its transmission. With sustained commitment to vaccination, strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again."

Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bolivia, Mexico, US and Canada no longer designated measles-free

As of November 13, PAHO said that the Americas region had reported 58,213 measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,806 cases during the same period last year.

The organization considers endemic transmission to be re-established when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country.

Canada had reached this status in November 2025, with Bolivia, Mexico and the US now deemed to have joined it.

The PAHO said that Canda had "interrupted the chain of transmission" that led to its designation and was working to regain elimination status.

Meanwhile, it said the other three countries "are implementing measures to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response."

World.title: Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
World.content:
The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

What does Russia mean by 1997?

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

What would be the consequences of a NATO withdrawal?

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

For more than 20 years, NATO allies have provided air policing over the Baltic states Image: Arnaud Dumontier/MAXPPP/dpa/picture alliance

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

Why isn't the mutual-defense clause enough?

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

Signing of the treaty establishing NATO in Washington on April 4, 1949 Image: epa/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

Who decides which alliances a country can join?

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

Was there a promise not to expand NATO eastward?

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

In 2022, the last Russia Council meeting was held at NATO's headquarters in Brussels Image: Olivier Hoslet/AFP

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Why is the demand back on the table?

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay
World.content:
The European Court of Human Rights has called for the release of imprisoned elected lawmaker Can Atalay. Atalay has been in prison for almost five years despite rulings from the Turkish Constitutional Court.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.

The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.

The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.

It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.

The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

No future in Turkey? Growing exodus of young Turks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.

From leading activist to a jailed member of parliament

As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.

He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup."

Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.

LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.

His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.

Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.

After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

World.title: La coalición compite por los votos de la izquierda en directo en La Moncloa: “El decreto está listo, portavoz”
World.content:
De izquierda a derecha, el ministro de Hacienda, Arcadi España, la vicepresidenta segunda y Ministra de Trabajo y Economía Social, Yolanda Díaz, la portavoz del Gobierno y ministra de Inclusión, Seguridad Social y Migraciones, Elma Saiz, y el ministro de Transformación Digital, Óscar López, durante la rueda de prensa posterior a la reunión del Consejo de Ministros, este martes en La Moncloa.

A solo 12 días de las elecciones, el Consejo de Ministros no puede ser otra cosa más que un escaparate electoral. Este martes, el Gobierno venía con artillería pesada para seducir a más de cinco millones de votantes: subida fuerte del salario mínimo (5,3%) y del sueldo de los funcionarios (4,5%). La semana pasada dio el primer paso para subir las pensiones a otros casi 10 millones de posibles votantes. En total, 15 millones de personas afectadas en dos consejos. Pese a las críticas de electoralismo, ha sido algo habitual en todos los gobiernos. Sin embargo, la novedad es que ahora los dos grupos que lo componen, PSOE y Frente Amplio, compiten electoralmente de forma descarnada —los socialistas se están llevando buena parte del voto que fue de Sumar, según todos los sondeos— y el pez pequeño de la coalición necesita imperiosamente frenar esa sangría y recordar que buena parte de las medidas del Ejecutivo, en especial algunas de las más valoradas, llevan su impronta.

Por eso este martes la rueda de prensa se ha convertido en una batalla amable, con sonrisas y bromas, pero con mucha carga de fondo entre la vicepresidenta Yolanda Díaz, de Sumar, y los tres ministros socialistas con los que compartía mesa: Arcadi España (Hacienda), Óscar López (Transformación Digital) y Elma Saiz (Seguridad Social y portavoz). Díaz no ha parado en ningún momento de lanzar pullas, gesticular, sonreír y bromear pero con mucho cálculo político para dejar claro quién tiene la paternidad de medidas como el registro horario o la prestación universal por crianza, que acaba de incluir el PSOE en su programa electoral. “Esto es la hegemonía”, decía Díaz con una sonrisa mientras los ministros socialistas se reían pero con cierta incomodidad. “Copiar no está mal si se copia bien”, insistía ella.

La estrategia del Frente Amplio, ya desplegada por el ministro Pablo Bustinduy, es clara: presionar al PSOE para que apruebe en estas dos semanas el registro horario y la prestación universal por crianza. “Nos han dado una campaña muy bonita hecha”, señalaba un dirigente de Frente Amplio. Y Díaz se puso a ello en el lugar más eficaz desde el punto de vista comunicativo: la rueda de prensa en La Moncloa con los ministros socialistas alrededor y todas las cámaras enfocando.

La vicepresidenta segunda y Ministra de Trabajo y Economía Social, Yolanda Díaz, junto al ministro de Hacienda, Arcadi España, durante la rueda de prensa posterior a la reunión del Consejo de Ministros, este martes en La Moncloa. Mariscal (EFE)

“Hemos estado hablando de esto con Arcadi [España] esta mañana”, revelaba Díaz. Ella no cortó en trasladar la presión y el reto mientras miraba a sus compañeros de Gobierno. “El reglamento [para el registro horario] está listo. Solo hay que firmarlo. No tiene que pasar ni por la diputación permanente. Además el ministro Bustinduy me dice que todos los partidos están dispuestos a votar la prestación universal por crianza”, presionaba. Elma Saiz, visiblemente incómoda, trataba de ganar tiempo.

—Contaremos las cuestiones que van al Consejo de Ministros cuando se alcance un acuerdo y se traigan, de momento seguimos trabajando”, intentaba cerrar. Y ahí Díaz, sonriendo, en voz más baja pero claramente audible, cortó a Saiz:

—El reglamento está listo, portavoz.

Después, España también esquivó la pregunta, aunque fuentes del Gobierno aclararon más tarde que no se van a llevar estas medidas que pide Sumar a los próximos consejos de ministros, que se dejan para después de las elecciones porque son una promesa electoral del PSOE, no algo que se pueda hacer en esta semana.

Díaz seguía protagonizando la escena y aprovechando así para mostrar las diferencias entre los dos partidos y hacer campaña por el Frente Amplio. Ella insistió en que en cuanto acabe la legislatura dejará la política definitivamente, pero sigue siendo un activo electoral muy evidente y en el Frente Amplio están tratando de convencerla de que haga más campaña e incluso en sectores del PSOE lo ven como buena idea, porque creen que ella activa el voto de la izquierda, como se vio en 2023. Ahí ella aprovechó para tirar contra el vicepresidente Carlos Cuerpo, con el que está teniendo tensiones internas similares a las que tuvo con su antecesora, Nadia Calviño. “No es el ministro Arcadi el que tiene un problema con el registro horario, ojo, es otro departamento”, decía de nuevo con una sonrisa en clara referencia al ministro de Economía.

La vicepresidenta segunda y Ministra de Trabajo y Economía Social, Yolanda Díaz durante la rueda de prensa posterior a la reunión del Consejo de Ministros, este martes en La Moncloa. Mariscal (EFE)

Pero aun así, cuando se le preguntó por cómo llega la coalición a estas elecciones, ahora que arrecia la competencia electoral entre sus dos partes, Díaz quiso hacer un balance muy positivo. “El Gobierno de coalición es un ejemplo de gestión política al más alto nivel en este país. Ustedes lo están viendo. Tenemos debates legítimos, como este del registro horario, que yo les digo que si lo llevan en el programa electoral lo podemos aprobar ya y dar una buena noticia. Pero la coalición es un ejemplo de gestión de las diferencias políticas para aportar soluciones a nuestro país. La coalición es un ejemplo que da absoluta serenidad. España es plural y ha entendido bien que la portavoz, Elma Saiz, ha hecho una regularización extraordinaria de inmigrantes, nosotros una reforma laboral, y que caminamos juntas. Este es el mensaje y esto es lo importante para seguir cambiando España. Esto es lo bonito de este Gobierno”, remataba mientras la portavoz le correspondía con una sonrisa amable. La coalición mantiene las formas, y evita la ruptura por si los números dieran para poder reeditarla, pero también está en campaña y el PSOE y Frente Amplio ahora sí pelean por un voto fronterizo dentro de la izquierda.

World.title: Sánchez se revuelve contra el ataque de Ayuso a los andaluces: “Andalucía se va a levantar, a movilizar y a darnos la victoria el 29-N”
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez ha salido este martes a responder a la presidenta madrileña, que el pasado domingo aseguró que la situación de la comunidad andaluza había llevado a muchos de sus ciudadanos a vivir en la Comunidad de Madrid. “Ayuso, la de la fruta, ha dicho que Andalucía, nuestra querida Andalucía, es una tierra decadente, la última de la fila y que es un desastre”, ha respondido el candidato socialista en un mitin en Albacete. “¡Y Feijóo, callado! Feijóo callado, no le vaya a pasar lo que le pasó a Casado", ha continuado en referencia a la abrupta salida del anterior presidente del partido después de criticar el enriquecimiento de familiares de Ayuso en pandemia. “Desde aquí nosotros decimos que Andalucía se va a levantar, se va a movilizar y nos va a dar la victoria también el próximo 29 de noviembre, reivindicando la buena política frente a la mala educación”, ha exclamado.

Sánchez respondía así a las palabras de la presidenta madrileña, erigida en su némesis política, cuando esta aseguró, el pasado domingo: “(...) Esa es la estrategia de la carcoma: poquito a poco va cayendo todo. La decadencia es tóxica y se pega en todas partes y después nos encontramos con una Andalucía socialista, que durante 40 años, gracias a esa red de gente garrapatera [sic] que vivía del dinero de todos, resulta que Andalucía —muchos de aquí sois andaluces y por eso estáis viviendo en la Comunidad de Madrid—: fracaso escolar, abandono escolar, corrupción, Andalucía la última siempre en puestos de trabajo, un desastre, siempre los centros de salud cerrados todas las tardes en verano porque estaban de vacaciones”, aseguró desde Móstoles sobre una comunidad que ahora lleva casi ocho años en manos de los populares.

La respuesta a Ayuso ha llegado también del líder de Adelante Andalucía, José Ignacio García, una formación en pleno auge según las encuestas y que lleva el andalucismo en su ideario. García ha instado a la presidente madrileña a que se “lave la boca” para hablar de los ciudadanos de Andalucía: “Que sepa usted, Isabel Natividad, que Madrid se ha levantado también con el esfuerzo de un montón de andaluces y andaluzas de clase trabajadora que se han ido a vivir allí y con su talento, con sus manitas han levantado lo que es Madrid hoy”. A eso ha añadido su explicación de por qué muchos andaluces siguen emigrando, como recalcó Ayuso en sus polémicas palabras. “Es por el centralismo que usted defiende y por un sistema que usted defiende, que es injusto con Andalucía, que siempre nos tengamos que ir nosotros de aquí”. Informa Eva Saiz.

Por parte de los correligionarios de Ayuso, los populares andaluces, este martes ha hablado el secretario general, Antonio Repullo, que ha asegurado que “evidentemente, se refería a la etapa del PSOE-A en la Junta” y ha calificado a la presidenta madrileña de ser “una amante de Andalucía”, recoge Diario de Sevilla.

Expresiones de andalufobia

Las palabras de Ayuso se suman al acervo de expresiones de tinte andalufóbicos proferidas por dirigentes del PP desde Madrid. En 2010, la entonces presidenta de la Comunidad, Esperanza Aguirre, criticó de una manera gráfica la decisión del presidente del Gobierno, el socialista José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, de reducir las peonadas necesarias para acceder al subsidio agrario en Andalucía. “Se han ido a Sevilla, han hecho un congreso y han hecho lo único que creen que debe hacer un Gobierno, que es utilizar el dinero de los contribuyentes para dar pitas, pitas, pitas”, reduciendo a los jornaleros a aves de corral.

Un año después Ana Mato, vicesecretaria general del PP y responsable de la campaña de Mariano Rajoy, aseguró que los niños andaluces estaban dando clase en el suelo porque no tenían siquiera mesas donde sentarse. Mato utilizó una fotografía publicada en prensa para denunciar las supuestas deficiencias de la enseñanza pública andaluza. Pero el director del colegio salió a explicar que los niños de la foto aparecían sentados en el suelo porque participaban en una actividad de cuentacuentos, no porque carecieran de pupitres.

“Íbamos a ser la California europea pero con bipartito parecemos Etiopía”, dijo en 2013 el portavoz adjunto del PP en el Congreso y diputado por Almería Rafael Hernando, criticando las medidas del Gobierno andaluz para garantizar tres comidas diarias a escolares desfavorecidos.

Cristina Cifuentes criticó en 2017, cuando ocupaba la presidencia regional, el que entendía era un agravio comparativo entre madrileños y andaluces. “Los madrileños están pagando 3.000 millones de euros para que los andaluces tengan sanidad, educación y demás”, aseguró. Le llovieron críticas por doquier, a derecha e izquierda del arco parlamentario de Andalucía.

En 2018, Isabel García Tejerina, vicesecretaria de acción sectorial del PP, comparó a los niños andaluces con los castellanos y leoneses. “En Andalucía lo que sabe un niño de diez años es lo que sabe uno de ocho en Castilla y León”, dijo criticando los resultados educativos de la comunidad más meridional de la Península durante los gobiernos socialistas. Las reacciones no solo llegaron desde el Ejecutivo andaluz, sino desde sus propios compañeros de filas, en el PP andaluz. Su líder, Juan Manuel Moreno, tuiteó: “No compartimos las palabras de Isabel García Tejerina. Los niños y profesores andaluces son de 10, solo les falta un Gobierno a su altura”.

La comparación no era del todo nueva. En 2008, la ya mencionada Ana Mato había dicho que “los niños andaluces son prácticamente analfabetos”. En aquella ocasión, la referencia eran los escolares de La Rioja. Las críticas también apuntan a los símbolos andaluces. En 2007, el eurodiputado Alejo Vidal-Quadras, entonces en las filas del PP, se refirió así a Blas Infante, el precursor de la autonomía, fusilado por los sublevados en la Guerra Civil y considerado de manera oficial como padre de la patria andaluza: “Infante, Dios lo tenga en su gloria, era un cretino integral”.

En 2006, antes de que Andalucía llevara a referéndum su reforma estatutaria, el presidente popular Mariano Rajoy se refirió a la inclusión de la expresión “realidad nacional” en él como un “cachondeo” y la presidenta del PP en el País Vasco, María San Gil, dijo que “a los andaluces, la realidad nacional les suena más a chirigota; no tienen la seriedad necesaria que tiene que tener una reforma estatutaria”. San Gil se sumaba a otras declaraciones del eurodiputado del PP Jaime Mayor Oreja que había relacionado el término realidad nacional en el Estatuto andaluz con el “fenómeno islamista”. En la consulta se terminó respaldando, con el 87,4% de los sufragios, el sí al Estatuto ya en 2007 (que incluía ese término en su preámbulo)... con el apoyo del PP andaluz.

La tradición también es que parte de esos dirigentes populares terminen pidiendo disculpas. A menudo consisten en que, después de usar Andalucía como ejemplo negativo, se aclare que no se trataba de una generalización, sino de una crítica específica a los Gobiernos socialistas.

Así, Aguirre señaló que la crítica de las “pitas, pitas” iba dirigida a Zapatero. Cifuentes, que pretendía criticar la gestión del Gobierno andaluz. Mato dijo luego que no era verdad que los niños andaluces fueran prácticamente analfabetos, aunque la disculpa quedó a medias: insistió en que lo eran mucho más que los riojanos: “Los niños andaluces no son prácticamente analfabetos, pero es verdad que son mucho más analfabetos que los de La Rioja”.

World.title: Feijóo comparece junto a Echeverría, en Eibar, en medio de un gran dispositivo policial y algunos gritos de “fascista”
World.content:
Decenas de agentes de la Ertzaintza controlaban los accesos a la plaza de Unzaga. La Policía Local había hecho cambios en el flujo del tráfico. Todo un potente despliegue preparado para la visita de Alberto Núñez Feijóo a Eibar (27.540 habitantes, Gipuzkoa) en su quinto día de campaña. El líder del PP ha recalado este martes en la ciudad industrial tras el ataque a Jon Echeverría, joven candidato —de 22 años— del Partido Popular por la provincia al Congreso, hace tres días en Hernani. “No nos van a callar, no vamos a dar un paso atrás en Euskadi ni en ningún lugar de España”, ha clamado Feijóo ante el micrófono, donde ha volcado su rabia contra el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, por amparar a “los violentos”. El líder del PP ha llegado sobre las 11.30 en su furgoneta negra. Fuera le esperaban decenas de personas que lo han recibido entre gritos de “fascista” y “kanpora” [fuera, en euskera]. Más allá de los chillidos, ambos dirigentes populares han podido comparecer ante los medios de comunicación —para cargar contra EH Bildu y contra Sánchez— y tomarse una fotografía con la papeleta del 29-N sin mayores problemas.

Eibar es considerada como la primera ciudad de España en declarar la II República. En el corazón de la urbe, la plaza de Unzaga, la bandera republicana ondeó por primera vez en la madrugada del 14 de abril de 1931. Casi un siglo después, EH Bildu logró aquí la victoria en las elecciones autonómicas del País Vasco y el Partido Popular quedó en cuarto puesto. Hoy, en la antesala de los comicios generales, Feijóo y Echeverría han pisado sus calles con la resaca del ataque al cabeza de lista al Congreso por Gipuzkoa y otros miembros de Nuevas Generaciones, que recibieron pedradas y fueron increpados en Hernani el sábado. “He querido pasarme por la provincia de Gipuzkoa simplemente para decirles que creemos en la libertad. Ningún rincón de España está reservado a quienes pretenden imponer sus ideas mediante la intimidación”, subrayó el líder del Partido Popular.

Feijóo cambió su agenda con el objetivo de parar en Eibar para hacer campaña con Echeverría antes de otro acto previsto en Bilbao. La elección de Eibar por parte del PP obedeció, precisamente, a que la urbe —encajonada en medio de las montañas— es una de las más próximas a Bilbao, pero ya en la provincia de Guipuzkoa. A primera hora de la mañana, mientras la Ertzaintza controlaba la zona, tres jóvenes colocaban una pancarta junto a carteles de campaña. Había de todos los principales partidos menos del PP y de Vox. “Faxismoa eta espainolismoa. Borrokatu!”, se leía en la tela colgada en una barandilla [¡Combatamos el fascismo y el nacionalismo español!, en euskera].

Un joven cuelga una pancarta en Eibar, este martes. V. M

Pocos minutos después llegó Echeverría a la plaza de Unzaga, donde el PP había instalado una carpa informativa y había aparcado el autobús de campaña. Decenas de personas se interesaban por la escena desde las terrazas de las cafeterías o los balcones de los edificios. Otros llegaron luego para lanzar proclamas contra los cargos del PP. “¡Son los cachorros de ETA!”, clamó Echeverría sobre quienes gritaban contra él luego en la plaza y sobre quienes perpetraron la agresión que sufrió, grabó y difundió en las redes sociales. La comparecencia conjunta se produjo, además, una jornada después de presentar el PP en Pamplona una de las propuestas de su programa: una ley de nietos vasca para que quienes abandonaron el País Vasco o Navarra por el terrorismo de ETA puedan votar en las elecciones autonómicas. Como ocurriera ayer en el mitin de la capital navarra, Feijóo ha vuelto a achacar el ataque a Echeverría a EH Bildu. Y elevó aún más el tono contra Pedro Sánchez.

“Un presidente digno de serlo, ante la agresión a pedradas de un candidato democrático al Congreso, ha de descolgar el teléfono y trasladarle su solidaridad. Un presidente digno de serlo ha de condenar este tipo de actuaciones, él personalmente”, sostuvo el líder del PP. La cuenta oficial del PSOE y dirigentes socialistas como Patxi López condenaron el ataque el domingo. “Un presidente digno de serlo ha de ordenar a los padres políticos de los violentos, que son sus socios en Madrid, que le han elegido presidente del Gobierno gracias a sus votos, que paren. Que paren de violentar la campaña de las elecciones generales”, añadió el líder del PP. “Sánchez tuvo tiempo para expresar ante Bildu el pésame por la muerte de un etarra, pero no ha encontrado ocasión para condenar una agresión a un candidato democrático al Congreso”, remachó. Fuentes de Génova aclaran que se refería al fallecimiento de Igor González Sola.

En Eibar, Feijóo ha defendido no haber presentado listas al Senado precisamente por la provincia en la que se encontraba Guipuzkoa, una de las tres circunscripciones donde los populares no concurren a la Cámara alta en favor de Vox. “Con todo lo que me diferencia de Vox, siempre me sentiré más cerca de Santiago Abascal que de Arnaldo Otegi”, ha dicho el líder del PP. “Aquí en Guipúzcoa lo hemos hecho para que Vox centralice los votos en el Senado”, ha añadido. “Lo que yo nunca haré es blanquear a los violentos y conseguir sus votos y su apoyo para ser presidente del Gobierno”, ha remachado.

Más inversión e infraestructuras en La Rioja

El líder del PP ha acudido esta tarde a un mitin en Logroño, La Rioja ―una comunidad que ha denominado como un “balón de oxígeno”― para el PP, en el que ha estado acompañado por la cabeza de lista por esta región, Cuca Gamarra, y el presidente autonómico, Gonzalo Capellán. Feijóo se ha comprometido a dos cosas para la región si consigue llegar a ser presidente del Gobierno: en primer lugar, “corregir el déficit de inversión en esta tierra y ejecutar el pacto de infraestructuras es justo, es necesario”, en concordancia con las palabras de Gamarra, que precisamente había dicho que, al ser la comunidad más pequeña (salvo Islas Baleares), se le trataba como a “ciudadanos de segunda”; y, en segundo, “poner nuevas frecuencias ferroviarias y las tenemos que poner desde Logroño a Madrid por La Rioja baja”.

El presidente de los populares se ha quejado de la gestión del Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez por endeudar a España “más que nunca”. Además, ha criticado que todas las medidas que se están aprobando durante este mes las “dejan a cuenta para que lo pague el siguiente”. También ha arremetido contra Sánchez por dividir a España en dos bloques opuestos para ganar las elecciones, lo que es, según ha dicho, “el buscar cómo podemos enfrentar a la mitad del país para que la otra mitad me vote, haga lo que haga, y ser presidente por los votos de Bildu o por los votos del independentismo catalán o vasco”. Incluso ha llegado a hacer mofa de que “como ya las dos manos derechas de Sánchez están en la cárcel, resulta que se ha hecho zurdo”.

World.title: Vox se frena y cede terreno al PP
World.content:
