El quinto ‘tracking’ de 40dB. indica que el PSOE prosigue su lenta escalada sin que apenas se muevan los bloques

Los primeros días de campaña no parecen haberle sentado bien a Vox, a tenor de los cuatro primeros trackings de 40 dB. para EL PAÍS y la Cadena SER. El beneficiado es el PP, que logra frenar sus fugas hacia la extrema derecha, lo que le reporta una cierta mejoría. El PSOE también prolonga su lenta escalada, aunque el reparto de fuerzas entre los bloques, claramente favorable al de la derecha, no sufre modificaciones reseñables.

Santiago Abascal, el líder de Vox, empezó la pasada semana con el viento a favor tras salir muy reforzado de su esperada entrevista con David Broncano. Dos días después, Abascal recibió duras críticas de algunos influencers con gran predicamento entre sus seguidores más jóvenes por haber cancelado la entrevista que había prometido al youtuber Jordi Wild. Desde entonces, el crecimiento de Vox ―que continúa siendo muy importante respecto a 2023― se ha frenado. En la última semana, la extrema derecha ha caído un punto, para situarse en el 17,5% de los votos.

Otro dato parece confirmar la tendencia. A finales de la pasada semana, Abascal llegó a rebasar por una décima en popularidad al líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo. En esta última entrega del estudio de 40dB., Feijóo le supera claramente por casi cinco puntos, con un 22% que le elige como preferido para presidir el Gobierno. Pedro Sánchez sigue en cabeza, con casi un 33% de apoyos.

La otra buena noticia para el PP es que logra detener la fuga de votos hacia la ultraderecha. Continúa siendo considerable —un 15%— pero supone cinco puntos menos que la pasada semana. Vox aún figura como el partido que capta más abstencionistas, si bien a poca distancia de PP y PSOE.

A la izquierda del PSOE, el Frente Amplio y las confluencias territoriales en su órbita experimentan una leve mejoría, pero su saldo en escaños no pasa de los 10, un tercio de los conseguidos por Sumar en 2023. Podemos se debate entre un solo escaño o quedar fuera del Congreso.

World.title: ¿Qué dice el promedio de encuestas? Consulta los sondeos en tiempo real
World.content:
El promedio de EL PAÍS se actualiza día a día, dando más peso a las mejores encuestadoras. Además, construye tu propio promedio

Se publican decenas de encuestas en una campaña. Son el mejor instrumento para predecir unas elecciones, sobre todo cuando las miramos juntas: eso hace nuestro promedio. Combina todos los estudios dando más peso a las encuestadoras que más aciertan. Ahora mismo, ese promedio sitúa al PP con el 31,2% de los votos, casi cuatro puntos por delante del PSOE (27,5%), y con Vox alrededor del 19%, cerca de su máximo.

En el gráfico puedes elegir entre tres promedios. El “medio” es el que usamos habitualmente; los otros dos sirven para comparar: “agresivo” (que reacciona antes a los cambios pero tiene más ruido), y otro “cauto” (que se mueve menos).

Los sondeos se han movido poco desde la convocatoria del 6 de octubre. El cambio más claro es un bajón del PP que estrecha su ventaja sobre el PSOE: era de 6 puntos y ahora es de 4. Nuestros cálculos dicen que el PSOE tiene ya un 20%-25% de probabilidad de ser primero.

Algo que también ha cambiado es la izquierda del PSOE. Hoy las encuestas estiman un 6,8% de voto para lo que hemos llamado Frentes (Frente Amplio y las coaliciones con Podemos, Compromís, Ara Més o Unidad del Pueblo Canario) y un 1,4% para Podemos, que solo cuenta donde concurre en solitario. Juntos rondan el 8,2% de voto, lejos del 12,3% que logró Sumar en 2023.

La suma de izquierdas y derechas

El número clave de las elecciones es el resultado por bloques. Ahora mismo la derecha suma el 52% de los votos (PP, Vox y SALF) y la izquierda, el 37,5% (PSOE, Frentes, Podemos y Adelante Andalucía). Son 14 puntos y medio de distancia, cuando en las generales de 2023 casi empataron, con 45,4% y 44% respectivamente.

La ventaja de la derecha creció entre 2024 y el verano de 2025, cuando sus votos pasaron del 48% al 52%. En campaña se ha reducido ligeramente, aunque todavía ronda los 14 puntos. Nuestra hipótesis inicial era que la izquierda, que partía desmovilizada, recuperaría terreno con la convocatoria electoral. Todavía pensamos que es la tendencia para las semanas que quedan.

El promedio también constata que las encuestadoras discrepan. Casi todas ponen al PP primero, pero con ventajas distintas: desde algo más de un punto de 40dB. hasta los seis y medio de NC Report. Solo SW Demoscopia sitúa al PSOE por delante, además del CIS. Pero el dato de este último es poco informativo porque el centro sobrestima a la izquierda desde 2018.

¿Y si corregimos los llamados sesgos? Algunas encuestadoras se desvían hacia la derecha o hacia la izquierda. Nuestro promedio no lo corrige por un motivo: esas desviaciones cambian de una elección a otra y casi nunca son sistemáticas. Pero podemos ver qué pasaría si lo hiciéramos: el siguiente gráfico permite corregir cada encuesta con el sesgo histórico de su casa.

El resultado depende de qué elecciones miramos. Con los errores de todas las elecciones desde 2018, generales y autonómicas, la ventaja del PP sobre el PSOE sube de 3,7 a 4,9 puntos: en conjunto las encuestas se han quedado cortas con la derecha. Pero en las generales ha pasado lo contrario: subestimaron a la izquierda. El caso más recordado es 2023: el último promedio de encuestas daba a la derecha cinco puntos y medio de ventaja, y en las urnas sacó solo 1,4. Si ajustamos las encuestas con sus sesgos solo en las tres generales desde 2018, la ventaja del PP baja a 2,1 puntos, pero la suma de derechas sigue claramente por delante.

Todos estos números son tentativos. Primero, porque las encuestas son una aproximación. Y segundo, porque todavía quedan dos semanas hasta el 29-N.

¿Cómo funciona el promedio?

Un promedio de encuestas suele ser más preciso que cualquier encuesta aislada: suma la muestra de todas y compensa en parte sus errores, porque mezcla la “cocina” de cada encuestadora. El nuestro funciona así:

1) Todas las encuestas. Usamos las de voto al Congreso publicadas desde las generales de 2023, salvo las encargadas por partidos y las que no tienen trabajo de campo propio. La mayoría las tomamos de Wikipedia.

2) Con distinto peso. Cada encuesta importa según su encuestadora, su muestra y su antigüedad. La nota de cada casa sale de nuestro comparador, que valora su error, su sesgo y si publica sus microdatos (las mejores pesan el doble que una casa normal). El peso de una encuesta se reduce a la mitad cada diez días y desaparece a los 30.

3) Cada casa cuenta una vez. De cada encuestadora pesa su último sondeo, para que no mande quien publica más.

4) Mira hacia atrás. El promedio de cada día solo usa las encuestas publicadas hasta entonces: la línea no se reescribe cuando llegan sondeos nuevos.

5) Tres ritmos. El promedio central y dos para comparar: el agresivo reduce el peso a la mitad cada 8 días y corta a los 14; el cauto, cada 30 y a los 60.

6) Las listas del 29N. Desde el 14 de octubre medimos las candidaturas nuevas, y las encuestas anteriores se traducen a ellas. SALF y Adelante Andalucía entran en el promedio poco a poco, a medida que las publican las encuestadoras.

7) El sesgo, aparte. La corrección del interactivo usa el error de cada casa en la ventaja entre bloques desde 2018, entero: enseña qué pasaría si las casas volvieran a fallar como de media.

8) El promedio es sólido, pero no infalible. Lo hemos probado con 41 elecciones desde 2018: cinco días antes de votar, falla 1,5 puntos por partido de media. Cambiar la ventana o los pesos lo mejora una décima como mucho. Cuando falla es porque fallan todas las encuestas a la vez, algo que ningún promedio puede corregir: por eso nuestro modelo añade esa incertidumbre.

Todas las encuestas

World.title: Pedro Sánchez concede su primera entrevista a una revista del corazón: “No imagino mi vida sin Begoña”
World.content:
El presidente del Gobierno y candidato del PSOE a las elecciones generales protagoniza este miércoles la primera página de ‘Lecturas’, y habla en la publicación de la campaña electoral y de su familia. “He tenido que renunciar a muchos momentos con mis hijas”, afirma

El presidente del Gobierno Pedro Sánchez y candidato del PSOE a las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre protagonizará este miércoles 18 de noviembre su primera entrevista en una revista del corazón. Así lo ha confirmado el director de la revista Lecturas, Luis Pliego, durante la tarde de este martes en el programa La tarde se mueve, de Telecinco, momento en el que ha revelado la portada de mañana y algunas de las declaraciones del líder socialista. Volcado de lleno en la campaña electoral, sentándose en platós de televisión de todas las cadenas de la televisión generalista y viajando por España con sus mítines, Sánchez ha sacado un hueco en su agenda para conceder la que probablemente es una de sus entrevistas más personales hasta la fecha.

La citada revista ha publicado algunas píldoras de lo que se podrá leer mañana: habla de sus hijas, de su mujer, Begoña Gómez, y también de sus padres y abuelos. “Una charla distendida acerca del pasado, del presente y del futuro. Un Pedro Sánchez que la sociedad no conoce”, describe la conversación en la publicación. Según su grupo editor, RBA, la revista tiene una tirada semanal de 98.000 ejemplares.

“Mis abuelos fueron personas humildes y trabajadoras. Conocieron el dolor de la emigración y las miserias de aquella época que hoy algunos añoran. Cuando era pequeño, los acompañaba a una escuela de adultos en Aluche, donde aprendían a leer y escribir”, le explica el presidente del Gobierno a Lecturas. Aunque la revista comparte algunas de las declaraciones, se guardan probablemente las más jugosas para que los lectores acudan a los quioscos y compren el ejemplar este miércoles.

“He tenido que renunciar a muchos momentos con mis hijas”, “no imagino mi vida sin Begoña” y “mi madre y yo estudiamos la carrera a la vez, verla esforzándose tanto fue una lección” son las frases que protagonizan la portada de la revista. Según Lecturas, lo que busca la entrevista es conocer más a la persona que se esconde detrás del político, sus preocupaciones personales y cómo es el día a día del presidente del Gobierno más allá de la política.

También se han publicado otras de sus frases en el adelanto en la versión digital: “Mi yo de niño estaría orgulloso de que siga creyendo en muchas cosas que aprendí. Que nadie es más que nadie y que merece la pena luchar por aquello en lo que crees”. Y: “Todas las etapas de nuestra vida conllevan un aprendizaje, sin duda. Lo importante no es tanto lo que ocurre, como lo que tú decides hacer con ella”.

Aunque es la primera entrevista que concede a una revista del corazón, no es la primera vez que protagoniza una portada de revista. En 2015, entonces como candidato socialista a La Moncloa, Sánchez emuló un retrato realizado al actor Steve McQueen por el reconocido fotógrafo Richard Avedon para la portada de Harper’s Bazaar. Era uno de los protagonistas de un reportaje que analizaba a la nueva generación de políticos españoles, y su foto es la que más dio que hablar. Entonces, la revista le presentaba como “un líder que encaja con el retrato robot de los emergentes, aunque vaya a lomos de un partido con 135 años de historia, para lo bueno y para lo malo”. También participaron Albert Rivera e Inés Arrimadas, Carolina Bescansa, Alberto Garzón y Beatriz Rodríguez.

El presidente del Gobierno ya estuvo el pasado domingo en Fuera de control, el magacín de las tardes del fin de semana de La Séptima, el nuevo canal en abierto, copresentado por Alba Carrillo y Marta Márquez. “Vamos a tratar temas de cultura, política, sociedad… También corazón. Va a ser un programa para personas que se sienten huérfanas en la televisión actual. Queremos que tenga cabida todo el mundo y abrir debates desde el respeto. Todas las opiniones serán bienvenidas, siempre y cuando estén dentro de los límites de los derechos humanos. Y tendrá un toque optimista. Estamos todos un poco crispados y es fundamental volver a la alegría”, contó la propia Carrillo en una entrevista publicada en EL PAÍS el pasado 31 de octubre.

Durante su entrevista, las presentadoras le pidieron, por ejemplo, que dijera algo bueno y malo de los otros tres candidatos a las elecciones del próximo 29 de noviembre. De Alberto Núñez Feijóo, dijo: “Viene de una tierra, Galicia, que está muy bien”; sobre Santiago Abascal: “Prefiero no contestar, me ponéis en una situación imposible”; y de Ada Colau dijo que es “una mujer comprometida, activista e hizo buenas cosas cuando estuvo en el Ayuntamiento de Barcelona”.

Durante el programa, Sánchez contestó varias preguntas sobre su vida personal y familiar. “¿Cómo concilias, con las niñas, con tu familia?”, le preguntó Márquez. “Difícil, pero yo cuento con una ventaja con la que vosotras no contáis: yo vivo donde trabajo. Eso significa que si tengo media hora libre, me acerco, hablo con ellas y vuelvo. Ese ir y venir lo practico mucho”, contestó. Y añadió: “Cuando tengo que prepararme una intervención o leer documentos, me voy a la residencia a leerlos y, aunque no esté con ellas, ellas saben que estoy allí. “Ahora son ellas las que deberían conciliar con su padre y con su madre, porque no les veo el pelo”, bromeó.

Durante la entrevista, contó cómo conoció a su esposa, Begoña Gómez: “Fue un flechazo a primera vista”. “Nos conocimos en una fiesta, empezamos a quedar, y teníamos 30-31 años… y todo fue muy rápido. Ella tenía su piso y su trabajo, y yo también. Así que a los 2-3 meses nos fuimos a vivir juntos”. Al año y medio tuvieron a su primera hija, y luego se casaron. En Fuera de control, el presidente reveló cómo fue esa proposición de matrimonio: “Fuimos a un restaurante de comida asiática, y no le puse el anillo en ningún sitio… Le dije que estaba enamorado y que me apetecía mucho casarme. Fue muy bonito porque en la boda nuestra boda estuvo con nosotros”, dijo, asegurando que hoy está todavía más enamorado de su esposa.

También contó cómo ha conseguido proteger la intimidad de sus dos hijas, Ainhoa y Carlota. “Ellas ven un poco la sobreexposición de su padre, y no les gusta un pelo. Es verdad que ha habido los típicos haters, los alvises de turno, que han intentado expandir imágenes suyas por las redes sociales…”, lamentó Sánchez. “Ellas son muy feministas, muy progresistas… han sufrido también mucho. Ellas son muy fuertes. Creo que están orgullosas”. Y añadió: “Cuando nos ven a Begoña y a mí con lo que estamos viviendo, ella, también a David, mi hermano [condenado a nueve años de inhabilitación por un delito de prevaricación administrativa], y nos ven bien, nos ven fuertes, de alguna manera se tranquilizan”. Y contó que en alguna ocasión han acabado abandonando algún local cuando algunos han empezado a cantar canciones con insultos dirigidos hacia él.

World.title: “Yo sí te voy a votar”: Adrián, el cocinero valenciano que compuso la canción viral de Sánchez en TikTok y no recibió respuesta del PSOE
World.content:
Óscar Puente, la exdelegada del Gobierno en Valencia Pilar Bernabé y usuarios anónimos se suman a esta composición creada en respuesta a una frase de la portavoz del PP Ester Muñoz

No está siendo una campaña sencilla de seguir en redes sociales. Ione Belarra hizo el pino —esto es literal— en su cuenta de TikTok hace unos días. Alberto Núñez Feijóo envió este lunes un mensaje a un programa de fútbol muy viral entre los jóvenes que se llama Línea de Cal y que se emite en YouTube. Aquí, dijo: “Killgore, maestro”. Killgore es un creador de contenido satírico, editor de vídeos, canciones virales —una sobre la selección de Curazao en el Mundial triunfó en las discotecas este verano— y es muy seguido entre la juventud, que estos días apoya al líder popular con mensajes en X. Santiago Abascal plantó a Jordi Wild el jueves. Y el domingo concedió una entrevista al mecánico más famoso de España, Ángel Gaitán, que cerró así la charla: “Pues tienes mi voto”.

Capturas de vídeos de la cuenta en TikTok de Adrián.

Sin duda, la campaña de este 2026 pasará a la historia por cómo los candidatos han apostado de lleno por marcar la agenda diaria en X, YouTube, Instagram y TikTok. Aquí el PSOE se ha encontrado con un aliado inesperado y anónimo. Hasta hoy. Se trata de un cocinero valenciano de 42 años que se llama Adrián. Adrián ha compuesto una canción con la ayuda de un programa de sonido de inteligencia artificial, a la que se han sumado a bailarla dirigentes socialistas y ciudadanos anónimos. El estribillo dice así: “Yo sí, yo sí te voy a votar [Pedro Sánchez]”. Fuentes de la dirección de Ferraz aseguran a este diario que no conocen a este chef que trabaja para una cadena hotelera. El propio Adrián lo confirma en una entrevista telefónica:

—Les envié la canción por redes y ni me contestaron.

Todo comenzó el 26 de octubre en Salamanca. Ese día, los populares dieron el pistoletazo de salida a la precampaña con un mitin junto a Alberto Núñez Feijóo y la portavoz popular en el Congreso. Ester Muñoz hizo un discurso de nueve minutos. A la mitad, más o menos, dijo: “¿Vas a llevarnos a cuatro años de enfrentamiento e incertidumbre? No te va a votar nadie, Pedro Sánchez, nadie”. Horas después, en una habitación de Valencia había un hombre de 42 años que estaba viendo el telediario y que acababa de ser operado de unas varices. Al escuchar estas palabras, habló a la tele desde el sofá, con su pareja delante:

–¡Pues yo sí te voy a votar, yo te voy a votar!

Se llama Adrián ―el apellido prefiere no mencionarlo para que no se le identifique― y cumplirá 43 años el próximo diciembre. Adrián nació en Guatemala y lleva más de 20 años viviendo en España. Relata que estudió magisterio y que no se dedica al mundo de las redes sociales, pero sí le gusta mucho TikTok. Ahí se creó una cuenta hace unos meses, visible, donde solo aparecen vídeos del PSOE y de Pedro Sánchez.

Aquella noche, tras ver el telediario, empezó a escribir una canción. “Porque yo primero escribo el boceto, como unas frases en una libreta, y luego ya la subo a la IA”. Dice que hizo hasta 20 versiones. Algunas están visibles (y tiene una hasta en árabe). “Quería que fuera pegadiza y mira, al final me gustó una y no esperaba que tuviera el tirón”. Acumula millones de visualizaciones. Tanto, que incluso algunos creadores de contenidos virales, como Kappa, compartieron su canción. No cobra por visualizaciones. “No me vendría mal”, dice.

Solo en las últimas 48 horas, numerosos usuarios y dirigentes como Óscar Puente o la exdelegada en el Gobierno en la Comunidad Valenciana Pilar Bernabé están bailando la canción que él mismo compuso con ayuda de la inteligencia artificial. Hasta el propio partido se ha sumado con cuentas afines en Instagram. El perfil La Bola Roja, creado hace cuatro días y al que siguen dirigentes socialistas y promueven vídeos de Sánchez, difundió el vídeo con el baile. El título dice así: “Ester, una cosita...”.

También presentadores, como Jorge Javier Vázquez, que ha publicado esta mañana el suyo.

Si aquel día contaba con 2.000 seguidores, hoy ya tiene 25.000 más. Adrián, eso sí, solo sigue a siete usuarios: todos del PSOE. “He intentado poner mi granito de arena porque estaba cansado de escuchar tantas tonterías y así frenar a la ultraderecha y dije, pues, este es el momento”.

—Los socialistas ahora sí usan su canción.

—No les pongo ningún pero porque quiero poner mi granito de arena.

Y lanza una crítica. “El PSOE no ha tenido cosas buenas con esto de la corrupción, pero bien vale lo bueno conocido que lo malo por conocer”. Adrián volverá a los fogones en unos días. Dice que su plato estrella es la paella valenciana, pero que el arroz meloso que guisa también está de rechupete.

—¿A Sánchez no le manda sus vídeos?

— A él le mando todos, pero nunca los ha visto.

World.title: Abascal justifica que su mujer cobre el bono social térmico porque es familia numerosa
World.content:
El candidato de Vox ha asegurado que es “familia numerosa especial” para justificar el cobro del cheque de 210 euros concebido para que familias vulnerables puedan pagar el recibo de la calefacción

El líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, ha justificado que su esposa, Lidia Bedman, sea beneficiaria del bono social térmico para familias vulnerables porque es familia numerosa, y ha prometido aumentar las cuantías y extender la ayuda a todas las familias. Según ha publicado InfoLibre, su esposa, Lidia Bedman, percibió en mayo un cheque de 210 euros correspondiente a la ayuda del año 2025, concebida para que familias vulnerables puedan pagar el recibo de la calefacción.

En declaraciones a los medios en Arrecife, capital de Lanzarote, Abascal ha indicado que bajo su techo viven sus cinco hijos, lo que convierte a su unidad familiar en “numerosa especial” y ha avanzado que no renunciarán a las ayudas previstas porque “son de justicia”. De hecho, ha recordado que el programa electoral de Vox recoge un “aumento” de estas ayudas y hacerlas “extensibles” al resto de las familias.

En concreto, el programa de Vox plantea que “todos los beneficios que ahora existen las familias numerosas se aumentarán y se extenderán a todas las familias de manera progresiva desde el primer hijo, intensificando las ayudas y bonificaciones en función del número de hijos”. “El dinero de los españoles está mucho mejor en manos de las familias que en manos de (el presidente, Pedro) Sánchez y sus amigos para que se lo gasten en putas y mordidas”, ha rematado.

World.title: VVD will support tax plan in Senate as cabinet avoids collapse
World.content:
All three coalition parties will support the cabinet’s tax plans for next year in the Senate, ending the stand-off that began last week when the right-wing VVD rejected its own finance minister’s budget settlement.

Senate group leader Tanya Klip confirmed that the party intended to vote in favour when the plans are debated on December 7.

The votes of the nine VVD senators, together with coalition partners D66 and CDA and the left-wing opposition parties Pro and Volt, will be enough to pass the bill.

The fiscal package was thrown into disarray last Thursday when the right-wing liberal VVD voted against it in the lower house, triggering a weekend of crisis talks and speculation that the government was about to collapse.

VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz called the minority coalition a “failed experiment” after the other coalition parties negotiated a deal with Pro and Volt to raise an extra €1 billion in income tax by increasing the tax rates on assets and savings.

Yesilgöz said her party had been wrong-footed by the amendment, which she called a “bad deal for the Netherlands”, and suggested D66 and CDA appeared to prefer a coalition with the left-wing Pro.

Weekend negotiations

But after three days of discussions behind closed doors on the Zwaluwenberg estate outside Hilversum and in the Catshuis, the prime minister’s official residence, the three parties agreed to carry on in government.

Prime minister Rob Jetten admitted at a press conference that he had been “too optimistic” about the chances of doing a deal with opposition parties on both left and right on the tax plans and said internal disputes within the coalition had had the “upper hand”.

Sybrand Buma, the former CDA party leader and vice-chairman of the Council of State who chaired coalition talks between the parties after last year’s election, will lead a new round of talks designed to improve relations between the government and parliament.

The cabinet will also come up with measures to help small and medium-sized businesses during the talks next year on the budget for 2028, Jetten said, in what was seen as a concession to the VVD.

The coalition parties said in a statement on Monday night that trust had been restored following the acrimonious budget debate last week, which led to D66 and CDA passing the tax plan with support from two fringe parties on the left.

But opposition leaders were sceptical of Jetten’s claims. Pro leader Jesse Klaver said: “The cabinet needs to set a course for itself and make choices”, otherwise “we’ll be back where we started”.

Joost Eerdmans, of the right-wing JA21, said the VVD had been right to demand a change of course, but commented: “We will find out in practice if we actually get a right-wing correction”.

World.title: Want to start really speaking Dutch? Read on…
World.content:
For so many internationals who have already taken Dutch language courses, their journey stops somewhere after heavy beginner grammar courses and before speaking truly takes hold.

Whether that’s due to book-focused courses, complicated grammar or futility and fear that you’ll never be able to get that guttural g sound right, life goes on and Dutch takes a back seat.

It’s for just that reason that NedLes, a homey Dutch school in Amsterdam Oost, developed its intensive, 2-week conversation course for those with at least an A2 level who want to start speaking Dutch in their daily lives.

“People want to stabilise their language level and feel confident enough to speak,” says Renske Berns, co-owner of NedLes.

Conversational boost

“Think of it as a conversational boost,” adds co-owner Welmoed Nijhout, speaking from their sunny and spacious office nearby the Oosterpark.

The intensive course immerses students in Dutch for 10 days, with two hours spent in class speaking and about four hours of preparation per class that you can do at home, at the school (on its sunny porch weather permitting!) or at the nearby public library.

“They’re not joking when they say intensive,” says Angely Diaz, an agile coach who moved to the Netherlands from Honduras in 2019. “You really have to commit to it, and I appreciate that. I’ve lived here for seven years already and really want to make progress this year. And NedLes is the only place I’ve found that really focuses on just talking, talking, talking!”

Podcasts

The small classes of 10 people maximum do that by starting off listening to a Dutch podcast, which students then discuss throughout the lesson. They also talk about daily topics, meaning you can carry what you’ve practiced with you outside the classroom and into the real world. There are no books used in class. (Yes, you read that right!)

“I can listen to podcasts more easily,” says Diaz of her progress since taking an intensive course. “But more than anything, it helped my self-confidence when speaking Dutch, to start the conversation in Dutch and resist switching to English.”

Student Stephen F., a classical musician from Toronto who moved to Amsterdam earlier this year with his husband (also a NedLes student!), agrees. He’s taken two intensive NedLes classes so far.

Muscle memory

“Both of them have helped me be less afraid to talk out loud in Dutch,” he says. “In class, I can speak well enough to be understood, but with mistakes. I still don’t get through many interactions in public that stay completely in Dutch without me or the other person switching to English, but when it does happen, I feel quite happy about it.”

And compared to other Dutch courses he’s taken online or at different schools, he says what he likes about NedLes is that “it doesn’t get bogged down in grammar rules, so you practice speaking more”.

“It’s a more organic way to learn than only following rules without getting the muscle memory of applying them,” adds Diaz. “And the teachers are very supportive and make the class engaging, fun, and most of all, a space to learn Dutch. Unlike other schools, they didn’t switch to English when we were confused but spoke in basic Dutch to make sure we understood. I appreciate that, because that’s how it goes in the real world!”

The next intermediate intensive course begins December 7, with another one following early in the new year. At only €625 a course, NedLes makes learning to speak Dutch affordable. What better holiday gift to give yourself than one that keeps on giving?

World.title: NL persistently falling short of obligations to disabled people
World.content:
People with disabilities in the Netherlands are structurally disadvantaged and lack the same opportunities as everyone else in daily life, according to the first report on how the country is meeting its obligations under the UN disability rights convention.

The convention, which the Netherlands ratified in 2016, commits governments to making sure people with disabilities can take full part in society, from work and housing to education and transport.

The public health institute RIVM, which carried out the monitor, said there was more attention for the more than two million people in the Netherlands with a disability than in the past. But it found persistent gaps in work, income and online access, the RIVM’s director Marith Volp told broadcaster NOS.

Some 36% of people with disabilities have a paid job, compared with 65% of people without, Volp said. People with disabilities also earn less on average, are more likely to live close to the poverty line and more often rent social housing rather than own a home.

Most Dutch websites and apps do not meet the rules on digital accessibility, the report said, although national government and council websites have more than commercial ones. Polling stations are also often a problem. Between 2022 and 2024, only 2% to 10% of the stations that councils had labelled accessible passed an independent test, NOS said.

Volp also said the RIVM saw a risk of social isolation, with people with disabilities facing barriers to playing sport and going to the cinema or theatre.

There has been some progress, however, with more people with disabilities in work than before, and more getting assistive home equipment. Public transport has also become more accessible, with fewer height differences at bus stops and more guide lines for blind people.

But much remains unclear because the information available is fragmented, the RIVM said. It made recommendations for better measurement so that policy can be adjusted.

The Netherlands ratified the convention in 2016, and in 2024 it published a national strategy with goals on work, housing, income, education, care, transport, culture, sport and safety. The cabinet aims to bring the position of people with disabilities into line with the convention by 2040. The RIVM will report every year until 2029.

In June, the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights (CRM) said the country was failing to keep its promises. In its survey of 1,800 disabled people, 35% said they worried about not having enough money in the future.

World.title: List of PFAS pollution sites “contaminated with errors”
World.content:
A list of sites contaminated with PFAS “forever chemicals” is riddled with mistakes, according to the local authorities who are responsible for overseeing the clean-up.

The government identified 57 sites that represent an “unacceptable risk” to the local environment because of high levels of PFAS chemicals, which are widely found in household and industrial waste.

But a survey by NOS of the 12 provinces and 29 local councils that manage the sites, at least half the locations are on the list even though they are not high-risk or the level has not been established.

Experts who spoke to NOS said the list was symptomatic of the chaotic way the government has handled PFAS pollution, and warned that while some locations are wrongly on the list, other places with high pollution levels were probably being overlooked.

The government in The Hague has compiled the list based on surveys of councils and provinces. The information gathering exercise is due to be completed in 2030.

But many authorities said there were administrative problems with the surveys. Groningen’s replies have not been included because they not submitted in the format required by the ministry, while Zuid-Holland said the “definition was not yet known”.

Schiphol not listed

Six of the 57 locations were recorded as having “no unacceptable risk” while another 20 were listed as “not yet known” and in five cases no data was recorded.

Some sites that are known to be major users of PFAS chemicals are absent from the list, including Schiphol airport, which Utrecht University professor and expert in toxicology Chiel Jonker called “one of the largest PFAS locations in the Netherlands where polluted water is pumped out”.

PFAS chemicals are widely used in packaging and products such as products such as shampoo, food packaging, cosmetics and paint.

Known as “forever chemicals” because they take an extremely long time to break down, they have been linked to some types of cancer, hormone disorders and damage to the immune system.

Hans Slenders, of the PFAS Expertise Centre, told NOS that the national government needed to take responsibility for tackling PFAS pollution. “The problem is much too complicated to be solved locally,” he said. “The ministry must take the lead.”

World.title: Jetten admits mistakes as VVD ministers back tax plan
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has admitted that he was “too optimistic” in his quest for broad support for his budget plan, which culminated in last week’s coalition crisis. The VVD ministers in the cabinet will now defend the tax plan that the party’s MPs voted against last week.

“We realise we have tested the patience of the whole country,” Jetten told a press conference on Tuesday morning, adding that financial decision making had been taken too lightly.

Jetten said the relationship in the coalition had been damaged. “We want to turn the page,” he said, “but it’s not as if we can put everything behind us.”

“Political intervention”

Deputy prime minister Dilan Yesilgöz, who called the minority cabinet a “failed experiment” on Friday, did not use the phrase when asked repeatedly at the press conference whether that was still her view.

On Wednesday she had said that if her coalition partners in the centrist D66 and the Christian Democrat CDA would rather form a coalition with the left, they should just say so.

She wouldn’t say whether the right-wing liberal VVD had won the “political reset” it had demanded. Instead, she called the appointment of Sybrand Buma to advise the coalition a “political intervention”.

“You want to go in a certain direction together,” she said. “We hope Mr Buma can lay the foundation for that. That could be structural agreements, partial deals.”

Buma, a former CDA leader who was informateur during the talks that led to the coalition last winter, has a month to help the cabinet agree a financial framework with opposition parties before budgets are drawn up, rather than fighting over them afterwards.

Business package

The tax plan, which shifts €1 billion from income tax to wealth tax, will not change this year, the Telegraaf reported. In return the coalition has promised a package for small and medium-sized businesses. The details won’t be worked out until spring.

Asked whether VVD senators would back the plan, Yesilgöz said that was up to the senate. The senate debate is provisionally set for December 7 and MPs are expected to debate the crisis on Wednesday.

World.title: More than half of Dutch students struggling with finances
World.content:
Students in the Netherlands are increasingly seeking financial support help from organisations set up to alleviate poverty, a survey by the hardship charity Armoedefonds has found.

Three-fifths of organisations said they had experienced an increase in applications, while the budget information agency Nibud said more than half of young people were struggling to make ends meet.

Earlier research by the Armoedefonds found that one-third of support agencies knew of young people who were unable to start or finish a study course because of financial problems.

Spokeswoman Lotte Meerhoff said discussing financial hardship was still a taboo for many young people.

“It’s good that more young people are seeking help, but it shows again how many young people are struggling with financial problems,” she told NOS. “And that can really affect your future in a negative sense.”

Nibud said 54% of young people were having trouble with their financial situation, compared to 40% two years ago. NOS said it had heard of some students doing three part-time jobs to pay the bills.

Financial institutions are offering more help in the form of payment plans or subsidies for essential equipment such as laptops, but Meerhoff said political solutions were needed too.

“We have seen young people’s financial problems growing for years,” she said. “Limiting their ability to pay in instalments on credit, which the political parties are focusing on now, is not enough. Young people need to have more to spend, and that means raising the minimum wage and student finance.”

World.title: Registrations to vote in Senate elections double since 2023
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

More than 80,000 Dutch citizens living abroad have registered to vote in next year’s provincial elections, more than double the number that signed up in 2023.

The electoral commission set up a special electoral college for non-resident citizens four years ago following a campaign by the lobby group Stichting Nederlanders Buiten Nederland (SNBN).

People living on the Caribbean islands of Bonaire, Sint-Eustatius and Saba were also given a vote for the first time.

Foreign residents do not choose representatives for a provincial assembly, but their vote counts towards the make-up of the Senate, which will be indirectly elected by the 12 provinces in May.

So far 82,393 people have registered to vote in the 2027 election, which takes place on March 17, according to the city council in The Hague, which is responsible for the electoral college.

Eelco Keij, chair of SNBN, said he was “positively stunned” by the size of the response, with 10 weeks to go until registration closes. “It’s exciting that so many people from abroad are willing to participate in the democratic process, which also indicates that they felt left out before.”

Dutch citizens can register until February 3 through the council’s website.

Four years ago 37,173 foreign citizens signed up. GroenLinks won the largest share of the overseas vote with 18.5%, while D66 took 16.3%.

The Labour party (PvdA), which has since merged with GroenLinks to form Progressief Nederland, took 8.4%, giving the left-wing combined list more than a quarter of the vote.

Not all parties in parliament contested the vote: the far-right PVV, farmers’ party BBB, the ChristenUnie and Denk were all absent from the ballot paper in 2023.

Keij said he hoped the heightened interest from voters would persuade parties to take the expat vote seriously this time. “There are always remainder seats, so this could be a tipping-point number for parties that are active abroad,” he said.

The BBB became the largest party in the provinces and Senate, taking 19.2% of the overall vote.

World.title: Jetten cabinet survives crisis as coalition agrees to carry on
World.content:
Rob Jetten’s minority cabinet will stay in office after four days of crisis talks. The three coalition parties have agreed to patch up the row over the 2027 tax plan and keep going.

The centrist D66, right-wing liberal VVD and Christian Democrat CDA said on Monday night that “intensive talks” had brought about a “restoration of trust”, public broadcaster NOS reported. No other party will be brought into the coalition.

The government information service RVD announced the deal at around 10pm, after more than nine hours of talks at the Catshuis, the prime minister’s official residence in The Hague.

Debate demanded

Opposition leaders were quick to react to the news. PRO leader Jesse Klaver said it was “totally irresponsible” for the VVD to vote against its own cabinet’s tax plan. “The big question for the whole country is: do we still have a cabinet?” he said. He wants a debate in parliament.

The local authorities’ association VNG, backed by the logistics lobby Evofenedex and the property developers’ association Neprom, had already urged the cabinet to sort out its differences and serve its full term.

Ministers are holding an extra cabinet meeting on Tuesday morning to hear what exactly was agreed. Jetten and his deputy prime ministers, Dilan Yesilgöz (VVD) and Bart van den Brink (CDA), are expected to explain the deal afterwards. MPs are likely to debate the situation on Wednesday, after Klaver’s request.

The three parties have also brought in Sybrand Buma, vice-president of the Council of State and a former CDA leader, to help them reach working agreements with opposition parties on the budget. Buma will mainly advise and won’t be making deals himself, NOS reported, quoting sources in The Hague.

Tax deal row

The row broke out when D66 and the CDA made a deal with left-wing PRO and pan-European party Volt. The deal raises wealth tax by €1 billion and uses the money to cut income tax.

The VVD said the deal broke the coalition agreement. On Thursday its MPs voted against the whole tax plan, which scraped through with the smallest possible majority, 76 of 150 seats.

The next day Yesilgöz called the minority cabinet a “failed experiment” that needed a “fundamental reset”. Jetten said the parties had to have “fundamental talks” to make improvements on a substantive, political and personal level.

The leaders spent the weekend at the De Zwaluwenberg estate in Hilversum, then moved to the Catshuis on Monday. According to NOS, they discussed breaking up the coalition or carrying on without the VVD, but both options were later dropped.

The coalition has just 66 of the 150 seats in parliament, so it needs opposition votes in both houses to pass legislation. The senate is due to vote on the tax plan in the week before Christmas.

World.title: Polish government seeks to introduce maximum gas prices for consumers

Poland’s government has announced plans to introduce a maximum price for natural gas to protect households from the continued impact of the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran earlier this year. The measure would be funded by a new special levy on certain energy companies. To enter into force, the bill must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record amount of legislation. Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk noted that gas prices have been at elevated levels due to the ongoing crisis around the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East, which is normally a major conduit for both oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). Tusk pointed out that the European gas benchmark price recently surpassed €100 per megawatt-hour (MWh), which was its highest level in four years. The figure has since fallen to around €85/MWh, though that is still more than double the level in January and February, before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Such costs are “unacceptable for any Polish family”, said the prime minister. “We can’t allow people to suffer because of decisions made abroad… about war in the Middle East. We don’t want Polish families to pay for it.” The government therefore wants to introduce a maximum price of 197.29 zloty (€44.15) per MWh (which is the level of the current state-regulated gas tariff) for the whole of 2027. The energy ministry estimates that this will save households that use gas for heating up to 1,863 zloty over the year. As well as individual households and housing cooperatives, the maximum price will also apply to entities providing important public services, such as schools, nurseries, hospitals and shelters. Companies selling gas to such consumers will then receive compensation from the state to cover the difference if the maximum price is below what the level of gas tariffs would normally be at that time. The costs of this compensation “will be largely covered by a new monthly gas levy” charged to “energy companies holding licences to trade natural gas with foreign countries and selling high-methane natural gas on the domestic market”, says the government. The levy would amount to 10% of net revenues from domestic sales of high-methane natural gas in 2027. Companies holding capacity rights amounting to less than 10% of the total capacity at entry points to Poland’s gas-transmission system would be exempt. While the legislation is unlikely to face obstacles in parliament, it remains unknown what Nawrocki’s position will be. The president has previously pushed for the government to lower energy prices. However, he also blocked a windfall tax on energy companies to subsidise fuel-price cuts, before eventually relenting. President @NawrockiKn has backed down and signed into law the government's proposed windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits, which he had previously blocked. In response, the government has reintroduced measures to lower prices at petrol stations https://t.co/icGEST8NAo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Earlier this year, analysis by Allianz, the world’s largest insurance company, found that Poland was among a group of 11 countries “most at risk” from a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Poland has become a growing consumer of gas in recent years. As the country has moved away from its traditional reliance on coal, gas has increasingly been used for both electricity generation and home heating. Last year, gas accounted for a record 13.2% of electricity production, up from just 2.7% in 2015. The latest figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that in 2024 almost 21% of households use gas for heating, up from 10% in 2015. Gas consumption reached its highest ever level in Poland this week – breaking a record set in 2021 – amid freezing winter temperatures and as the fuel continues to play a bigger role in the country's energy mix https://t.co/2wEWLPCV9l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 10, 2026 The majority of gas consumed in Poland is imported – around 82% last year, according to the energy ministry. Around 43% of imports arrive in the form of LNG, delivered to a terminal at Świnoujście on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast. Last year, most of that LNG came from the United States (accounting for 30.7% of Poland’s total gas imports) and Qatar (11.2%). However, LNG exports from Qatar have been severely impacted by the difficulties around the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this month, Polish state energy giant Orlen exercised its right to terminate one of its two long-term LNG contracts with QatarEnergy, citing “the ongoing force majeure”. However, Orlen insisted that the decision “does not affect the security of gas supplies”. Most of Poland’s remaining gas imports come via the Baltic Pipe, which opened in 2022 and brings gas from Norway via Denmark. World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a disputed takeover by a group of judges backed by the government. The National Bank of Poland (NBP), which holds the tribunal’s accounts and is headed by a governor appointed under the former government, said it was not the bank’s role to determine which side was legally entitled to represent the institution. Narodowy Bank Polski wstrzymał realizację zleceń płatniczych Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Powodem jest spór o to, kto jest uprawniony do reprezentowania TK i dysponowania środkami zgromadzonymi na jego rachunkach bankowych – poinformował NBP.https://t.co/KXwEBL6j9k pic.twitter.com/0h90bPdTLO — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 16, 2026 Last month, eight judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority – but five of whom the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, has refused to swear in – took control of the court. They declared that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, both of whom were appointed to the TK under the former government, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties and launched disciplinary proceedings against them. Święczkowski denounced the move as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the court’s other six judges, also appointed under the former government. A few days later, Święczkowski submitted a statement to the NBP identifying himself as the sole person authorised to manage the TK’s accounts. Later that week, after the newly elected judges held their first meeting and made several key decisions, the NBP said it had also received documents “indicating, in principle, other persons authorised to dispose of the funds held in the Constitutional Tribunal’s bank accounts”. Meanwhile, Święczkowski also issued a legal challenge against the TK takeover at the Supreme Court, which on 10 November issued a ruling revoking the order to suspend Święczkowski and Sochański. However, the validity of that ruling is disputed. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge who has claimed leadership of the TK, said that only the tribunal itself can decide on the issue. Disciplinary hearings for Święczkowski and Sochański are due to begin later this week. Święczkowski, nevertheless, sent the Supreme Court ruling to the national bank as evidence that he remained the person legally entitled to manage the tribunal. The dispute around Poland's constitutional court risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/mtgutqSTQh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 The NBP’s governor by Adam Glapiński, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government and is a longtime associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. On Monday, the NBP announced that it would suspend all payment orders relating to funds held in the TK’s accounts, citing “a set of documents, which mutually cancel each other out”. “This means that payment orders are not executed, regardless of who initiates them,” the NBP said in a statement. “The National Bank of Poland has no authority to decide who is legally entitled to control the Constitutional Tribunal.” Finance minister Andrzej Domański criticised the decision, accusing the central bank of becoming embroiled in the political dispute. “The National Bank of Poland should safeguard its independence, including its political independence,” Domański said. He added that the government would “explore all available options” to secure funding for the TK and ensure that it can continue functioning. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also condemned the NBP’s move, saying its “invocation of a non-existent document [the disputed Supreme Court ruling] to block funding for a constitutional body is…an attempt to protect an entrenched system”. Święczkowski expressed satisfaction that the NBP had denied access to the “usurpers” trying to take over the court but argued that he, as the legitimate chief justice, should be given control over the accounts, reports news website Onet. Prezes Narodowego Banku Polskiego próbuje paraliżować Trybunał Konstytucyjny, powołując się na rzekome orzeczenie Sądu Najwyższego z 10.11.2026 r.. Problem w tym, że ten papier wygląda jak wydany z pieczątką z ziemniaka, a w obiegu są już jego trzy różne wersje. Najpierw Bogdan… pic.twitter.com/7rWELZFIF0 — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 16, 2026 Recent events follow a decade-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative PiS government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. However, Nawrocki has refused to accept the oath of most of those judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. World.title: Kraków church holds mass for perpetrator of deadly attack just metres from where he shot victims
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. The historic St Mary’s Basilica in Kraków has hosted a holy mass for Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out the recent attack in the city and later died of injuries sustained in a shootout with police. The six people who died in the attack and more than a dozen who were injured were shot by Oskiński on the square where the church stands, some of them just a few metres from its doors. St Mary’s Basilica says that the mass is “an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime”. On the afternoon of 7 November, Oksiński launched his attack on Kraków’s famous market square, which was packed with locals and tourists. He shot at random from his car while driving through the square and surrounding streets before police managed to bring his rampage to an end. Later that same day, the dead bodies of Oksiński’s parents and sister were found in his home. They had each been shot in the head while sleeping. Two days after the attack, Oskiński himself died in hospital. On Sunday, Łukasz Wantuch, a former city councillor, shared a photograph of an announcement that there would be “a holy mass for the late Michał Oksiński and the deceased members of his family” at the Roman Catholic St Mary’s Basilica on Monday morning. The church, built in the 14th century, is one of the most famous in Poland and dominates the skyline in Kraków’s historic, UNESCO-listed city centre. It stands on one corner of the market square, just a few steps from where some of Oksiński’s victims were shot. “I won’t hide the fact that I find this somewhat shocking,” wrote Wantuch. He noted that the announcement referred to the “blessed memory” (świętej pamięci) of Oksiński. However, that phrase is standard usage in Polish to refer to someone who has died (the equivalent ot the English “late”). “But perhaps that is what faith is about: praying even for a murderer,” added Wantuch. Among the more than 1,000 comments under his Facebook post, many agreed with that sentiment. “The whole of Christianity is based on forgiving the unforgivable,” wrote one. “I don’t think anyone needs God’s mercy more [than Oksiński],” said another. However, some others were critical of the fact that the mass was being held in that particular church among the dozens in Kraków. “It is the height of impudence that they’ll celebrate mass for him in the very church he murdered in front of,” wrote one commenter. Later on Sunday, St Mary’s Basilica issued a statement, signed by parish administrator Father Mariusz Słonina, saying that the holy mass “is a private initiative of one of the priests, not of St Mary’s Parish”. However, Słonina added that “praying for the deceased is an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime, a lessening of the perpetrator’s responsibility, or a trivialisation of the suffering of the victims”. Local news service KR24 reported that uniformed police officers were posted outside the church for today’s mass while plainclothes officers were inside, with one of them right next to the altar. Three priests were present, including Słonina, who presided over the mass. Only around a dozen faithful were in attendance, with KR24 suggesting that many did not even seem aware for whom mass was being held. Separate private funeral ceremonies will take place for Oksiński, his parents and sister, who lived in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 160 km from Krakow. On Sunday, their family issued a statement asking the media to “respect the privacy, dignity and mourning of our family and loved ones”. Meanwhile, police and prosecutors continue to investigate the possible motive behind Oksiński’s attack, which they are treating as a terrorist offence. Last week, the justice minister said that there were “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the perpetrator’s online activity. Two police officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, who were seriously injured in the shootout that debilitated Okisński, have been recovering in hospital after undergoing emergency surgery. World.title: Poland detains neo-Nazi teens accused of terrorist plot
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has detained and charged three teenagers who are allegedly linked to “an international neo-Nazi network” and had been planning terrorist attacks, including with the use of homemade explosives. The arrests were announced on Monday morning by Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, who revealed that the suspects are Polish citizens. Two are aged 17 and one is 16. “The teenagers not only promoted Nazi and fascist ideology but had also already taken steps toward committing terrorist offences,” wrote Siemoniak. Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 3 obywateli RP, 16-latka i dwóch 17-latków, związanych z międzynarodowym środowiskiem neonazistowskim. ▶️ Nastolatkowie nie tylko propagowali ideologię nazistowską i faszystowską, ale podejmowali już działania zmierzające do popełniania… — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 16, 2026 The National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that the trio were “fascinated by the activities of an international neo-Nazi terrorist organisation…[that] has an ideology based on hatred against people of Jewish descent, immigrants, black people, the LGBT community, politicians and state security officials”. Though prosecutors did not name the organisation, they said that members of it have been involved in planning terrorist attacks in the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom. In some countries, including the UK, Canada and Australia, it has been outlawed and designated a terrorist group. Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) had found that the three suspects’ online communication indicated “an interest in constructing explosive devices, modifying weapons and using such items to carry out terrorist activities”. During a search of the home of one of the 17-year-olds (named only as “suspect 1”), officers found chemicals that are precursors for the production of explosives. That suspect has also been charged with possession of a so-called pipe bomb, which prosecutors say he wanted to “transfer to a neo-Nazi terrorist group”. Suspect 1 was found to have discussed with the other 17-year-old, named as suspect 2, how to construct an explosive device and detonate it in a specific residential building where someone they knew lived. Suspect 1 had also “incited extremist behaviour and hate-motivated violence” in his online activity, while the 16-year-old, named as suspect 3, had “promoted fascist content” (a crime in Poland) and encouraged someone to assault another person based on their race. Each suspect has been charged with three crimes, relating variously to terrorist offences, possession or attempted production of explosives and weapons, promoting Nazism, fascism and racial hatred, and inciting others to commit violence based on racial differences. Prosecutors note that Polish law generally allows people to face full criminal liability from the age of 17. The two 17-year-olds have therefore been placed in adult pretrial detention, while the 16-year-old is being held in a juvenile facility. Śledztwo w sprawie neonazistów i planowanych aktów terroru kryminalnego Szczegóły w komunikacie: ⬇️https://t.co/dQpdgiTYJD — Prokuratura Regionalna w Gdańsku (@Prok_Regio_GDA) November 16, 2026 The arrests come in the context of recent concerns over radicalisation of young people in Poland. Earlier this month, a 24-year-old carried out a terrorist attack in the city of Kraków, killing six people by firing a rifle from his car. He had earlier killed his parents and sister in their home. In the aftermath of the attack, justice minister Waldemar Żurek revealed that investigators had found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the attacker’s online activity, though he emphasised that the motive was yet to be determined. In the space of a few days last month, three knife attacks took place in Polish schools, resulting in one case in the death of a member of staff. Dozens of young people were arrested in the aftermath for making threats and/or possessing weapons. In September, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them has been charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. World.title: Ukraine blames Russia for graffiti glorifying WWII Ukrainian nationalists on Polish monuments
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around a dozen public monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two nationalist partisan group that was responsible for the massacre of Poles and Jews. Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia, which has previously been accused by the Polish authorities of orchestrating provocative graffiti on monuments. W sobotę, 14 listopada, w Warszawie doszło do kolejnych dwóch dewastacji pomników. Napisy „Slava UPA” pojawiły się na Pomniku Bohaterów Getta przed Muzeum Historii Żydów Polskich POLIN oraz na Pomniku Żołnierzy 1 Armii Wojska Polskiego przy ulicy Andersa 13. To kolejna odsłona… pic.twitter.com/Y7NDsfpjxn — Miejski Reporter (@MiejskiReporter) November 14, 2026 The latest spate of vandalism was first reported in early November in the western city of Poznań, where three World War two memorials were painted with graffiti saying “Glory to the UPA” (Slawa UPA). While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Local police in Poznań told the Gazeta Wyborcza daily that they were searching for a young man dressed in black who is believed to be the culprit, but have so far not been able to identify him. Similar graffiti was subsequently reported on seven monuments, including ones dedicated to Polish World War Two heroes and anti-communist protests that took place in 1970, in Gdańsk and Gdynia, neighbouring cities on Poland’s northern Baltic coast. On Friday, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian on suspicion of “painting offensive slogans propagating hatred”. They shared blurred-out images of the suspect as well as cans of spray paint. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments. If convicted, he could face up to three years in prison. Previously, on Tuesday this week, MOST, a Polish-based Belarusian independent media outlet, published findings that an anonymous person on messaging service Telegram, which is popular among Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians, had been offering $500 plus travel expenses for a job in Poznań. When an undercover MOST journalist responded to the advert, he was told that the job would involve spray painting “Glory to the UPA” on monuments. The recruiter confirmed that the job was illegal, “but if you cover your face and do everything quickly, they won’t find you”. They also revealed that similar jobs were available in other Polish cities, including Warsaw, Wrocław and Lublin. Subsequently, similar inscriptions appeared in Warsaw on the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, which honours the Jews who rose up against their German-Nazi oppressors in 1943; a monument commemorating the Polish First Army, which fought in World War Two; and a monument to sappers who served in the war. The vandalism was condemned by Poland’s Jewish Historical Institute (ŻIH), which called it a “disgraceful attack on the memory of the victims of the Holocaust and the heroes of Jewish resistance”. Noting MOST’s findings and the vandalism of other monuments, ŻIH said that “this points to the possibility of an organised provocation intended to incite hatred and divide society”. Warsaw police told PAP that they are investigating and seeking to identify the perpetrator. An unnamed police source also told Gazeta Wyborcza they see the incidents in all four cities as related to one another, pointing to the similar style of the inscriptions. On Sunday afternoon, Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, condemned the vandalism and shared images of the municipal authorities cleaning the graffiti off the Ghetto Heroes Monument. “Given the scale of similar incidents in other cities, we must consider the possibility that this is a planned provocation,” added the mayor. “Let us not let ourselves be divided – the authorities are working to identify both those who carried out these acts and those who ordered them.” Nie ma zgody na wandalizm w Warszawie. Minionej nocy służby miejskie wyczyściły pomniki oszpecone przez wandali – między innymi Pomnik Bohaterów Getta. Sprawców szuka policja. Patrząc na skalę podobnych incydentów w innych miastach, musimy brać pod uwagę, że mamy do czynienia… pic.twitter.com/5xMgPhnHf8 — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) November 15, 2026 A day earlier, on Saturday, the Ukrainian embassy had also condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation”. “In our view, these unlawful acts are a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states, and in Poland in particular,” wrote the embassy. “The objective is clear: to incite hostility between Poles and Ukrainians, undermine mutual trust, and weaken support for Ukraine.” Writing in both Polish and Ukrainian, the embassy appealed to Ukrainians “not to be tempted by offers of ‘easy money’ in exchange for painting graffiti, damaging property, or carrying out other illegal tasks” and to report any such offers to the Polish police. “Let us respect the laws of the country in which we reside, as well as historical memory and each other’s dignity,” they added. “Polish-Ukrainian solidarity is our shared strength. Let us not allow the enemy to destroy it.” Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians. Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases. In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the massacres, which Poland recognises as a genocide. Ukraine rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting for independence. The issue has recently flared up again this year after President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That sparked widespread anger in Poland and prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of his country’s highest honour. World.title: Polish president vetoes law on removing harmful online content, warning of “censorship”
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed a government bill creating new powers to block harmful online content. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the measures were too far-reaching and could be abused to introduce “censorship”. Government figures have strongly criticised the president’s decision, arguing that it will leave young people in particular more exposed to dangerous content. It also means that Poland still has not fully implemented the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA). ❌ Nie dla cenzury Internetu! pic.twitter.com/WusnK7LImD — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026 Previously, in January this year, Nawrocki had vetoed an earlier bill intended to implement the DSA, describing the measures as “Owellian”. That prompted the government to split the legislation in two. In September, Nawrocki agreed to sign one of those bills, which appointed the president of the Office of Electronic Communications (UKE) as Poland’s digital services coordinator, responsible for overseeing enforcement of the DSA. A second bill was then needed to introduce the actual powers to block harmful online content. In October, it was approved in parliament by the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The right-wing and far-right opposition either voted against it or abstained. Among the new powers included in the legislation were authorisation for the heads of UKE and the National Broadcasting Council (KRRiT) to order the blocking of online content containing violence or threats based on race, nationality, ethnicity, religion or political affiliation. It also allowed the immediate blocking, at the request of a prosecutor or the police, of content involving the acceptance of a contract to commit murder or inciting or assisting in suicide or self-harm. “Perpetrators of serious crimes should not be allowed to use the internet to spread violence and threats,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. “The state must have effective tools to quickly respond to such threats. The safety of internet users must transcend political divisions.” The government also argued that last month’s series of stabbings in schools and this month’s deadly terrorist attack in Kraków – which have raised concern about the online radicalisation of young people – have emphasised the importance of tough controls over digital content. There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister. His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 However, on Friday, the final day by which the president had to make a decision on the bill, Nawrocki announced that he was vetoing it. He argued that “the government has clearly mixed up European obligations with its own political interests”. The measures in the bill threaten to create a “censorship official” and “essentially give the government arbitrary control and the ability to decide what we can and cannot say, write or publish, said the president. Decisions on whether content is permitted or not should be “the exclusive competence of the justice system and independent judges”, he argued. Nawrocki also said that the powers in the vetoed bill were “disproportionate”, allowing an entire domain to be blocked due to a single example of illegal content. “The security of citizens cannot be a pretext for weakening their freedoms,” said Nawrocki. “We must not create a false choice: either the security or the freedom of its citizens. A responsible state must ensure and balance both.” Dlaczego Prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki zawetował ustawę o DSA? ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/1BUJVFEftl — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026 Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski, however, said that the president was “not defending free speech” but instead “once again siding with global [digital] platforms and allowing them to decide what users see”. “The vetoed provisions concerned illegal content, not opinions or views expressed online,” added the ministry, which also noted that all decisions on blocking content were subject to appeals and judicial review. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, accused Nawrocki of “waging war on the government at the expense of Polish children and Polish security”, which would both be threatened by the absence of the vetoed measures. Z prezydenckiego weta zadowoleni są hejterzy, rosyjskie farmy trolli, pedofile, ekstremalni nihiliści i lobbyści. Ofiarami tego weta są polskie dzieci, rodzice, bezpieczeństwo wszystkich obywateli. Tego nie da się w żaden sposób usprawiedliwić. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) November 14, 2026 Aleksandra Wójtowicz, an analyst on new technologies at the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), told the Fakt newspaper that the measures do “not in any way relate to alleged censorship”. They are intended to force digital platforms to remove illegal content, she explained. Wójtowicz added that the measures would actually have protected free speech by giving Polish users whose accounts were unjustly deleted by social media platforms the right to appeal against those decisions outside of the platform itself. However, Nawrocki’s veto was praised by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party. Czarnek told TV Trwam that the proposed measures had been intended to “fight the opposition” rather than actual hate speech. A new hub has opened at the University of Oxford to support research cooperation with Poland, offering grants for academic projects, visits, training and workshops. The Oxford Poland Hub, which its organisers describe as Poland’s first initiative of its kind anywhere in the world, will also hold public events exploring Polish history, language and culture. We’re proud to have worked on the Oxford-Poland Hub & helped make it a reality together with great partners 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Huge thanks to: 🔹 @UniofOxford & @JesusOxford, esp. Prof Paulina Kewes & Dr Marek Naczyk 🔹 Ministry of Science and Higher Education & Minister @MarcinKulasek 🧵 pic.twitter.com/LghfpOhptC — Polish Embassy UK 🇵🇱 (@PolishEmbassyUK) November 12, 2026 “The launch of the Oxford-Poland Hub is an exciting new chapter in Oxford’s longstanding relationship with Poland,” said the University of Oxford’s vice-chancellor, Irene Tracey. “[It] will create new opportunities for academic exchange, collaborative research and partnership between Oxford and Poland.” The centre is initially funded for three years by Poland’s National Agency for Academic Exchange (NAWA), with support from the science and higher education ministry. It will operate within The Oxford Research Centre in the Humanities (TORCH). “The Oxford Poland Hub…gives us a permanent institutional presence at one of the world’s leading academic centres,” said Wojciech Karczewski, NAWA’s director general. “We see it as an investment in long-term partnerships that will enable researchers from Poland and Oxford to tackle increasingly ambitious research challenges together.” The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and one of the most prestigious. It ranked first globally in the latest Times Higher Education World University Rankings. The new centre will offer grants of up to £5,000 (26,400 zloty) to support research projects or academic visits and up to £10,000 for academic workshops. Training scholarships are due to be introduced from the hub’s second year. All researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford will be eligible to apply for funding if their work involves collaboration with researchers based in Poland. The hub will focus on humanities and social sciences as well as cooperation with Oxford’s libraries and museums. The hub will also organise public lectures, exhibitions and events related to Polish history, language and culture for the academic community and Oxford’s residents, including its Polish community. 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Oxford-Poland Hub oficjalnie otwarty! Polska nauka zyskuje nowe możliwości współpracy z Uniwersytetem Oksfordzkim. W uroczystym otwarciu wziął udział minister nauki i szkolnictwa wyższego Marcin Kulasek. Centrum powstało dzięki współpracy Ministerstwa Nauki i Szkolnictwa… pic.twitter.com/bZaCdM3Y53 — Ministerstwo Nauki i Szkolnictwa Wyższego (@MNiSW_GOV__PL) November 10, 2026 The hub was inaugurated on Monday at Jesus College, one of Oxford University’s colleges, with Poland’s science and higher education minister, Marcin Kulasek, and Rafał Wiśniewski, chargé d’affaires at the Polish Embassy in London, among those attending. “Poland and the United Kingdom have for many years developed strong cooperation in science and higher education through joint research projects, academic mobility programmes and institutional partnerships,” Kulasek said. “The Oxford–Poland Hub opens a new chapter in this cooperation.” The centre is directed by Paulina Kewes, a professor of English literature at Oxford who was born in Poland. Professor Norman Davies, the renowned historian of Poland and an honorary fellow at St Antony’s College, Oxford, attended the launch. The inaugural lecture, given by Dariusz Wójcik, a professor at the National University of Singapore and honorary research associate at the University of Oxford, discussed Maria Czaplicka, the renowned Polish academic who in 1916 became Oxford’s first female lecturer of anthropology. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
