No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Sofya Samodelkina Breaks Into World’s Top 10 Figure Skaters
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Sofya Samodelkina has reached a career-best 10th place in the updated International Skating Union (ISU) world rankings, earning 2,881 points after improving her previous position by three places.

Her rise followed a strong performance at Skate America 2026, the fourth stage of the Grand Prix series, held in Everett, United States, on Nov. 12-15. After placing 11th in the short program with 61.03 points, Samodelkina scored 137.56 points in the free skate, setting a season best and finishing fifth overall with 198.59 points.

During the free skate, she became the first Kazakh female figure skater to perform a triple Axel, an ultra-C element, at an official international competition.

Japan’s Ami Nakai won the event with 236.81 points, followed by Russia’s Alexandra Ignatova with 213.90 and Japan’s Rino Matsuike with 211.63.

Samodelkina has earned 14 ranking points across two Grand Prix events, having also finished fifth at Skate Canada. She is preparing for the second half of the season, including the Four Continents Figure Skating Championships, scheduled for Almaty in February 2027.

Her achievement means Kazakhstan now has representatives in the top 10 of both singles world rankings. Olympic champion Mikhail Shaidorov holds second place in the men’s standings with 4,261 points.

World.title: Air Astana to Launch Direct Almaty-Tokyo Flights This November
World.content:
ASTANA – Air Astana will launch regular direct flights between Almaty and Tokyo’s Narita Airport on Nov. 30, operating twice a week.

The route was discussed at a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev and Seiichi Tajima, Assistant Vice-Minister for International Aviation at Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, on the sidelines of the Seventh ICAO Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7), the ministry reported on Nov. 17.

Lastayev said the launch of direct flights would restore air connectivity between the two countries after a long interruption and support business, tourism, investment and cultural ties.

The flights will be operated on Airbus A321LR aircraft. According to Air Astana’s schedule, the flight from Almaty to Tokyo will take approximately seven hours and 30 minutes, while the return journey will take nine hours and 25 minutes. Ticket sales opened on Oct. 2.

Lastayev and Tajima also discussed prospects for expanding air services and cooperation between their national carriers.

They also addressed cooperation within the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). Lastayev congratulated the Japanese side on electing Toshiyuki Onuma as President of the ICAO Council, marking the first time a representative from the Asia-Pacific region has held the position.

The officials emphasized the importance of continued dialogue and cooperation on international aviation platforms to promote safety, sustainability and efficiency in civil aviation.

World.title: Kazakhstan Joins ICAO Conference to Shape Global Aviation Agenda Toward 2050
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is taking part in the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7) of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which opened in Montreal, Canada, on Nov. 16 and brought together representatives of 193 member states and international aviation organizations to discuss the future of global air transport.

The conference focuses on key priorities for the aviation industry, including air transport liberalization, stronger international connectivity, infrastructure investment, digitalization, innovation and sustainable development.

According to the ministry, the Kazakh delegation is led by Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev and includes Civil Aviation Committee Chair Saltanat Tompiyeva, Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to ICAO Timur Tlegenov, ministry officials and representatives of the country’s aviation industry.

The opening ceremony featured remarks by ICAO Council President Toshiyuki Onuma, UN Tourism Secretary-General Shaikha Al Nuwais and Canadian Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon. ICAO Secretary-General Juan Carlos Salazar also delivered a presentation.

Addressing participants, Onuma highlighted the aviation sector’s reliance on international cooperation, emphasizing that global air travel depends on common standards and mutual trust established under the 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation.

He stressed the need for ICAO to remain responsive to technological advances, evolving markets and increasingly complex operational requirements.

ATConf/7 marks the first worldwide air transport conference in 13 years, following the sixth edition in March 2013. Its agenda reflects significant changes in the global aviation landscape and the need to adapt regulatory and economic frameworks to emerging industry challenges.

The conference agenda covers aviation’s long-term development toward 2050, investment in airport and aviation infrastructure, regulatory cooperation, emergency preparedness and consumer protection. Participants will also discuss ways to strengthen international air connectivity, improve economic and regulatory frameworks, and enhance the aviation sector’s competitiveness and resilience.

An extraordinary ICAO Assembly is also scheduled to open on Nov. 19. Its main objective is to elect four additional member states to the ICAO Council following the expansion of its membership from 36 to 40 countries. The assembly is also expected to adopt a ministerial declaration.

For Kazakhstan, participation in the conference provides an opportunity to advance its aviation priorities, exchange international expertise and strengthen cooperation with foreign governments and international organizations.

The delegation is also expected to hold bilateral meetings and discuss prospects for developing Kazakhstan’s civil aviation sector.

Kazakhstan’s participation underscores its commitment to international aviation cooperation and contributes to the development of a safe, competitive and sustainable global air transport system.

World.title: Uzbekistan and Oman Advance $5 Billion Cooperation Package Across Key Sectors
World.content:
ASTANA – Uzbekistan and Oman are advancing nearly 30 agreements and contracts worth approximately $5 billion across energy, industry, transport, finance and other sectors, as part of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s state visit to Oman.

During the visit, Mirziyoyev met with representatives of major Omani businesses led by Abdulsalam al-Murshidi, President of Oman’s Investment Authority, to discuss expanding investment cooperation and implementing joint projects, the President’s press service reported on Nov. 16.

The talks focused on increasing the Uzbek-Omani Investment Company’s authorized capital and developing projects in mining, electrical engineering, chemicals, renewable energy, construction, transport and logistics, infrastructure and agriculture.

The officials also discussed establishing an Uzbek-Omani Business Council to strengthen direct engagement between companies. They agreed to form a joint working group to advance the proposed initiatives and review progress quarterly.

The business meetings followed the Uzbek-Omani Business Forum held in Muscat on Nov. 16, which brought together more than 150 business representatives from both countries. The forum resulted in the signing of a package of cooperation documents covering energy, industry, transport and logistics, finance, agriculture and technology.

The two countries are also seeking to expand bilateral trade and investment. Trade reached approximately $2.3 million in 2025 and increased by more than 70% in the first nine months of 2026 to $3.3 million, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.

World.title: Airbus Expects Central Asia Air Traffic to Nearly Triple by 2045
World.content:
ASTANA – Passenger air traffic in Central Asia is projected to nearly triple by 2045, reaching 242 billion revenue passenger kilometers, as rising incomes, economic growth and an expanding population fuel demand for air travel, Airbus said at a Nov. 17 briefing in Tashkent.

Passenger traffic in Central Asia increased from 16 billion revenue passenger kilometers in 2005 to 89 billion revenue passenger kilometers in 2025, representing an average annual growth rate of 9%, said Jérôme Chaptal, director in strategic analysis and global market forecasting at Airbus.

By 2045, the figure is expected to rise by a further 153 billion revenue passenger kilometers to 242 billion, representing an average annual growth rate of 5.1%.

“The most important thing is that air traffic in this region will triple over the next 20 years. Globally, we expect it to double, while in Central Asia it will grow threefold,” Chaptal said, attributing the stronger regional outlook partly to faster population growth.

According to Airbus, several factors are expected to drive demand, including economic growth, rising incomes and demographic expansion. The company projects that the region’s population will increase by 23 million by 2045, while the number of people with middle-level incomes will grow by 26 million.

Chaptal also pointed to growing economic activity and trade within Central Asia as factors supporting passenger and cargo traffic. Europe and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) are expected to remain important markets for regional connectivity, alongside expanding commercial links with other destinations.

Global aviation growth

The briefing also examined broader trends in global aviation. Airbus expects worldwide passenger traffic to nearly double over the next 20 years, supported by rising demand for air travel, particularly in emerging markets.

Chaptal highlighted China and India as major contributors to future growth. By 2045, China’s aviation market is expected to reach a scale comparable to Europe’s current market, while India’s market could reach a level similar to China’s today.

He also identified Asia, India, Africa and South America as regions with strong growth potential, contrasting them with more mature markets such as Europe and North America.

“Central Asia’s geographical position between Europe and Asia could further strengthen its role in international air connectivity, particularly along routes linking the two regions through the Middle East,” Chaptal said.

He noted that airlines’ decisions to expand their networks would depend on several factors, including market demand, geopolitical developments and the flexibility to adjust routes when airspace restrictions or other disruptions affect operations.

Rising passenger demand to reshape global aircraft fleet

The projected increase in passenger traffic will require substantial expansion and renewal of the global aircraft fleet.

According to Chaptal, the number of passenger aircraft with at least 100 seats is expected to increase from 23,310 in 2025 to 45,550 by 2045. Meeting this demand will require 42,060 new aircraft deliveries. Of these, 22,240 will support fleet growth, while 19,820 will replace older aircraft.

Air cargo is another important area of growth, Chaptal said, noting that freight transportation has demonstrated resilience amid global disruptions.

Airbus also forecasts significant expansion of the global freighter fleet. The number of cargo aircraft in service is expected to rise from 2,360 in 2025 to 3,460 by 2045.

The company projects demand for 2,670 new freighters over the period. Of these, 1,580 will replace older aircraft, while 1,090 will contribute to fleet expansion. Around 790 existing aircraft are expected to remain in service in 2045.

The forecast reflects both growing demand for air cargo and the need to modernize aging fleets. Chaptal also pointed to the resilience of air freight amid geopolitical disruptions, fuel supply challenges and extreme weather events.

As Kazakhstan pushes to become a regional aviation hub, Airbus is also deepening its presence across multiple sectors, from passenger aircraft to military transport and space technology.

World.title: Kazakhstan Seeks to Increase Domestic Content in $8 Billion Oil and Gas Procurement Market
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is stepping up efforts to expand domestic manufacturers’ access to government and corporate procurement, with local content accounting for 55.4% of purchases by companies in the country’s fuel and energy sector during January-September. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov has called for stronger support for local suppliers, broader use of long-term contracts and reforms to simplify the registration of Kazakh manufacturers at a Nov. 17 government meeting.

According to Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov, procurement of goods, works and services by companies in the fuel and energy sector reached 3.55 trillion tenge (US$8 billion) in the first nine months of 2026. Approximately 1.9 trillion tenge ($4.3 billion) went to domestic suppliers.

The government is seeking to increase local content in oil and gas projects by introducing minimum requirements of 30% for goods and 80% for works and services in subsoil-use contracts.

Major oil operators expand cooperation with local suppliers

Three major oil and gas operators are paying particular attention to procurement: Tengizchevroil, Karachaganak Petroleum Operating and North Caspian Operating Company.

Following an industry forum and open days held in October, the companies signed 10 memorandums of cooperation and 27 contracts with domestic manufacturers.

Their combined procurement of goods, works, and services reached 2.8 trillion tenge ($6.3 billion) in 2025, up 4% from the previous year.

Long-term supply agreements and offtake contracts are another mechanism intended to provide local manufacturers with predictable demand.

Since the beginning of this year, subsoil users have signed 75 long-term contracts with Kazakh manufacturers worth 79.7 billion tenge ($179 million). National oil and gas company KazMunayGas has signed another 42 offtake contracts worth 668.9 million tenge ($1.5 million).

These agreements allow manufacturers to secure buyers before expanding production capacity or investing in new facilities.

Government targets gaps in procurement

Bektenov highlighted the potential to increase domestic manufacturers’ participation in procurement by companies developing Kazakhstan’s solid mineral resources.

According to him, the share of goods purchased from domestic manufacturers in this segment stands at just 17%.

He instructed the Ministry of Industry and Construction, together with the Ministry of Energy, to identify products and procurement volumes Kazakh companies could supply.

The government also plans to address administrative barriers affecting access to procurement.

The digital register of Kazakhstan commodity producers, introduced earlier this year, has registered approximately 2,600 manufacturers and more than 70,000 product lines. More than 50,000 applications have been processed.

However, businesses have raised concerns about delays in confirming their status as domestic producers. Bektenov instructed the relevant ministries to improve the register, integrate it with government databases, and convert the registration procedure into a government service within three months, with set deadlines for processing applications.

Long-term contracts and local production

Bektenov also called for wider use of offtake agreements, under which buyers commit to purchasing products from manufacturers over an agreed period.

He instructed the Ministry of Industry and Construction, the Ministry of Finance and the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs to remove procurement barriers and increase the volume of contracts with domestic manufacturers by the end of the year.

The relevant ministries, together with subsoil users, must also identify products and volumes suitable for domestic procurement and approve a 2027 plan for long-term agreements and offtake contracts.

“Development of domestic production and protection of the domestic market are an unconditional priority of the government’s economic policy,” Bektenov said.

He emphasized that budget-funded purchases should prioritize Kazakh products when domestic alternatives are available, arguing that public spending should support local businesses and strengthen the country’s manufacturing base.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans 200 Industrial Projects Worth $3.8 Billion to Expand Manufacturing
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to launch 200 industrial projects worth more than 1.7 trillion tenge (US$3.8 billion) by the end of this year, aiming to expand domestic manufacturing, reduce import dependence and create more than 17,000 jobs.

At full capacity, the projects are expected to generate approximately 1.5 trillion tenge ($3.3 billion) in annual output, including 500 billion tenge ($1.1 billion) in export-oriented production. Minister of Industry and Construction Yersaiyn Nagaspayev presented the plans at a Nov. 17 government meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov.

Manufacturing output increased by 9.3% in January-October. Of the 200 planned projects, 125 have already been launched, attracting 900 billion tenge ($2 billion) in investment. The remaining projects are nearing completion, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

The new facilities will produce goods ranging from railway wheels and gear components to press equipment, laminate flooring, drip irrigation systems and aluminum coffee capsules. The projects are expected to create 17,300 jobs, including 5,500 in rural areas.

Automotive and railway manufacturing

A key element of the government’s industrial strategy is introducing an industrial cluster model designed to connect large manufacturers with domestic suppliers, small and medium-sized businesses, research institutions and service companies. Automotive and railway engineering have been selected as pilot sectors.

Kazakhstan already produces batteries, tires, multimedia systems and vehicle seats. Local manufacturers have also begun stamping bus body components using steel supplied by domestic producer Qarmet. This year, new production lines for heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems, flooring and truck engine blocks have been launched.

Further localization projects are planned in Kostanai and Almaty. Kostanai is expected to launch an automotive components facility with an annual capacity of up to 60,000 units, while Almaty is preparing to localize the production of wiring harnesses, brake lines and fuel pipes.

The government is also seeking to expand domestic heavy-truck production. Kazakhstan has already established production operations involving international brands such as HOWO, SITRAK and Scania. Volvo truck production is planned for Almaty by the end of the year, while negotiations with Mercedes-Benz are underway.

Investment in oil and gas equipment

The energy sector is another priority for localization. Kazakhstan is working with international and domestic original equipment manufacturers to establish 15 new production facilities supplying goods required by the oil and gas industry. The projects are valued at 37.7 billion tenge ($84.7 million).

Between 2022 and 2025, the country localized 10 such production facilities worth 7.9 billion tenge ($17.7 million), creating more than 350 jobs.

The government has also raised the reimbursement threshold for international certification costs from 3,000 to 15,000 monthly calculation indices, allowing domestic manufacturers to receive up to 60 million tenge ($134,818).

According to Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov, seven Kazakh manufacturers in the oil and gas sector have already supplied products to markets in Europe, North America and Asia.

Construction materials and agriculture

Kazakhstan aims to increase the share of domestically produced construction materials in the internal market from 73% to 80% within three years.

The government plans to attract investment into the production of insulation materials, ceramic tiles, composite materials and facing products. The initiative is linked to the Khalyktyq Qurylys, or the People’s Construction program, which is expected to receive approximately 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.6 billion) from the National Fund.

Agriculture is also receiving substantial support. Gross agricultural output increased by 5.2% in the first 10 months of this year, reaching 8.9 trillion tenge ($20 billion).

Concessional agricultural lending reached 1.2 trillion tenge ($2.7 billion) this year, while domestic manufacturers accounted for 95% of agricultural machinery purchases, supported by preferential leasing programs.

Bektenov said the government would continue supporting local manufacturers through access to financing, industrial cooperation and guaranteed demand for their products.

World.title: Kazakhstan and IMF Discuss Economic Outlook and Priorities for Sustainable Growth
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s economy is expected to maintain steady growth this year and accelerate in 2027, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), as Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov met with the fund’s mission chief for Kazakhstan, Amina Lahreche, on Nov. 16, to review the country’s economic outlook and discuss further cooperation.

The meeting focused on the findings of the IMF’s latest mission, Kazakhstan’s ongoing institutional and economic reforms, and priorities for strengthening macroeconomic stability and sustainable growth, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Bektenov briefed Lahreche on the country’s institutional reforms, including the new Constitution, which entered into force in July, and the government’s efforts to develop the digital economy and establish new drivers of economic growth in line with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s directives.

He highlighted the importance of continued expert engagement with the IMF and drawing on international experience to improve Kazakhstan’s economic policymaking.

“Our dialogue continues through regular missions, targeted consultations and the provision of technical assistance by the IMF to government agencies. I hope the recommendations following the current mission will serve as a useful guide for further improving the country’s macroeconomic and macroprudential policies,” Bektenov said.

Lahreche presented the mission’s findings and gave a positive assessment of Kazakhstan’s macroeconomic situation, noting the country’s economic potential and its development priorities.

“We arrived in Kazakhstan shortly after the President delivered his address and outlined important priorities for infrastructure development and investment in human capital. We recognize Kazakhstan’s significant economic potential. We hope our dialogue and recommendations will contribute to sustainable economic growth that takes citizens’ needs into account,” she said.

According to the IMF’s October outlook, Kazakhstan is set to maintain stable economic growth in 2026, with growth expected to accelerate next year. The fund also noted that Central Asian economies, including Kazakhstan, have demonstrated resilience to external shocks, supported by ongoing reforms.

The IMF identified price stability, better coordination of monetary and fiscal policies, rebuilding fiscal buffers and trade diversification among the key priorities for the region.

Kazakhstan’s economic indicators showed continued expansion in January-October. GDP grew by 4.5%, while fixed-capital investment increased by 4.9% to 18.3 trillion tenge (US$41.1 billion).

Growth was recorded across industry and agriculture, with particularly strong performance in manufacturing-related sectors. Machinery manufacturing expanded by 22.2%, while pharmaceuticals grew by 50.9%. Agricultural output increased by 5.2%.

Following the meeting, the government reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining constructive engagement with the IMF and expanding cooperation in areas with potential for mutual benefit. Relevant government agencies will review the fund’s proposals and recommendations.

Lahreche said at a press briefing on Nov. 17 that the country’s large-scale construction and infrastructure investment program could support economic growth, projected at 4.6% in 2026 and 4.8% in 2027, but also fuel inflation if productivity gains fail to keep pace with increased public spending.

World.title: ‘Traffic jams are not caused by buildings’: Yerevan mayor responds to prime minister’s wife
World.content:
Yerevan mayor responds to Anna Hakobyan over traffic jams

“Traffic jams are caused by cars, not buildings. Armenia is experiencing economic growth and an inflow of money. People now have more opportunities – and they are buying cars,” Yerevan Mayor Tigran Avinyan said today.

He was effectively responding to Anna Hakobyan, the wife of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. A few days ago, she posted a video on social media showing traffic jams in the capital. She said Yerevan was gradually becoming “the most unfriendly city” to live in.

The prime minister’s wife asked what the authorities should do to prevent life in the city and getting around it from becoming “a reason for a heart attack”. She pointed to economic growth, the rapid construction of new buildings, a rising population, more cars on the roads and an influx of tourists.

“Some people have a professional duty to find an answer to this question. But this task is far more difficult than issuing construction permits to companies investing millions of dollars. ‘Approved’ is a magic stamp that requires minimal effort but has an enormous impact [on the situation],” Hakobyan stressed.

According to the mayor, the city authorities issued a record 108 permits for apartment blocks and residential complexes in 2021. Those are the buildings now being completed and handed over to residents. Avinyan noted that the authorities have not issued as many permits in any year since then. For example, they issued just 37 in 2025.

The mayor acknowledged that the current situation is causing a certain degree of “tension” – and said he shares those concerns. However, Avinyan called for an analysis of the problems and appropriate solutions.

Tigran Avinyan’s explanation apparently failed to satisfy Anna Hakobyan. She immediately posted another video, this time about the “catastrophic traffic jams”. In her post, the prime minister’s wife urged women drivers to stop being patient:

“Keep noisy objects in your cars. Every time you find yourself stuck in traffic for hours, make a loud noise. Make it loud enough for those who have a duty to use their brains and solve the problem to hear you.”

Prime minister’s wife: “You need an astronaut’s health to get from point A to point C”

In her first post, Anna Hakobyan said that getting around the capital required “an astronaut’s health” – in other words, a strong cardiovascular and nervous system.

She also expressed confidence that scientific disciplines exist that can help calculate how many cars Yerevan will have in 25 years, based on current development trends. They can also help determine what measures the authorities need to take now to prepare for that future.

Hakobyan suggested that, alongside the buildings springing up across the city “like mushrooms after rain”, the authorities should build flyovers, as well as elevated, underground and bypass roads.

“You have to actively seek out this knowledge yourself. Nobody will serve it up on a silver platter as a ready-made, multi-million-dollar project that only needs a ‘approved’ stamp,” she said, again alluding to the construction permits issued in the capital.

In her view, traffic planning must take into account how much the population could grow in the coming years and how many more cars the city might have.

“What will happen if between 300,000 and 500,000 people return to their homeland to live permanently over the next five years? And what if 250,000 of them bring their own cars? What are we going to do? Will the same number of people have to leave so that we can all fit on the streets?” Anna Hakobyan asked.

Mayor: “Possible solutions will be presented to the public”

According to Yerevan Mayor Tigran Avinyan, traffic congestion in the capital has three main causes: the growing number of private cars, driving culture and the need to give public transport priority.

He said the city authorities would soon present various possible solutions for public discussion. Avinyan outlined some of the measures under consideration:

fully separating bus lanes from other traffic;

introducing measures to reduce traffic violations;

restricting car use on public health grounds.

On the last point, the mayor clarified that the restrictions would not apply to vehicles coming to Yerevan from other regions. He said the aim was to reduce the overall number of cars within the city.

Tigran Avinyan believes the growing number of private cars is the main cause of traffic jams. He argues that public transport should take priority.

He expects new road construction to help improve traffic flow to some extent. However, he warned that new roads alone would not solve the problem. They would soon become congested again unless the authorities introduced measures such as restrictions on car use, dedicated lanes and tougher fines.

The mayor also addressed environmental concerns. Avinyan identified nitrogen dioxide as a specific pollutant whose levels in Yerevan are rising rapidly year after year as the number of cars increases. He said it causes lung and respiratory diseases.

“The most dangerous thing is that children are the first to suffer from these problems,” Avinyan stressed.

First lady’s appeal

In response to the Yerevan mayor’s remarks, Anna Hakobyan published a new video, saying that people had thanked her for raising the issue.

“They tell me: ‘At last, someone has had the courage to speak about this.’ Every day, hundreds of thousands of people suffer in Yerevan’s traffic jams. So does complaining about the situation now require ‘courage’?”

Hakobyan urged women drivers to stop putting up with the situation and called on men to show greater determination. She suggested that women should make a loud noise whenever they get stuck in traffic.

In her view, government institutions never hear complaints that people “do not dare to voice”.

“Otherwise, we might end up blaming the previous authorities for Yerevan’s traffic jams [the current government, led by her husband, often blames its predecessors for various problems]. If Armenia’s economy had developed in a balanced way over the past 30 years, and the number of cars had increased gradually rather than exponentially, the situation in the Armenian capital would be completely different today,” she said.

Yerevan mayor responds to Anna Hakobyan over traffic jams

World.title: ‘Сake will be divided without us’: Analyst on Georgia’s foreign policy
World.content:
According to analyst Paata Zakareishvili, the appointment of Giorgi Zurabashvili, first deputy foreign minister, as the Georgian prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia gives the Kremlin a new channel for direct political communication with Georgia’s foreign ministry. This could pave the way for existing negotiation formats to be weakened.

Russia has already established contact with the new special representative, Giorgi Zurabashvili. His Russian counterpart will be Mikhail Galuzin, Russia’s deputy foreign minister. According to the Russian side, the main topics for discussion will include increasing trade and tourism, expanding transport links and promoting cultural exchanges between the two countries.

Paata Zakareishvili believes that placing the special representative’s post within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is a dangerous decision. In his view, the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia should be an independent figure, rather than a serving senior official in the foreign ministry.

“Georgia and Russia have not maintained diplomatic relations since the August 2008 war. At the same time, Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and the political confrontation between the two countries require a special format for relations.

“It was precisely for these reasons that the Karasin-Abashidze format was established. Under this arrangement, Georgia’s former special representative, Zurab Abashidze, met with Russia’s deputy foreign minister, Grigory Karasin,” the analyst says.

According to Zakareishvili, the format was important because it kept talks with Russia on practical issues separate from discussions about the conflicts. It also allowed Georgia’s foreign ministry to make its position clear during international negotiations.

“Russia constantly says that diplomatic relations with Georgia should be restored. The Georgian authorities remain silent on this issue. Against this background, they have suddenly taken a step in Russia’s favour. Russia needs to ‘get its foot in the door’ of Georgia’s foreign ministry and hold talks with the first deputy minister,” Zakareishvili says.

He is particularly concerned about the possible weakening of the Geneva International Discussions. Established after the 2008 war, the talks involve representatives of Georgia, Russia and the United States, as well as the European Union and the OSCE. Zakareishvili believes the Georgian authorities’ latest moves could eventually be aimed at reducing the importance of this international format in favour of direct bilateral contacts.

According to the analyst, the replacement of Lasha Darsalia as Georgia’s representative at the Geneva talks also carries symbolic significance. Zakareishvili says Darsalia clearly articulated Georgia’s position during the negotiations and regularly used the term “occupation” when referring to Russia’s actions.

“The time will come when they start singing a new tune: ‘Georgia’s foreign ministry is already dealing with Russia, so why do we need Geneva?’ Their primary aim is to weaken the Geneva format, which is visibly losing ground,” Zakareishvili predicts.

He also believes that the location of the first meeting between Giorgi Zurabashvili and Mikhail Galuzin will be particularly important. He considers holding the meeting in Moscow a disastrous political move, as it would give Russia an opportunity to symbolically demonstrate that it controls the process.

In Zakareishvili’s view, Prague would be the most logical venue, as it hosted meetings between Karasin and Abashidze for years.

“Russia needs symbolic victories. If the meeting takes place in Moscow, the message will be that Russia is in control of the process. That must not be allowed under any circumstances,” the analyst says.

Zakareishvili also links the Georgian authorities’ new approach to relations with Russia to a shift in the country’s foreign policy. In his assessment, the government is gradually moving away from the European Union and NATO, while seeking to build closer ties with Russia without making any formal commitments to direct integration or cooperation with Moscow.

In this context, the analyst also points to the possibility of Article 78 of Georgia’s Constitution being repealed. It obliges state authorities to take all necessary measures to ensure the country’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

According to Zakareishvili, the initiative to ban opposition parties and the Georgian authorities’ efforts to secure a constitutional majority are part of a broader political process that could undermine the institutional foundations of Georgia’s commitment to Western integration.

Paata Zakareishvili

“It is not Bidzina Ivanishvili who is Russia’s project, but Russia that is Ivanishvili’s project. For now, however, this suits Russia. Russia has other priorities at the moment, and it is not Russia that is working on Georgia – it is Ivanishvili who is working for Russia,” Zakareishvili says.

In his assessment, the message the Georgian authorities are sending to the Kremlin is this: Georgia no longer intends to move towards the European Union and NATO, but it also has no plans to join the political and economic blocs established by Russia. Zakareishvili believes the authorities are using this approach to preserve room for political manoeuvre while avoiding public discontent that an overt shift towards Russia could trigger.

The analyst believes that if the authorities continue with their current policy, by the time Bidzina Ivanishvili’s political influence comes to an end, support for Georgia joining the EU and NATO could be significantly weakened, leaving the political space open to groups advocating neutrality.

Turning away from Brussels and the threat to Georgia’s role as a transit hub

Another key focus of Zakareishvili’s criticism is Georgia’s absence from a ministerial meeting in Brussels dedicated to security and connectivity.

The meeting brought together representatives of the European Union, Central Asian countries, Armenia and Azerbaijan. Zakareishvili sees Georgia’s absence not simply as a diplomatic mistake, but as a significant loss for the country’s long-term economic and geopolitical interests.

He says the connectivity ministerial was not about EU enlargement. Its main focus was the development of transport, energy and economic links across the region – an area in which Georgia could play an important role because of its geographical position.

According to the European Commission’s 2026 enlargement report, Georgia’s EU integration process remains suspended, and the country’s position has deteriorated further compared with the previous year. The Commission says the Georgian authorities took no steps during the reporting period to implement the nine recommendations set out as conditions for advancing the country’s EU accession process.

Zakareishvili stresses that international transport and trade routes are constantly changing. A country that does not take part in the relevant negotiations may eventually lose the opportunity to benefit even from its own geographical advantages.

“If Georgia does not take part, someone else will take its place and share the spoils! If you do not show up to a party, the party will go on without you – and someone else will eat the slice of cake that was meant for you,” he says.

In the analyst’s view, Georgia should pay particular attention to the development of a new transport corridor through Armenia, including the so-called “Trump Route”, which could significantly reshape the transport geography of the South Caucasus.

Zakareishvili fears that if Georgia does not actively participate in regional connectivity projects, a significant share of international freight could bypass the country. Georgia would then lose the economic and political advantages built up over decades through its Black Sea ports, railway, pipelines and East-West transit corridor.

The analyst draws a historical parallel with the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan oil pipeline and the Baku-Tbilisi-Erzurum gas pipeline. He says that, as a result of political decisions made at the time, these projects were routed through Georgia rather than Armenia. But the situation could now change: new transport routes in the region could allow Armenia to become a transit country at Georgia’s expense.

Zakareishvili believes Turkey will play a particularly important role in this process. The development of new routes and the redistribution of transport flows could increase the importance of Turkish ports and Mediterranean routes, affecting the competitiveness of Georgia’s Black Sea ports.

“As long as Georgia has pipelines and ports, and still has a chance to take part somewhere, to get a foot in the door and claim a share – if not a piece of the cake, then at least a seat at the table – it should do so. Otherwise, these processes will move forward without Georgia,” Zakareishvili says.

In his view, the authorities’ refusal to attend international meetings, justified on the grounds of protecting the country’s dignity and sovereignty, could in reality damage Georgia’s economic interests.

“EU candidate status is becoming little more than a formality”

Zakareishvili identifies the Georgian authorities’ decision to suspend political dialogue with the European Union as one of the main reasons for the country’s growing distance from Brussels.

In November 2024, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Georgia would not put the opening of EU accession talks on the agenda until the end of 2028. The announcement came after the EU had effectively suspended Georgia’s accession process and stepped up its criticism of the government’s policies.

Zakareishvili believes that instead of meeting the conditions set by the European Union, the Georgian authorities chose political confrontation. He says candidate status alone does not mean progress towards membership: the country must fulfil specific commitments.

The analyst points to Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro as examples of countries that continue to implement reforms as part of their efforts to move closer to the EU.

“The European Union did not write an application saying, ‘I want Georgia to join.’ It was Georgia that said it wanted to join the European Union. It is all very well to want to join the EU, but you need to look at its standards, its economy and its relations. The EU’s conditions include judicial reform, de-oligarchisation and many other things that the ruling Georgian Dream party does not like,” Zakareishvili says.

In his assessment, the EU’s declining political attention to Georgia is not limited to deteriorating diplomatic relations. The country could also gradually be left out of regional developments in which its geographical position and transit potential once gave it a significant advantage.

The analyst warns that Georgia’s international role is not determined by geography alone. A country may lie on a transit corridor on the map, but to gain real economic and political benefits, it must take part in the processes shaping the region’s future transport, energy and security architecture. Otherwise, Georgia risks finding itself surrounded by new political and economic partnerships while remaining on the sidelines.

Paata Zakareishvili on Georgia-Russia relations

World.title: Part of Crimean Bridge collapses into sea: what damage to one of Kremlin’s key propaganda symbols means
World.content:
On 17 November 2026, the Crimean Bridge, which spans the Kerch Strait, was severely damaged in another Ukrainian attack. Video footage and photographs circulating online appear to show a large metal arch and a section of the road deck collapsing into the sea. Both road and rail traffic across the bridge have been suspended.

The attack is particularly significant because the Crimean Bridge is a vital land corridor linking the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed in 2014, with Russian territory. Moscow has also used the bridge to supply its military forces.

For years, the Crimean Bridge was regarded as one of Vladimir Putin’s largest infrastructure projects and a symbol of Russian control over Crimea. Its damage creates several problems at once: it complicates Russian military logistics, increases the cost of supplying Crimea and shows how difficult it is for Moscow to secure one of its most heavily protected strategic assets.

It is important to note that the collapse on 17 November was preceded by an attack on 16 November, which also reportedly damaged the bridge’s structure. This means the bridge has been hit in a series of successive strikes rather than in a single isolated incident.

According to Anton Herashchenko, an adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister, the attack involved a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. Russian authorities confirmed the attack and the suspension of traffic across the bridge, but have yet to issue an official statement about its collapse.

The Russian outlet Agentstvo reports that federal television channels did not mention the attack on the Crimean Bridge in their morning news bulletins. Instead, they covered strikes on several bridges in Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine.

The collapsed Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

What does the collapse of the bridge arch mean from an engineering perspective?

To understand the scale of the damage to the Kerch Bridge, it is important to know how it is constructed.

The bridge is approximately 19 kilometres long and consists of two independent parallel structures: one carries road traffic and the other railway traffic.

Both structures rest on concrete supports. However, the navigable section of the Kerch Strait features large metal arch structures that support the corresponding spans and provide sufficient clearance for ships to pass underneath.

According to reports published on 17 November, a roughly 227-metre-long arch of the road bridge collapsed into the sea, along with the section of road deck connected to it. The adjacent railway arch was also damaged but has not collapsed.

Why does this matter?

The arch is not a decorative feature of the bridge but a key load-bearing element. Its damage means that the load in the affected section can no longer be safely distributed.

This creates several technical problems:

Damage to the load-bearing structure: After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles.

After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles. Risk of damage to adjacent elements: The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans.

The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans. Safety of the railway infrastructure: The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure.

The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure. Possible disruption to shipping: Debris from the collapsed structure could also obstruct the shipping channel used by vessels.

It is important to stress that the collapse of the arch does not mean the entire 19-kilometre bridge has been destroyed. However, one of its most important sections has been damaged. Restoring traffic will require a detailed structural assessment, the removal of debris and the necessary engineering and repair work.

Rebuilding such a large load-bearing element is a far more complex, time-consuming and costly process.

What does the collapse of the Kerch Bridge mean symbolically?

For Russia, the bridge is one of the most visible political symbols of the annexation of Crimea.

When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, one of Moscow’s main challenges was establishing a land link between the peninsula and Russian territory, as the Kerch Strait separates Crimea from Russia’s Krasnodar Krai. By building the bridge, the Kremlin overcame this geographical barrier.

Vladimir Putin personally championed the project. In May 2018, he drove a lorry across the bridge and officially opened its road section. The event was broadcast on Russian state television and became an important part of the Kremlin’s propaganda narrative.

For Moscow, the bridge carried several key messages:

Consolidation of the annexation of Crimea: The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory.

The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory. Putin’s political project: Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities.

Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities. Demonstration of Russian control: The bridge signalled that Moscow intended to maintain a long-term presence in Crimea and had no plans to return the peninsula to Ukraine.

Russia decided to build the bridge in 2014, following its annexation of Crimea. Construction began in 2016. The road section opened on 15 May 2018, while rail traffic began in December 2019.

The bridge is considered one of the longest in Europe. Its construction cost around 228 billion roubles (approximately $3.5–3.8 billion at the exchange rate at the time).

The project involved extensive engineering work. The structure includes supports on both land and underwater, while specially designed high arches allow ships to pass through the navigable section of the strait.

After the first explosion in 2022, the damage to the bridge was seen in Ukraine as an important moral and symbolic victory. At the time, Al Jazeera reported that the attack had heightened the perception of Russia’s vulnerability.

Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

How many times has Ukraine attacked the Kerch Bridge before?

Before the attack on 17 November 2026, Ukraine had carried out three major successful operations against the Kerch Bridge. Ukrainian officials subsequently confirmed or acknowledged responsibility for them.

The strike on 16 November 2026, which directly preceded the attack on 17 November, should also be treated as a separate incident.

8 October 2022: First major explosion

A lorry travelling across the bridge exploded, damaging several road spans and causing some of them to collapse. The blast also set fuel tankers on a passing railway train on fire. Four people were killed.

Ukraine subsequently acknowledged its involvement in the attack. Repairs to the damaged sections took several months.

Damage to the Kerch Bridge on 8 October 2022

17 July 2023: Sea drone attack

Ukraine attacked the bridge using Sea Baby naval drones. The road section sustained damage, and one of its spans collapsed. Two civilians were killed in the attack, and their child was injured.

Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), later confirmed that Ukrainian forces had carried out the operation.

Sea drone attack on the Kerch Bridge in 2023

3 June 2025: Underwater explosion

Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) detonated explosive devices near the bridge’s underwater supports. According to the Ukrainian side, the blast had an estimated force of 1,100 kilograms of TNT.

The SBU said the operation had been in preparation for several months and that the bridge’s supports had sustained significant damage. The agency claimed that the structure had been left in a critical condition.

Underwater explosion on the Kerch Bridge in 2025

16 November 2026: Another strike

The Ukrainian drone attack damaged the bridge’s structure. Russian authorities initially described the damage as minor, but traffic across the bridge was temporarily suspended and later partially restored.

16 November 2026: Another strike on the Kerch Bridge

What did Russia use the Kerch Bridge for?

For Russia, the bridge was not just a transport link for Crimea’s population. It was also one of the key logistical routes used in its war against Ukraine.

Military role

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the bridge acquired particular strategic importance. It allowed Russia to transport military supplies from its territory to Crimea and then onwards to the occupied regions of southern Ukraine.

These supplies included:

military equipment and armoured vehicles;

ammunition and weapons;

fuel and other military supplies;

military personnel and logistical resources.

The bridge allowed Russian forces to move military supplies relatively quickly from Russian territory to Crimea and then distribute them towards the front line in southern Ukraine.

In March 2024, Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), said Russia had significantly reduced its use of the bridge to transport military equipment following Ukrainian strikes.

According to Maliuk, 42–46 trains carrying weapons and ammunition crossed the bridge every day before the attacks. After the strikes, that number fell to four or five.

Civilian and economic role

The bridge is also an important transport route for Crimea’s residents and tourists.

It was used to deliver:

food;

fuel;

consumer goods;

construction materials;

various industrial products.

The bridge also carried passenger trains and cars travelling between Russia and Crimea.

A prolonged disruption would therefore affect not only military supplies but also everyday economic life in Crimea, the cost of delivering goods and the tourism industry.

The collapsed section of the Kerch Bridge

What alternatives does Russia have?

Disabling the Kerch Bridge does not mean that Russia will lose the ability to supply Crimea altogether.

Moscow can use the land corridor through the occupied parts of southern Ukraine. It links Russia’s Rostov region with the occupied territories of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and Crimea.

However, this route has several drawbacks. It is significantly longer, runs close to active combat zones and is itself vulnerable to Ukrainian strikes.

Russia could also use the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, but it would not be able to fully replace the bridge’s capacity.

Disabling the Kerch Bridge therefore represents a serious logistical blow to Russia, even if Moscow continues to supply Crimea via alternative routes.

Why is this attack significant?

From a military perspective, Russia is losing – at least temporarily – one of its most important transport corridors, which it used to supply its forces in Crimea and southern Ukraine.

From an economic perspective, a prolonged closure of the bridge will increase the cost of supplying Crimea and put additional pressure on alternative transport routes.

From a political perspective, it is another blow to Putin’s project, which has become a symbol of Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

It is also particularly significant that the bridge was considered one of Russia’s most heavily protected strategic assets. It was guarded by air defence systems, maritime barriers and other security measures. Yet Ukraine has managed to strike it repeatedly.

However, the ultimate strategic impact will depend on how long the bridge remains out of service, how severe the damage is to its supports and the adjacent railway structure, and how quickly Russia can increase the capacity of alternative routes.

One thing is clear: the Kerch Bridge is one of the most important symbols Putin has created since the annexation of Crimea. Its repeated damage sends Moscow a clear message: in its war against Ukraine, no infrastructure asset is safe or beyond reach.

World.title: EU foreign policy chief: ‘Syria must withdraw recognition of occupied territories in Georgia and Ukraine’
World.content:
EU foreign ministers have called for closer relations with Syria. However, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that any association agreement with Syria should include a commitment not to recognise the occupied territories of Georgia and Ukraine, alongside commitments to protect human rights.

Kallas made the remarks at a press conference following a meeting of EU foreign ministers.

According to Kallas, EU member states agreed that maintaining relations with Syria was important. Without EU engagement, other actors would fill the existing political and diplomatic vacuum in the country.

Kallas said the EU was considering signing an association agreement, negotiations on which began in 2008. The agreement would provide a common framework for cooperation between the two sides. At the same time, the EU would begin work on a new mandate to modernise the agreement.

“The question now was the status of the agreement. Negotiations on it took place in 2008, quite a long time ago. So the question arose as to whether we should make changes to it.

“The EU works in such a way that decision-making takes time. That is why the compromise would be to sign the 2008 association agreement. This would give us a framework within which we could work on all the issues that matter to both sides. At the same time, together with the Council, we will begin work on developing a new mandate for a modernised agreement,” Kallas said.

Kaja Kallas

Kallas said EU foreign ministers had called for several key issues to be addressed in the agreement. These include clear conditions on human rights protection and a commitment not to recognise the occupied territories of Georgia and Ukraine.

She explained that the issue concerned the territories whose independence was recognised by Bashar al-Assad’s regime.

“We are now working in technical groups on the details, both technical and legal, but we are making progress,” the EU foreign policy chief said.

At the press conference, Kallas also commented on the architecture of European security. She said that Russia had been a party to several international agreements that laid the foundations for European security. However, the main problem was not the existence of these documents, but Moscow’s failure to honour its commitments.

In this context, Kallas cited the Helsinki Final Act, the Paris Agreement and the Budapest Memorandum.

“The problem is not with the agreements themselves, nor with Ukraine’s position on this issue. The problem is that Russia violates these agreements and fails to comply with their terms. So the main question is: how can we restore the European security architecture?” Kaja Kallas said.

Background

On 29 May 2018, the regime of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad recognised the independence of Georgia’s occupied regions of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). Tbilisi responded by severing diplomatic relations with Damascus. The EU condemned the decision on the same day, saying it violated international law and the principles of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Assad’s decision followed Russia’s military intervention in the Syrian civil war. Moscow was one of the main supporters of Assad’s government, and Damascus’s move was seen as serving the Kremlin’s interests.

In June 2022, Syria also recognised the independence of Ukraine’s occupied territories of Donetsk and Luhansk. Ukraine responded by severing diplomatic relations with Syria.

Assad’s regime fell in December 2024, and a new government took power in Syria. Against this backdrop, Tbilisi called on Damascus to withdraw its recognition of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region.

Ukraine restored diplomatic relations with Syria in September 2025. The association agreement now under consideration by the EU could therefore mark a new stage in relations with Syria. However, the territorial integrity of Georgia and Ukraine remains one of the key conditions in this process.

World.title: Old links on Aliyev’s X account redirected users to opposition videos: cyberattack or global vulnerability?
World.content:
Interference with Ilham Aliyev’s X account

On 15 November, links in some old posts on President Ilham Aliyev’s account on X redirected users to videos featuring opposition politicians and bloggers, as well as footage of protests. Most of the posts dated from 2010–2011. The links led to videos featuring Ali Karimli, chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, and bloggers Mehman Huseynov and Gabil Mammadov.

The posts themselves remained unchanged, but the links they contained began directing users to different pages. The altered links remained accessible for several hours, and users shared the posts across social media.

That evening, the Azerbaijani president’s press service issued a statement:

“Cyberattacks are currently targeting the social media accounts of Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Relevant agencies are taking the necessary measures to prevent these attacks and investigate the incident.”

The statement did not specify which platforms had come under attack, how the attacks were carried out or who was behind them.

Similar incidents affected the accounts of several prominent politicians, government agencies and companies around the world on the same day. This raises the question:

Were the president’s accounts actually hacked, or was the incident the result of a global vulnerability that affected numerous accounts, including those of Donald Trump and McDonald’s?

Trump, Gates and Burger King among those affected by similar incidents

According to a CNN investigation published on 15 November, links in old posts by politicians, government agencies and companies on X began redirecting users to unrelated videos, images and websites over the weekend.

The largest number of such cases involved the personal account of US President Donald Trump. Links in at least 12 of his posts began directing users to other websites. Similar changes affected posts by Bill Gates dating from 2010 and former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau from 2011.

A link in a 2011 Burger King post listing the locations of its restaurants redirected users to a page listing Nazi concentration camps. A link in one of McDonald’s posts led to a page about the 11 September attacks. Similar cases also affected posts by the FBI, the US Department of Defence and former Vice-President Mike Pence.

All the links had been shortened using Bitly, a service that turns long web addresses into shorter ones. The service was widely used on Twitter, now known as X, between 2009 and 2014. According to CNN, Bitly links do not expire, and users with paid subscriptions can change the addresses to which they redirect.

Bitly said it had identified “an issue that allowed malicious actors to reuse some old, inactive links”. The company said it had suspended the accounts used to change the links and deactivated the links themselves. However, Bitly did not say who was behind the activity.

No password required

An attack of this kind does not require access to an account password. The original post remains unchanged; only the destination address of the shortened link changes. As a result, someone clicking a link in a post published by the president 15 years ago ends up on a completely different page.

IT expert Osman Gunduz also believes that the problem stems not from hacked accounts but from a security vulnerability in Bitly’s system. He recommended that government agencies and other organisations check their old links, deactivate potentially dangerous ones and use their own domains wherever possible.

Ari Lightman, a professor of digital media at Carnegie Mellon University, told CNN that many old accounts remain inadequately monitored. He described the situation as “problematic”.

Government agencies have not yet confirmed that the incident involving the president’s account was linked to a Bitly vulnerability. The president’s press service has issued no further statements on the matter.

Who appears in the videos?

The videos feature some of the most vocal critics of the Azerbaijani authorities.

Ali Karimli, chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, has been under arrest since November 2025. Authorities accuse him of actions aimed at violently seizing power. Karimli rejects the charges, calling them fabricated and politically motivated. The investigation ended in October. If convicted, he faces a prison sentence of 12 years to life. On 12 November, he received the Magnitsky Human Rights Award in London.

Blogger Mehman Huseynov was sentenced to two years in prison in 2017 on defamation charges. He was released in March 2019. Following the incident, Huseynov sarcastically “thanked” the president on Facebook for sharing a video featuring him: “Thank you, Mr President!”

Blogger Gabil Mammadov, who lives abroad, has been convicted in absentia in Azerbaijan. The Baku Court of Serious Crimes sentenced him to 16 years in prison.

What does “cyberattack” mean?

In the past two months, the Azerbaijani authorities have reported cyberattacks for the second time. On 13 October, more than 100 government websites came under attack. At the time, the State Service for Special Communication and Information Security said when the attack began, which systems it targeted and that its impact had been limited. The agency blamed an unnamed “foreign hacker group”. However, the pro-Iranian group 313 Team, which is believed to operate in Iraq, claimed responsibility. Its members said they had acted in protest against the ban on wearing hijabs in schools.

The statement about the attack on the president’s accounts, however, provided no similar details.

Previous cyberattacks on social media accounts in Azerbaijan have mainly targeted independent media outlets. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, an international press freedom organisation, almost all Azerbaijani-language posts disappeared from Meydan TV’s Facebook page in June 2020. In August this year, eight independent Azerbaijani media outlets operating in exile issued a joint statement. They said a series of coordinated copyright infringement complaints had led to the suspension of several of their Facebook and Instagram accounts.

This time, the incident affected the president’s own account. It remains unclear who changed the links and why they chose opposition videos as the new destinations. Bitly has not disclosed who owned the accounts it suspended.

Interference with Ilham Aliyev’s X account

World.title: “Relations with Russia cannot be restored”: Georgian prime minister on the country’s foreign policy
World.content:
Kobakhidze on Georgia-Russia relations

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze spoke at National Business Association conference on 16 November, commenting on relations with Russia and the European Union, prospects for political stability in the country and economic development.

Kobakhidze confirmed that dialogue with Moscow would continue. A first meeting is planned shortly between Georgia’s new special representative for relations with Russia, Giorgi Zurabashvili, and Russia’s deputy foreign minister Mikhail Galuzin. Various issues are expected to be discussed.

However, Kobakhidze stressed that two main obstacles prevent full restoration of relations with Russia: its occupation of Georgian territories – Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia), and its recognition of them as “independent”.

“Georgia’s leadership will not reverse its decision on this issue. It cannot be reversed,” the prime minister said.

Speaking about Georgia’s relations with the European Union, Irakli Kobakhidze criticised European bureaucracy, saying it was failing to take Europe’s real interests into account.

He argued that closer relations with Georgia should be one of Europe’s top priorities.

“Against the backdrop of isolation from Russia and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Georgia remains Europe’s only land gateway to the east.

When you artificially create a problem at a time like this, when you obstruct open and transparent dialogue, it shows that European bureaucracy is once again acting against Europe’s objective interests,” Kobakhidze said.

Irakli Kobakhidze also spoke about the importance of political stability in the country.

He said the government had managed to protect Georgia from attempts at destabilisation funded by foreign forces.

He described the adoption of a law restricting foreign funding for NGOs and media as one of the important steps in this process.

Context: The law has been strongly criticised by the EU and international organisations, which warn that it threatens civil society, restricts media freedom and undermines democratic standards in Georgia.

“Recently, we have managed to ensure political stability, which was not easy. We had to take very bold and decisive steps to protect our country, including from external threats, and to safeguard our sovereignty and independence,” he said.

According to Kobakhidze, stability is a necessary condition for the consistent development of the economy and business.

He also stressed that Georgia’s economic growth was underpinned by an effective economic framework, legislation and a strong government team.

He singled out Minister of Economy and Sustainable Development Mariam Kvrivishvili for special praise.

News in Georgia

World.title: Verbal clash, insults and fistfight live on Armenia’s Public TV channel
World.content:
Fight on Armenia’s Public TV channel

People in Armenia are discussing a heated exchange on Armenia’s Public Television. During the programme Big Debate, political analyst Harutyun Mkrtchyan and journalist Boris Murazi traded insults and swore at each other before getting into a fight live on air. They kicked each other. The presenters had to call security staff into the studio, but even they could not calm the angry guests down.

Presenter Tatev Danielyan reminded the participants that thousands of people were watching the programme. “This is a sign of disrespect — not only towards each other, but also towards the viewers,” she said. Presenter Petros Ghazaryan added that the broadcaster would not cut the footage from the recorded programme and would show it on air.

However, the Television and Radio Commission criticised the decision to broadcast the footage unedited.

The commission members expressed “concern” over the programme makers’ position and editorial policy.

“Open displays of violence and insults cannot be justified by the participants in the discussion, the heated nature of the debate, an attempt to boost ratings or even formal compliance with the principle of impartiality,” they said.

The commission also expressed “bewilderment” that the programme had not aired live but had been recorded in advance, yet the broadcaster had chosen not to remove the scenes of violence.

Vasak Darbinyan, chairman of the Public Broadcaster’s Council, disagreed with the Television and Radio Commission. He asked what the commission expected the broadcaster to do when programme guests behaved in an “unrestrained and vulgar” manner.

“I think it was perfectly normal for the Public Broadcaster to show all of this on air. What, should they have hidden the truth and portrayed these public figures as ‘sweet and innocent’? Should they have said: ‘You know, they are actually very nice people, even though they may swear or kick each other on air’? Did you expect a ‘sanitised’ version? Why should people not know what they are really like?” Darbinyan said.

What led to the on-air fight

During a debate on opposition consolidation, political analyst Harutyun Mkrtchyan said:

“Mr Murazi, if I’m not mistaken, the press has reported that you provided sexual services to former Armenian President Serzh Sargsyan.”

Journalist Boris Murazi called it disgraceful to publish such allegations:

“I could provide similar services to the adult female relatives of those making such claims, their mothers, for example.”

Tensions escalated when Murazi urged Mkrtchyan to behave himself, calling him “ara”. This is an informal and contemptuous way of addressing a man. In Armenia, the term is considered rude and derogatory.

A verbal altercation followed, with both men using obscene language. A standard censoring tone drowned out the swearing on air.

After the exchange, the programme guests resorted to violence. They punched and kicked each other.

Television and Radio Commission statement on the “legitimisation of violence on air”

The Television and Radio Commission says that the Public Broadcaster, which should set an example for other TV companies, has a duty in such situations to:

comply with legal requirements;

avoid stirring up emotions among viewers;

prevent the legitimisation of violence on air.

Amendments to the Law on Audiovisual Media prohibit the distribution of information that promotes violence and cruelty in audiovisual programmes.

The commission members said that, beyond legal requirements, broadcasters must also follow ethical and professional standards. These should take priority when covering any events involving scenes of violence:

“After all, there are professional techniques that can neutralise provocations by participants in a discussion, defuse tensions, prevent violence and steer the debate in a constructive direction — especially when the programme is not live but recorded in advance.”

The Television and Radio Commission regulates the Public Television broadcaster. The commission members therefore called on the broadcaster to comply with the established standards on scenes of violence, hate speech and insults.

Social media reactions

Opinions on social media were divided. Most users condemned both the incident and the decision to broadcast it. However, some supported one side or the other in the dispute.

Here are some of the comments posted on social media:

“Shame on everyone who agrees to appear as a guest on Public TV after this.”

“Whatever you say, things were not as bad on Public TV as they are in parliament. That’s a whole different level… You should be ashamed of yourselves. You have turned our country into a laughing stock in the eyes of the whole world.”

“Another show, another talentless performance. When will people learn to ignore these characters and stop falling for their provocations?”

“Everything was right. Murazi put up with it for long enough. He should have put that ill-mannered representative of the Civil Contract party [a reference to a supporter of the ruling party] in his place much earlier.”

“Shame on them. We all spit on the National Television and Radio Commission and everyone holding a senior public office in Armenia. Or perhaps they will mistake our spit for raindrops?”

“It is unclear why these politicians hate each other so much. They should get down to work instead!”

“The Civil Contract party will give Harutyun Mkrtchyan a pat on the back. As for Boris Murazi’s behaviour, they will say: ‘See what a lesson the opposition has taught this pro-government propagandist?’ In the end, matters of national importance will sink to the level of Murazi and Mkrtchyan. And all of us will watch our own country’s decline over a glass of bitter wine.”

Fight on Armenia’s Public TV channel

World.title: Moscow and Tbilisi prepare to resume dialogue
World.content:
The Kremlin has established contact with Giorgi Zurabashvili, the Georgian prime minister’s new special representative for relations with Russia. His Russian counterpart will be Mikhail Galuzin, a deputy foreign minister responsible for Russia’s policy towards the South Caucasus. The Russian Foreign Ministry told the Izvestia newspaper.

“Russia has consistently advocated building pragmatic and mutually beneficial relations with Georgia,” the ministry said.

According to Moscow, the main topics for talks between the two sides will include increasing trade and tourism, expanding transport links and promoting cultural exchanges between the two countries.

The Russian Foreign Ministry has also given the new format broader political significance, saying it is effectively linked to the resumption of Russian-Georgian dialogue, which began in 2012 and continued for almost a decade.

Giorgi Zurabashvili, Georgia’s first deputy foreign minister, was appointed the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia in late October 2026. He has retained his post at the ministry. However, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has clarified that Zurabashvili will represent Georgia in relations with Russia specifically in his capacity as a special representative.

Giorgi Zurabashvili

Tbilisi has therefore given its informal dialogue with Moscow a higher political status and a clear mandate.

At the same time, Irakli Kobakhidze says Georgia’s position on restoring diplomatic relations with Russia remains unchanged. The government has no plans to reconsider its decision on this matter.

Reaction in Georgia

Georgian opposition politician Zurab Japaridze criticised the decision, saying the authorities were moving step by step towards restoring relations with Russia. He said the ultimate goal could be the reopening of a Russian embassy in Tbilisi.

He also criticised bilateral talks with Russia without the participation of international partners. In his view, Georgia should not be left alone at the negotiating table with Moscow.

Speaking to journalists, Irakli Kobakhidze said that Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and its recognition of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) as independent states remained the main obstacles to restoring diplomatic relations.

However, he said that despite Georgia’s firm and unchanged position on restoring diplomatic ties, the dialogue between the special representatives would continue actively. The two sides would discuss all issues covered by the format.

The date and venue of the first meeting between Galuzin and Zurabashvili remain unknown. Kobakhidze said the meeting would probably take place soon, but not necessarily in Tbilisi or Moscow. It could be held in a third location.

How dialogue between Tbilisi and Moscow resumed after the 2008 war

Diplomatic relations between Georgia and Russia were severed after the August 2008 war. Immediately after the war ended, Moscow recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. Tbilisi responded by cutting diplomatic ties, which have never been officially restored.

However, after a change of government in Georgia in 2012, Tbilisi made an attempt to normalise relations with Moscow. The new ruling Georgian Dream party said that a constant state of confrontation with Russia was not in the country’s interests and that cooperation on practical issues was possible without changing Georgia’s position on territorial integrity or its foreign policy course.

As part of this policy, in November 2012, then Georgian Prime Minister Bidzina Ivanishvili appointed Zurab Abashidze as his special representative for relations with Russia. His Russian counterpart was Grigory Karasin, a deputy foreign minister.

Zurab Abashidze and Grigory Karasin

Their first meeting took place on 14 December 2012 in Switzerland. It was the first direct round of talks between Georgian and Russian representatives since 2008.
