The two sides agreed to continue the dialogue on a regular basis, focusing mainly on trade and economic relations, humanitarian issues and cultural exchanges.

The format later became known as the Karasin–Abashidze talks. Meetings were held mostly in Prague, and their agenda was deliberately limited. The sides could discuss trade, transport links, tourism and humanitarian issues, but not Georgia’s territorial integrity or security.

Talks on the latter issues continued within the framework of the Geneva International Discussions, established after the 2008 war with the mediation of the EU, the UN and the OSCE. Tbilisi stressed that the Karasin–Abashidze format should not replace or undermine the Geneva talks.

The launch of the dialogue also brought practical results. After Russia imposed an embargo in 2006, its market reopened to Georgian wine and mineral water in 2013. Some freight transport links resumed, trade between the two countries expanded, and exports of Georgian products to Russia increased. Regular flights and transport links later became part of the agenda as well.

However, improved economic relations did not break the political deadlock. Moscow continued to maintain military and political control over Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region and did not reverse its decision to recognise them as independent states. Meanwhile, the Georgian authorities maintained that the country’s territorial integrity and its right to determine its own foreign policy were not up for negotiation.

In 2023, Russia lifted visa requirements for Georgian citizens and ended its ban on direct flights to Georgia. Tbilisi described these decisions as unilateral steps, but economic and transport links between the two countries expanded further.

Dialogue between Moscow and Tbilisi

World.title: Kyrgyzstan's foreign trade grows 16.6% in January-September 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Kyrgyzstan's foreign and mutual trade in goods reached $14.1 billion in January-September 2026, increasing by 16.6% year-on-year, according to the National Statistical Committee of Kyrgyzstan.

The committee reported that the country's mutual trade with other Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states amounted to $5.2 billion, up 11.3% compared with the same period of 2025. Exports to EAEU countries decreased by 8.2%, while imports increased by 16.5%.

According to Trend's calculations, the growth rate of Kyrgyzstan's total foreign and mutual trade accelerated by 24.9 percentage points compared with January-September 2025, when trade turnover declined by 8.3%.

Meanwhile, the growth rate of mutual trade with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states accelerated by 16.6 percentage points, from a 5.3% decline in January-September 2025 to an 11.3% increase in the same period of 2026.

Russia accounted for 61.5% of Kyrgyzstan's mutual trade with EAEU countries, while Kazakhstan's share stood at 35.2%, the report says.

Trend's calculations show that Russia's share decreased by 4.3 percentage points compared with January-September 2025, when it stood at 65.8%. Kazakhstan's share, meanwhile, increased by 3.4 percentage points, from 31.8% to 35.2%.

Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan is implementing its National Export Development Programme for 2025-2028 under the Made in Kyrgyzstan brand. The programme focuses on promoting domestic products abroad, facilitating trade, improving access to finance and strengthening national quality infrastructure.

The country is also developing transport and logistics infrastructure to expand access to regional markets. One of the major projects is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which is expected to strengthen transport links between China and Central Asia. In September 2026, Kyrgyzstan's National Investment Agency signed a memorandum on establishing the Sary-Tash international transport and logistics center along the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan-Afghanistan route, with potential access to Pakistan.

Agricultural production and processing are another focus of export development. In October 2026, the state institution Kyrgyz Export launched a programme to help fruit, berry and vegetable producers prepare their products for international certification and enter markets in the European Union and the United Arab Emirates. The initiative forms part of the Made in Kyrgyzstan export programme.

World.title: Iran plans to raise Tang-e Bijar gas output to 8 million cubic meters/day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Iran is implementing development projects to increase gas production at the Tang-e Bijar field, according to the Iranian Central Oil Fields Company (ICOFC), said Mahmoud Nasiri, executive director of Iran's Western Oil and Gas Production Company.

"During the winter months, production from the Tang-e Bijar gas field is planned to reach 250 million cubic meters. Preparatory work has been carried out at the field, including repairs, and it is fully prepared for production," he said.

Nasiri noted that plans to build a gas pressure-boosting station at the field are currently at the engineering research stage. Implementation of the project will create conditions for more sustainable production from Tang-e Bijar's gas reserves.

He also stressed the need to manage gas consumption during the winter months. Efforts to reduce consumption should begin in residential apartments, where indoor temperatures should be maintained at appropriate levels. He explained that saving gas is not intended to deprive the population of access to it, but rather to prevent unnecessary energy waste.

According to Trend's calculations based on ICOFC data, efforts are underway to increase daily production at the Tang-e Bijar gas field from 7 million to 11 million cubic meters of gas and from 8,500 to 13,000 barrels of gas condensate.

The Tang-e Bijar gas field is located 70 kilometers southwest of the city of Ilam, in Iran's western Ilam Province. Gas extracted from the field is transported to the Ilam gas processing plant and, after processing, supplied to the country's gas network for consumption.

World.title: Azerbaijani fighter becomes two-time European kudo champion
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Azerbaijani athlete Vusal Aliyev won the gold medal at the European Kudo Championship held in Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria.

Competing in the 270 category, the Azerbaijani representative claimed the European title for the second time.

On his way to the final, Aliyev defeated athletes from England and Lithuania. In the decisive bout, he overcame an Armenian-origin opponent representing Bulgaria and took the top spot on the podium.

Thus, Aliyev added another achievement to his record as Azerbaijan's only world champion and a two-time European champion in kudo.

World.title: Azerbaijan, US discuss expanding agricultural cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. As part of his visit to the US, a delegation of Azerbaijan led by Minister of Agriculture Majnun Mammadov met with a US delegation led by Deputy Secretary of Agriculture Stephen Vaden.

During the meeting, the sides discussed expanding agricultural cooperation between Azerbaijan and the US, increasing bilateral trade in agricultural products, and exploring prospects for cooperation in scientific research and innovation.

Minister Majnun Mammadov briefed the US side on measures underway to strengthen Azerbaijan’s scientific capacity in agriculture, modernize research institutes, and align their activities with international standards. He emphasized the importance of launching joint scientific research projects and field trials with the US Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Agricultural Research Service (ARS) and the National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA).

The minister also highlighted ongoing efforts to develop agriculture in the liberated territories using a modern, climate-resilient, and digitally enabled model. Noting that Garabagh and East Zangezur have been declared green energy zones, he stated that US scientific research expertise could make a significant contribution to developing agricultural production systems in these territories in line with international standards.

Stephen Vaden noted that work was underway to conclude a memorandum of understanding between the agriculture ministries of the two countries. He added that the draft memorandum prepared by the Azerbaijani side had been submitted to its US counterpart and was under discussion.

Vaden emphasized the US side's interest in expanding cooperation under the memorandum in biotechnology, as well as livestock breeding and selection. The sides also discussed studying Azerbaijan's experience in these fields and exchanging expertise.

They also discussed ways to expand trade in agricultural products and strengthen bilateral trade ties. They exchanged views on prospects for agricultural cooperation, the exchange of expertise, and the draft memorandum of understanding between the two ministries.

World.title: One Nation plans to cut 90 per cent of refugee intake and scrap parent visas
World.content:
One Nation has unveiled a plan to cut Australia's refugee intake by 90 per cent and scrap a visa program for the parents of migrants.

Party leader Pauline Hanson pledged to cut the yearly refugee intake from 20,000 places to 2,000 and prevent thousands of parent and grandparent visas from being granted each year.

She said while Australia was "built on migration" it could no longer "afford it".

"It's called tough love, but my love is for the Australian people first and foremost," she said.

In September, One Nation announced its plan to cut 750,000 temporary visa holders over three years, with migration falling in each of the first three years under what it calls "net-negative migration".

Loading...

After that, the annual net overseas migration would be capped at 130,000.

That plan targeted international students and the immediate families of skilled migrants, and the party insisted at the time it would not have a negative impact on the economy, although it was never modelled by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO).

'Policy for the long term'

Senator Hanson said scrapping parent visas and the majority of the refugee intake would cut Australia's migration spend by $100 billion over the decade, based on One Nation analysis drawing from Treasury data that has also not been modelled by the PBO.

She said it would not be appropriate to have the policy costed by the PBO because it "only does it for about a year" and her policy was over the "long term".

"You can't do this modelling — humanitarian and parents — you can't do it," she said.

Pauline Hanson says the proposal would save taxpayers $100 billion over the decade. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

The PBO has powers to access government data that is not otherwise publicly available, and has previously provided long-term economic analysis and costings for other political parties upon request.

Senator Hanson said parents of migrants already in Australia on bridging visas, of which there were about 157,000, would have their application fee refunded, but would ultimately have to leave the country unless they applied for a different pathway to stay.

How Labor, the Coalition and One Nation's migration cuts compare One Nation wants negative migration in its first years, the Coalition has promised to more than halve it, while Labor has announced measures to ensure migration actually falls to its target of 225,000.

Under the current scheme, the government caps how many parent and aged parent visas are issued each financial year, with the current rate at 8,500 compared to 7,060 last financial year.

"We're not saying your parents can't come out ... if you want to bring your parents out, you will sponsor them, under the sponsoring parent program," she said.

"We can't even provide the aged care beds for Australians, let alone anyone else coming to this country.

"They have not contributed to this country, they have not paid a lifetime of taxes, and my responsibility is to the Australian people."

Wholesale cuts to humanitarian intake

The party has long vowed to withdraw Australia from the UN Refugee Convention and reinstate the use of temporary protection visas, which critics say leave asylum seekers in an unethical limbo.

Backpacker policy backflip Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has increased the cap on third-year working holiday visas by 20,000 places after backlash from agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors.

This newest proposal would cut the refugee intake by 90 per cent, which Senator Hanson argued would still be above the average per capita intake of other OECD countries.

"We can't afford it any longer," Senator Hanson said.

"You're not just going to have an open door for these people to come in anymore."

Foreign Minister Penny Wong disputed One Nation's claim and said Australia made a "very small contribution" to the global refugee intake.

"There are countries which take more refugees, there are countries which take fewer. We think this is the right balance," she said.

Penny Wong says Australia makes a modest contribution to the global humanitarian intake. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

In August, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese personally intervened to quash speculation the government would reduce the refugee intake from 20,000 to 13,750.

The Coalition has promised to halve the intake to 10,000.

Earlier this week, Labor wound back its planned cuts to the backpacker intake as the government also chases lower migration numbers, after hospitality, farming and tourism sectors warned major changes to the visa scheme would have a detrimental impact on their industries.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has maintained the government is committed to its 225,000 net overseas migration figure.

World.title: Netanyahu ally ousted as speaker of Israeli parliament
World.content:
Israel's parliament has voted to install a new speaker backed by rivals of Benjamin Netanyahu in what could mark a first step towards rolling back the prime minister's political agenda.

The 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, elected Matan Kahana, a member of the centre-right Yashar party led by Gadi Eisenkot, Mr Netanyahu's main opponent in last month's deadlocked election.

Mr Kahana won with 66 votes in his favour, with 52 members of parliament voting for another candidate. He replaces Amir Ohana, a member of Mr Netanyahu's Likud party.

"The Knesset of Israel is the home of all citizens of the State of Israel, and I intend to be the speaker for everyone," Mr Kahana told the parliament.

In Israel's parliament, the speakership wields considerable influence, including over what legislation is voted on.

This means that even while Mr Eisenkot struggles to form government, Mr Kahana will have power to advance bills prioritised by the Eisenkot-led bloc and those backing the former general.

Gadi Eisenkot (centre) has been given first go at trying to form a government over incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu, bottom right. (Reuters: Ronen Zvulun)

These include establishing an independent inquiry into the October 7 attack, which Mr Netanyahu has opposed; imposing term limits on the prime minister, and; repealing laws passed by the previous Netanyahu-led government which critics say limit the powers of the judiciary.

The Likud party condemned the vote, saying Mr Kahana was elected with "the votes of terror supporters".

The criticism is consistent with attacks Mr Netanyahu lobbed at Israel's Arab-led parties during the election campaign — attacks the parties condemned as racist and discriminatory.

Members of the Eisenkot-led bloc have also been appointed to chair several key parliamentary committees, which play an important role in advancing legislation.

The parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government, after a deadlocked general election stripped Mr Netanyahu of his majority but left his main rivals with no clear path ‌to power.

Aftermath of election stalemate

Israel's President Isaac Herzog has tasked Mr Eisenkot with forming government, but the former military chief will likely need to compromise on some campaign promises in order to secure the support needed to rule.

Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a new coalition government is established. (Reuters: Ronen Zvulun)

Mr Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until a government is formed. His right-wing Likud's alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats.

Mr Eisenkot's Yashar party and coalition partners hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel's Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Mr Eisenkot in their opposition to Mr Netanyahu.

Five ways Israeli negotiations could go Gadi Eisenkot's path to power could involve some creative political arithmetic and manoeuvring. So, what are the options from here?

If no-one is able to form government, another election will be held next year.

Netanyahu has sought to cast doubt on the election results by baselessly alleging voter fraud by Arabs, who make up a fifth of the population.

Election officials have said they are ⁠investigating, but have seen no evidence of fraud that could have influenced the outcome.

On Sunday, Israel's Channel 12 News reported that law enforcement was investigating if officials in Mr Netanyahu's office had deliberately planted information that led to an inquiry into alleged vote-buying in Arab communities.

Mr Netanyahu's office dismissed the Channel 12 report as "false".

Reuters

World.title: Death of woman and toddler at Melbourne lake to be probed by coroner
World.content:
Victoria Police will prepare a report for the coroner following the death of a woman and a toddler in Melbourne's northern suburbs yesterday.

Police said they were called to Aitken Boulevard in Craigieburn after a 36-year-old woman and 2-year-old child were found unresponsive in the water just before 1pm.

The pair were pulled from the water and CPR was performed but both died at the scene.

"The deaths are not being treated as suspicious," police said.

The Aitken Creek waterway and surrounding parkland is a recreational reserve with walking and cycling paths, several pedestrian bridges, and connects to a local golf course.

Police are preparing a report for the Coroner. (ABC News)

There was a large police presence at the location throughout yesterday afternoon.

The local council said it was "deeply saddened" by the deaths.

"This is a heartbreaking incident for their family, loved ones and the broader Craigieburn community," Hume City Council said in a statement.

"Council extends its deepest sympathies to everyone affected during this difficult time.

"We acknowledge the emergency services personnel and first responders who attended the scene, as well as members of the community who may have witnessed or responded to the incident."

World.title: It may feel inhumane, but a racehorse in landfill is common practice
World.content:
Late on Tuesday afternoon, the body of Melbourne Cup racehorse So You Are was found in a skip bin at a rubbish tip in Sydney.

This story contains content that may be distressing to some readers.

The five-year-old gelding had been rushed to an equine specialist with severe colic (a gastro-intestinal illness), and was euthanised when the issue could not be resolved. A builder at the tip filmed the body and posted the video.

The vet hospital said its contracted provider took the horse to the landfill where it should have been buried promptly. It has apologised.

Racing NSW, which is conducting an investigation, stated So You Are was awaiting burial when the video was recorded.

What normally happens when horses die or are euthanised?

An adult horse weighs around 500 kilograms, and a burial pit needs at least two metres of soil over the carcass.

Many horse owners cannot bury a dead horse at home — they may not own a property or may lack the space or distance from water bodies to do it safely.

It is common practice for vets to dispose of dead horses at licensed landfills, and NSW Department of Primary Industries guidance lists licensed landfill as the preferred disposal option in most instances. The standard procedure is for carcasses to be placed in designated areas and covered without delay.

Some horses killed by captive bolt tools (where compressed gas or a specialised cartridge delivers high-velocity impacts) or firearms may be accepted by knackeries for rendering or use in pet food.

However this option is not available if drugs have been used to euthanise the horse.

Why the euthanasia drugs matter

Vets usually euthanise horses with an overdose of a barbiturate, given intravenously.

The drug will depress breathing, brain activity and, ultimately, the heart. During the euthanasia process it will be carried by the blood stream throughout the body, leading to high concentrations in organs such as the kidneys, lungs and liver.

Because it is slow to break down, the drug will remain in tissue long after death. This can poison animals that consume the carcass.

In one reported case, dogs were poisoned after scavenging a partly buried horse that had been euthanised two years earlier.

Studies of composted horse carcasses have found the drug still present in compost and liquids leaching from the soil.

A review of reported cases found most poisoned wild animals were scavenging birds, and 86 per cent of those were eagles or their relatives. Dogs are the most often reported domestic victims.

Why a skip bin is a problem

Prompt and deep burial removes this risk. A carcass in an open skip, even for a short time, is within reach of birds and may be moved on with general waste rather than deeply buried.

If left in the bin for an extended period, the decomposition process can lead to unpleasant odours and carcasses can be a breeding ground for flies, which can transmit disease.

There are health risks posed by the disposal of a horse in a skip bin. (Facebook: Gregg Jowett)

The risks of secondary poisoning are well understood by the veterinary profession, which is why vet practices establish relationships with local landfills.

How So You Are came to be in the bin instead of buried, and for how long, is for the investigation to establish.

Why a horse in a skip bin shocks us

Much of the reaction to the video has nothing to do with how So You Are was euthanised under veterinary care.

Many are reacting to the sight of a specific horse, a Melbourne Cup runner with a brand on his shoulder, lying among building waste as if he were household rubbish.

Such treatment seems a callous contradiction to industry narratives of how much care horses receive and how well they are loved.

It contravenes our expectations of how the body of a deceased equine "athlete" should be treated. The reverent burial of champions such as Makybe Diva appear to honour the service given by horses to racing.

Tuesday's video makes visible something that is usually hidden. Even after the best veterinary care, dead horses end up in local tips.

Landfill burial may appear more respectful than a skip bin, but its purpose is sanitary and to protect wildlife: it is still burial in a rubbish dump.

A dead horse has no welfare

For So You Are, the dumping of his body in the bin is not an animal welfare issue. Welfare concerns what an animal experiences: pain, fear, comfort, pleasure. A dead horse experiences nothing and has no interest in what happens to its body.

The distress belongs to the people who cared for him, and the real risk is to the animals that might eat from the carcass.

For the horse, what mattered was how he lived and how he died.

By the hospital's account, he received emergency care and was euthanised under anaesthesia; about as good an end as a horse with fatal colic can have.

If this case makes us care more about horses, that attention belongs with the living: how they are housed, trained, raced and retired, and whether their deaths are timely and humane.

Cathrynne Henshall is a post-doctoral fellow at the School of Agricultural, Environmental and Veterinary Sciences at Charles Sturt University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

World.title: Live: Keen Victorian voters queue up for first morning of early voting
World.content:
Data centres have become an increasingly hot topic politically, both in Australia and internationally.

Local councils and neighbourhoods have been increasingly wary about data centres being built near them, with calls for a moratorium on new approvals.

Nowhere has this been clearer than in West Footscray, where community pushback to power poles caused tech giant NextDC to delay expansions to its data centre.

(ABC News: Kyle Harley)

The pushback from locals against data centres has found support from both the Greens and One Nation.

The Greens have called for an immediate moratorium on all new AI data centre projects and compensation for affected communities, while One Nation has pledged a ban on data centres on agricultural land and to protect neighbourhoods with stricter regulations and community consultation.

(ABC News: John Gunn)

But Labor and the Coalition have been more muted in their response to data centres.

Labor have promised stricter regulations around locations, drinking water and energy usage. The Coalition has also promised to more tightly regulate data centres and create buffer zones around residential areas.

But neither party has pledged a ban or moratorium. With the state staring down the barrel of a major debt hole, the financial incentives behind data centres may become even more important.

(ABC News)

The government said the data sector delivered $5.8 billion in capital expenditure into Victoria in 2025.

The Victorian Treasury also said in its budget papers that data centres will feature heavily in the state's economic future, with the value of commercial building approvals related to data centres exploding in Victoria.

In a property category the Victorian treasury says mainly comprises data centres, figures show approval value rising from just $1.2 billion in the year-to-September 2024, to $8.96 billion in the year-to-September 2026.

In a release in January, the Carroll government said AI could bring $30 billion in GSP (Gross State Product, the state equivalent of GDP) over the next 10 years, underpinned by projects such as NextDC's $2 billion AI factory in Fisherman's Bend.

Let us know what you think about data centres, and if the AI debate will be shaping your vote in the coming election.

World.title: Why Pachinko author Min Jin Lee loves Australia's TAFE system
World.content:
In 1997, a financial crisis swept across Asia, swiftly ending the region's postwar period of rapid economic growth.

It was a dramatic reversal in fortune for the four "Asian Tigers" — Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan — which had not long before been celebrated as the Asian Miracle.

"Several Asian countries had a terrible time in which they over-borrowed, and they couldn't pay back their loans," Min Jin Lee, the author of bestselling novel Pachinko, tells ABC Radio National's The Book Show.

Listen to the podcast Your favourite fiction authors share the stories behind their latest books on ABC Radio National's The Book Show.

As the crisis gripped the region, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) intervened with a $US40 billion ($58 million) bailout for the worst-affected countries, Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea.

The effect on South Koreans was profound.

"Korea was eventually allowed to pay back its loan, but that period was so devastating for so many people who didn't have generational wealth," Lee says.

" If you had money … you walked away great. But the average person, they lost their education, they lost their homes, they lost their jobs. "

Education was already important to South Koreans, seen as one of the few avenues to higher social status.

After the financial crisis, South Koreans went to more extreme lengths to educate their children, making many sacrifices to send their kids to elite schools in Korea and abroad.

But the emphasis on education came at a cost, further entrenching the hagwon system, which sees South Korean students spending most of their time studying.

Lee explores hagwon culture among the Korean diaspora in her latest book, American Hagwon, a sweeping social novel which follows the Koh family from South Korea to Australia and the US.

What is a hagwon?

A hagwon, also known colloquially as a cram school, is a for-profit tutoring business that operates outside the state school system.

"The hagwon is a very central part of being a Korean person," Lee says.

In South Korea, education is seen as fundamental to career success.

"A middle school can affect a high school, high school could affect a university, and a university can affect your job," Lee says.

"People tend to think that if you don't make those right moves, then your life will be more difficult."

Most students, four out of five, attend hagwons, many commencing when they are five years old.

By the time Korean students reach high school, they typically study 14 hours a day.

Min Jin Lee moved to the US in 1976, when she was seven years old. (Supplied: Elena Seibert)

After school finishes at 4 or 5pm, students head straight to their hagwon, where they study subjects like English, maths and science until 10pm or later.

Many hagwons specifically prepare children for the highly competitive university entrance exam, the College Scholastic Ability Test, also known as the Suneung.

Relatively few who sit the gruelling eight-hour exam gain entry into the country's most prestigious universities, which, in turn, can lead to successful careers in top-tier companies.

Failing the test is common. In American Hagwon, Bo, the eldest Koh child and a bright, diligent student, sits the test numerous times, a huge investment of time and money.

But hagwons are not just for exam preparation.

"In Korea, if you get married and you want to learn how to cook dinner, you go to a hagwon," Lee says.

"If you want to learn how to tap dance in Korea, you go to a hagwon. If you want to become a police officer or a postal worker and you have to take a civil service exam, you go to a hagwon."

A polarising topic

In American Hagwon, Helen Koh conscientiously sets aside money from the commissions she receives in her job at a luxury department store to pay for her children's extracurricular expenses.

But after the financial crisis, referred to in shorthand as "IMF", money becomes scarce.

"Min Jin Lee is a master of building rich, character-led stories," ABC critic Rosie Ofori Ward said in her review of American Hagwon. (Supplied: HarperCollins Australia)

Although both Koh parents went to top Korean universities, educating their three children is beyond their means. Helen must scrimp to pay her children's hagwon fees.

Hagwons in South Korea are big business, with Koreans spending $29 billion on private education in 2022.

In a country where 70 per cent of students go to university, it's an almost unavoidable cost that many families, like the Kohs, find difficult to bear.

It's no coincidence South Korea's fertility rate is in sharp decline, with the country reporting the lowest birth rate in the world.

"It's probably the central reason that people are not having children in Korea," Lee says.

" The cost of raising a child and the cost of her education is so extraordinary and forbidding that a lot of people are saying, 'I don't want to do it.' It's that important. "

Hagwon culture contributes to other social problems. South Korea has a high incidence of depression among young people and one of the world's highest suicide rates.

The government has made efforts to reform the sector, introducing measures such as a curfew, but hagwons remain an integral part of the Korean education system.

"It's a very polarising topic," Lee says.

"If you ask the average Korean person, 'What do you think about hagwons?' they'll give you the eye roll, like they're so frustrated by it.

"And yet, almost all parents send their kids to hagwons; almost all Koreans that you'll meet have experienced some hagwon in their lives, especially if they're living on the peninsula."

How Australia compares

It's a tension Lee seeks to capture in her novel.

One character, Lion, runs a hagwon in California that puts student welfare above profit and results.

But his example is the exception.

As Lee's novel shows, Korean families invest huge resources in educating children, paying thousands for extra tutoring and specialised exam application services.

Faced with a rigid and inaccessible education system in South Korea, many families opt to educate their children abroad, in countries like Australia and the US.

'If you get cancer, you will go bankrupt': Anna Funder on life in the US The award-winning author, who burst onto the literary scene with her debut, Stasiland, in 2003, discusses writing, AI and the rise of fascism.

But Lee acknowledges the American system isn't perfect, despite its prestige.

American Hagwon also highlights problems with the US system: its entrenched inequality, spiralling costs and transactional philosophy that treats students as commodities.

For Lee, the Australian education system provides an intriguing alternative to those in Korea and the US.

"I was so amazed by HECS and TAFE," she says.

"In America, we don't have anything like that. When you talk to the average Australian person who went to a very fine university … they don't freak out about the cost of it because they're like, eventually you pay it back."

In the US, where higher education is much more expensive, the stakes are much higher.

"If you had the cost of a house hanging over your head, which is what the average American thinks, then you would be very upset about how much your college tuition is, and you would think carefully about what kind of jobs you get."

Lee was also impressed by universal health care and the protective effect it has on society.

"[The US] is a cruel place," she says.

"The reality of every American [is] you have to pay for your own health care. If you get cancer and you don't have a job, you can't get treatment. If you have a house, you have to sell the house to pay for it."

Stories of diaspora

American Hagwon is the third novel in Lee's Diaspora Quartet charting the movement of Koreans across the globe.

Her writing is an attempt to understand the role of migration and borders in a world that is constantly changing.

"I believe that diaspora is a permanent condition now," she says, pointing to the increased displacement of people, both voluntary and forced, due to economic, environmental and educational factors around the world today.

October's best books A dystopian tale of life in a failed America, a family saga set in the world of Korean cram schools and two books about virtuosic musicians are among this month's best reads.

Her first novel, Free Food for Millionaires (2007), follows a young Korean American woman and Ivy League graduate as she navigates the tension between her family's heritage and her life in the US.

Next was Pachinko, a story of Korean migration to Japan spanning the 20th century. A finalist for the 2017 National Book Award for Fiction, the novel was adapted for television in 2022.

Lee is currently working on the quartet's final instalment, The Marshall Plan, which examines the Korean diaspora in Europe after World War II.

"I focus on Koreans, but what I really focus on is the movement of bodies and how our movement is changing us and how our environment is also being affected by our presence," she says.

" Because once you go somewhere, not only are you changed, but we change others. "

American Hagwon is published by Fourth Estate.

World.title: Sandpaper-centric response to Khawaja's story shows Australia still growing
World.content:
A short disclaimer before we get things started — if you're hoping for more sandpaper revelations, then this story isn't the one for you.

Usman Khawaja's 430-page autobiography, Sabr, has dominated the news cycle in Australia since its release earlier this month.

Unfortunately for Khawaja, virtually none of the discourse following the release has actually been about Sabr, the theme that has been the staple of not only his cricketing career, but his life.

'They cut a bit different': Khawaja opens up on facing racism growing up Usman Khawaja speaks out on a range of topics beyond Sandpapergate, including where he felt he belonged in Australia, the racist stereotyping he faced and his early mental health struggles coping with cricket failures.

You can argue that perhaps he should have seen that coming, and maybe he did, but the reaction remains disappointing.

Sabr is an Arabic word used in Urdu, and other languages across the Muslim world. The closest translation in the English language is patience, although it is also related to endurance, perseverance and persistence. It is one of the key tenets of Islam, the faith Khawaja devoutly follows

While Khawaja's book dedicates an entire chapter to the infamous sandpaper scandal from Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa, when you actually read the book, you realise the whole episode is a very small part of his story.

That so much of the response to Khawaja's book has been centred around sandpaper rather than his actual story shows that Khawaja will once again be forced to summon up a healthy dose of sabr.

The reaction also shows that despite all its progress when it comes to multiculturalism and the understanding of it, Australia still has a long way to go.

While Khawaja may be disappointed at the response, he will not be surprised at it. He has needed to practice sabr his whole life, well before he'd faced a ball for Australia.

Throughout Khawaja's story, you are able to see a young man who matures and deals with every single setback better than the previous one. Sabr isn't something that you master once and then it sits like a trophy on a mantelpiece. Rather, it is something you practise constantly and, as Khawaja constantly mentions in his book, it is incredibly tough to keep doing.

Khawaja played 88 Tests for Australia and scored 16 centuries despite being dropped on eight separate occasions. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Jason McCawley)

Khawaja never professes to deal with any issue perfectly, nor does he consider himself a perfect human, but it becomes evident that he is ever progressing.

There are several occasions throughout his career when Khawaja butts heads with someone, only to form strong relationships with them later on. Darren Lehmann, Australia's coach during the sandpaper scandal, is notably one of those characters.

One of the big questions surrounding Khawaja's sandpaper chapter from his critics has been: "Why now? Why not let sleeping dogs lie?"

Once you read his entire story, it is obvious that living with a lie over the past eight years became entirely impossible for Khawaja to do, especially when it involved seeing two of his closest cricketing mates, Steve Smith and David Warner, taking the blame for something he himself was also complicit in.

Usman Khawaja dedicates the Sandpaper chapter in his book to his oldest friend on the team: David Warner (left). (Getty Image: Alex Davidson, ICC)

Throughout the journey, Khawaja constantly fights the same old stereotypes us South Asians deal with, as he is called lazy and selfish among other things. They are the same stereotypes that have been thrust upon him once again in the wake of him sharing his story.

Whether you like it or not, Khawaja is undoubtedly one of this country's most important cricketers.

Modern-day Australia is a cultural melting pot, not simply white, and Khawaja is the perfect representation of it.

Khawaja is unashamedly a Pakistani-born Muslim, but he is a very modern-day Aussie despite not being born here.

Usman Khawaja's stories involving his mother Fozia and father Tariq are entirely relatable to anyone of a South Asian background. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock, Cricket Australia)

This is a man who never goes a day without doing his five prayers, but is also happy to sledge Hollywood actress Dakota Johnson on a call with her then-husband, Coldplay's Chris Martin, about "yanks" not knowing anything about cricket. You don't get more Aussie than sledging a Hollywood star.

He also mimics LeBron James and Snoop Dogg with his celebrations after scoring centuries and calls himself the "People's Champ" like kids around the country might after achieving similar feats.

That Khawaja is still the only cricketer of South Asian descent to have enjoyed a solid career for Australia is an indictment on the sport's pathways in this country.

Cricket Australia needs only look at the multicultural make-up of some of Australia's other national teams — the Socceroos, the Matildas, the Wallabies or the Kangaroos — to see there is a serious representation problem. There is a reason why those teams are much more universally loved than the men's Test team currently is.

The Socceroos are one of a number of Australia's national teams that better represent the country's multicultural reality. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

It can also look within its own sport at the likes of South Africa, England and New Zealand and understand that the answer simply cannot be that Australia's South Asian diaspora happens to be less talented at cricket than its counterpart in other countries.

Khawaja has often spoken about not supporting the Australian team because its players didn't look like him, but rather looked like the guys bullying him at school as he grew up.

While his representation was important for the South Asian community throughout Khawaja's career, the Aussie team still isn't really fully loved, even with him in it.

The dream scenario for a lot of us when watching Australia during Khawaja's career was for him to make a century but Australia to be all out for 200 in the very same innings.

Usman Khawaja and current Australian captain Pat Cummins (right) have been pivotal in changing the team's culture for the better in recent years. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Khawaja's hope is that in time, more representation allows for all of us in the South Asian community to fall in love with the Australian team, just as he did in the late 90s.

He, along with Pat Cummins and other veterans, have been pivotal in the culture of the team changing and being more accepting and accessible to those who aren't white Australians.

Khawaja may no longer be on our TV screens, but he has paved the way for other South Asian cricketers to represent Australia. The hope is that their path to the Test side is much easier than what he encountered.

Whether that is in this generation of players or in future generations remains to be seen.

That is ultimately the purpose of him releasing his book, not getting royalties after "snitching" about Sandpapergate.

If you're wondering what is actually the most important part of the book if not the sandpaper chapter, Khawaja actually tells you.

It is chapter 20, titled: "Gratitude, mindfulness, patience."

That is what Usman Khawaja's legacy is. Not sandpaper.

World.title: Grieving husband drives body donation changes after wife's wishes not met
World.content:
Susan Lewis loved studying at university and planned to donate her body to science to help others learn.

"She thought she'd give something back to society," her husband Warren Lewis said.

"That's one of the best charities in the lot, donating yourself."

But when the 79-year-old died in Batemans Bay on the New South Wales South Coast on a weekend in September, her wishes were unable to be carried out.

Photos of Susan hang on the wall of Warren Lewis's house. (ABC News: Jacinta Counihan)

Miscommunication between the hospital, the funeral service provider and the University of Wollongong meant her body was not embalmed in time.

"On Monday morning, the university rang me to say they hadn't received my wife," Mr Lewis said.

"It really hurts.

"It hurts more than the heart; it really hurts your whole body."

Warren and Susan Lewis were married for 52 years. (ABC News: Jacinta Counihan)

There are 17 anatomy programs tied to universities across Australia that accept whole-body donation.

If a body is accepted, it is either embalmed or frozen, and can then be used for up to eight years in NSW.

Ideally, that process should happen within 48 hours.

"After a certain period, a couple of days, we can't embalm the body sufficiently for us to use that donation because the body changes after a period of time of death," University of Wollongong anatomy committee chair professor Deirdre McGhee said.

At the time of Ms Lewis's death, the University of Wollongong did not have a body donation coordinator on call over the weekend, on public holidays or during the academic shutdown period.

It has since forged a partnership with Macquarie University to allow weekend donations to be received there.

Professor McGhee said the partnership happened because of Mr Lewis's advocacy.

"I said [to him], 'Well, good on you because you initiated this,'" she said.

" You've made a change and your wife would be proud of you. "

Barriers to body donation

Regardless of their intentions, not everyone can donate their body for scientific research.

Deirdre McGhee says the University of Wollongong accepts up to 20 bodies each year. (Supplied)

Characteristics that can invalidate a donation at the time of death include infectious diseases or skin lesions.

At the University of Wollongong, bodies weighing less than 45 kilograms or more than 95kg are also ruled out.

"If they're too big, then we actually can't fit them in our cool room … and if they're very, very emaciated, then we can't use them for teaching," Professor McGhee said.

University of Sydney research affiliate Rebekah Jenkin said up to 1,500 donated bodies were accepted each year into programs across Australia, but the number of bodies that were not accepted was "quite high".

"Most programs in Australia are at capacity," Dr Jenkin said.

Rebekah Jenkin says Australia has more potential body donors than programs can accommodate. (Supplied)

"As the majority of bodies are embalmed and that process takes 12 to 18 months, each donor's body is held in the mortuary for that period before it is used for anatomical examination.

" We have many more donors or potential donors in Australia than what we can actually accommodate. "

Lab capacity and cost of refrigeration

Macquarie University body donation program director Richard Appleyard said the university's facilities could hold up to 60 embalmed and frozen bodies for its anatomy, surgical skills and orthopaedic research programs.

But he said the capacity and cost of running an anatomy lab placed restraints on how many bodies could be accepted.

Richard Appleyard says it can take the university up to two years to prepare a body for use. (Supplied)

"Probably the vast majority of donors that aren't accepted into a program is because of a capacity issue, where there's not enough refrigeration space to hold that person," he said.

"With our capacity, we're in a pretty good place where we have quite a lot of storage for bodies here and we have a higher turnover than perhaps the other universities."

A research paper by Dr Jenkin estimated more than 10,000 clinicians, students, anatomists and researchers accessed tissue from local body donors every year.

Donated bodies are important for undergraduate and postgraduate medical and allied health training. (Supplied: Macquarie University)

Professor McGhee said despite the costs of running an anatomy lab, it was essential for teaching allied health and medicine.

"It's like a mechanic going to fix a car and not knowing what's in the engine," she said.

" How can you fix the body if you don't understand its structure and how it works? "

More public information

An Australian Law Reform Commission report reviewing human tissue legislation, including standardising body donation laws across the country, is due to be tabled in federal parliament by November 25.

Dr Jenkin said she wanted to see more data publicly available on body donation, including a register detailing options for organ donors.

"The Australian community is incredibly supportive of body donation, even though it's something that's not very well known or talked about," she said.

About 1500 David Jones workers are bracing to be told later this week that they have lost their jobs as the department store’s receivers prepare to permanently close 19 stores. Representatives for retail worker union SDA (Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association) met with receivers from FTI Consulting late last week and were advised only 170 roles, or 10 per cent, would be saved from 1689 jobs lost as a result of the closure of 18 stores in Australia and one in New Zealand. With seven stores in NSW set to shut, about 720 of the 1500 roles to disappear are based in the state, most of whom work in customer service. Jeremy Piper With seven stores in NSW set to shut, about 720 of the 1500 roles to disappear are based in the state, most of whom work in customer service. “We’re very disappointed with the very low number of 170 redeployments,” Smith told this masthead on Wednesday morning.



“We’re talking about a very low number, compared to the number of redundancies … It’s a missed opportunity to reset service levels at David Jones.” Related Article Exclusive

David Jones collapse Westfield owner is scoping out replacements for David Jones In an initial creditor’s meeting yesterday morning, David Jones’ administrators said an employee consultation process was underway and indicated impacted staff would find out “in the coming days”. In NSW, David Jones employs about 100 staff in its Hornsby store and roughly 115 at Warringah Mall, in Sydney’s northern beaches. Parramatta employs about 90 staff while Wollongong has about 85 employees. David Jones in Campbelltown hires approximately 80 workers, as does Woden in Canberra. Green Hills hires about 50 workers. The 170 redeployed roles will be predominantly in beauty and cosmetics counters at other stores, Smith said, as well as a limited number of roles in sales and management.

Loading “You’ve got to have enough staff on the floor to take the money off the customers who want to give it to you. World.content:

The owner of the Melbourne Cup runner discovered in a public skip bin in Sydney has blasted those responsible for the disposal of the racehorse’s body as Premier Chris Minns weighed into the controversy, saying: “We expect these things not to happen”. The handling of So You Are’s remains has placed the racing industry under scrutiny to address systematic shortcomings. Loading It was only 15 days ago that So You Are started as one of the favourites in the Melbourne Cup before finishing eighth in the race. On Tuesday, this masthead revealed the deceased horse had been found in skip bin at the Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre in southern Sydney after suffering a severe bout of colic and being euthanised.



Minns, whose government appoints the board of racing industry controlling body Racing NSW, told reporters on Wednesday the incident was “distressing for everyone involved and needed to be fully investigated”. “I’m not sure about the sequence, the reasons why a Melbourne Cup runner ends up in a skip bin in Lucas Heights, but we expect to get to the bottom of it,” Minns said. So You Are before competing in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington earlier this month. Racing Photos via Getty Images Minns said he expected retired racehorses to be dealt with humanely and in most cases rehomed, and said the industry needed to find better ways of disposing dead horses. “We expect these things not to happen,” he said.



Editor's pick Opinion

Racing integrity So You Are’s horrifying final fate in a skip bin with an old couch is beyond unacceptable Neil Breen National sports editor So You Are’s owner and breeder Stuart Ramsey is also demanding answers, taking aim at the veterinary clinic which organised the disposal of the horse’s body after being unable to save him. REC Equine Specialists has admitted it did not know what happened to deceased horses after they were taken away from its Horsley Park hospital by contractors. “Heads should roll,” Ramsey said. Weirey [trainer Darren Weir] got life for a jigger. This is worse. “At the end of the day they’re professional people and they should be treated like professional people. They’ve done the wrong thing and should be gone. This is the worst thing to happen in my lifetime.



“These horses try their heart out and they’re allowed to do what they like to them.” Waste management giant Cleanaway said So You Are had been transported to its Lucas Heights facility in a small tipper truck and held in a skip bin before burial because it was unsafe for the vehicle to approach the landfill. Veterinarians who treat racehorses are licensed by racing authorities and can face penalties, including deregistration. Ramsey said he had been travelling in western Queensland when So You Are fell ill on Monday and was rushed to emergency surgery from a spelling paddock near Camden. So You Are’s trainer, Bjorn Baker, was distraught, he said.



So You Are was found dead and dumped in a skip bin at Lucas Heights in Sydney. Facebook “I was in western Queensland and very hard to contact. They contacted me as soon as they could. Bjorn rang me and he was very upset,” Ramsey said. “I was speaking to him the other morning and he broke down. His wife had to get on the phone, the poor bastard.” Ramsey had been joined by about 30 long-time friends at Flemington to see So You Are compete in the Melbourne Cup a fortnight ago and could not envisage what was to come. He said he was devastated to lose the horse and learn how its body had been left in a skip bin before being buried but was more concerned for the family of apprentice jockey Izzy Neale, who died 10 days ago following a race fall in central western NSW. “She was 22. I’m bloody 74. She hadn’t lived,” he said. “We lost a daughter 20 years ago. There is always someone worse off than yourself.”

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has wrongly claimed Donald Trump’s war in Iran has not contributed to inflation, while confirming her crackdown on parent visas could force more than 10,000 parents and grandparents out of the country. Described as “MAGA-first” by Liberals including Andrew Hastie, Hanson declined to say on Wednesday whether she wanted Trump to wind down the conflict, which has spiked global oil prices and which the Reserve Bank has repeatedly said is adding to Australia’s pre-existing inflation problem. Pauline Hanson speaking in Canberra on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “That’s not up to me to decide whether Donald Trump should end the war,” Hanson told reporters in Canberra. “No country like Iran should have nuclear weapons. “Cost of living was not due to the war in Iran. That’s been bad management by an absolutely incompetent government that has driven it up. Even [bank governor] Michele Bullock from the RBA has called it out time and time and time again. It’s out of control spending by the current government.”





The populist-right party released an uncosted estimate, based on its own analysis of Treasury figures, that cutting parent visas and slashing the refugee intake by 90 per cent could save federal and state taxpayers $140 billion over decades. However, the policy did not reference the cost of repaying the nearly $50,000 fee already paid by many people in the 161,000 in the parent visa backlog, some of whom die waiting to be accepted. Immigration analyst Abul Rizvi said the cost of refunding would be about $1 billion. Making matters more complicated, Rizvi said at least 13,000 had applied for parent visas while living onshore on different visas, including bridging visas. Asked if those already living in Australia would be able to stay after their parent visa fee was refunded, Hanson said: “They can’t.” Her comments raise the spectre of a future Hanson-led government pushing thousands of parents and grandparents to depart the country.



Rizvi, previously a senior migration bureaucrat in the Howard government, said many parent visa holders performed a childcare role for grandchildren, which did not show up in Treasury estimates that suggest parent visa holders cost the taxpayer more than $500,000 over their lifetimes. The visa holders are immediately eligible for Medicare but must wait 10 years for benefits such as the age pension or unemployment benefits. The $500,000 figure stems from the fact that the people come to Australia as older people, meaning they use services in the same way as other Australians, but do not contribute to tax revenue because they did not spend their working lives here. The parent visa also requires a financial guarantee of $10,000 by the person’s sponsor in case the parent is forced to draw on benefits. Minister for Foreign Affairs Penny Wong. Alex Ellinghausen Foreign Minister Penny Wong described the changes as “very harsh on many families”.



“I’d say to many of our multicultural communities, the ending of parent visas would be very harsh on so many families in Australia,” Wong told reporters. Hanson’s policy also pledged to cut refugee visas from 20,000 to 2000 per year. Wong said the world was facing “unprecedented people movement” and that Australia’s refugee intake was a “very small contribution” on the global stage. “Refugees also make such a great contribution to Australia. [Businessman and former chairman of Westfield] Frank Lowy was a refugee,” Wong said. “I think we all spoke about the Socceroos and the way in which that team represented multicultural Australia. “I know that [One Nation] think dividing Australians is the best response to the politics of the time. I take a different view.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Experts backed ‘homely units’ for young offenders. Labor wants them in prison
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian election Experts backed ‘homely units’ for young offenders. Labor wants them in prison Patrick Hatch November 18, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Duelling pledges by Labor and the Coalition to lock up more young people for low-level crimes have been slammed by drug, alcohol and youth justice experts, who say the plans will not address the core drivers of youth offending. Liberal leader Jess Wilson announced on Sunday a $60 million plan to establish prison “boot camps” where repeat low-level youth offenders will be sent to learn “discipline” through farm work, other labour and education. Labor reopened the Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre earlier this year to handle the growing number of young offenders held on remand. Paul Jeffers That followed a promise by Premier Ben Carroll to spend $204 million over two years establishing a youth rehabilitation detention system, where young people could be detained for up to 12 months for crimes such as theft, vandalism and minor assaults. But experts say the Labor proposal is a distortion of what those at the coalface have been asking for.



Youth crime has become a major headache for Labor in the lead-up to this month’s state election after a spike in youth offending following the COVID-19 pandemic. Rates of crimes committed by kids aged 12 to 17 jumped 24 per cent between 2019 and 2025. Offending rates fell 9.6 per cent last year. Victoria Police chief commissioner Mike Bush earlier this year called for graduated mandatory sentencing for serious offences, including young people who needed “clarity” about the consequences of their actions. But YSAS (Youth Support and Advocacy Service) chief executive Andrew Bruun said Labor’s announcement was a blow to the leaders in the drug and alcohol sector, who had spent close to a decade working on a plan for youth mandatory rehabilitation orders.



Magistrate Jennifer Bowles kicked off that work after growing frustrated with the number of young people before the children’s court with severe substance abuse problems who were not accessing voluntary drug and alcohol rehabilitation services. In 2014, Bowles published a study into programs in Sweden, England, Scotland and New Zealand where young people at extreme risk from substance abuse and sexual or criminal exploitation could be treated in a secure environment. Twenty-four leading experts from the drug and alcohol and youth justice sectors have been part of a steering committee for the implementation of Bowles’ “What Can Be Done” model, intended to be a “circuit breaker” to stop children’s lives spiralling out of control. Carroll referenced Bowles’ work when announcing the policy on Sunday, but Bruun said Labor’s plan was a serious distortion of her proposal.



Bruun said a critical element of Bowles’ proposal for mandatory rehabilitation was that they would be non-punitive health and welfare orders issued based on clinical need, not criminal offending. Related Article Crime ‘You are meant to be greater’: The bold plan to stop youth crime – at the hospital bedside Under Bowles’ proposal, treatment would be at “homely units” for up to six months, but with regular monitoring so the young person’s order could be relaxed as soon as they improved. It would be followed up with 12 months of intensive community care. In contrast, Labor has promised “youth rehabilitation detention” that judges could order at sentencing as an alternative to a community corrections order for low- and mid-level offences, including theft, vandalism, property damage and minor assaults. Sentences could be up to 12 months, including at the Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre, which closed in 2023 before the state government reopened it earlier this year to handle the swelling number of young offenders being held on remand.



“We’re trying to look at an option which is going to break that cycle for young people and give them a chance to actually treat the underlying issues and symptoms that are driving their involvement in unsafe and harmful behaviours,” Bruun said. “But in this case, if you sentence young people and have them in larger numbers in a youth justice precinct, what is the difference between [this and] youth justice detention?” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has laid out a policy of “boot camp” for young offenders. Eddie Jim Bowles, who still serves as a reserve magistrate, declined to comment when contacted by The Age. Labor said it would start with places for about 500 young people over the first two years, which is roughly 10 times the capacity Bowles’ work suggested would be necessary to treat the small number of extreme cases who needed mandatory rehabilitation.



The Coalition promised to introduce mandatory therapeutic orders based on Bowles’ work ahead of the 2018 election but has not revived the policy this campaign. Instead, Wilson on Sunday promised to send low-level young offenders to “boot camps” where they would be forced to do farm work and other labour, as well as education and training, at the former Dhurringile Prison near Shepparton. National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Legal Services chief executive Nerita Waight. “This is about instilling the discipline and respect that so many young offenders have not learned throughout their life, and crucially giving them the skills they need to get on the right path,” Wilson said. The “boot-camp” orders would apply to offenders aged 14 to 17 who had repeatedly committed low-level offences such as graffiti and vandalism, she said.



Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service CEO Nerita Waight said she was disappointed both major parties were promising to lock up more children rather than pursue evidence-based approaches to improve community safety. “We have a long history of child labour camps in this country, the harmful effects well documented in the Bringing Them Home report and Yoorrook,” Waight said. “You cannot punish children into submission.” Loading Joel McGregor, a senior lecturer in criminology at Swinburne University, said evidence from around the world showed that military-style boot camps did not work in reducing youth crime. Queensland ended a short-lived youth boot-camp program in 2015 after finding it was expensive and ineffective.



“The thing about boot camps is it looks like the government is doing something, and that’s important; people want to feel safe in their communities. But it doesn’t address those underlining factors,” McGregor said. Related Article Victorian election ‘No evidence’ that $40m youth crime program reduces offending “Getting young people involved in education and training, addressing drug or alcohol misuse, addressing trauma – those are the things that we know stop young people participating in crime.” McGregor said both major parties’ youth detention policies risked sending low-level offenders into environments where they would be negatively influenced by other detainees and in fact become more likely to reoffend. Justice Reform Initiative executive director Mindy Sotiri said the two major parties’ “evidence-free” policies would push children deeper into the justice system, and remove them from family, school and community when those connections mattered most.



“We know that the earlier a child is locked up, the more likely they are to keep cycling through the system, which means more victims and greater cost to taxpayers in the years ahead,” Sotiri said. “Whatever else prisons for children are, they have never been rehabilitative.” Victorian Greens justice spokesperson Katherine Copsey said Labor and the Coalition were “locked in a grotesque competition to see who can announce the cruellest headline and lock up the most children”. It cost Victoria $7304 per day to keep a young person in prison in 2025, or almost $2.6 million per year, according to the Productivity Commission. In 2023, 56 per cent of young people released from prison were back in jail within 12 months, the commission found. Victoria’s private schools will reclaim their place as the No.1 football nurseries in the country at this year’s AFL draft. Early predictors suggest that a third of the first 20 names to be called out by AFL clubs across Thursday and Friday nights will be students from Melbourne’s exclusive, high-end secondary schools. Top-10 draft prospect Arki Butler played his school football with Brighton Grammar. AFL Photos That is in stark contrast to last year. Only three of the top 20 picks from the class of 2025 were from the privileged private sector – Penleigh and Essendon Grammar School student Cooper Duff-Tytler joined the Eagles at No.4, Richmond took Camberwell Grammar’s Sam Grlj at No.8, while the Eagles also took Josh Lindsay, of Geelong Grammar, at No.19.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Who will your AFL club draft? Our expert prediction of the first round A large chunk of last year’s top 20 consisted of interstate selections – five south-east Queenslanders, four South Australians, two from NSW and one from Western Australia. There were also three state school recruits last year. The Eagles plucked No.1 pick, Willem Duursma, from Foster Secondary College after he shot to prominence as captain of Talent League team Gippsland Power, while Rowville Secondary College threw up pick 11 Xavier Taylor (Eastern Ranges) and pick 16 Lachy Dovaston (Eastern Ranges). However, this year, only three of the projected top 30 have been educated at government secondary schools, with likely No.1 selection Dougie Cochrane attending Henley High School in Adelaide, top-10 prospect Clancy Snell going to Mirboo North Secondary College, and Caylen Murray attending Maroochydore State High in Queensland. Once again, Brighton Grammar is expected to continue its proud history of nurturing gun teenagers.



Brighton Grammar student Tyson Bradley is expected to go in the top 20 in the 2026 AFL draft. AFL Photos The Brisbane Lions’ premiership-winning brothers, Will and Levi Ashcroft, were educated at Brighton, as was Essendon captain Andy McGrath, who was taken at No.1 in 2016, and Greater Western Sydney star Josh Kelly, who joined the Giants at No.2 in 2013. The school had five draftees in 2024. The Age’s draft expert Marc McGowan is predicting two Brighton Grammar products will be snapped up in the top 10 on Thursday night – Arki Butler at No.4 and Tyson Bradley at No.10. Butler started at Brighton Grammar in year seven, while Bradley’s father was a former student, and he joined in year 10. The Age’s phantom rankings have 10 teenagers from the Associated Public Schools of Victoria (APS) competition making the top 40 – two from Brighton Grammar, two from Geelong Grammar, two from St Kevin’s College, two from Wesley College and one each from Haileybury and Caulfield Grammar.



“The first 18 programs now are really well resourced,” Brighton Grammar director of coaching Simon McPhee told The Age on Tuesday. “We’ve got strength and conditioning coaches and a rehab coordinator, we’ve got good help from a medical point of view, and then we’ve got good coaching [at the schools].” McPhee highlighted three members of the Haileybury College coaching staff as a prime example – former AFL captains in Matthew Lloyd, who is head coach, Scott Pendlebury and Aaron Hamill. “Obviously, it’s good for the schools and the APS program when we get kids into the AFL system,” McPhee said.



Related Article AFL 2026 He ‘shrunk’ this year, but this draft hopeful could be one of the AFL’s biggest achievers “But we also take a lot of pride when the boys go on to play VFL footy, and VAFA footy. “We just want to prepare the boys to play the highest level they can, and obviously, it’s nice for the school when a few make it to the top.” Brighton Grammar won this year’s first APS grand final, beating Caulfield Grammar by nine points, after the competition shifted away from awarding the premiership to the team that finished on top. Butler and Bradley were part of that premiership-winning outfit, as was another Brighton draft hopeful Jasper Williams.

World.title: Tinkering with consent laws won’t stop rapists like Russell Brand. Here’s what might
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCrime Opinion Tinkering with consent laws won’t stop rapists like Russell Brand. Here’s what might Jenna Price Columnist November 18, 2026 — 11:43am

November 18, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anyone who thinks changing age of consent laws will single-handedly stop sexual assault has lost their minds. That won’t do a single thing to stop rape except to further criminalise rapists. Sure, good outcome. Not that jail stops them from proclaiming their innocence. Russell Brand at court, before being convicted of rape. Getty Images Russell Brand confessed to conservative podcaster Megyn Kelly that he slept with a 16-year-old – Mia Latter – when he was 30. He was an “immature 30-year-old”. And then, vomit, he said that a power imbalance – such as being famous – “involves exploitation”. OK, late bloomer, take some responsibility then. As Latter told The Times: “He was a very successful man who had a lot of power and sway in the industry, whereas I was a 16-year-old with no life experience, no sexual experience and no prior relationships. What was my level of maturity meant to be?” Do we think any other rapists will really care? Age is not the issue – it’s the power imbalance. I only wish we could legislate against men wielding power. Our lives would be better for it.



We’ve got two – maybe three – huge tasks to stop sexual assault and all of them require brutal and confronting community action. And if you think the problem is confined to the powerful, here’s the truth. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, more than 30,000 women were victims of sexual assault in 2025. There were 10,000 police-recorded offenders. About half were convicted in a criminal court. And so many women never report. Mia Latter has accused Russell Brand of raping her when she was 16. Getty Images for Academy Museum of Motion Pictures Our first task will make many men – and some women – stick their fingers in their ears and go la la la. End male entitlement (sure, to women’s bodies but to much more). No-one wants to hear about undoing this behaviour because it is challenging to do. Some men don’t believe it exists. So I’ll leave you to it while at the same time putting it number one on my list to stop rape, so you know it’s the most important. Number two. The last time I wrote about what women could do to protect themselves I got into helluva trouble (think hard before you drink with men). Victim-blaming! Anti-feminist! Make men responsible. OK then, but see point one. If men can’t or won’t change (and I believe they can and will when they understand the benefits), women have to do what they can to protect themselves from dinosaurs, from raptors, from those men who act sweet but are sour as hell. Number two, two parts. Thanks to the work of Chanel Contos and collaborators, we’ve all endorsed the enthusiastic consent concept. Hell yes!



Now? Teach, hell no! It won’t stop rapists with intent. But beneath the flashy examples of celebrity sexual assault (and sadly, more to come) we have an ocean of women having sex in ways they don’t want it. For every rape victim, there are women subjected to practices such as strangulation, too afraid to say no. Women are brought up to fear boys and men, to concede even if they don’t want to. We need more fury and fight. And we need to start teaching that concept from day one in nappies. Related Article Opinion

Comedy Shocked by Russell Brand and David Walliams? You shouldn’t be Which brings me to gender roles. I have no idea how this happens but by the age of two, young girls want to be Elsa. Co-opt the princess movement and start Princess Jiu-Jitsu, a compulsory physical activity for girls across the world, ages five and onwards. Sure, dress up in your flowing blue dress but also know how to fend off attackers while using the lion killer. Keys held tightly in your fist won’t work against someone bigger and stronger. Think this is trivialising? Apparently the first task, to rid us all of male entitlement, is too hard. Won’t be fixed in my lifetime. The good news is that affirmative consent laws have seen changes in the courtrooms. So says the woman who co-wrote the book on Australian rape trials, Julia Quilter, a professor of law at the University of Wollongong.



“They are actually having some changes in the courtroom, from the most recent study we’ve just done,” she says. “It has taken us a long time to get the law to accept you don’t have to resist, shout ‘no’ or fight back … the Crown is being good at not requiring a ‘fight’ response and recognising that it is common to ‘freeze’ during sexual violence. The law now also places an obligation on the accused to explain what they said or did to affirm consent and the Crown is actively pursuing lines of questioning that place that responsibility on the accused. These are important and good developments.” Jennifer Power, professor at La Trobe University and leader of the Australian Secondary Students and Sexual Health Survey, says it’s possible a bigger age gap leads to more vulnerability in relationships with a substantially older adult: higher rates of sexual violence, unwanted sex, unwanted pregnancies. Lack of experience, lack of money, less agency. She reminds me kids are usually sexually active in many different ways before they turn 16. The consumption of pornography has changed sexual vocabulary. There’s a distance between what the law says is rape, and how thousands of women feel participating in sex they don’t want. Power says when we talk to our kids about sex we need to reach beyond the cringe moment, lean forward and say: “You have my full permission to tell someone to go away. You never have to be polite if you are uncomfortable. You don’t have to be polite for a man. Sex should be something you enjoy. If you don’t enjoy it, don’t do it.” Saying no will never stop a rapist. I would prefer a world where we didn’t have to rely on women to predict, prevent, protect against rape. Until we end male entitlement, that can’t happen. Jenna Price is a regular columnist. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Republicans, MAGA demand answers over spate of tech outages as Trump says ‘that’s life’
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTechnology & democracy Republicans, MAGA demand answers over spate of tech outages as Trump says ‘that’s life’ Michael Koziol November 18, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
