Washington: Republicans and MAGA activists are demanding answers over a string of outages and technical failures that have halted air travel, hit the big banks and even impacted communications inside one of the United States’ most secret government agencies. There is growing doubt among lawmakers and the public that the incidents are unrelated, even as officials insist the problems have been caused by maintenance issues rather than cyberattacks or nefarious activity. A customer using a Bank of America ATM in Renton on Monday. Some people are choosing to stockpile cash amid the tech outages. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson On Tuesday (US time), internal communications at the National Security Agency – which specialises in signals and code-breaking – experienced an outage that was first reported by CNN. The NSA later confirmed there had been a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance”. Also on Tuesday, an internal update disrupted core services at tech giant Apple including Apple Music, the App Store and iCloud. The company said many systems were back up and running, and it was working to restore the others.



It followed service interruptions at major US banks on Monday, and a brief outage in systems used by United Airlines, as well as last week’s problems with air traffic control that led the Federal Aviation Administration to ground departing flights for nearly five hours and a major outage with Microsoft systems. Related Article Updated

Network outage Apple suffers outage sparked by software update The flurry of outages – many of which were short – has dominated cable news, water cooler conversations and discussions on Capitol Hill this week, and prompted alarm. One former Australian official in Washington, who did not want to be named, told this masthead they recently withdrew a stockpile of cash because of the technology failures. There is also some evidence of panic buying. Chief financial officer of retail giant Costco, Gary Miller, told Bloomberg News that the company had seen increased purchases of rice, canned goods, water, generators and batteries, beginning in late October.



On Fox News, former FBI special agent Darren Mott said people who were worried may want to withdraw cash, put it in a safe, have supplies of water on hand and generally make their lives more analog. Related Article Analysis

Network outage One router, one bug. How routine upgrades caused worldwide chaos But officials maintain there is no cause for alarm. “This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state. We’ve looked very closely,” said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on CNBC television on Tuesday afternoon. “What I think is going on here … is many people are patching their systems. They know that their legacy systems have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated, they don’t work well with new systems.”



There have been mixed messages about the potential role of artificial intelligence in the outages. On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said a man who was “very smart with tech” told him that one possible cause of the outages was old systems being overwhelmed by much faster programs driven by artificial intelligence. “That kind of makes sense to me,” he told Fox News. But the next day, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said AI definitely didn’t play a role in last week’s air traffic control problem, which officials say began when old copper wires were being replaced by fibre optic cable. Donald Trump downplayed the tech failures while speaking to reporters in Manila. “It’s life … it’s fine,” he said. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein US President Donald Trump, who was meeting world leaders in Manila, told reporters he was not concerned about the spate of outages. “It’s life,” he said. “When you’re big and powerful, and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”



Some Republicans expressed doubts about the official narrative, however, or suggested that the incidents must be linked. Josh Hawley, a Republican senator from Missouri, said his initial reaction was that it must be a cyberattack, and called for members of Congress to be briefed. Republican senator Josh Hawley said he did not believe the spate of outages was a coincidence and Congress must be briefed. Bloomberg “All of these outages – maybe it’s because somebody unplugged a router in Arkansas or whatever. Frankly, I find that really hard to believe,” Hawley said. “We need to know what’s going on, the American people deserve to know … If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world. You can’t tell me that all of this is just happenstance.”



Hakeem Jeffries, the leader of the Democrats in the House of Representatives, echoed calls for a briefing. And Republican majority leader in the Senate John Thune, pointed to possible foul play. “It’s fair to say there are a lot of bad actors out there who would love to do damage to the United States,” he said. “Whether it’s banking or transportation or our communications networks, we have to be on top of our game.” MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who is close to the president, said he should come home immediately. Greg Kahn/The New York Times Laura Loomer, a MAGA social media influencer who has Trump’s ear and has pushed conspiracy theories in the past, said it was “obvious” that the US was being attacked by Iran with assistance from China and Russia. “Our leaders are lying to us,” she wrote on X. “This is very clearly a coordinated cyberattack. President Trump should come back to the United States.”



Tricia McLaughlin, who recently served as chief spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security, told her followers: “Americans aren’t stupid. We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.” Related Article Opinion

Aviation I’m an air traffic controller and can explain the US shutdown better than the White House Geoff Fairless Aviation safety specialist Meanwhile, the FBI was forced to clarify a bulletin it published last week warning that cybercriminals and state-aligned hackers were exploiting an AI-powered penetration testing platform called ARTEX to automate attacks against businesses and organisations around the world. When the FBI’s Dallas bureau posted a link to the week-old bulletin on Tuesday, it went viral, leading the FBI to issue a note stressing: “It is not a new announcement, and the FBI has not issued any additional warning since.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
Joel Leavitt has forced the commission to be adjourned briefly as he requested legal advice after he was asked whether he threatened violence and stood over a labour hire firm to get $165,000.

Leavitt’s bank account records were shown to the inquiry, and the bikie said they revealed he was “battling” before a $165,000 payment from BK Labour arrived last year.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis has become more blunt today, telling Leavitt: “The commission has evidence that you didn’t do any work for BK Labour. I ask you now: Did you do any work for the money that you charged?”

Leavitt responded: “I was out trying to work a lot of places at that time, and tried to do the best … for … JVL Consulting that I could do.”

Kourakis then explicitly asked if Leavitt extorted BK Labour, telling him: “Given the paucity of your answers in giving any detail of the work that you did, and on the basis of the evidence that the commission has, an inference, a finding I could make, is that you did not do any work, and that the sending of the invoice was you standing over BK Labour to get a large amount of money because you needed it badly, am I right or wrong?”

About 1500 David Jones workers are bracing to be told later this week that they have lost their jobs as the department store’s receivers prepare to permanently close 19 stores. Representatives for retail worker union SDA (Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association) met with receivers from FTI Consulting late last week and were advised only 170 roles, or 10 per cent, would be saved from 1689 jobs lost as a result of the closure of 18 stores in Australia and one in New Zealand. With seven stores in NSW set to shut, about 720 of the 1500 roles to disappear are based in the state, most of whom work in customer service. Jeremy Piper With seven stores in NSW set to shut, about 720 of the 1500 roles to disappear are based in the state, most of whom work in customer service. “We’re very disappointed with the very low number of 170 redeployments,” Smith told this masthead on Wednesday morning.



“We’re talking about a very low number, compared to the number of redundancies … It’s a missed opportunity to reset service levels at David Jones.” Related Article Exclusive

David Jones collapse Westfield owner is scoping out replacements for David Jones In an initial creditor’s meeting yesterday morning, David Jones’ administrators said an employee consultation process was underway and indicated impacted staff would find out “in the coming days”. In NSW, David Jones employs about 100 staff in its Hornsby store and roughly 115 at Warringah Mall, in Sydney’s northern beaches. Parramatta employs about 90 staff while Wollongong has about 85 employees. David Jones in Campbelltown hires approximately 80 workers, as does Woden in Canberra. Green Hills hires about 50 workers. The 170 redeployed roles will be predominantly in beauty and cosmetics counters at other stores, Smith said, as well as a limited number of roles in sales and management.



“We’ll keep working with receivers to see if we can change that number, but it doesn’t look positive so far,” Smith said. Loading “You’ve got to have enough staff on the floor to take the money off the customers who want to give it to you. If you don’t have enough staff, you don’t turn the business around.” The SDA has contacted a number of other retailers as well as the wider business industry to see where David Jones workers can be retrained or hired elsewhere. “It’s a tight time hiring now. World.content:

The owner of the Melbourne Cup runner discovered in a public skip bin in Sydney has blasted those responsible for the disposal of the racehorse’s body as Premier Chris Minns weighed into the controversy, saying: “We expect these things not to happen”. The handling of So You Are’s remains has placed the racing industry under scrutiny to address systematic shortcomings. Loading It was only 15 days ago that So You Are started as one of the favourites in the Melbourne Cup before finishing eighth in the race. On Tuesday, this masthead revealed the deceased horse had been found in skip bin at the Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre in southern Sydney after suffering a severe bout of colic and being euthanised.



Minns, whose government appoints the board of racing industry controlling body Racing NSW, told reporters on Wednesday the incident was “distressing for everyone involved and needed to be fully investigated”. “I’m not sure about the sequence, the reasons why a Melbourne Cup runner ends up in a skip bin in Lucas Heights, but we expect to get to the bottom of it,” Minns said. So You Are before competing in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington earlier this month. Racing Photos via Getty Images Minns said he expected retired racehorses to be dealt with humanely and in most cases rehomed, and said the industry needed to find better ways of disposing dead horses. “We expect these things not to happen,” he said.



Editor's pick Opinion

Racing integrity So You Are’s horrifying final fate in a skip bin with an old couch is beyond unacceptable Neil Breen National sports editor So You Are’s owner and breeder Stuart Ramsey is also demanding answers, taking aim at the veterinary clinic which organised the disposal of the horse’s body after being unable to save him. REC Equine Specialists has admitted it did not know what happened to deceased horses after they were taken away from its Horsley Park hospital by contractors. “Heads should roll,” Ramsey said. Weirey [trainer Darren Weir] got life for a jigger. This is worse. “At the end of the day they’re professional people and they should be treated like professional people. They’ve done the wrong thing and should be gone. This is the worst thing to happen in my lifetime.



“These horses try their heart out and they’re allowed to do what they like to them.” Waste management giant Cleanaway said So You Are had been transported to its Lucas Heights facility in a small tipper truck and held in a skip bin before burial because it was unsafe for the vehicle to approach the landfill. Veterinarians who treat racehorses are licensed by racing authorities and can face penalties, including deregistration. Ramsey said he had been travelling in western Queensland when So You Are fell ill on Monday and was rushed to emergency surgery from a spelling paddock near Camden. So You Are’s trainer, Bjorn Baker, was distraught, he said.



So You Are was found dead and dumped in a skip bin at Lucas Heights in Sydney. Facebook “I was in western Queensland and very hard to contact. They contacted me as soon as they could. Bjorn rang me and he was very upset,” Ramsey said. “I was speaking to him the other morning and he broke down. His wife had to get on the phone, the poor bastard.” Ramsey had been joined by about 30 long-time friends at Flemington to see So You Are compete in the Melbourne Cup a fortnight ago and could not envisage what was to come. He said he was devastated to lose the horse and learn how its body had been left in a skip bin before being buried but was more concerned for the family of apprentice jockey Izzy Neale, who died 10 days ago following a race fall in central western NSW. “She was 22. I’m bloody 74. She hadn’t lived,” he said. “We lost a daughter 20 years ago. There is always someone worse off than yourself.”

World.title: Hanson stands doubles down on plan to deport grannies
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalImmigration Hanson stands doubles down on plan to deport grannies Paul Sakkal November 18, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has wrongly claimed Donald Trump’s war in Iran has not contributed to inflation, while confirming her crackdown on parent visas could force more than 10,000 parents and grandparents out of the country. Described as “MAGA-first” by Liberals including Andrew Hastie, Hanson declined to say on Wednesday whether she wanted Trump to wind down the conflict, which has spiked global oil prices and which the Reserve Bank has repeatedly said is adding to Australia’s pre-existing inflation problem. Pauline Hanson speaking in Canberra on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “That’s not up to me to decide whether Donald Trump should end the war,” Hanson told reporters in Canberra. “No country like Iran should have nuclear weapons. “Cost of living was not due to the war in Iran. That’s been bad management by an absolutely incompetent government that has driven it up. Even [bank governor] Michele Bullock from the RBA has called it out time and time and time again. It’s out of control spending by the current government.”





The populist-right party released an uncosted estimate, based on its own analysis of Treasury figures, that cutting parent visas and slashing the refugee intake by 90 per cent could save federal and state taxpayers $140 billion over decades. However, the policy did not reference the cost of repaying the nearly $50,000 fee already paid by many people in the 161,000 in the parent visa backlog, some of whom die waiting to be accepted. Immigration analyst Abul Rizvi said the cost of refunding would be about $1 billion. Making matters more complicated, Rizvi said at least 13,000 had applied for parent visas while living onshore on different visas, including bridging visas. Asked if those already living in Australia would be able to stay after their parent visa fee was refunded, Hanson said: “They can’t.” Her comments raise the spectre of a future Hanson-led government pushing thousands of parents and grandparents to depart the country.



Rizvi, previously a senior migration bureaucrat in the Howard government, said many parent visa holders performed a childcare role for grandchildren, which did not show up in Treasury estimates that suggest parent visa holders cost the taxpayer more than $500,000 over their lifetimes. The visa holders are immediately eligible for Medicare but must wait 10 years for benefits such as the age pension or unemployment benefits. The $500,000 figure stems from the fact that the people come to Australia as older people, meaning they use services in the same way as other Australians, but do not contribute to tax revenue because they did not spend their working lives here. The parent visa also requires a financial guarantee of $10,000 by the person’s sponsor in case the parent is forced to draw on benefits. Minister for Foreign Affairs Penny Wong. Alex Ellinghausen Foreign Minister Penny Wong described the changes as “very harsh on many families”.



“I’d say to many of our multicultural communities, the ending of parent visas would be very harsh on so many families in Australia,” Wong told reporters. Hanson’s policy also pledged to cut refugee visas from 20,000 to 2000 per year. Wong said the world was facing “unprecedented people movement” and that Australia’s refugee intake was a “very small contribution” on the global stage. “Refugees also make such a great contribution to Australia. [Businessman and former chairman of Westfield] Frank Lowy was a refugee,” Wong said. “I think we all spoke about the Socceroos and the way in which that team represented multicultural Australia. “I know that [One Nation] think dividing Australians is the best response to the politics of the time. I take a different view.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Experts backed ‘homely units’ for young offenders. Labor wants them in prison
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian election Experts backed ‘homely units’ for young offenders. Labor wants them in prison Patrick Hatch November 18, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Duelling pledges by Labor and the Coalition to lock up more young people for low-level crimes have been slammed by drug, alcohol and youth justice experts, who say the plans will not address the core drivers of youth offending. Liberal leader Jess Wilson announced on Sunday a $60 million plan to establish prison “boot camps” where repeat low-level youth offenders will be sent to learn “discipline” through farm work, other labour and education. Labor reopened the Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre earlier this year to handle the growing number of young offenders held on remand. Paul Jeffers That followed a promise by Premier Ben Carroll to spend $204 million over two years establishing a youth rehabilitation detention system, where young people could be detained for up to 12 months for crimes such as theft, vandalism and minor assaults. But experts say the Labor proposal is a distortion of what those at the coalface have been asking for.



Youth crime has become a major headache for Labor in the lead-up to this month’s state election after a spike in youth offending following the COVID-19 pandemic. Rates of crimes committed by kids aged 12 to 17 jumped 24 per cent between 2019 and 2025. Offending rates fell 9.6 per cent last year. Victoria Police chief commissioner Mike Bush earlier this year called for graduated mandatory sentencing for serious offences, including young people who needed “clarity” about the consequences of their actions. But YSAS (Youth Support and Advocacy Service) chief executive Andrew Bruun said Labor’s announcement was a blow to the leaders in the drug and alcohol sector, who had spent close to a decade working on a plan for youth mandatory rehabilitation orders.



Magistrate Jennifer Bowles kicked off that work after growing frustrated with the number of young people before the children’s court with severe substance abuse problems who were not accessing voluntary drug and alcohol rehabilitation services. In 2014, Bowles published a study into programs in Sweden, England, Scotland and New Zealand where young people at extreme risk from substance abuse and sexual or criminal exploitation could be treated in a secure environment. Twenty-four leading experts from the drug and alcohol and youth justice sectors have been part of a steering committee for the implementation of Bowles’ “What Can Be Done” model, intended to be a “circuit breaker” to stop children’s lives spiralling out of control. Carroll referenced Bowles’ work when announcing the policy on Sunday, but Bruun said Labor’s plan was a serious distortion of her proposal.



Bruun said a critical element of Bowles’ proposal for mandatory rehabilitation was that they would be non-punitive health and welfare orders issued based on clinical need, not criminal offending. Related Article Crime ‘You are meant to be greater’: The bold plan to stop youth crime – at the hospital bedside Under Bowles’ proposal, treatment would be at “homely units” for up to six months, but with regular monitoring so the young person’s order could be relaxed as soon as they improved. It would be followed up with 12 months of intensive community care. In contrast, Labor has promised “youth rehabilitation detention” that judges could order at sentencing as an alternative to a community corrections order for low- and mid-level offences, including theft, vandalism, property damage and minor assaults. Sentences could be up to 12 months, including at the Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre, which closed in 2023 before the state government reopened it earlier this year to handle the swelling number of young offenders being held on remand.



“We’re trying to look at an option which is going to break that cycle for young people and give them a chance to actually treat the underlying issues and symptoms that are driving their involvement in unsafe and harmful behaviours,” Bruun said. “But in this case, if you sentence young people and have them in larger numbers in a youth justice precinct, what is the difference between [this and] youth justice detention?” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has laid out a policy of “boot camp” for young offenders. Eddie Jim Bowles, who still serves as a reserve magistrate, declined to comment when contacted by The Age. Labor said it would start with places for about 500 young people over the first two years, which is roughly 10 times the capacity Bowles’ work suggested would be necessary to treat the small number of extreme cases who needed mandatory rehabilitation.



The Coalition promised to introduce mandatory therapeutic orders based on Bowles’ work ahead of the 2018 election but has not revived the policy this campaign. Instead, Wilson on Sunday promised to send low-level young offenders to “boot camps” where they would be forced to do farm work and other labour, as well as education and training, at the former Dhurringile Prison near Shepparton. National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Legal Services chief executive Nerita Waight. “This is about instilling the discipline and respect that so many young offenders have not learned throughout their life, and crucially giving them the skills they need to get on the right path,” Wilson said. The “boot-camp” orders would apply to offenders aged 14 to 17 who had repeatedly committed low-level offences such as graffiti and vandalism, she said.



Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service CEO Nerita Waight said she was disappointed both major parties were promising to lock up more children rather than pursue evidence-based approaches to improve community safety. “We have a long history of child labour camps in this country, the harmful effects well documented in the Bringing Them Home report and Yoorrook,” Waight said. “You cannot punish children into submission.” Loading Joel McGregor, a senior lecturer in criminology at Swinburne University, said evidence from around the world showed that military-style boot camps did not work in reducing youth crime. Queensland ended a short-lived youth boot-camp program in 2015 after finding it was expensive and ineffective.



“The thing about boot camps is it looks like the government is doing something, and that’s important; people want to feel safe in their communities. But it doesn’t address those underlining factors,” McGregor said. Related Article Victorian election ‘No evidence’ that $40m youth crime program reduces offending “Getting young people involved in education and training, addressing drug or alcohol misuse, addressing trauma – those are the things that we know stop young people participating in crime.” McGregor said both major parties’ youth detention policies risked sending low-level offenders into environments where they would be negatively influenced by other detainees and in fact become more likely to reoffend. Justice Reform Initiative executive director Mindy Sotiri said the two major parties’ “evidence-free” policies would push children deeper into the justice system, and remove them from family, school and community when those connections mattered most.



“We know that the earlier a child is locked up, the more likely they are to keep cycling through the system, which means more victims and greater cost to taxpayers in the years ahead,” Sotiri said. “Whatever else prisons for children are, they have never been rehabilitative.” Victorian Greens justice spokesperson Katherine Copsey said Labor and the Coalition were “locked in a grotesque competition to see who can announce the cruellest headline and lock up the most children”. It cost Victoria $7304 per day to keep a young person in prison in 2025, or almost $2.6 million per year, according to the Productivity Commission. In 2023, 56 per cent of young people released from prison were back in jail within 12 months, the commission found. World.content:
SportAFLDraft The private schools finding their way back to the top of AFL draft lists Danny Russell November 18, 2026 — 11:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Victoria’s private schools will reclaim their place as the No.1 football nurseries in the country at this year’s AFL draft. Early predictors suggest that a third of the first 20 names to be called out by AFL clubs across Thursday and Friday nights will be students from Melbourne’s exclusive, high-end secondary schools. Top-10 draft prospect Arki Butler played his school football with Brighton Grammar. AFL Photos That is in stark contrast to last year. Only three of the top 20 picks from the class of 2025 were from the privileged private sector – Penleigh and Essendon Grammar School student Cooper Duff-Tytler joined the Eagles at No.4, Richmond took Camberwell Grammar’s Sam Grlj at No.8, while the Eagles also took Josh Lindsay, of Geelong Grammar, at No.19.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Who will your AFL club draft? Our expert prediction of the first round A large chunk of last year’s top 20 consisted of interstate selections – five south-east Queenslanders, four South Australians, two from NSW and one from Western Australia. There were also three state school recruits last year. The Eagles plucked No.1 pick, Willem Duursma, from Foster Secondary College after he shot to prominence as captain of Talent League team Gippsland Power, while Rowville Secondary College threw up pick 11 Xavier Taylor (Eastern Ranges) and pick 16 Lachy Dovaston (Eastern Ranges). However, this year, only three of the projected top 30 have been educated at government secondary schools, with likely No.1 selection Dougie Cochrane attending Henley High School in Adelaide, top-10 prospect Clancy Snell going to Mirboo North Secondary College, and Caylen Murray attending Maroochydore State High in Queensland. Once again, Brighton Grammar is expected to continue its proud history of nurturing gun teenagers.



Brighton Grammar student Tyson Bradley is expected to go in the top 20 in the 2026 AFL draft. AFL Photos The Brisbane Lions’ premiership-winning brothers, Will and Levi Ashcroft, were educated at Brighton, as was Essendon captain Andy McGrath, who was taken at No.1 in 2016, and Greater Western Sydney star Josh Kelly, who joined the Giants at No.2 in 2013. The school had five draftees in 2024. The Age’s draft expert Marc McGowan is predicting two Brighton Grammar products will be snapped up in the top 10 on Thursday night – Arki Butler at No.4 and Tyson Bradley at No.10. Butler started at Brighton Grammar in year seven, while Bradley’s father was a former student, and he joined in year 10. The Age’s phantom rankings have 10 teenagers from the Associated Public Schools of Victoria (APS) competition making the top 40 – two from Brighton Grammar, two from Geelong Grammar, two from St Kevin’s College, two from Wesley College and one each from Haileybury and Caulfield Grammar.



“The first 18 programs now are really well resourced,” Brighton Grammar director of coaching Simon McPhee told The Age on Tuesday. “We’ve got strength and conditioning coaches and a rehab coordinator, we’ve got good help from a medical point of view, and then we’ve got good coaching [at the schools].” McPhee highlighted three members of the Haileybury College coaching staff as a prime example – former AFL captains in Matthew Lloyd, who is head coach, Scott Pendlebury and Aaron Hamill. “Obviously, it’s good for the schools and the APS program when we get kids into the AFL system,” McPhee said.



Related Article AFL 2026 He ‘shrunk’ this year, but this draft hopeful could be one of the AFL’s biggest achievers “But we also take a lot of pride when the boys go on to play VFL footy, and VAFA footy. “We just want to prepare the boys to play the highest level they can, and obviously, it’s nice for the school when a few make it to the top.” Brighton Grammar won this year’s first APS grand final, beating Caulfield Grammar by nine points, after the competition shifted away from awarding the premiership to the team that finished on top. Butler and Bradley were part of that premiership-winning outfit, as was another Brighton draft hopeful Jasper Williams.



Editor's pick Series

AFL 2026 AFL draft 2026 “The school system, I think, complements the [AFL] Talent League,” McPhee said. “In the Talent League they look for the athletic profiles of the boys and showcase that, whereas the schools produce a different style of footy, a little bit more contested. “The kids really embrace playing for their school and playing with their mates, so there’s character traits that come through in the school as well … we help prepare them pretty well.” McGowan’s predicted rankings have two students from Ballarat’s St Patrick’s College going top 20 – Ethan Drever at No.2 and Archie Elliott at No.18 – while Parade College is also looking at two top 20 selections with Sam Gayfer at No.11 and Toby Krasna at No.15. World.title: Tinkering with consent laws won’t stop rapists like Russell Brand. Here’s what might
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCrime Opinion Tinkering with consent laws won’t stop rapists like Russell Brand. Here’s what might Jenna Price Columnist November 18, 2026 — 11:43am

November 18, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anyone who thinks changing age of consent laws will single-handedly stop sexual assault has lost their minds. That won’t do a single thing to stop rape except to further criminalise rapists. Sure, good outcome. Not that jail stops them from proclaiming their innocence. Russell Brand at court, before being convicted of rape. Getty Images Russell Brand confessed to conservative podcaster Megyn Kelly that he slept with a 16-year-old – Mia Latter – when he was 30. He was an “immature 30-year-old”. And then, vomit, he said that a power imbalance – such as being famous – “involves exploitation”. OK, late bloomer, take some responsibility then. As Latter told The Times: “He was a very successful man who had a lot of power and sway in the industry, whereas I was a 16-year-old with no life experience, no sexual experience and no prior relationships. What was my level of maturity meant to be?” Do we think any other rapists will really care? Age is not the issue – it’s the power imbalance. I only wish we could legislate against men wielding power. Our lives would be better for it.



We’ve got two – maybe three – huge tasks to stop sexual assault and all of them require brutal and confronting community action. And if you think the problem is confined to the powerful, here’s the truth. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, more than 30,000 women were victims of sexual assault in 2025. There were 10,000 police-recorded offenders. About half were convicted in a criminal court. And so many women never report. Mia Latter has accused Russell Brand of raping her when she was 16. Getty Images for Academy Museum of Motion Pictures Our first task will make many men – and some women – stick their fingers in their ears and go la la la. End male entitlement (sure, to women’s bodies but to much more). No-one wants to hear about undoing this behaviour because it is challenging to do. Some men don’t believe it exists. So I’ll leave you to it while at the same time putting it number one on my list to stop rape, so you know it’s the most important. Number two. The last time I wrote about what women could do to protect themselves I got into helluva trouble (think hard before you drink with men). Victim-blaming! Anti-feminist! Make men responsible. OK then, but see point one. If men can’t or won’t change (and I believe they can and will when they understand the benefits), women have to do what they can to protect themselves from dinosaurs, from raptors, from those men who act sweet but are sour as hell. Number two, two parts. Thanks to the work of Chanel Contos and collaborators, we’ve all endorsed the enthusiastic consent concept. Hell yes!



Now? Teach, hell no! It won’t stop rapists with intent. But beneath the flashy examples of celebrity sexual assault (and sadly, more to come) we have an ocean of women having sex in ways they don’t want it. For every rape victim, there are women subjected to practices such as strangulation, too afraid to say no. Women are brought up to fear boys and men, to concede even if they don’t want to. We need more fury and fight. And we need to start teaching that concept from day one in nappies. Related Article Opinion

Comedy Shocked by Russell Brand and David Walliams? You shouldn’t be Which brings me to gender roles. I have no idea how this happens but by the age of two, young girls want to be Elsa. Co-opt the princess movement and start Princess Jiu-Jitsu, a compulsory physical activity for girls across the world, ages five and onwards. Sure, dress up in your flowing blue dress but also know how to fend off attackers while using the lion killer. Keys held tightly in your fist won’t work against someone bigger and stronger. Think this is trivialising? Apparently the first task, to rid us all of male entitlement, is too hard. Won’t be fixed in my lifetime. The good news is that affirmative consent laws have seen changes in the courtrooms. So says the woman who co-wrote the book on Australian rape trials, Julia Quilter, a professor of law at the University of Wollongong.



“They are actually having some changes in the courtroom, from the most recent study we’ve just done,” she says. “It has taken us a long time to get the law to accept you don’t have to resist, shout ‘no’ or fight back … the Crown is being good at not requiring a ‘fight’ response and recognising that it is common to ‘freeze’ during sexual violence. The law now also places an obligation on the accused to explain what they said or did to affirm consent and the Crown is actively pursuing lines of questioning that place that responsibility on the accused. These are important and good developments.” Jennifer Power, professor at La Trobe University and leader of the Australian Secondary Students and Sexual Health Survey, says it’s possible a bigger age gap leads to more vulnerability in relationships with a substantially older adult: higher rates of sexual violence, unwanted sex, unwanted pregnancies. Lack of experience, lack of money, less agency. She reminds me kids are usually sexually active in many different ways before they turn 16. The consumption of pornography has changed sexual vocabulary. There’s a distance between what the law says is rape, and how thousands of women feel participating in sex they don’t want. Power says when we talk to our kids about sex we need to reach beyond the cringe moment, lean forward and say: “You have my full permission to tell someone to go away. You never have to be polite if you are uncomfortable. You don’t have to be polite for a man. Sex should be something you enjoy. If you don’t enjoy it, don’t do it.” Saying no will never stop a rapist. I would prefer a world where we didn’t have to rely on women to predict, prevent, protect against rape. Until we end male entitlement, that can’t happen. Jenna Price is a regular columnist. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Republicans, MAGA demand answers over spate of tech outages as Trump says ‘that’s life’
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTechnology & democracy Republicans, MAGA demand answers over spate of tech outages as Trump says ‘that’s life’ Michael Koziol November 18, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: Republicans and MAGA activists are demanding answers over a string of outages and technical failures that have halted air travel, hit the big banks and even impacted communications inside one of the United States’ most secret government agencies. There is growing doubt among lawmakers and the public that the incidents are unrelated, even as officials insist the problems have been caused by maintenance issues rather than cyberattacks or nefarious activity. A customer using a Bank of America ATM in Renton on Monday. Some people are choosing to stockpile cash amid the tech outages. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson On Tuesday (US time), internal communications at the National Security Agency – which specialises in signals and code-breaking – experienced an outage that was first reported by CNN. The NSA later confirmed there had been a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance”. Also on Tuesday, an internal update disrupted core services at tech giant Apple including Apple Music, the App Store and iCloud. The company said many systems were back up and running, and it was working to restore the others.



It followed service interruptions at major US banks on Monday, and a brief outage in systems used by United Airlines, as well as last week’s problems with air traffic control that led the Federal Aviation Administration to ground departing flights for nearly five hours and a major outage with Microsoft systems. Related Article Updated

Network outage Apple suffers outage sparked by software update The flurry of outages – many of which were short – has dominated cable news, water cooler conversations and discussions on Capitol Hill this week, and prompted alarm. One former Australian official in Washington, who did not want to be named, told this masthead they recently withdrew a stockpile of cash because of the technology failures. There is also some evidence of panic buying. Chief financial officer of retail giant Costco, Gary Miller, told Bloomberg News that the company had seen increased purchases of rice, canned goods, water, generators and batteries, beginning in late October.



On Fox News, former FBI special agent Darren Mott said people who were worried may want to withdraw cash, put it in a safe, have supplies of water on hand and generally make their lives more analog. Related Article Analysis

Network outage One router, one bug. How routine upgrades caused worldwide chaos But officials maintain there is no cause for alarm. “This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state. We’ve looked very closely,” said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on CNBC television on Tuesday afternoon. “What I think is going on here … is many people are patching their systems. They know that their legacy systems have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated, they don’t work well with new systems.”



There have been mixed messages about the potential role of artificial intelligence in the outages. On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said a man who was “very smart with tech” told him that one possible cause of the outages was old systems being overwhelmed by much faster programs driven by artificial intelligence. “That kind of makes sense to me,” he told Fox News. But the next day, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said AI definitely didn’t play a role in last week’s air traffic control problem, which officials say began when old copper wires were being replaced by fibre optic cable. Donald Trump downplayed the tech failures while speaking to reporters in Manila. “It’s life … it’s fine,” he said. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein US President Donald Trump, who was meeting world leaders in Manila, told reporters he was not concerned about the spate of outages. “It’s life,” he said. “When you’re big and powerful, and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”



Some Republicans expressed doubts about the official narrative, however, or suggested that the incidents must be linked. Josh Hawley, a Republican senator from Missouri, said his initial reaction was that it must be a cyberattack, and called for members of Congress to be briefed. Republican senator Josh Hawley said he did not believe the spate of outages was a coincidence and Congress must be briefed. Bloomberg “All of these outages – maybe it’s because somebody unplugged a router in Arkansas or whatever. Frankly, I find that really hard to believe,” Hawley said. “We need to know what’s going on, the American people deserve to know … If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world. You can’t tell me that all of this is just happenstance.”



Hakeem Jeffries, the leader of the Democrats in the House of Representatives, echoed calls for a briefing. And Republican majority leader in the Senate John Thune, pointed to possible foul play. “It’s fair to say there are a lot of bad actors out there who would love to do damage to the United States,” he said. “Whether it’s banking or transportation or our communications networks, we have to be on top of our game.” MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who is close to the president, said he should come home immediately. Greg Kahn/The New York Times Laura Loomer, a MAGA social media influencer who has Trump’s ear and has pushed conspiracy theories in the past, said it was “obvious” that the US was being attacked by Iran with assistance from China and Russia. “Our leaders are lying to us,” she wrote on X. “This is very clearly a coordinated cyberattack. President Trump should come back to the United States.”



Tricia McLaughlin, who recently served as chief spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security, told her followers: “Americans aren’t stupid. We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.” Related Article Opinion

Aviation I’m an air traffic controller and can explain the US shutdown better than the White House Geoff Fairless Aviation safety specialist Meanwhile, the FBI was forced to clarify a bulletin it published last week warning that cybercriminals and state-aligned hackers were exploiting an AI-powered penetration testing platform called ARTEX to automate attacks against businesses and organisations around the world. When the FBI’s Dallas bureau posted a link to the week-old bulletin on Tuesday, it went viral, leading the FBI to issue a note stressing: “It is not a new announcement, and the FBI has not issued any additional warning since.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Building Bad royal commission LIVE updates: Bikie Joel Leavitt says dull safety paperwork was easier after ‘a big line’ of cocaine
World.content:
Joel Leavitt has forced the commission to be adjourned briefly as he requested legal advice after he was asked whether he threatened violence and stood over a labour hire firm to get $165,000.

Leavitt’s bank account records were shown to the inquiry, and the bikie said they revealed he was “battling” before a $165,000 payment from BK Labour arrived last year.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis has become more blunt today, telling Leavitt: “The commission has evidence that you didn’t do any work for BK Labour. I ask you now: Did you do any work for the money that you charged?”

Leavitt responded: “I was out trying to work a lot of places at that time, and tried to do the best … for … JVL Consulting that I could do.”

Kourakis then explicitly asked if Leavitt extorted BK Labour, telling him: “Given the paucity of your answers in giving any detail of the work that you did, and on the basis of the evidence that the commission has, an inference, a finding I could make, is that you did not do any work, and that the sending of the invoice was you standing over BK Labour to get a large amount of money because you needed it badly, am I right or wrong?”

World.title: Weather: Heavy rain hits North Island, mainly Waikato
World.content:
Wild weather in the upper North Island has downed trees and powerlines, as a thunderstorm watch remains in place for the area.

Fire and Emergency said it had responded to five weather-related callouts since 6am on Wednesday, mostly in the Waikato region.

Three of those were for trees, branches or power lines that had come down, one was for flooding due to a blocked drain, and one for a leaking roof, shift manager Josh Pennefather said.

A yellow heavy rain watch remains in place until 4pm for Auckland and Waikato, and until 7pm for Coromandel, Great Barrier and Northland.

A watch is also in place for eastern Bay of Plenty and Tai Rāwhiti until 11pm.

MetService earlier forecast periods of heavy rain, with thunderstorms and localised downpours. During these times, rainfall amounts may approach warning criteria, the agency warned.

There was a moderate chance of the watches being upgraded to a warning, MetService said.

Weather watches

Severe weather watches are issued when severe weather is possible, but not yet imminent or certain.

When a watch is in place, people are urged to stay alert and keep an eye on local forecasts for updates.

Watches are generally issued one to three days in advance of potential severe weather.

World.title: Saying goodbye to Maketū Pies
World.content:
Sharon Brettkelly goes to Maketū on the day its famous pie factory closes to see how locals are taking the news.

Audio player for " Mourning Maketū Pies " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2646500%2Fsaying-goodbye-to-maketu-pies

Slap bang in the middle of Maketū's main street is a big industrial building that has been the backbone of the Bay of Plenty town for several decades.

Until Friday, when the Maketū Pies factory closed, putting more than 20 local people out of work.

It is another chapter in the town's long commercial history which dates back to the arrival of the first Te Arawa waka 600 years ago.

The pies are not the town's only claim to fame. Among the celebrated locals past and present are sisters Kasey and Kārena Bird, winners of MasterChef New Zealand in 2014; political leader and diplomat, Sir Charles Moihi Bennett who grew up there in the early 1900s; and the local fish and chip shop is immortalised in Robyn White's 1975 painting.

In this seaside village of 1400, everyone knows someone who has worked at the factory.

The closure comes as no surprise, but the 'for sale' sign on the building gives it finality.

"It's gone a little bit ghostly today," says Irirangi Nicholas, who proudly wears Maketū tattooed on her neck. "It's been a staple in our village for a long time."

Irirangi Nicholas (left) and Ramona Tapsell at Maketū's fish and chip shop Sharon Brettkelly/The Detail

From her home on the hill behind the town, she has watched staff packing up the factory.

"Over the last 18 months to two years, they've done really well at getting a resurgence and getting the rapport of their customers back. They've done really well this year, so it's really sad to see that, but it's more sad to see a lot of whānau being put out just before Christmas as well."

The company has been struggling since 2019 when it previously went into receivership.

It was bought two years ago by Montana Group, but the new owner was up against ageing factory infrastructure. The plant needed a complete rebuild and it went into voluntary solvent liquidation in 2024.

Montana said production at the current level was not sustainable and this time there was no rescuer after attempts to find a buyer failed.

Ironically, on the day the factory closed, local leaders gathered across the road to celebrate a milestone of another community champion. Maketū Health and Social Services marked 30 years since it was set up as a charitable trust by a group of local women with the aim of addressing and supporting equity for Māori.

Chief executive Huhana Smith calls it a significant moment in history.

"It's a bit of a juxtaposition where we're celebrating and then we're losing the iconic pie shop. And more particularly, our concern is with all the families involved because there's going to be a lot of people affected by this," she says.

"Some haven't worked anywhere else. So as a hauora, we're impacted because a lot of them are family members of staff here. But all I'd like to say is that we will do everything we can to support them in any way we can."

The hauora is helping workers with resumes and finding jobs, but a recent food drive was not as successful as previous years.

People of Maketu. Top left: Luke Wilson and his son Daniel-Joe Wilson / Top Right: Huhana Smith / Bottom Left: Lyn Potaka / Bottom Right: Philippa Boyd and Owen Emery Sharon Brettkelly/The Detail

"We knew that would be impacted," says Smith. "But still, people gave, just out of pure kindness. So with that in mind, I think there is some hope."

Locals told The Detail seasonal jobs can be found in surrounding kiwifruit orchards and at the local AFFCO meat works. But Luke Wilson says he may move his family closer to Te Puke where there are more opportunities.

The Western Bay of Plenty is one of the fastest growing regions in the country and its leaders have recently signed a deal to deliver 35,000 new jobs over 10 years.

That's not soon enough for Wilson who has two teenagers needing jobs, though he is reluctant to leave the town.

"It's home," he says.

Former pie factory worker Lyn Potaka says she has stocked up the freezer with the pies to feed the family at Christmas.

"I used to work on the table, making the pies from scratch. We had a girl that rolled out the pastry. In those days, it used to be by hand.

"Quite an amazing business, really, in such a small community as well."

Local mum Philippa Boyd says she has bought pies for dinner to mark the closure.

The factory was a bonus for local people as they didn't need to travel for work.

"Sometimes they would come and go, but they always knew it would be there for them. And now that option's gone, it will probably put pressure on some households."

Boyd says she hopes the building will be bought and used for "something bigger and better".

Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here.

World.title: Opportunity Party deputy predicts a 'pretty gnarly negotiation period'
World.content:
The Opportunity Party deputy leader says its going to be a "pretty gnarly negotiation period," as the party prepares for any discussions to form a government.

Daniel Eb says there's multiple scenarios they need to be thinking about, but there's no value in speculating ahead of it.

Speaking to RNZ's Midday Report, he said he was on the party's negotiating team, and their bottom lines were a good starting point.

"It's an unusual thing to do with the bottom lines, but I think the payoff at this point in time in the sort of cycle is is pretty clear."

Audio player for " Opportunity Party's Daniel Eb discusses entering Parliament " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics/2658175%2Fopportunity-party-deputy-predicts-a-pretty-gnarly-negotiation-period

Opportunity Party's Daniel Eb discusses entering Parliament Midday Report Download MP3 10m

Host Guyon Espiner asked how difficult it would be for Opportunity to maintain its support, if it were to be a minor party propping up a government with the risk of becoming subsumed by the governing parties.

Eb said it would be silly to discount the last couple of years, and the way in which ACT and New Zealand First had sought to maintain their support despite being in government.

"There are benefits and disadvantages to all types of scenarios going forward."

He said the potential of being subsumed by the major parties was "probably one of the biggest advantages of something like the crossbenches, which is something we've maintained as a possible pathway for us".

"But again, we've got to see what happens with the specials.

"We've got to understand who we might be sitting around the table with, and all of those factors will come into it.

World.title: Police inspectors added to audit of staff phone and computer use
World.content:
Police inspectors are now being included in an internal audit of staff internet use to see what material they have on their phones and comupters.

A rapid review of staff internet use was sparked by the resignation of disgraced former Deputy Police Commissioner Jevon McSkimming, after child sexual exploitation and bestiality material were found on his work devices.

It was later agreed that there would be additional internet usage checks for all existing staff in senior leadership teams including the commissioner, assistant commissioners, executive directors and district commanders.

That review concluded with no concerns raised.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Police earlier said ongoing regular checks of all staff device use, including leaders, would continue and had been implemented as part of Police's routine practice.

Checks on staff seeking promotion to the ranks of superintendent or above would also be conducted, in line with the Independent Police Conduct Authority's recommendation following the McSkimming scandal.

In response to questions from RNZ, police's chief of staff Cassandra Anderson said police were "committed to transparency and have put in place routine reviews into technology use for Inspector-level staff".

"This is not a new review, instead an extension of the previous reviews and audits that police have carried out on staff.

"The routine review seeks to strengthen information security, and covers the 24 months prior to October 2026, which ensures an increased level of reassurance regarding any potential misuse of police systems and devices."

Following completion of the review, any person appointed into an Inspector-level position would be subject to a 12-month internet usage audit.

"This is a substantial but crucial piece of work that remains in progress. Therefore, we are unable to comment on any outcomes to date.

"We continue to focus ensuring all police staff live our values, by displaying professionalism and integrity at all times."

RNZ asked if any misuse had been identified so far, and if so how many investigations were underway.

World.title: Magnitude 5.7 quake strikes east of Arthur's Pass
World.content:
Two earthquakes jolted residents up and down the country on Tuesday evening.

GeoNet said a magnitude 5.7 tremor struck 15 kilometres southeast of Arthur's Pass at 11.30pm, at a depth of 5km, with strong shaking near the epicentre.

More than 14,000 people reported feeling the quake, some as far south as Invercargill and as far north as Auckland.

Most described the shaking as weak to light.

A second, weaker quake struck a quarter of an hour later, at 11.44pm, in the same spot.

GeoNet said this one was a magnitude 3.2, at a depth of 4km. Just under 1200 people reported having felt it.

Earth Sciences New Zealand seismologist Sam Taylor-Offord said the magnitude 5.7 earthquake occurred near Cass in Arthur's Pass about 40km southeast of the Alpine Fault.

"This is really normal for the area. All of the mapped faults we have in the area have that same kind of trend and sense of motion," he said.

The bulk of reports came from people in north Westland and central Canterbury, he said.

Taylor-Offord said there could be aftershocks for weeks or months following the quake.

It was unlikely the quake had any influence on the Alpine Fault.

"Because the separation in space and the size of this earthquake and the way that it's moved, there's not going to be much if any loading on the Alpine Fault," he said.

However, the likelihood of the Alpine Fault rupturing in the near future remained high, Taylor-Offord said.

"It's a hazard I'm sure most people are aware of but should be thinking about in their plans and their knowledge of what to do in an earthquake."

'Felt deep and distant'

One RNZ listener in Christchurch said last night's first quake "felt deep and distant" and went on for about a minute: "Grandma awake!"

Another in the Christchurch suburb of Redwood described being "restless and shaken yet again".

Maree said the quake was "quite strong" in Fendalton, and described it as the strongest she had felt in the last seven years.

In New Brighton, Alison hadn't yet gone to bed and felt "a gentle rocking motion", while fellow resident Liz said she was "awake and didn't feel a thing".

Colleen said her bed was swaying in Rangiora.

Ilam resident Brian Thomas said his wooden bungalow shook abruptly: "I was instantly awakened, remembering the 2010 quake."

Mike from Westport described it as a "short shake, not strong", while Freda in Avonside said "it was very strong, my house shook and furniture rocked".

Arthur's Pass Cafe & Store owner Sean Moran said last night's earthquake felt like a rolling shake through his house.

"I heard quite a noise, then the house started shaking so it was quite slow in coming but pre-empted with noise," he said.

"It sort of rolled on afterwards so quite a rolly one rather than a jolty one."

Moran said he received texts from his children in Christchurch and Rolleston, who also felt the shaking.

He said there was no damage in the village.

Fire and Emergency's southern communications centre had no callouts related to the quake.

Selwyn mayor Lydia Gliddon said the earthquake brought back some memories and it was a reminder for residents to be prepared.

In Lyttelton, Chris and partner were both woken from deep sleep. A listener in Karitāne, Dunedin, said they could still feel the "rolling motion" an hour later.

The quakes follow an earlier weak tremor on Tuesday, at 12.40pm. The magnitude 3.3 quake's epicentre was 15km southwest of Arthur's Pass, at a depth of 5 km. Only three people reported noticing it.

World.title: Black Cap Rachin Ravindra returns 'rested and mentally fresh'
World.content:
Black Caps batter Rachin Ravindra is hoping some nervous energy will work in his favour as he returns to cricket after a three-month injury break.

Ravindra is expected to slot straight back into the New Zealand line-up for the first Test against India starting at the Basin Reserve on Thursday.

The 26 year old dislocated his right shoulder during a promotional shoot with broadcaster Sky in September.

"Super excited to get going again," Ravindra said on the eve of the Test. "I think watching the guys play on TV, you get a little bit of FOMO, you want to be out there and I'm super looking forward to it especially in Wellington."

His last game was for the Welsh Fire in The Hundred in August.

"It's been a lot of rehab, from dislocation it's been eight weeks. I had a great support group of doctors, physios and trainers and being able to do a lot of batting in the last three or four weeks."

Ravindra was initially assigned to return for the ODI series against India, but had that delayed as he continued to rehabilitate However he doesn't expect the extended break to be a problem.

"We're so used to playing so much cricket, so hopefully I can draw back on the experience and my test experience so far.

"It's been a little while since the test group has come together and we all remember it against England and what we did over there, so hopefully like I say, draw on that form and experience and then do what we do."

Rachin Ravindra batting against England, at Trent Bridge in Nottingham in June. www.photosport.nz

Ravindra has played 115 games for New Zealand, with the last of his 24 Tests the series winning game against England at Trent Bridge in June.

He is viewing the time off as a positive.

"Hopefully, it's a blessing in disguise. I think you sort of have to have that mindset and opinion to keep going forward.

"It's tough playing a lot of cricket and sometimes tough not playing enough cricket, so it's definitely a balance. Hopefully, it will mean I'm rested and mentally fresh."

In 24 Tests Ravindra averages 47.82 with five centuries. He has also taken 11 wickets.

Black Caps Test squad

Tom Latham (C), Tom Blundell (WK), Devon Conway, Jacob Duffy, Matt Henry, Kyle Jamieson, Daryl Mitchell, Henry Nicholls, Glenn Phillips, Rachin Ravindra, Dean Foxcroft, Nathan Smith, Blair Tickner, Will Young.

Black Caps v India - Test Series

1st Test - November 19th-23rd, Basin Reserve, Wellington

World.title: Volunteer firefighters abused, harassed over emergency siren in Taranaki
World.content:
Audio player for " Waverley fire siren silenced after complaints about noise " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/emergencies_local/2654390%2Fvolunteer-firefighters-abused-harassed-over-emergency-siren-in-taranaki

Waverley fire siren silenced after complaints about noise Nine To Noon Download MP3 16m

A siren alerting volunteer firefighters to emergencies has been silenced in the small south Taranaki town of Waverley after abuse on social media, a FENZ manager says.

The volunteer firefighters are now relying on personal phones or pagers to alert them to emergencies after a decision was made to stop using the siren.

Fire and Emergency Taranaki district manager David Utumapu told Nine to Noon the siren had been turned off temporarily to give volunteer firefighters a break from what has been happening on social media.

It would "cool the area down" and provide a breather so people could reassess what had been happening, he said.

Previously, the brigade averaged about 50 callouts in a year covering fires, traffic accidents and medical emergencies.

However, recently the number of sirens going off had tripled because the volunteer firefighters and St John Ambulance had joined the First Responder Programme so that callouts for medical emergencies to isolated areas could be reached more quickly.

The volunteer firefighters received some training from St John so they could help if they reached the scene before an ambulance from a larger town such as Hāwera.

While some Waverley residents were supportive of the siren being used at all hours, some were angry at the increase, he said.

Firefighters had been subject to behaviour that was "below the line", he said.

"We just don't think our brigade needs to be the meat in the sandwich in that conversation."

'Totally unacceptable' behaviour

Taranaki District Council Patea Ward councillor Brian Rook said the main issue was that only a small number of residents had applied "totally unacceptable" pressure on the brigade.

"I'm talking about taking over meetings, personal harassment and it's just not on.

"These volunteers .... are not paid to do what they're doing and they do an absolutely incredible job."

The former police officer said the siren might go off three or four times in the early hours on occasions, but most callouts occurred during the day.

He didn't want the siren to be turned off permanently but would support a curfew in an effort to have the siren operational most of the time.

"We can't rely on technology at times, even at 2 o'clock in the morning ...the siren is a good backup and it's also a good reminder that someone is in trouble, someone needs help now."

The siren was the most reliable system with phone alerts via an app and pagers which were being phased out next year as the lesser favoured options, Utumapu said.

So far data had shown it was not "overly high risk" to either turn off the siren or have a curfew so it wasn't used overnight.

World.title: Smoking rate under 6% for first time
World.content:
The daily smoking rate has dropped by 0.8 percent, the latest New Zealand Health Survey finds.

The Ministry of Health is currently working on proposals to reform legislation around smoking, following Cabinet decisions in September.

It is the first time the smoking rate has been below 6 percent, dropping to 5.9 percent from 6.7 percent.

Associate health minister Casey Costello said it meant 32,000 fewer people were smoking daily.

"The results show the progress that's been made from a consistent approach.

"That's better for them and their families and the wider health system."

Associate health minister Casey Costello RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

She said the smoking rate had halved over the last six years, with numbers particularly low in young people.

Daily smoking for 25-34 years olds had the largest fall in smoking from 7.9 percent to 5.6 percent.

She said the figures put New Zealand's smoking rate at the second lowest in the OECD, which includes 38 countries.

However, Costello said older smokers, and Māori and Pacific peoples still needed to be targeted.

Māori smoking rates sat at 13.9 percent, having more than halved in the past six years.

"The progress New Zealand has made means that those who currently smoke cigarettes are mostly older, long-term smokers and throughout the Smokefree work, they have been the most difficult group to get to quit."

She said the country needed to build on its approach - warning of the harms of smoking, increasing financial cost, and providing quit support, including access to vapes.

Vaping stays the same

Vaping rates have remained largely the same since the last annual report, with 11.2 percent reporting daily vaping today compared to 11.7 percent.

"It's also important to continue to focus on the dangers posed by the illicit tobacco market and strengthen the regulatory framework to support the operational response that is in place," Costello said.

Action for Smokefree campaign group said it was encouraging to see rates starting to drop after stalling for a few years.

Director Ben Youdan said, "We have been immensely successful at smoking prevention. Smoking rates are now well below 5% for those under 25, and we almost have a smokefree generation for those under 35."

However, he said the smoking population had changed over recent years, being increasingly made up of older adults who have smoked for decades.

Youdan was pleased to see the daily vaping rate for teenagers between 15 and 17 had dropped from 12.8 percent to 8 percent.

However, he said the results were not good for Māori men. They have not changed since 2023/24, plateauing at 14.4 percent.

Meanwhile, there has been a further decline for Māori women from 15.4 percent to 13.5 percent.

World.title: Bears handed grudge match for Perth's first NRL game
World.content:
Perth will host Manly in its maiden NRL game, with the two warring parties from the Northern Eagles merger to face off in the Bears' long-awaited return to the competition.

Some 25 years after the breakdown of their unhappy marriage forced North Sydney into hibernation, the Bears will resume their rivalry with Manly in round one of 2027.

The NRL confirmed the opening round fixtures on Wednesday, with Perth's clash against the Sea Eagles listed for Perth Stadium in the Sunday afternoon slot.

With Parramatta, Gold Coast, Melbourne and Wests Tigers locked in for Las Vegas the previous week, reigning premiers the Sydney Roosters will kick off the season on Australian soil against Brisbane on March 4.

Scott Drinkwater will face his old club North Queensland the following night when St George Illawarra takes on the Cowboys, while Canterbury travel to the Warriors for the other Friday match.

Mal Meninga will coach the Bears in their inaugural season. (Supplied: Perth Bears)

Grand finalist Newcastle and minor premier Penrith will clash at Newcastle International Sport Centre in one of the most anticipated games of the round on the Saturday night.

The Dolphins will also host Cronulla in Redcliffe for the Saturday evening fixture, before Canberra and South Sydney close out the round on Sunday night at Canberra Stadium.

But it is the Bears' first fixture that is of most interest ahead of the full draw being released later this week.

Perth had hoped to play South Sydney in its first match, given the Rabbitohs and Bears faced off on the first day of competition in 1908.

But turnaround times meant that was not possible, with the NRL having traditionally stuck with the Roosters-Rabbitohs rivalry on Friday night in round two.

Instead, the Bears' clash with Manly shapes up as a fitting start to their life as a club in Perth.

The two teams have a genuine rivalry in Sydney's northern suburbs that dates back to 1947, when Manly entered the competition and took several Bears players.

So fierce was it in the early days, historians recount tales of the sides coming to blows at a function they both attended in Manly's maiden season.

Officials are hopeful of a sold-out Perth Stadium to mark Perth's entry as the NRL's 18th team, before most of the club's home matches are played at Perth Rectangular Stadium.

Perth has already been installed as clear wooden-spoon favourites for next year, having built a workmanlike roster that lacks marquee talent.

But they will no doubt draw inspiration from the Dolphins' entry to the competition in 2023, when they shocked the Roosters 28-18 in their opening game.

AAP

World.title: So You Are owner outraged by treatment of dead horse's remains
World.content:
So You Are's owner-breeder has demanded a full investigation after the Melbourne Cup runner's body was found in a skip at a Sydney tip, insisting "heads have got to roll".

Stuart Ramsey said it was a "bloody disgrace" the gelding was left in the bin while awaiting burial at Sydney's Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre.

The grisly sight was uncovered by a Sydney man, with online footage outraging industry participants and anti-horse racing activists alike.

Bjorn Baker's promising stayer fell ill at a spelling farm after finishing eighth in Australia's most famous race on November 3.

He was rushed to the REC Equine Specialists veterinary clinic at Horsley Park in Sydney's west after showing signs of colic on Monday morning.

Surgery could not save the horse and he was euthanased under anaesthesia.

Racing NSW said its ongoing investigations found So You Are was being held temporarily while awaiting burial when the footage was recorded.

While REC has apologised, renowned breeder Ramsey, of boutique Hunter Valley farm Turangga Stud, wants answers and accountability over the disposal of the five-year-old, which earned $1.4 million from eight career wins.

"There should be a full investigation. Heads have got to roll, simple as that," Ramsey said.

"He was more than just a racehorse. He brought our family together, and to think of the stress the family are under now because of this. It's a bloody disgrace.

"We took 30-odd people down to Melbourne for the race. So You Are brought us all together, as only a horse can do.

"It's very sad that it's happened."

Loading...

REC's managing partner Jonathan Lumsden said the centre had spoken with So You Are's owners and trainers to apologise.

He said the veterinary practice did not carry out the burial, but took "full responsibility" for choosing the service provider and arrangements.

"He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," Lumsden said in a statement.

Ramsey, who said he had not been contacted by REC, was not satisfied with its explanation.

"So they should take responsibility. It wasn't the contractor's fault; it was their fault. They were in charge of the horse," he said.

"They didn't even give us the option of burying him up at Turangga … they should all be out, gone.

"I don't mean everyone, but the bosses and the people who've made the decisions."

So You Are finished eighth at this year's Melbourne Cup. (Getty Images: Racing Photos/Pat Scala)

Ramsey said racehorses were among the best-looked-after animals in the world and spoke of his affinity for So You Are.

"He meant so much to us," he added.

The treatment of So You Are's remains has sparked strong criticism from animal welfare groups.

"There is always the option to bury the horse or have the horse cremated," Coalition for the Protection of Racehorses campaign director Elio Celotto said.

"However, it is more expedient to dump the horse at a local tip. This is business as usual for an industry where profit is always more important than sentiment."

Victorian Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said the case should force the industry to confront serious questions about duty of care.

"The racing industry breeds these horses and profits from them but fails the most basic obligation to treat them with dignity after death," she said.

Racing NSW said "appropriate action" would be taken if any wrongdoing was discovered in its ongoing investigation .

"Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process," it said.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner."

AAP

World.title: 'Terrible' Socceroos downed by Jordan as Popovic decision looms
World.content:
Tony Popovic's Socceroos have been deservedly beaten 2-0 in Qatar by a Jordanian side that had not previously won in 2026.

Jordan scored once in each half, had a penalty saved by Patrick Beach and what looked a good goal ruled out for offside.

Popovic described the first period as "terrible", and while Australia did improve in the second, any hope of a comeback disappeared when substitute Daniel Arzani was sent off for two bookings inside six minutes. He was on the pitch for 15 minutes.

"We got what we deserved," Popovic said.

"A real contrast from the other night against Qatar. They came with a lot of energy, they were fresh, they were focused, they were more aggressive than us and it showed."

The one positive for Popovic and Football Australia, as they prepare to negotiate over a new contract, is that the Socceroos were at their best when they were at their youngest.

When Arzani was dismissed in the 80th minute, he was, at 27, the team's second-oldest player after Jason Geria (33). The other nine were aged 19 to 23.

But after 26 matches in 26 months (12 wins, seven losses), the 53-year-old's future is in limbo. Talks on a new contract, he says, should take place "in the next couple of months", but he admitted beforehand this could be his final game.

"We have to learn, all of us; me included," he said.

"There are some big lessons tonight. This has been a reality check for all of us. There's a lot of work to do."

Popovic had chosen the same XI that started Friday's impressive 3-0 win over Qatar, but it soon became clear this would be a very different match.

Rennes winger Mousa Al-Taamari was particularly influential as Jordan poured forward, and it was no great surprise when he won a 31st-minute penalty.

Al-Taamari took it himself, but it was poor — yet still a good save with his feet by Beach.

But two minutes later, the Australian keeper was beaten. Lucas Herrington lost possession and Al-Taamari was released. Running away from Paul Okon-Engstler, he turned Souttar inside-out, then tucked his shot inside the near post.

Souttar was replaced at half-time by Herrington's older brother Diesel, who made his debut against Qatar.

He was part of an improved performance as Australia stemmed the flow of Jordanian attacks, albeit without mounting much threat of their own.

Popovic made further changes soon after the hour and subs Kasey Bos and Marcus Younis twice almost combined for an equaliser.

But Arzani, having been booked for hauling down Al-Taamari, was late on Abdallah Nasib to receive a second card.

A man down and pushing forward, Australia left gaps. The assistant referee's flag saved them when Odeh Fakhouri went through to score in the 93rd minute, but there was no escape a minute later.

Herrington and Alessandro Circati failed to deal with a long ball and Ghaith Al-Madadha found Ali Olwan, who produced a composed finish.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Smith's next move confirmed after LIV Golf collapse
World.content:
Cameron Smith has found a new home after the demise of LIV Golf, joining the European Tour, albeit on a limited basis.

Australian superstar Smith, along with several other former LIV players, including compatriot Lucas Herbert, has agreed to a deal that involves invites to a "specific number of tournaments".

These will not include the tour's highest-profile Rolex Series events, but smaller ones at which the presence of the former LIV players would "add value", the European Tour said on Tuesday.

The 2022 British Open winner joins a raft of former players on the now-defunct rebel circuit to have joined the European Tour, known as the DP World Tour.

They are headlined by big-hitting Bryson DeChambeau, who signed just before the deadline, and former world number one Jon Rahm. DeChambeau joins in "category one" status, meaning the American can play in whichever tournaments he chooses.

However, it looks as though he will not feature in the two Australian events that open the tour: The Australian PGA Championship at The Lakes, Sydney, starting on November 26, followed by the Australian Open at Melbourne's Kingston Heath, opening on December 3.
